teacher: White’s second move develops the king’s knight to its natural square, eyeing the e5 pawn and keeping the modest edge that existed after 1.e4 e5. The engine confirms that the move is the best available, with the evaluation slipping only a tenth of a pawn to +0.24. Black can answer with …Nc6, which simply eliminates the immediate pressure on the e5 pawn, after which the main line continues 3.Bb5 a6 4.Ba4. Overall, the move preserves White’s slight advantage while completing basic development.
student: White develops the knight to its natural square f3, keeping the modest edge that existed after 1.e4 e5. The engine rates it as the best continuation and notes that the evaluation stays at roughly +0.24 for White, with no material change. Black’s most accurate reply would be …Nc6, which simply eliminates the pressure on the e‑pawn. In short, Nf3 preserves White’s slight advantage while completing development.

teacher: Black’s …Nf6 brings the last undeveloped piece to its natural square, completing development without altering the material balance. The engine rates it as the best continuation, keeping the evaluation essentially unchanged at roughly equal. In the principal variation the game could proceed 5.d3 d6 6.a4 O‑O, preserving the balance.
student: Black’s …Nf6 develops the knight to its natural square and leaves material perfectly balanced, so the engine still judges the position as roughly equal with only a tiny edge for White. The engine rates this as the best continuation, noting that any alternative would have cost Black about a hundredth of a pawn in evaluation. In the principal variation White can continue with d3, after which Black may answer …d6 and both sides can safely castle.

teacher: By pulling the bishop back to b6 Black eliminates the immediate threat to it, keeping the evaluation essentially unchanged with a small edge for Black. The retreat also leaves Black’s bishop on b6 pinning White’s f‑pawn to the king, while White’s bishop on c4 continues to pin Black’s f‑pawn, creating a tense mutual‑pin situation. The engine rates the position at about –0.26 pawns for Black and marks the move as excellent, confirming that Black has preserved the slight advantage without incurring any new problems.
student: By retreating the bishop to b6 Black eliminates White’s immediate pressure on that piece, and the move also creates a pin – the bishop now attacks the white pawn on f2 while the white bishop on c4 continues to pin the f‑pawn to the black king. The engine rates the position virtually unchanged, with Black still holding a slight edge of about a quarter of a pawn. In the principal line White would try h3, after which Black can continue with …Nd4, keeping the initiative. This precise defensive resource therefore earns an “excellent” label for its soundness and long‑term implications.

teacher: White’s knight jump to a4 is a clear mistake because it leaves the pawn on e4 undefended, allowing Black to capture it with Nxe4. That capture would give Black a material edge and swing the evaluation to a clear advantage of roughly a pawn in Black’s favour. The engine’s top‑choice, h3, would have kept the e‑pawn safe and preserved only a slight edge for Black (‑0.26), avoiding the tactical loss altogether.
student: By playing Na4 White leaves the pawn on e4 en prise, allowing Black to capture it with Nxe4. This simple tactical error costs White roughly a pawn’s worth of evaluation, turning a slight disadvantage into a clear one‑pawn deficit. The engine indicates that the correct continuation was h3, which would have kept material equal and avoided the loss of the e‑pawn. Consequently, Na4 is rightly marked as a mistake.

teacher: Black’s 8…Bd7 is a clear mistake, turning a position that was about a pawn better for Black (‑1.45) into a slight edge for White (+0.31). By moving the c8‑bishop to d7 Black missed the tactical shot 8…Nxe4, which would have captured the pawn on e4 and preserved the advantage. Instead White can simply play Re1, removing the threat to the e4‑pawn and leaving Black’s f2‑pawn en prise, after which the engine’s line continues with …Bg4 and White consolidates. The move therefore costs Black roughly one‑and‑three‑quarters of a pawn.
student: By playing …Bd7 Black does nothing to meet White’s pressure – the bishop on b6 already pins the f‑pawn and White still has the powerful pin on the f7‑pawn with his bishop on c4. The engine shows that this retreat costs roughly two pawns, turning a clear Black edge into a slight White advantage. A far stronger continuation would have been …Nxe4, which captures the pawn on e4 and keeps material balanced. After …Bd7 White can simply play Re1, removing the threat to the e‑pawn and leaving the f2‑pawn vulnerable.

teacher: By playing axb6 Black eliminates White’s knight on b6 and removes the threat to the a8 rook, simultaneously making the a‑file semi‑open for Black’s rook to use. The capture also leaves Black with doubled pawns on the b‑file, but the position remains essentially the same in evaluation, with Black still a shade better. This accurate response resolves the tactical pressure while preserving Black’s slight advantage, justifying the “excellent” label.
student: By taking on b6 Black eliminates White’s active knight and at the same time opens the a‑file, giving the rook on a8 a useful semi‑open line while also removing the immediate danger to that piece. The capture does leave Black with doubled pawns on the b‑file, but the material balance remains equal and the engine still judges the position as only marginally better for Black – roughly a third of a pawn. With White’s bishop on c4 pinning the f7‑pawn, Black can continue with …Na5, keeping the pressure alive. This precise exchange therefore earns an “excellent” label.

teacher: White’s 10.c3 is a clear mistake; instead of the more active 10.b5, it does nothing to make use of the bishop pair or the pin on f7 and simply leaves the e‑pawn hanging. Black can reply 10…Nxe4, capturing the pawn on e4 and gaining material, which pushes the evaluation to about a pawn and a half in Black’s favour. The engine rates the move as a loss of roughly 1.3 pawns, whereas the best continuation would have been 10.b5.
student: White’s quiet c3 does nothing to meet Black’s looming …Nxe4, and after it Black can simply capture the pawn on e4, leaving White with a weakened centre and a clear material deficit. The engine shows that this mistake costs roughly a pawn‑and‑a‑half, turning a slight Black edge into a much larger one. In contrast, the more accurate 10.b5 would have kept the balance, as shown by the principal variation. Consequently, the move is rightly marked as a mistake.

teacher: Black’s 12…d5 seems tempting because it would make the d‑file semi‑open for Black, but it immediately allows White to capture with 13 Bxd5. After that capture the white bishop on d5 pins the f7‑pawn to the black king, a concrete drawback that turns a two‑pawn lead into only about a pawn’s worth of advantage. The engine’s preferred move was 12…Bg4, which would have kept pressure on f7 without conceding the d‑pawn. By playing …d5 Black gave up the pawn and the strong pin, costing roughly a pawn’s worth of evaluation.
student: By playing …d5 Black opened the d‑file and allowed White’s bishop to capture with check, after which the bishop would pin the f7‑pawn to the black king and remove the pressure on that bishop. This concession costs Black roughly two pawns of evaluation – the engine’s assessment drops by about 1.7 pawns compared with the previous position. The engine’s preferred continuation was 12…Bg4, which would have kept the advantage without giving White the chance to exchange on d5. Consequently, despite being up a pawn in material, Black’s position is now only marginally better.

teacher: White eliminates Black’s central pawn with Bxd5, removing the immediate threat to the bishop and pinning the f‑pawn to the king on g8. After the forced Nxd5 the material balance is restored, the d‑file becomes semi‑open for Black and the bishops now face each other on opposite colours, which dampens any sharp tactics. This exchange lifts White’s evaluation by roughly a third of a pawn, turning a clearly worse position into only a slight disadvantage.
student: By playing Bxd5 White eliminates the immediate danger to his bishop and forces Black’s best reply Nxd5, after which the d‑file becomes semi‑open for Black while the bishops end up of opposite colour. The capture also creates a pin on the f7‑pawn against the black king, but it does not win material because Black can simply recapture with the knight. Although the engine still judges Black to be a little better – roughly three‑tenths of a pawn – the move improves White’s standing by about a third of a pawn, making it the clear best choice.

teacher: By capturing on d5 Black eliminates White’s active bishop and forces an exchange that restores material equality after the inevitable Qxd5. The resulting opposite‑colour bishop situation leaves White’s lone bishop on c1 with only one safe square, while Black’s rook on the semi‑open a‑file remains well‑placed. If White does recapture, the queen on d5 will pin the f‑pawn to the king, further restricting Black’s pawn moves. The move therefore preserves Black’s slight edge, changing the evaluation by only a few hundredths of a pawn.
student: By taking on d5 Black eliminates White’s active bishop and forces an immediate queen trade that leaves both sides with bishops of opposite colour. After the inevitable Qxd5 the position features a semi‑open a‑file for Black’s rook on a8 while White’s remaining bishop on c1 is cramped to just one safe square, giving Black modest long‑term chances despite being down material. The engine rates the capture as excellent, noting that it keeps Black’s slight edge essentially unchanged – the evaluation shifts by only about three hundredths of a pawn. In the principal line White would recapture with Qxd5, after which Black can continue with …Re8 and later meet White’s Nxe5 with …Nxe5, preserving the pressure.

teacher: White’s queen captures the knight on d5, removing a key defender and, by virtue of the queen’s new placement, pins the f‑pawn to the black king. After Black’s most natural reply Re8 the pawn on f7 would be left en prise, giving White immediate tactical pressure. The engine’s evaluation barely changes (about a tenth of a pawn), confirming that the move keeps the material balance and is the best – indeed an excellent – continuation in a position where the bishops are of opposite colour and Black’s a‑file rook is active.
student: By taking on d5 White eliminates Black’s active knight and simultaneously pins the f‑pawn to the black king, so the pawn cannot move without exposing the king. The capture also leaves the material balance untouched while keeping the position roughly equal – the engine still judges Black to be a shade better, about three‑tenths of a pawn. With opposite‑coloured bishops and White’s bishop on c1 confined to its single safe square, the exchange does not worsen White’s standing despite Black’s rook already enjoying the semi‑open a‑file. Black’s most natural reply would be …Re8, after which the pinned f7‑pawn becomes vulnerable, but even that line does not improve Black’s standing.

teacher: Black’s 14…Be6 develops the last minor piece to a sensible square, keeping the a‑file pressure of the semi‑open a‑file and respecting the opposite‑colour‑bishop structure in which White’s bishop on c1 is already cramped. However, the move also allows White to exchange queens with Qxd8, after which Black recaptures with the a‑rook and the game heads toward an even endgame, erasing the slight edge Black enjoyed earlier (the evaluation slipped from about a third of a pawn in Black’s favour to a roughly equal position). The engine’s top‑choice, 14…Re8, would have preserved the queen but would have left the f‑pawn en prise, so Be6 was a solid, “good” alternative even though it cost Black roughly a third of a pawn.
student: By playing …Be6 Black places the bishop on an active diagonal while White’s bishop on c1 remains cramped, but the move does not improve Black’s standing – the evaluation slides from a slight edge to near equality, costing about three‑quarters of a pawn. The engine judged Re8 to be stronger because it would have kept more pressure, even though it leaves the f7‑pawn vulnerable. After …Be6 White could capture with Qxd8, forking the c7‑pawn, the a8‑rook and the f8‑rook, yet the resulting line still leaves Black without any concrete compensation. Consequently the move is good in principle but sub‑optimal compared with the best continuation.

teacher: Black’s …f5 tries to push the kingside pawn majority and to get rid of the danger to the pawn on h7, but the pawn thrust also tears open the pawn cover in front of his king. In a middlegame with opposite‑colour bishops and a semi‑open a‑file already serving Black’s rook, this weakening costs roughly a pawn of the earlier advantage, pulling the evaluation from a clear pawn‑plus to only a slight edge. The engine indicates that the far stronger continuation would have been 15…Bd5, which would have preserved the king’s safety and kept the advantage. White can now meet the move with 16.Qe2, removing the remaining threat to the queen.
student: By playing …f5 Black tries to advance his kingside pawn majority and eliminate the immediate danger to the h‑pawn, but the move also loosens the pawn shield in front of his own king. This concession lets White answer with Qe2, removing the pressure on the queen and leaving Black’s slight edge evaporating – the evaluation drops by roughly a pawn. The engine indicates that the far stronger continuation would have been …Bd5, keeping the initiative without conceding the king‑side safety. Consequently, …f5 is a clear mistake, costing Black about a pawn’s worth of advantage.

teacher: White’s queen steps back to e2, eliminating the immediate threat that hovered over it.  By doing so the material balance stays level and the evaluation remains essentially unchanged, with Black still a shade better (roughly a quarter‑pawn).  In a position defined by opposite‑coloured bishops—where White’s lone safe bishop square is c1 and Black’s rook already exploits the semi‑open a‑file—this retreat is a precise way to preserve the equilibrium.  The engine’s line would continue with …Re8, after which White can meet it with d3 and keep the tension.
student: By retreating the queen to e2 White eliminates the immediate danger that had been hanging over it, thereby preserving material and keeping the position balanced. With opposite‑coloured bishops and Black’s rook already exploiting the semi‑open a‑file, the move also sidesteps any further pressure from Black’s pieces. The engine rates Qe2 as an excellent continuation, noting that the evaluation stays virtually unchanged – Black remains only a fraction of a pawn ahead. In the principal line Black would continue with …Re8, after which White can meet it with d3, followed by …b5 and then Bg5.

teacher: By pushing …e4 Black expands his kingside pawn majority (four pawns against White’s three) and further limits the already cramped White bishop on c1, while his rook on a8 enjoys the semi‑open a‑file. The advance does, however, give White the immediate pawn break d3, which can hit the e‑pawn and equalise the game; the engine’s principal line continues d3 Bd5 dxe4 fxe4. Although the move is still “good”, it costs Black roughly a fifth of a pawn – the evaluation slides from a slight Black edge to an almost equal balance – and the engine preferred the more precise …Re8 to retain the advantage.
student: By playing …e4 Black pushes his kingside pawn majority forward, gaining space and preparing to expand along the long diagonal. The advance also leaves White’s bishop on c1 with very few safe squares in an opposite‑colour‑bishop ending, while Black already enjoys a semi‑open a‑file that can be used by the rook on a8. Nevertheless, the engine rates Re8 as the superior continuation because it would keep more pressure without conceding the small edge that …e4 gives up – the evaluation slips from about a quarter‑pawn advantage for Black to near equality. White could answer with the thematic pawn break d3, striking at the newly created e‑pawn.

teacher: White’s 17.Nd4, intended to eliminate a threat to the knight, actually walks into a simple capture: Black can play …Nxd4, after which White’s c‑pawn recaptures and Black’s queen takes back, leaving White a piece down. The evaluation therefore collapses from an essentially equal position to a clear two‑pawn advantage for Black, confirming the move as a blunder. The engine’s preferred continuation was 17.d3, a pawn break that would have struck at Black’s e4 pawn and kept material balance. In a game with opposite‑coloured bishops and a semi‑open a‑file favouring Black, preserving the knight was far more important than the modest relief the move offered.
student: White’s 17.Nd4 was meant to eliminate the immediate danger to the knight, but it walks straight into a tactical shot: after …Nxd4 Black not only wins the piece but also eliminates the pressure on the bishop on e6 while keeping the initiative. The engine shows that this blunder swings the evaluation from an almost equal balance to a clear Black advantage of about two pawns, whereas the correct continuation would have been the pawn break d3, striking at Black’s e‑pawn and preserving material equality. In short, Nd4 costs White roughly two pawns of value and hands Black a comfortable lead.

teacher: Black eliminates White’s knight on d4, thereby removing the direct threat to the bishop on e6. After White is forced to recapture with cxd4, the c‑file becomes semi‑open for White but Black gains a clear structural edge: White is left with isolated and doubled pawns on the d‑file while Black is up three points of material (a knight) and the engine still evaluates the position as about two pawns better for Black. The exchange therefore leaves the overall assessment essentially unchanged, with Black still much better. In the continuation White would capture on d4, Black would reply Qxd4, and Black’s rook can continue to exploit the semi‑open a‑file.
student: By playing …Nxd4 Black eliminates the immediate danger to his bishop on e6 and forces an exchange that leaves White with isolated and doubled pawns on the d‑file while giving Black a clear semi‑open c‑file. After the inevitable cxd4 the material balance is restored, but the resulting structural weakness compensates for any temporary loss in the engine’s eyes, keeping Black’s advantage at roughly two pawns. The capture also exploits the fact that White’s bishop on c1 is cramped – it has only one safe retreat – whereas Black already enjoys active play along the semi‑open a‑file. In short, the move neutralises the tactical threat without conceding material, preserving Black’s sizable edge.

teacher: By capturing the knight on d4 White eliminates the immediate danger to the queen on e2 and clears the way for a semi‑open c‑file, which is the most sensible way to meet Black’s threat. After the forced …Qxd4 the pawn on f2 becomes pinned to the king, and White is left with an isolated queen’s pawn on d2, but the exchange restores material balance without conceding anything further. The engine rates the move as the best available, improving White’s standing by roughly a tenth of a pawn, although Black still enjoys a clear advantage of more than two pawns.
student: By playing cxd4 White eliminates the immediate danger to the queen on e2 and forces the natural reply Qxd4, after which the c‑file becomes semi‑open for White’s pieces. The capture also leaves White with an isolated queen’s pawn on d2, but it does not win material because Black can simply recapture with the queen. Although the engine still judges Black to be clearly better—about two pawns ahead—the move improves White’s standing by roughly a tenth of a pawn, making it the best continuation in this opposite‑colour‑bishop ending.

teacher: Black’s 19…Bc4 puts the bishop on the c4‑square, with opposite‑coloured bishops; the queen on d4 already pins the f‑pawn and White’s bishop on c1 has only one safe square. The move is good enough to keep Black’s material edge (up a pawn) and a sizable advantage of roughly a pawn, yet it is not the engine’s top choice. The engine preferred 19…Rad8, which would have improved rook coordination while preserving the pressure. By opting for Bc4 the evaluation slipped by about four‑tenths of a pawn, turning a very strong position into a still much‑better one for Black.
student: By playing …Bc4 Black places his bishop on a safe diagonal while the opposite‑coloured bishops and the queen’s pin on the f‑pawn keep White’s pieces cramped. The move does not improve Black’s already sizable edge – the evaluation slips by about four‑tenths of a pawn compared with the engine’s top choice …Rad8. Nevertheless, it remains a good move because it preserves the pressure without creating new weaknesses.

teacher: White’s retreat Qd1 is a clear mistake, worsening the score by roughly a pawn as the engine notes. By moving the queen the immediate threat to it disappears, but the pawn on f2 remains en prise under Black’s queen on d4, which is already pinning the pawn to the king; Black can simply capture on f2 and increase his material lead. The engine’s top choice, Bb2, would have aimed for a queen exchange after Rad8 – a line that keeps Black’s advantage much smaller. Consequently the move costs White about a pawn of material and a significant swing in the evaluation.
student: By playing Qd1 White does eliminate the immediate danger to the queen, but it leaves the pawn on f2 hanging because Black’s queen on d4 pins that pawn to the white king on g1. The engine shows this costs roughly a pawn and pushes Black’s advantage from about –1.7 to –2.7, leaving Black a full pawn ahead. A far stronger try would have been Bb2, which keeps the bishop active while avoiding the pin and preserving material balance. Consequently, the move is rightly judged a mistake.

teacher: Black’s queen retreat to d5 keeps the material edge but leaves the g7 pawn exposed, so the move only modestly preserves the advantage. It does remove the immediate threat to the queen, yet it is inferior to the engine‑recommended Qd6, which also leaves the pawn on g7 en prise. White can answer with Rc1, removing the threat to the rook on c1 and costing Black roughly half a pawn of evaluation.
student: By playing …Qd5 Black eliminates the immediate danger to its queen, but the move leaves the g‑pawn hanging – it can be taken by White’s rook on e1. The engine rates the move as “good” yet notes that it costs Black about half a pawn compared with the optimal continuation …Qd6, which would have removed the same threat while keeping the g‑pawn defended. After …Qd5 White could answer with Rc1, removing the pressure on the rook and preserving the slight edge. In short, the move is solid but not the most accurate way to maintain Black’s advantage.

teacher: White eliminates the immediate danger to the rook by retreating it to c1, a move that the engine rates as the best and improves his standing only marginally (about a few hundredths of a pawn). With opposite‑colour bishops and each side’s rook already on its own semi‑open file, the tactical balance of the position is preserved. Black can answer with …Qd6, which would defend the pawn on c7 and keep the fight going.
student: By playing Rc1 White eliminates the immediate danger to his rook, allowing it to stay active while the bishops remain of opposite colour and each side’s pieces enjoy their own semi‑open files. The engine rates this as the best continuation, keeping the evaluation virtually unchanged – Black still holds about a pawn advantage but the position remains roughly balanced. Black can reply with …Qd6, which would remove the pressure on the c7 pawn, after which White could continue with f3 and later bring the rook back to d8.
violations: calls the position equal at -1.51

teacher: White’s queen hop to h5 tries to put pressure on the g‑pawn, but Black can simply meet the idea with …Rf7, which eliminates the threat to g7. That defensive resource leaves White a little worse; the evaluation slides from about a pawn down to roughly a pawn‑and‑a‑third down, and Black even remains a full pawn ahead in material. The engine’s top choice, f4, would have kept more tension in the position, while the opposite‑colour bishops and the semi‑open a‑ and e‑files give each side modest activity that White’s queen sortie does not exploit. Consequently, Qh5 is only a “good” move and not the optimal continuation.
student: White’s queen retreat to h5 does little more than keep the pieces active in an already opposite‑colour‑bishop ending where both sides have their own semi‑open files – the white rook on e1 and the black rook on a8 each enjoy a line that can be exploited. By moving off the queenside, White allows Black to answer with …Rf7, which simply eliminates the pressure on the g7 pawn and leaves Black still a clear pawn ahead. The engine rates the move as “good” but notes it costs roughly a third of a pawn compared with the optimal continuation, after which White could have played f4 instead. Consequently, despite being the best available option, Qh5 modestly worsens White’s standing.

teacher: By pushing …f4 Black hoped to unleash the queen on d5 against White’s queen on h5 and to press the kingside pawn majority, but the pawn thrust simply opens the line for White to reply Qxd5+ – a checking capture that trades queens and erases Black’s initiative. Consequently the evaluation slips from a clear pawn advantage to only a modest edge, costing roughly six‑tenths of a pawn. The engine points out that the far more precise …Rf7 would have eliminated the immediate threat to the g7‑pawn and kept Black’s advantage intact. Although Black remains up a pawn, the inaccuracy has given White the only sensible way to neutralise the attack.
student: By playing …f4 Black tries to uncover the queen on d5 and push the kingside pawn majority forward, but the move also allows White to answer with Qxd5+, winning the queen that was previously attacking h5. The engine rates this as an inaccuracy, noting that it costs Black roughly two‑thirds of a pawn compared with the optimal continuation Rf7, which would have removed the threat to the g7 pawn. After …f4 White can simply capture on d5 with check, after which Black must recapture and continue with …f3, leaving Black still a pawn ahead but with a much reduced edge.

teacher: White’s 24 Qg4 looks attractive because it threatens a direct mate with Qxg7#, but it completely overlooks the far stronger tactical shot that was available. The engine shows that 24 Qxd5+ would have captured Black’s queen on d5 with check, preserving material equality and keeping the initiative, whereas the played move allows Black to meet the threat with …Rf7, simply defending the g‑pawn and leaving Black a full pawn ahead. The resulting evaluation swings from a modest Black edge to a clear one‑pawn disadvantage for White, confirming the move as a mistake.
student: White’s 24.Qg4 looks tempting because it creates an immediate mating idea – Qxg7# – but it does nothing to meet Black’s looming …Rf7, which would simply eliminate the pressure on the g‑pawn and allow Black to keep the initiative. The engine shows that the far stronger continuation was 24.Qxd5+, a checking capture that wins the black queen outright. By opting for Qg4 White allowed Black to reply Rf7, after which the evaluation slipped by roughly a pawn, leaving Black clearly better. In short, the move cost White about a pawn in material and a clear edge for Black.

teacher: Black’s rook slides to f7, eliminating the immediate danger to the pawn on g7 and reinforcing the king‑side pawn shield. With opposite‑colour bishops and each side’s rook already active on a semi‑open file, the move simply consolidates Black’s material edge—now a full pawn—and nudges the evaluation a quarter‑pawn deeper in Black’s favour. White’s most logical try would be the pawn break f3, hitting at Black’s e‑pawn, after which Black can continue with …Re8, keeping the pressure on the centre.
student: By playing Rf7 Black eliminates the immediate danger to the g‑pawn, thereby preserving the one‑pawn material edge and nudging the evaluation a little deeper into Black’s favour (+0.25 pawn). The move also leaves the opposite‑colour‑bishop structure intact while both sides continue to use their respective semi‑open files—White’s rook on e1 and Black’s rook on a8. If White tries the natural pawn break f3, Black can answer with …Re8, keeping the pressure on White’s centre. This subtle defensive resource therefore earns the “best” label.

teacher: Black tried the pawn break 25…f3, hoping to strike at White’s g‑pawn and open the f‑file. In reality White can simply capture 26.gxf3, and after the forced exchange the evaluation collapses from a clear two‑pawn lead to only a slight edge for Black – a loss of roughly two pawns of advantage. The engine indicates that the far stronger continuation was 25…h5, which would have preserved Black’s substantial lead. Consequently the pawn push is a clear blunder, even though the position features opposite‑colour bishops and semi‑open a‑ and e‑files.
student: Black’s …f3 was intended as a pawn break against White’s g‑pawn, but after the natural capture gxf3 the pawn structure collapses: White ends up with isolated, doubled f‑pawns while Black’s own pawn chain becomes vulnerable. The engine shows that this blunder costs roughly two pawns of evaluation, turning a clear –2.7 advantage into only a slight edge for Black. In contrast, the more accurate …h5 would have kept the pressure without creating those structural weaknesses. Consequently, Black’s position deteriorates sharply despite still being up one pawn in material.

teacher: White’s 26 g3 is a clear blunder. Instead of the simple 26 gxf3, which would have captured Black’s pawn on f3, White merely pushed the pawn, leaving the enemy pawn alive and allowing Black to keep a material edge. The engine’s evaluation jumps from a slight Black advantage (‑0.35 pawn) to a decisive one (‑3.2 pawns), turning a modest disadvantage into a winning position for Black. With opposite‑coloured bishops and both rooks already active on their respective semi‑open files, the missed capture proved especially costly.
student: White’s quiet g3 does nothing to meet Black’s active pawn and simply hands over the initiative. By ignoring the more forcing capture gxf3, White allows Black to keep the pawn on f3 and, with the bishops of opposite colour, the rook on a8 already exploiting the semi‑open a‑file, the evaluation swings from a slight edge for Black to a decisive one – roughly three pawns in Black’s favour. The engine rates the move as a blunder, costing about two and a half pawns compared with the correct continuation.

teacher: Black’s queen move to f5 is a serious blunder because it walks into a direct queen capture: White can simply play Qxf5, winning the queen and forking the rook on f7 and the pawn on h7 (the fork can be answered by Rxf5). This exchange drops Black’s evaluation from a decisive –3.2 pawn advantage to only about –1.1, roughly a two‑pawn swing in White’s favour. The engine’s top‑choice, …h5, would have avoided this tactical shot and preserved Black’s winning edge. Consequently the move costs Black a clear winning edge, though material advantage (up a pawn) remains, and turns a winning position into a merely better one.
student: By playing …Qf5 Black walks straight into a tactical shot: White can capture the queen with Qxf5, after which Black recaptures Rxf5 and then plays Bd4, forcing an exchange on a3 that leaves Black still down a pawn. The engine’s evaluation drops by roughly two pawns, turning a decisive –3.2 advantage into only about a pawn’s worth. The blunder was therefore unnecessary; the simple pawn push h5 would have kept Black’s edge intact. In short, the move costs Black almost a full pawn in evaluation.

teacher: White removes Black’s queen with Qxf5, forking the rook on f7 and the pawn on h7, but the queen can be captured. After the forced Rxf5 the material balance is restored, leading to a rook‑and‑minor‑piece ending in which Black remains clearly better (about a pawn and a half). The exchange also leaves Black’s pawn on g7 en prise, a weakness White can try to exploit in the continuation (Kh2 Rd5 Re3). Although the move worsens White’s evaluation, no alternative avoided the queen loss, so Qxf5 is the best practical choice.
student: By playing Qxf5 White wins Black’s queen with a fork that attacks both the rook on f7 and the pawn on h7. After the forced Rxf5 the queens disappear and the game simplifies into a rook‑and‑minor‑piece ending where each side has one rook and a few pieces, leaving the evaluation at roughly –1½ pawns in Black’s favour. The capture also leaves the pawn on g7 en prise, but it is the most accurate continuation because any other try would allow Black to retain his advantage.

teacher: By playing …Rxf5 Black eliminates the queens, turning the battle into a rook‑and‑minor‑piece ending where he already enjoys a pawn advantage. The capture also removes White’s pressure on the h7‑pawn and the rook that had been on f5, while Black’s rook on a8 can continue to exploit the semi‑open a‑file. Although the pawn on g7 becomes a target after the exchange, the engine’s evaluation remains essentially unchanged, still clearly favoring Black. This precise simplification preserves the material edge and is therefore judged excellent.
student: By taking on f5 Black eliminates White’s queen and instantly converts the game into a rook‑and‑minor‑piece ending, leaving Black a clear pawn ahead. The capture also removes the immediate danger to the h7 pawn and the rook that had been under fire, while Black’s rook now sits on the semi‑open a‑file opposite White’s rook on e1. Although the exchange leaves the g7 pawn vulnerable, the engine still rates the position as “clearly better” for Black – roughly a pawn’s worth – and the move keeps the advantage essentially unchanged. This precise simplification makes Rxf5 an excellent choice.

teacher: By pushing …h5 Black tries to press its kingside pawn majority, but the move also creates a weakness in the pawn shield around the king. White can immediately answer with the pawn break g4, striking at the newly advanced pawn and exploiting the now‑weakened cover, which is why the evaluation collapses from a clear 1.7‑pawn advantage for Black to only a slight edge. The engine considered Rd5 the correct move, keeping the rook active without compromising Black’s king safety. Consequently, despite being up a pawn, Black’s position is now only marginally better.
student: By pushing …h5 Black not only fixes White’s pawn on h4 but also tears open the pawn shield in front of his own king, weakening the safety of the monarch while leaving the dark‑squared bishop still cramped behind its own pawns. The engine shows that this concession costs roughly a pawn, turning a clearly better position for Black into only a slight edge. A far stronger continuation would have been Rd5, which keeps the king safe and preserves the larger advantage. After …h5 White can immediately strike with g4, attacking the newly advanced pawn.

teacher: Black steps the king to f7, a move that surprisingly strengthens the position even though it weakens the pawn cover in front of the monarch. In this rook‑and‑minor‑piece ending White’s dark‑squared bishop is hemmed in by its own pawns, so the slight king‑safety concession can be tolerated and the evaluation improves by roughly a third of a pawn in Black’s favour (from about –0.7 to –1.0). Although the engine preferred 29…Be2, Kf7 still yields the best practical result, increasing Black’s material edge to about a pawn.
student: By moving the king to f7 Black steps out of the pawn shield that had been protecting it, but this also loosens the pawn cover in front of the monarch. The engine still judges the position as clearly better for Black – roughly a pawn’s worth – yet the evaluation improves by about a third of a pawn after the move. Although the suggested continuation would be 29…Be2, Kf7 is nevertheless a strong defensive try that modestly strengthens Black’s edge.

teacher: White’s 30 .Rc4 is a serious blunder because the rook on c4 is left en prise. Black would capture it with 30…Bxc4, after which the pawn on e4 becomes vulnerable and can be captured with Rxe4, turning a modest disadvantage into a decisive one. The evaluation therefore drops from about a pawn down to a winning five‑pawn deficit, and Black even emerges a pawn up. The safer alternative would have been 30 .Rg1, which would have kept the rook protected.
student: By playing Rc4 White leaves the rook completely exposed – it can be taken immediately with …Bxc4, after which Black’s pawn on e4 becomes vulnerable. The engine shows that this blunder turns an already inferior position into a decisive one for Black, worsening the evaluation by roughly five pawns. The correct continuation would have been Rg1, keeping the rook safe and preserving White’s chances. Consequently Black emerges with a clear winning edge.

teacher: By playing Rxe4 White finally opens the e‑file, allowing the remaining rook to bear down on Black’s king while also winning the pawn on e4. In this rook‑and‑minor‑piece ending White’s dark‑squared bishop remains hemmed in by its own pawns, but the open file gives the heavy pieces a direct line of pressure. The engine rates the move as the best available, improving White’s evaluation by roughly a tenth of a pawn, although Black still holds a decisive advantage. Black’s most accurate reply would be …Bd5, which removes the threat to the bishop on d5.
student: By taking on e4 White opens the e‑file, allowing his heavy pieces to bear down on Black’s king while the newly opened file gives him active play in this rook‑and‑minor‑piece ending. The capture also leaves Black with the defensive resource …Bd5, which would remove the immediate pressure on the bishop that was created by the pawn grab. Although the engine still judges Black to be decisively better – roughly five pawns ahead – the move improves White’s standing by about a tenth of a pawn, making it the best continuation available.

teacher: Black’s 31…Bd3 simply retreats the bishop to a safe square, eliminating the immediate threat to that piece. Although the move is solid, it is not the strongest continuation; the engine preferred 31…Bd5, which would have removed the same threat while preserving a more active bishop, and the chosen move costs Black about a quarter‑pawn of its winning edge. White can now meet the bishop with 32 Re3, removing the pressure on the rook and leading to a line such as Bf1+ Kh2 Bc4.
student: By playing …Bd3 Black simply steps the bishop out of the immediate danger it faced, eliminating White’s pressure on that piece. The engine still judges the position a decisive win for Black – roughly five‑and‑a‑half pawns ahead – but notes that the move costs about a quarter pawn compared with the optimal continuation. The engine preferred …Bd5, which would have removed the same threat while keeping the evaluation marginally higher. After …Bd3 White can answer with Re3, removing the threat to the rook on e3.

teacher: White retreats the rook to d4, thereby eliminating the threat to the rook on d4. In this rook‑and‑minor‑piece ending White’s dark‑squared bishop is already cramped by its own pawn chain, so the move is a pragmatic way to preserve material. Nevertheless, the engine indicates that the more precise Re3 would have removed the threat to the rook on e3 and would have kept the evaluation roughly the same, whereas Rd4 costs about a quarter of a pawn and leaves Black with a decisive advantage of roughly five pawns.
student: White’s 32.Rd4 simply steps the rook out of danger, eliminating Black’s immediate pressure on that piece. In this rook‑and‑minor‑piece ending – with White’s pawn structure locked on dark squares and his dark‑squared bishop cramped – the move does little more than preserve the rook, and it even nudges the evaluation a touch deeper into Black’s favor (about a quarter of a pawn worse for White). The engine judged Re3 to be superior because it would have removed the threat to the rook on e3, keeping the balance tighter. Consequently, while Rd4 is a good defensive try, it is not the optimal continuation.

teacher: By playing …Be2 Black merely removes the immediate threat to the bishop, but the move allows White to unleash a powerful rook check. White can answer with Rd7+, forking the king on f7 and the pawn on b7 while the rook’s move also uncovers the bishop on b2’s attack on the g7‑pawn, forcing the Black king to move and leaving Black still up about five pawns. The engine’s best reply was …Rd5, which would have preserved the decisive advantage, whereas …Be2 costs roughly one pawn of material and drops the evaluation from a winning –5.8 to –4.7, justifying the “mistake” label.
student: By playing …Be2 Black merely sidesteps the immediate danger to the bishop, but the retreat allows White’s rook to jump to d7 with a fork that attacks both the b‑pawn and the king on f7 while also uncovering a discovered attack on the g7 pawn. This tactical shot turns an already decisive edge into a modest loss – roughly a pawn’s worth – because Black missed the far stronger continuation Rd5, which would have kept the initiative alive. Consequently the evaluation drops from about a five‑pawn lead to just under four pawns, even though Black remains clearly ahead in this rook‑and‑minor‑piece ending where White’s dark‑squared bishop is cramped.

teacher: White’s rook check on d7 is the only move that keeps any chances, for it simultaneously attacks the black king and the b7 pawn while uncovering the bishop on b2’s line to the g7 pawn. After the forced king move (the engine’s line continues 33…Ke6), White can capture on g7, regaining material and creating further threats, but the position is still a decisive Black advantage. The move is therefore the best available, even though it costs White roughly a third of a pawn in the evaluation.
student: White’s rook jump to d7 checks the black king while simultaneously forking the b‑pawn and the king, and because the rook also skews the king onto the same line as the g7 pawn it opens a discovered attack on that pawn with the bishop on b2. The engine rates this as the best continuation, even though it still leaves Black with a decisive material edge – roughly five pawns ahead. After the forced …Ke6, White can capture on g7, but Black will then continue with Bc4 and later g4, preserving the winning advantage.

teacher: White retreats the bishop to c3, thereby eliminating the immediate threat to the pawn on d2.  In doing so the a3 pawn becomes en prise, and the position remains a decisive Black advantage of roughly five pawns.  The engine, however, judged the checking move Rg6+ to be stronger, as it would give check and keep the pressure on Black’s king.
student: White’s retreat Bc3 eliminates the immediate danger to the d‑pawn, but it also leaves the a3 pawn hanging. The engine still judges Black to be decisively ahead – roughly five pawns down – so the move does not improve White’s standing at all. In fact, the engine preferred the checking move Rg6+, which would have forced Black into an awkward king walk. By opting for Bc3 White missed that chance and the position remains a losing one for White.

teacher: Black finally wins the a‑pawn, opening the a‑file and leaving White with an isolated pawn on b4, which looks attractive in this rook‑and‑minor‑piece ending. Yet the capture costs Black a little – the evaluation slips from roughly a 4.8‑pawn win to about a 4.5‑pawn win – and it gives White the checking resource Rg6+ in the continuation. The engine prefers 35…Bd3, which would have kept a larger advantage. So 35…Rxa3 is a good, material‑winning move, but it is not the most accurate choice.
student: By taking on a3 Black wins a pawn and opens the a‑file, leaving White with an isolated pawn on b4 while his dark‑squared bishop remains cramped behind its own pawns. The capture also leaves White’s king exposed to checking ideas such as Rg6+, which can be met by Kf5 before White continues with Rf6+. Although the engine rates the move “good” and still judges Black to be decisively better, it costs about a third of a pawn compared with the optimal continuation …Bd3, which would have preserved more of Black’s winning edge.

teacher: Black’s 36…Rxc3 captures the white bishop and, although the rook on c3 is left en prise, it forces the only sensible reply 37.dxc3, which removes the threat to the rook on c3 and simultaneously opens the d‑file for Black’s other rook. With the d‑file now open, Black’s rooks become far more active and the pawn on d2 – poorly defended – comes under fire, while the c‑file ceases to be a semi‑open line for White. The exchange does not win material, but it deepens Black’s decisive advantage, improving the evaluation by about four‑tenths of a pawn.
student: By playing Rxc3 Black eliminates White’s active bishop and forces an immediate trade that opens the d‑file while leaving the rook on c3 temporarily en prise. After White’s natural reply dxc3, the capture both removes the threat to the pawn on c3 and restores material balance, but it also closes the c‑file for White, giving Black a clearer line in this rook‑and‑minor‑piece ending where his pawns sit on light squares opposite White’s dark‑square pawns. The engine rates the move as the best, improving Black’s already decisive edge by roughly four‑tenths of a pawn.

teacher: By playing dxc3 White eliminates Black’s rook on c3, opens the d‑file and removes the immediate danger to the pawn on c3, so the c‑file is no longer semi‑open for White. In this rook‑and‑minor‑piece ending White’s pawns remain fixed on dark squares while Black’s are fixed on light squares, and Black still holds a decisive material edge of two pawns. Black can answer with Rd1, which threatens mate by Rh1#. Thus, although the move is the best available and keeps the evaluation essentially unchanged, the position remains winning for Black.
student: By playing dxc3 White eliminates Black’s active rook on c3, opening the d‑file while removing the immediate danger to the pawn that had just moved there. The capture also closes the c‑file for White, leaving the position in a rook‑and‑minor‑piece ending where both sides’ pawn structures are locked on opposite colours. Although the engine still judges the position as a decisive Black advantage, this exchange is the best continuation available because it neutralises Black’s most forcing idea – …Rd1 would threaten an immediate mate with Rh1#. In short, the move preserves White’s chances without worsening the already losing score.

teacher: Black’s …b5 does fix White’s pawn on b4 on a dark square and eliminates the immediate danger to the pawn on b5, but the move is a mistake because it gives White the pawn break g4, striking at the h5 pawn and opening lines against Black’s king, while also abandoning the far stronger Rd1, which would have threatened mate with Rh1#. As a result the engine’s assessment falls from a decisive –5.07 to –3.52, a loss of roughly one and a half pawns, even though Black still retains a winning edge.
student: By playing …b5 Black fixes White’s pawn on b4 on a dark square and eliminates the immediate danger to the pawn that had just moved there, but the move does nothing to improve his already decisive edge in this rook‑and‑minor‑piece ending. The engine shows that the far stronger continuation would have been Rd1, which threatens an immediate mating blow with Rh1#. Instead, after …b5 White can answer with the pawn break g4, striking at the h5 pawn and eroding Black’s advantage by roughly one and a half pawns. Consequently the evaluation drops from a five‑pawn lead to about three‑and‑a‑half pawns – a clear mistake.

teacher: White’s 38.Rb6 tries to pin the c6‑pawn to Black’s king, but the move does little to curb Black’s decisive threats. Black can reply with 38…Rd1, threatening an immediate Rh1# and forcing a forced line (Kh2 Rf1 Rxc6+) that leaves White in a hopeless position. The engine indicates that the far stronger try was 38.g4, a pawn break that attacks the h5‑pawn and offers the best practical chances. By opting for the pin instead, White’s evaluation slid from a roughly three‑pawn disadvantage to about five pawns, a clear worsening of about one and a half pawns.
student: White’s 38.Rb6 tries to pin the c‑pawn to Black’s king by occupying the b‑file, but it does nothing to stop Black’s looming threats. After the move Black can reply …Rd1, which immediately threatens mate with Rh1#, while the engine shows that the far stronger continuation would have been the pawn break g4, striking at Black’s h‑pawn and keeping more counterplay. By playing Rb6 White’s evaluation slipped from a decisive –3½‑pawn disadvantage to an even larger –5½‑pawn deficit, turning a losing position into a clearly winning one for Black. The mistake therefore costs roughly a pawn and hands Black a clear winning edge in this rook‑and‑minor‑piece ending.

teacher: Black’s king walk to d6 is a clear mistake: the evaluation drops from a decisive –5.1‑pawn edge to about –3.6, a loss of roughly one and a half pawns. By stepping away from the active rook on d5, Black forfeits the winning continuation Rd1, which would have threatened an immediate mate with Rh1#. In the resulting position the material balance (Black up two pawns) remains, but the winning chances are markedly reduced. The engine’s line after 38…Kd6 continues with …Rb8, allowing White a check on f1 and giving Black even less scope.
student: By moving the king to d6 Black missed the far stronger …Rd1, which would have threatened an immediate mate with Rh1#. The engine’s evaluation therefore slipped by roughly one and a half pawns, turning a decisive –5‑pawn edge into only about –3½ pawns. In this rook‑and‑minor‑piece ending White’s pawn structure remains locked on dark squares while Black’s sits on light squares, but the missed mating idea costs Black the chance to convert his material lead.

teacher: White tries the pawn break g4, hoping to strike at Black’s h‑pawn, open the g‑file and create a passed pawn on h4. Black can simply reply hxg4+ (check) and after White’s forced king capture, Black continues with Rd1, leaving White with isolated f2 and h4 pawns and a position about a half‑pawn worse; the evaluation slides from a decisive Black advantage of roughly three and a half pawns to over four pawns. The engine rates the move only as “good” and points out that Rb8 would have been a better try, preserving material and avoiding the forced check. Consequently Black’s winning edge increases.
student: White tries to activate his pieces by playing g4, a pawn break that strikes at Black’s h‑pawn. After the natural reply hxg4+ the g‑file becomes semi‑open for White while the h‑file opens for Black, and White ends up with an isolated h‑pawn and a passed pawn on h4, but the exchange also leaves him with isolated f‑pawns. The engine rates the move as “good” yet notes it costs roughly half a pawn compared with the optimal continuation Rb8, which would have kept the balance more favorable for White. Consequently Black remains decisively ahead in this rook‑and‑minor‑piece ending.

teacher: Black’s forcing capture with check not only wins the pawn on g4 but also forces White’s king onto g4, opening the g‑file for Black’s rook and leaving the h‑file semi‑open on Black’s side. After the inevitable Kxg4, White is left with isolated f2 and h4 pawns and a new passed pawn on h4, while Black’s bishop and rook gain active lines in a rook‑and‑minor‑piece endgame. The exchange restores material balance, so Black keeps the decisive –4‑pawn advantage essentially unchanged. This precise check therefore consolidates Black’s winning position.
student: By playing hxg4+ Black forces the white king to capture, opening the g‑file and leaving White with isolated pawns on f2 and h4 while also giving Black a semi‑open h‑file. After the forced Kxg4 the material balance is restored but Black’s position remains clearly better – the engine still evaluates the position as a decisive win for Black. The continuation Rd1 followed by Rb7 and Rh1 shows how Black can continue exploiting the newly opened lines in this rook‑and‑minor‑piece ending.

teacher: Black’s 40…Bd1 is a mistake because it forgoes the far more active 40…Rd1 and lets White answer with the simple pawn push h5, leaving that pawn en prise and giving White some counterplay. The engine’s evaluation slides from a decisive –4.28 pawns to –2.82 pawns, a loss of roughly one and a half pawns for Black. In this rook‑and‑minor‑piece ending, where White’s pawns are fixed on dark squares and Black’s on light, the bishop retreat does not improve Black’s position, whereas the rook move would have maintained the pressure.
student: By playing …Bd1 Black missed the far stronger …Rd1, which would have kept more pressure in this rook‑and‑minor‑piece ending. The bishop retreat does nothing to stop White’s looming pawn push h5, after which the pawn on h5 becomes en prise, allowing White to generate counterplay. As a result the evaluation slipped by roughly one and a half pawns, leaving Black still clearly ahead but with a much smaller edge than before.

teacher: The capture on f2 wins a pawn and gives Black a passed pawn on f3, but it also makes the f‑file semi‑open for White and, more seriously, allows White to check with Rd8+. That check **skewers** the Black king on d6, and when the king moves the bishop on d1 behind the rook is exposed and can be taken, erasing the pawn gain and shrinking Black’s lead. The engine marks the move a mistake, costing roughly a pawn compared with the best continuation Kc7, which would have preserved a much larger advantage. As a result Black’s winning edge drops from a decisive to a comfortable, but far smaller, margin.
student: By playing Rxf2 Black wins a pawn but opens the f‑file for White and leaves the black king vulnerable to a checking skewer. After the capture White can reply with Rd8+, forcing the king to move and exposing the bishop on d1, which costs Black about a pawn’s worth of evaluation. The engine therefore marks the move as a mistake, noting that Kc7 would have kept the king safe and preserved the larger advantage. In short, the capture creates new threats while leaving Black’s king in danger.

teacher: White exploits the line of Black’s king on d6 and bishop on d1 by delivering Rd8+, a checking skewer that forces the king to move. After the forced Ke5 the bishop on d1 is left en prise, so White can capture it with Rxd1. In this rook‑and‑minor‑piece ending the move keeps the evaluation essentially unchanged, leaving White still about three pawns down but preserving active chances with the advanced passed pawns on h5 (White) and f3 (Black).
student: White’s Rd8+ delivers a checking skewer that attacks Black’s king on d6 while simultaneously exposing the bishop on d1 behind it. After the forced …Ke5, the bishop becomes en prise, allowing White to capture with Rxd1 and keep the initiative in this rook‑and‑minor‑piece ending. The engine rates the move as the best possible, improving White’s standing by just a few hundredths of a pawn but leaving Black still clearly ahead – roughly two and a half pawns down.
violations: describes a capture that did not happen

teacher: By moving the king to e5 Black both centralises the monarch and leaves the black bishop on d1 hanging, forcing White to decide whether to capture it. If White takes with Rxd1, Black’s king can march to e4 and the rook will swing to g2, exploiting the distant white king and the two passed pawns on h5 and f3. This active king infiltration turns the material edge into a decisive winning advantage, as reflected by the evaluation swing of almost a pawn in Black’s favour. The engine therefore rates Ke5 as the best continuation.
student: By stepping to e5 Black not only improves his king’s activity but also forces White to give up the bishop on d1 with Rxd1, after which Black can continue with Ke4 and keep the pressure. The engine rates this as the best move, lifting the evaluation by roughly a pawn and turning a sizable edge into a decisive one. In this rook‑and‑minor‑piece ending both sides have advanced passed pawns – White’s h‑pawn and Black’s f‑pawn – so the king move consolidates Black’s already large advantage.

teacher: White removes Black’s last bishop with 44 Rxd1, turning the battle into a pure rook ending. With only opposite‑flank passed pawns left – White’s h5 versus Black’s f3 – material is equal, but the engine still judges Black as winning by about three pawns, and the move improves White’s score by only a few hundredths of a pawn. The engine’s continuation would be …Ke4, White Kh3, …Rg2 and White h6, yet the evaluation stays essentially unchanged. As the best move, Rxd1 simply preserves the most resilient defensive chances in a losing position.
student: By taking on d1 White eliminates Black’s last bishop and forces the game into a pure rook ending. The capture leaves material equal but preserves White’s dangerous passed pawn on h5 while Black still enjoys his own distant passed pawn on f3, so the engine rates the move as the best possible – it nudges the evaluation from a three‑pawn disadvantage to virtually the same score. In the principal line Black would continue with Ke4, after which White can meet it with Kh3, keeping the balance in this losing position.

teacher: White’s check with Rd4+ looks natural in a rook ending, but it actually deepens Black’s decisive edge, pushing the evaluation from a three‑pawn disadvantage to more than four pawns. By giving the check White allows Black’s king to step further into White’s position (the engine’s line continues Ke3), and the resulting rook‑and‑pawn race favours Black even more. The engine indicates that the simple king move Kh3 would have been far less costly, keeping the disadvantage around the original level. Consequently the check is an inaccuracy that costs White about 0.8 pawn of evaluation.
student: White’s Rd4+ simply checks the black king while leaving his own king vulnerable to …Ke3 and allowing Black to continue with …Rd6, after which White can try Rd6 again but still loses ground. The engine shows that this inaccuracy costs roughly eight‑tenths of a pawn, pushing the evaluation from a three‑pawn disadvantage for White to about four pawns – a decisive Black edge. In contrast, the best move Kh3 would have kept the king safe and avoided giving Black the easy reply …Ke3. Consequently, the check does not improve White’s chances and actually deepens the already losing position.

teacher: White’s 46 Rf4 simply shuffles the rook to a defensive square without creating any new threats, allowing Black’s winning edge to creep from roughly four‑and‑a‑half pawns to almost five. The engine’s preferred continuation, 46 Rd6, would have kept more pressure and, after the natural checking idea 47 Rg2+, would have left Black’s advanced f‑pawn vulnerable. By opting for the quieter rook move, White gives Black a modest but clear increase in the decisive advantage.
student: White’s rook slides to f4, but it does nothing to stop Black’s looming …Rg2+ check that would leave the f‑pawn hanging and further cramp White’s king. The engine rates the move as a moderate worsening for White – roughly four‑tenths of a pawn – because after 46.Rf4 Black can continue with 46…Rg2+ – a checking move that also attacks the now‑undefended f‑pawn. In contrast, the computer’s top choice was 46.Rd6, which would have kept more pressure on Black’s king and avoided the immediate tactical liability. Consequently, despite being “good”, Rf4 costs White about half a pawn in this already losing rook ending.

teacher: By playing 46…Kd3 Black walks straight into a forced rook fork. White can answer with Rxf3+, checking the king while simultaneously attacking the rook on f2; after 47…Rxf3 48.Kxf3 Black loses the rook and the evaluation swings from a decisive Black edge to a decisive White advantage, roughly a nine‑pawn swing. The engine’s preferred move was 46…Rg2+, which would have given check and left the pawn on f3 en prise, keeping Black’s chances alive.
student: By moving the king to d3 Black walks straight into White’s tactical shot Rxf3+, which not only wins the rook but also forks the black king on d3 and the white king on g4. The engine shows that this blunder swings the evaluation by almost ten pawns in White’s favour – the score jumps from a decisive Black edge to a decisive White edge. The correct continuation would have been Rg2+, a checking move that leaves the f‑pawn vulnerable but avoids the fork altogether. Consequently, Kd3 costs Black roughly nine pawns of material value.

teacher: White exploits the cramped black king with Rxf3+, a checking fork that attacks both the king on d3 and Black’s rook on f2. The rook is left en prise and Black can capture it, but the forced exchange opens the f‑file for White’s remaining rook and leaves the position with an advanced passed pawn on h5 and a decisive winning advantage, the evaluation slipping only a fraction of a pawn. This continuation forces the exchange and preserves White’s material edge in the rook ending.
student: White’s rook capture on f3 checks the black king while simultaneously attacking the opposing rook on f2, creating a fork that forces Black to answer with …Rxf3. After the forced exchange the material balance is restored, but the resulting open f‑file leaves White’s rook active in this rook ending where he already has an advanced passed pawn on h5. The engine rates the move as good – it costs only about a sixth of a pawn compared with the previous evaluation – yet it remains the best continuation because it preserves White’s decisive edge.

teacher: By taking the rook on f3, White eliminates Black’s last heavy piece and forces the game into a king‑and‑pawn ending, keeping the decisive material edge. The capture also leaves White with an advanced passed pawn on h5, while the kings are now directly opposed. Black’s best reply would be Kxc3, grabbing the pawn on c3, but even after that White’s evaluation stays around +4.6 pawns, confirming the move’s excellent quality.
student: By taking the rook on f3 with the king, White eliminates Black’s last heavy piece and steers the game into a pure king‑and‑pawn ending where his advanced passed pawn on h5 remains a potent asset. The capture leaves the evaluation virtually unchanged at about +4½ pawns, confirming that White still enjoys a decisive edge despite being down one pawn overall. Black’s most natural reply would be Kxc3, after which White can continue with h6 and later capture on b4, preserving the winning advantage.

teacher: Black’s king captures the pawn on c3, eliminating the last central pawn, opening the c‑file and leaving White with an isolated pawn on b4. White still enjoys a far‑advanced passed pawn on h5, and the engine still judges the position a decisive White advantage, virtually unchanged (about a seventh of a pawn swing). For a losing king‑and‑pawn ending this was the best practical try, and the move is therefore rated excellent.
student: By taking on c3 Black eliminates White’s last central pawn, leaving White with an isolated pawn on b4 in this pure king‑and‑pawn ending. The capture also opens the c‑file for White but does not alter the material balance, so the engine still judges White to be decisively ahead. In fact the evaluation stays virtually the same – about four and two‑thirds of a pawn in White’s favour – confirming that Kxc3 was the optimal continuation.

teacher: By taking on b4 Black wins a pawn and leaves a passed pawn duo on b5 and c6, giving him the only realistic chance to generate counterplay in this king‑and‑pawn ending. The capture also leaves the b‑file semi‑open for White, but the material gain offsets that drawback, as reflected by the evaluation improving by roughly a sixth of a pawn from Black’s point of view. White still retains a decisive advantage thanks to the advanced h‑pawn, yet Kxb4 is objectively the best move in the position.
student: By taking on b4 Black eliminates White’s last central pawn, turning the b‑file into a semi‑open line that can be exploited later while also leaving Black with two passed pawns on b5 and c6 in this pure king‑and‑pawn ending. The capture improves Black’s standing by roughly a sixth of a pawn, even though White still enjoys a decisive edge thanks to his advanced h‑pawn. In the engine’s continuation White would try h6, after which Black can head for Kb3 and then push …b4, keeping the pressure alive.

teacher: By pushing the pawn to h6 White creates a passed pawn on the kingside, turning a solitary pawn into a decisive outside majority in this king‑and‑pawn ending. The new passed pawn not only increases White’s winning margin (the engine’s evaluation rises by roughly two‑thirds of a pawn) but also gives the king a clear target while Black is left with only the b‑ and c‑pawns on the opposite wing. This advance is therefore the strongest continuation, improving White’s already decisive position.
student: By pushing h6 White creates a passed pawn deep in Black’s camp, turning his lone kingside pawn into a concrete asset even though it will be isolated. In this pure king‑and‑pawn ending the new passer gives White a clear long‑term target while preserving the already decisive edge – the engine’s evaluation rises by about two‑thirds of a pawn. The move therefore solidifies White’s winning chances without conceding any material disadvantage.

teacher: By pushing the pawn to h7 White creates an isolated passed pawn on the seventh rank, the only pawn left on the kingside and a clear 1‑vs‑0 majority. In this pure king‑and‑pawn ending the pawn is already a decisive asset, and the engine rates the move as the best, improving the evaluation by roughly a sixth of a pawn. Black’s remaining pawns on b5 and c5 are far on the queenside, while White’s king on g4 can advance, as the continuation Kb3 – Kf3 – c4 – Ke3 illustrates. The position remains a winning one for White despite being down a pawn in material.
student: By pushing h7 White creates a passed pawn deep in Black’s camp, turning his lone kingside pawn into a concrete asset even though it will be isolated. In this pure king‑and‑pawn ending the new passer gives White a clear long‑term target while Black’s remaining pawns on b5 and c5 remain vulnerable, which explains why the engine rates the move as the best and rewards it with a modest gain of about a sixth of a pawn. The continuation suggested by the engine would see Black’s king march to b3, after which White can bring his own king to f3 and later step onto e3, preserving the decisive edge.

teacher: By playing …c4 Black creates a passed pawn on the c‑file and advances his queenside pawn majority (two pawns versus none).  The move leaves the material balance in Black’s favour – he is up a pawn – but it does not improve the overall picture: White’s h‑pawn is still far advanced and the engine still judges the position a decisive White advantage, with the evaluation only slipping by about a tenth of a pawn for Black.  Although the engine preferred the more precise Kb3, the c4 push is still an excellent technical try in this king‑and‑pawn ending.
student: By pushing …c4 Black creates a second passed pawn on the queenside, extending his two‑pawn majority in this pure king‑and‑pawn ending. The advance does not alter the overall balance – White still enjoys a decisive edge of roughly four and three‑quarters pawns – but it keeps Black’s chances alive by giving him a concrete target to attack. Although the engine preferred the quieter Kb3, the pawn push is nevertheless judged excellent because it preserves Black’s material edge while generating counterplay.

teacher: Promoting the h‑pawn to a queen turns the position into a queen endgame and opens the h‑file for the new queen. The engine rates the move as excellent and the evaluation stays virtually unchanged, with White still winning by about four and a half pawns. Black’s only sensible reply is to bring the king forward, for example …Kc5, but the newly created queen endgame leaves White in full control despite Black’s advanced passed pawn on c4.
student: By promoting on h8 White converts the game into a pure queen ending and opens the h‑file, giving Black’s king limited counterplay while his own pieces become more active. The engine rates the move as excellent, noting that the evaluation stays at roughly +4½ pawns – essentially unchanged from before. In this line Black can try Kc5, after which White would continue with Kf3, followed by …c3 and Ke3, keeping the decisive material edge intact.

teacher: Black’s king steps to b2, staying close to the advanced passed pawn on c3 but not improving the position; the evaluation remains at roughly a five‑pawn advantage for White. The engine, however, rates 54…Kb4 as marginally stronger, preferring the king a square farther up the board. After 54…Kb2 White can continue with the forcing line Qf2+ – Kb1 – Qd4 – Kc2, keeping the decisive material edge. In short, the move is safe but it forgoes the slightly better king‑move suggested by the engine.
student: Black’s king steps to b2, keeping it safe in this queen‑ending where White already enjoys a decisive material edge and an advanced passed pawn on c3. The engine rates the move as essentially neutral – the evaluation remains at about +5½ pawns for White – but it does not improve Black’s chances. A more accurate continuation would have been Kb4, which the engine flags as the best alternative. After Kb2 White can continue with Qf2+, after which Black must retreat to Kb1 before White plays Qd4 and Black replies Kc2.

teacher: White had a decisive edge after the forcing Qf7+ Kb2, but the quiet Qb7 is a blunder that throws away that advantage. By moving the queen away, White forfeits the winning checking idea Qf2+, which the engine identifies as the best move. After Qb7 Black can simply advance the passed pawn with …c2, and even the forcing continuation Qxb5+ Ka2 Qa4+ only brings the evaluation down to roughly equal. The missed check would have preserved White’s winning advantage.
student: White’s retreat Qb7 is a serious blunder that turns a decisive +5‑pawn edge into an almost equal position – the evaluation drops by about five pawns. The engine shows that the correct continuation was the checking move Qf2+, which would have kept the initiative and preserved the large advantage. By playing Qb7 instead, White allows Black to advance the passed pawn with …c2, after which the line continues Qxb5+ Ka2 Qa4+. In short, the move costs White roughly half its winning chances.

teacher: Moving the king to c1 is a catastrophic error: it abandons Black’s only active piece, the passed pawn on c2, and lets White’s queen infiltrate with tempo while the Black king is driven further from the action. The engine shows that a simple Ka2 would have kept the pawn defended and maintained the balance, whereas after 56…Kc1 White can improve with Kf3, Black replies Kd2, then White plays Qb2, leading to a winning queen‑and‑pawn ending, leaving White up the equivalent of eight pawns and a decisive advantage.
student: By moving the king to c1 Black walks into a losing queen‑endgame where White’s king can march in with Kf3 and then capture the last black pawn, turning a balanced position into a decisive one for White. The engine shows that the simple retreat Ka2 would have kept the balance, whereas Kc1 lets White win the extra eight points of material. In this line White also enjoys a clear edge – the evaluation jumps from equality to about six pawns in White’s favour.

teacher: By moving the king to d1 Black walks into a direct queen fork. After 57…Kd1 White can answer with Qd3+, checking and simultaneously attacking the king on d1 and the advanced pawn on c2, a line that forces mate in nine (for example Qd3+ Kc1 Ke2 Kb2 …). The position was already a decisive white advantage (+5.63 pawns), but this blunder turns it into a forced loss; the engine’s best reply, Kd2, would have avoided the immediate mating net.
student: By moving the king to d1 Black walks straight into White’s forcing line. After …Kd1 White can play Qd3+, checking the king and simultaneously attacking the advanced passed pawn on c2, which leads directly to a forced mate in nine. The engine shows that the correct defence was Kd2, keeping the king out of danger and preserving any chance to survive. Consequently the position collapses from a clearly losing one for Black to an immediate loss.

teacher: White’s check Qf1+ looks natural, but it forfeits the winning tactic that was available. The engine’s best continuation, Qd3+, would fork the black king on d1 and the advanced pawn on c2. By playing Qf1+ White gives up that fork and the forced mate in nine, settling instead for a decisive material edge of roughly five pawns. In short, the move turns a forced win into a winning but less precise position.
student: White’s checking move Qf1+ looks natural but it allows Black to slip the king away with Kd2, after which White can continue with Qe2+, Kc3, Qe5+. The engine shows that the far stronger try was Qd3+, which would have forked the black king on d1 and the advanced passed pawn on c2 while keeping the mating net intact. By opting for Qf1+ White forfeits the forced mate in nine and instead wins about five pawns, turning a win into a merely winning position. In short, the check costs White the immediate forced mate and turns a decisive edge into a comfortable but not forced one.

teacher: Black’s king steps onto c3, the only move that keeps the evaluation essentially unchanged (the engine shows a swing of only +0.03 pawns) even though the advanced passed pawn on c2 is now left en prise. In this queen‑endgame the king’s move continues to defend the pawn, and White’s most forcing reply would be the checking move Qe5+. After the likely sequence Qe5+ Kc4 Ke4 Kb3 the assessment remains a decisive White advantage, confirming Kc3 as the best defensive try.
student: By moving to c3 Black brings his king into the centre of this queen‑ending and keeps the dangerous passed pawn on c2 alive, even though it becomes temporarily en prise. The engine rates the move as the best possible, with the evaluation barely shifting from +5.30 to +5.27 – essentially unchanged in practical terms. White’s most forcing continuation would be Qe5+, after which Black can answer Kc4 and continue with Ke4, Kb3 etc., but the position remains clearly winning for White.

teacher: White’s check with Qe3+ is a serious blunder, wiping out the roughly five‑pawn winning edge it enjoyed a moment earlier. Although the move does give check, it allows Black’s king to step away and leaves the dangerous passed pawn on c2 untouched, so the position collapses to an almost equal balance (+0.17). The engine shows that the correct continuation was the more forcing Qe5+, which would have kept the decisive advantage. In short, the check loses the winning momentum and turns a winning queen‑endgame into a roughly level one.
student: White’s checking move Qe3+ looks natural but it walks straight into Black’s counter‑play. After the forced …Kb2, White can continue with Qd2 and then Qb4+, yet the engine shows that this sequence leaves Black with a king on b2 and a dangerous passed pawn on c2, erasing White’s earlier +5‑pawn edge and reducing the evaluation to roughly equality. The correct continuation would have been Qe5+, which also checks while keeping the initiative in the queen ending. By playing Qe3+ instead, White surrendered about five pawns of value.
violations: names a king on b2, but there is none

teacher: Black’s king steps onto b2, directly supporting the far‑advanced passed pawn on c2 and cementing the king’s position in front of it. In this queen‑endgame the move modestly improves Black’s standing – the engine rates the change as roughly a sixth of a pawn – and leaves the evaluation essentially equal. White’s most forcing reply would be the checking move Qb6+, after which Black can calmly answer Ka2 and, after White’s Qc5, return to Kb2, keeping the pawn safe. This precise king maneuver is judged the best possible continuation.
student: By stepping to b2 Black brings his king into the centre of this queen‑ending and directly attacks White’s queen with …Qb6+, forcing the white queen to give check. The engine rates the move as the best, improving Black’s standing by about a sixth of a pawn even though White remains up eight points of material. After the forced line Qb6+ Ka2 Qc5 Kb2 the game heads into a queenside pawn race where Black’s advanced passed pawn on c2 will dominate.
violations: describes a check that did not happen

teacher: White improves the safety of his king by stepping to e2, while keeping the queen on e3 ready to meet any promotion. The evaluation stays exactly balanced, showing that the move does not alter White’s standing in this queen‑endgame. The engine, however, considered the more forcing Qb6+ – a checking move – to be the optimal continuation. After a possible …c1=Q the newly promoted queen would be left en prise, so White’s position remains secure.
student: White’s king steps to e2, keeping the material edge intact and leaving the evaluation at equality in this queen‑ending where Black’s advanced passed pawn sits on c2. The engine notes that the more forcing continuation would have been Qb6+, delivering a check that after …c1=Q leaves the newly placed queen en prise. By opting for Ke2 instead, White avoids any immediate tactical liability while preserving the balance.

teacher: By queening on c1 Black converts the pawn into a queen and opens the c‑file, stepping into a queen‑ending. Although the new queen on c1 is left en prise, the move is still the strongest because White’s best reply would be Qe5+. The engine’s evaluation remains roughly equal and material stays level, so 61…c1=Q is rightly marked as the best move (!!).
student: By promoting on c1 Black not only creates a new queen but also opens the c‑file in this pure queen ending. The engine rates the move as the best choice, leaving the evaluation at equality despite material being level. White’s most forcing reply would be Qe5+, checking and removing the threat to the queen on e5, after which Black can continue with …Qb5+ followed by …Qb2+. This sequence preserves the balance while giving Black active counterplay.

teacher: White meets the danger to his queen by sliding it to b6 with check, thereby both removing the immediate threat on the queen and forcing Black’s king to move in this queen‑endgame. The move leaves the material balance unchanged and the evaluation stays roughly equal, although the engine judges Qe5+ — which also eliminates a queen‑threat while checking — to be marginally more accurate. After Qb6+ Black must step the king (for example Ka1), after which the queens continue to trade checks such as Qa5+ and Qb5+.
student: White’s Qb6+ both eliminates Black’s immediate danger to the queen and delivers a check in this pure queen‑ending. The engine rates it as a solid continuation that leaves the balance untouched – the evaluation remains roughly equal. Nevertheless, the engine preferred Qe5+, which would have removed the same threat while giving an even sharper check.
