Black can immediately answer with …Qc5+, forking the king on g1 and the a‑pawn while also removing the threat to the bishop on f8, which leaves White’s position even more vulnerable – the engine’s evaluation slides from a four‑pawn disadvantage to almost five pawns. The move therefore costs roughly eight‑tenths of a pawn and is rightly judged an inaccuracy. The engine’s preferred continuation was Kg2, keeping the king safer and avoiding the fork.

teacher: By taking on d2 Black captures a bishop, but the rook immediately lands en prise and White can recapture with Nxd2, restoring material balance. Nevertheless the exchange eases Black’s defensive task against White’s advanced passed pawn on d5, and the engine’s evaluation jumps by roughly a pawn in Black’s favour. The engine’s top alternative, Qc5+, would have forked the king and the a‑pawn while also removing the threat to the bishop on f8, but Rxd2 still improves the position enough to keep Black’s decisive advantage.
student: By playing Rxd2 Black eliminates White’s active bishop on d2, but the rook lands on a square that can be taken immediately. After the forced Nxd2 the material balance is restored, leaving Black with a four‑pawn lead in a position where White’s passed pawn on d5 and his dark‑square pawn structure give him little counterplay. The engine rates the capture as a significant improvement – roughly a pawn’s worth – yet it is not the most accurate continuation; Qc5+ would have forked the king on g1 and the a‑pawn while also removing the threat to the bishop on f8. In short, the move wins a piece but does not exploit the tactical possibilities available.

teacher: By playing Nxd2 White captures the rook on d2, turning a material deficit into a one‑pawn lead and improving the evaluation by roughly a third of a pawn. The capture leaves White’s advanced passed pawn on d5 untouched while both sides’ pawn structures stay fixed on opposite colours. Black can reply with the forcing Qc1+, which forks the king on g1, the newly placed knight on d2 and the a‑pawn, leaving the a7‑pawn en prise; White would have to meet the check with Nf1 before Black can continue with Bc5+. Nonetheless, Nxd2 is the engine’s top choice and the only move that modestly improves White’s position.
student: By taking on d2 White wins a rook, turning his one‑pawn lead into a full rook for a pawn advantage. The capture also leaves Black’s queen vulnerable to a fork after …Qc1+, which would attack the king on g1, the knight on d2 and the a‑pawn while leaving the a7 pawn hanging. Although Black still enjoys a decisive edge, Nxd2 is the strongest continuation because it improves White’s evaluation by roughly a third of a pawn.

teacher: Black’s queen delivers a spectacular check on c1, forking the white king on g1, the knight on d2 and the pawn on a3. White can only interpose with Nf1, but that move leaves the knight on f1 en prise, after which Black can continue Bc5+ and Qc2+, consolidating a clear advantage; the engine rates the move as a gain of about a pawn, deepening Black’s winning advantage to roughly –6½. Although the a7 pawn becomes temporarily vulnerable, the decisive fork more than compensates, which is why the move is marked as a brilliant “best” choice.
student: Black’s queen jumps to c1 with a checking fork that hits White’s king on g1, the knight on d2 and the a‑pawn, while also leaving the a7 pawn undefended. The engine rates this as the best continuation, improving Black’s already decisive edge by roughly a pawn (+1.03). If White replies with the natural Nf1, the knight would be left en prise, allowing Black to continue with …Bc5+ and later …Qc2+. This precise tactical blow consolidates Black’s winning chances despite White’s dangerous passed pawn on d5.

teacher: White’s only sensible try is 36.Nf1, even though it places the knight on f1 where it can be captured. The move preserves White’s extra pawn and the advanced passed pawn on d5, but it does cost a little – the engine’s evaluation slips from a decisive Black edge of about six‑and‑a‑half pawns to roughly seven pawns. Black can exploit the hanging piece with 36…Bc5+, forking the king on g1 and the a‑pawn, and after 37.Kg2 White would have to meet the ensuing 37…Qc2+ with 38.Kh3. Nonetheless, given the position’s constraints, Nf1 is still the best continuation for White.
student: White’s retreat Nf1 does leave the knight hanging, but it is the best continuation because any other try would allow Black to increase the pressure with …Bc5+, forking the king on g1 and the a‑pawn while also removing the threat to the bishop on c5. After that checking blow White can meet Kg2 and then continue with Qc2+, keeping the initiative alive despite the looming loss. The engine still judges the position a decisive Black advantage, though the evaluation slips by about half a pawn after the move.

teacher: Black answers with 36…Bc5+, a checking move that also forks the white king on g1 and the pawn on a3. In the engine’s line White’s most natural reply, 37.Re3, would leave the rook on e3 en prise, allowing Black to continue 37…Bxe3+ and maintain the winning position. Although the evaluation slips by only about a fifth of a pawn, Black remains clearly winning with a decisive advantage, making Bc5+ the correct and best continuation.
student: Black’s bishop jump to c5 checks the white king while forking the king on g1 and the pawn on a3, thereby removing the immediate danger to the bishop itself. The engine rates it as the best continuation, even though White can answer with Re3, which would leave the rook on e3 hanging. After that reply Black can capture on e3 with check, preserving the decisive edge despite being down a pawn. The evaluation slips by only about two‑tenths of a pawn, but Black remains clearly ahead in this winning middlegame.

teacher: White’s king‑step to g2 looks natural but it walks into Black’s queen check Qc2+, after which White must reply Kh3 and Black can continue with Qf2 and a timely …d6, deepening the already decisive edge; the evaluation slides from about –6.8 to –7.4 pawns, a moderate worsening for White. The engine preferred Re3 instead – even though it would leave the rook en prise – because it at least offers more resistance than the passive king move. Consequently Kg2 is an inaccuracy, costing roughly half a pawn in the assessment.
student: White’s king step to g2 does little to improve his already cramped position and actually lets Black increase the pressure – the engine now evaluates the position about half a pawn worse for White than before. By moving the king instead of the more active rook lift Re3, White missed the chance to keep the rook safe and allowed Black to continue with …Qc2+, a checking move that further limits White’s options. The move therefore costs White roughly half a pawn in evaluation despite remaining up one pawn of material.

teacher: Black continues with the forcing Qc2+, delivering a check that drives White’s king to the edge of the board. The move leaves the evaluation essentially unchanged, preserving Black’s decisive advantage even though White is up a pawn, because Black enjoys a superior pawn structure – White’s pawns are fixed on dark squares while Black’s are fixed on light squares and White’s advanced passed pawn on d5 is already under pressure. In the principal continuation White would likely answer Kh3, after which Black can reply Qf2 and follow up with …d6 and …Ne4, keeping the winning pressure.
student: Black’s Qc2+ simply checks the white king while preserving his overwhelming material edge – the engine still evaluates the position as a decisive Black advantage, even though White is technically a pawn up. By forcing the king to move, Black keeps the pressure and maintains the initiative that underlies the already‑deciding score. The continuation suggested by the engine would be Kh3, after which Black can continue with …Qf2, keeping the initiative alive.

teacher: After Black’s forcing queen check, White’s only sensible reply is Kh3, which the engine flags as the best move. The king steps to h3, escaping the check while preserving the advanced passed pawn on d5 and the mutually fixed pawn structure (White’s pawns locked on dark squares, Black’s on light). The move only marginally worsens White’s already losing position—by about a sixth of a pawn—so Black still enjoys a decisive advantage. According to the engine, Black would likely continue with Qf2, after which White can push d6, but Black can answer Ne4, after which White can capture on e4.
student: White’s king steps to h3, the engine‑recommended move that keeps it out of Black’s attack while preserving the advanced passed pawn on d5 and the dark‑square pawn structure. The evaluation slips by about a sixth of a pawn, leaving Black still with a decisive edge, but no alternative would improve White’s chances further. In the principal variation Black can continue with …Qf2, after which White may try d6, followed by …Ne4 and a possible exchange on e4.

teacher: Black answers White’s central d4 thrust with the natural developing move Nf6, keeping the evaluation essentially unchanged and preserving material equality. The engine rates the move as excellent and confirms it as the best reply, with the most likely continuation being c4 followed by e6 and then Nf3 – d5. This simple development maintains the balance and leaves Black well‑placed for the ensuing opening battle.
student: Black’s reply …Nf6 is an excellent developing move that simply brings the knight into play without altering the balance – the engine still evaluates the position as roughly equal, with only a tiny swing of about three‑hundredths of a pawn against Black. By completing development, Black keeps material level and maintains the status quo in this opening phase. The engine predicts White will likely continue with c4, after which Black can answer …e6 and later strike in the centre with …d5, confirming the soundness of the move.

teacher: White’s 2.c4 is the engine‑recommended continuation, preserving the tiny edge that White already enjoyed after 1.d4 Nf6. The move leaves material level and only nudges the evaluation from +0.18 to +0.21, essentially keeping the position equal but marginally better for White. In the principal variation Black would likely answer …e6, after which White can develop with Nf3 and meet a …d5 thrust by recapturing on d5 with the c‑pawn.
student: White’s second move c4 is judged the best continuation, nudging the evaluation from a tiny edge for Black to a slight advantage for White – an improvement of about three‑hundredths of a pawn. The engine predicts that Black would most naturally answer …e6, after which White can develop with Nf3 and later capture on d5, keeping the balance intact. In short, the pawn thrust preserves material equality while giving White a modest but tangible edge in the opening.

teacher: White eliminates Black’s pawn on d5, removing the immediate threat to the pawn that had just advanced there. After the expected recapture Nxd5 the material balance is restored, so White is no longer up a pawn, and the c‑file becomes semi‑open for White while the d‑file becomes semi‑open for Black, leaving the evaluation only slightly in White’s favour. The engine, however, judged Qb3 to be the sharper continuation because it would have removed the threat to the pawn on c4 and kept a marginal edge. Nonetheless, cxd5 is a sound capture that leaves the position essentially unchanged.
student: By playing cxd5 White eliminates Black’s pawn on d5 and immediately opens the c‑file for his pieces while giving Black a semi‑open d‑file after the natural reply Nxd5. The capture also removes the immediate threat to the pawn that had just advanced to d5, but it does not win material – the engine still evaluates the position as only a slight edge for White. Although the move keeps the evaluation essentially unchanged, the engine prefers Qb3, which would have removed the threat to the pawn on c4 without conceding the c‑file advantage. In practice, however, the exchange leaves White with a modest material lead and a comfortable semi‑open line.

teacher: By capturing on c3 White eliminates Black’s knight and the immediate threats to the queen on d1 and the pawn on e4, while the b‑file becomes semi‑open for White’s pieces. The trade does leave White with an isolated pawn on a2 and the c‑file is no longer semi‑open, but the engine rates the move as the best, keeping White a shade better (about a tenth of a pawn). Black can now try the pawn break c5, striking at White’s d4 pawn, as the most natural reply.
student: By playing bxc3 White eliminates Black’s active knight on c3, removing the immediate danger to both the queen on d1 and the pawn on e4 while also opening the b‑file for future play. The capture does leave White with an isolated pawn on a2, but it preserves material equality and nudges the evaluation from a slight edge for Black to a modest advantage for White (about a tenth of a pawn). Black can reply with the thematic …c5, striking at White’s d4 pawn, yet the engine still rates bxc3 as the best continuation.

teacher: Black meets White’s central space with the thematic …c5, a pawn break that strikes directly at the d4 pawn and seeks to open lines for his pieces. The engine rates it as the best continuation, and the evaluation stays essentially unchanged – White remains only a hair better (+0.22). In the principal variation White can answer with Be3, after which Black can safely castle and bring the queen to a5.
student: Black’s …c5 is a timely pawn break that strikes directly at White’s central pawn on d4, challenging its stability and opening lines for his pieces. The engine rates it as the best continuation, keeping the evaluation virtually unchanged – White remains only a fraction of a pawn ahead. In the principal variation White would develop with Be3, after which Black can safely castle and continue with …Rc1 and …Qa5, preserving the balance.

teacher: White’s 11 c4 is a solidifying move that reinforces the strong d5 pawn and limits Black’s already cramped pieces, but it also allows Black to play …b6, which simply removes the pressure on the c5 pawn and trims White’s edge. The engine evaluates the position after 11 c4 as only slightly better for White (+0.57) instead of the clear pawn‑plus advantage it had (+1.03), reflecting a moderate loss of about half a pawn. In contrast, the computer‑recommended 11 h4 would have kept a larger edge. Overall, 11 c4 is a good move that improves the position, yet it is not the most accurate continuation.
student: White’s 11.c4 tries to open lines for his pieces but does nothing to improve the cramped situation of his king, which remains stuck in the middle while Black already enjoys a comfortable setup with the king safely castled and both bishops limited. The engine rates the move as a moderate worsening – roughly half a pawn – because it allows Black to meet the thrust with …b6, removing the pressure on the pawn on c5 and keeping the balance. A more accurate continuation would have been 11.h4, which the engine flags as the best move. Consequently White’s advantage shrinks from about a pawn to just under half a pawn.

teacher: White retreats the queen to d2, a solid but modest move that simply connects the rooks while leaving the king in the centre and the f‑bishop still cramped to only two safe squares. The engine rates it as “good”, yet it costs White about a tenth of a pawn compared with the sharper  h4 , which would keep more pressure on Black’s kingside. After Qd2 Black can reply e5, gaining space and further exploiting White’s uncastled king. Consequently the evaluation slips from a slight +0.57 to about +0.44.
student: White’s queen retreat to d2 does little more than preserve the slight edge it already enjoyed – the engine’s evaluation slips by about a tenth of a pawn and the move is judged “good” but not optimal. By moving the queen instead of the more active h4, White misses the chance to increase pressure on Black’s central pawn structure, especially since the king remains stuck in the middle while Black has already castled. The position therefore stays roughly equal, with White’s bishop on f1 limited to just two safe squares.

teacher: Black’s 12…Ba6 is an inaccuracy that merely shuffles the c8‑bishop to a6 without improving Black’s stance. After the move White can continue with h4, gaining space on the kingside, and the evaluation swings from a slight White edge to roughly a pawn’s worth in White’s favour. The engine’s top choice was …e5, showing that Ba6 missed a stronger continuation. As a result White’s position is now clearly better by about a pawn.
student: By playing …Ba6 Black does nothing to improve his already‑castled position and simply hands White the chance to increase the edge. The engine shows that the far stronger continuation would have been …e5, which keeps the balance and leaves White’s slight advantage at roughly +0.4 pawn. After …Ba6 White can continue with h4, after which Black’s best reply is h5, followed by Bd3 and e6, leaving White clearly better – now about a pawn ahead. In short, the move costs Black roughly eight‑tenths of a pawn and is rightly marked as an inaccuracy.

teacher: Black’s 14…Qa4 is an excellent move that leaves the material balance unchanged and only lets White’s edge **grow** by a few hundredths of a pawn (the evaluation moves from +1.27 to +1.32). By relocating the queen while Black’s king is safely castled and White’s king still sits in the centre, Black maintains a solid defensive stance. Nevertheless, the engine rates the pawn break 14…e6 – striking at White’s d5 pawn – as the superior continuation. In the most likely line White can reply with Bh6, pinning the g7 bishop to the rook on f8, after which Black would have to capture and meet Qxh6 with …f6.
student: By moving the queen to a4 Black places it on the same rank as White’s king and keeps the material balance untouched, so the engine’s assessment stays roughly the same – White remains about a pawn ahead. The move also leaves Black safely castled while White’s king is still stuck in the centre. Although the engine preferred the more ambitious pawn break …e6, which would strike directly at White’s d5 pawn, Qa4 is an excellent defensive resource that preserves the status quo without worsening Black’s position.

teacher: White’s 15 Bh6!! puts the bishop on h6, pinning Black’s g7‑bishop to the rook on f8 and sharpening the pressure on Black’s king‑side. Black can reply with 15…Qb4, attacking White’s queen on d2 (which currently defends the bishop on h6). White can then capture on g7 with 16 Bxg7; after 16…Kxg7 White continues with 17 h5, keeping the edge. The move nudges the evaluation from about a pawn to roughly +1.4, confirming it as the best continuation.
student: By playing Bh6 White creates a direct pin of Black’s bishop on g7 against the rook on f8, tightening the pressure on that piece even though White’s own king remains in the centre and Black has already castled. The engine rates the move as the best, improving White’s advantage by roughly a tenth of a pawn. Black could try …Qb4, which would attack the newly placed bishop and also pin White’s queen on d2 to the king, but White can meet it with Bxg7 and then continue with h5, keeping the initiative.

teacher: By playing Bxc4 Black finally wins the pawn on c4, creating a passed pawn on c5 and opening the c‑file for White. Yet this concession allows White to increase the pressure – after Black’s move the evaluation jumps from a modest +1.4 pawn to a clear +2.0 pawns in White’s favour, and White can continue with Bxg7. The move is an inaccuracy because Black missed the far stronger Qb4, which would have pinned White’s queen on d2 to the king on e1 and attacked the poorly defended bishop on h6. Consequently, the material gain is outweighed by the deterioration of Black’s position.
student: By playing …Bxc4 Black wins a pawn but opens the c‑file for White and leaves the bishop on g7 vulnerable to capture, allowing White to reply Bxg7. The engine rates the move an inaccuracy because it lets White’s advantage swell from roughly a pawn to more than two pawns – a loss of about half a pawn for Black. A far stronger try would have been …Qb4, which both attacks the poorly defended bishop on h6 and pins the white queen to the king, preserving the pressure that the position otherwise lacked. Consequently, despite being up a pawn, Black’s position becomes significantly worse after this capture.

teacher: By taking on e2 Black eliminates White’s last bishop, converting the position into opposite‑colour bishops and surrendering the bishop pair. The capture also uncovers the a4‑queen’s line, now targeting the pawn on e4, and creates the concrete threat Bxf8 to win the rook. Although the exchange wins a piece and leaves the evaluation essentially unchanged at roughly a two‑pawn advantage for White, it is the only move that preserves Black’s chances. The engine’s line would continue Bxf8, after which White could answer Bxf3, gxf3 and Black would recapture on f8.
student: By playing …Bxe2 Black wins the white bishop and simultaneously uncovers the queen’s line to the e‑pawn, creating an immediate threat that can be met with …Bxf8. The capture also leaves Black with a bishop on e2 while the bishops are now of opposite colours, giving Black a small material edge despite White still being about two pawns ahead. Although White retains the active rook on the semi‑open c‑file, the engine rates the move as the best continuation, keeping the evaluation essentially unchanged at roughly +2 pawns.

teacher: Black’s bishop captures on f3, forking the g‑pawn and the e‑pawn, but the fork is short‑lived because White can simply take back with gxf3. After the recapture the material balance is restored, the bishop is gone, and White is left with an isolated h‑pawn and doubled pawns on the f‑file, yet White still enjoys a well‑over‑a‑pawn advantage (+2.58). The engine, however, judged Ba6 to be stronger – it would have removed the immediate threat to the bishop on a6 without conceding the exchange.
student: By playing Bxf3 Black creates a fork on g2 and e4, forcing White to capture with gxf3. After the forced recapture the g‑file becomes semi‑open for White, White’s h‑pawn is left isolated and his f‑pawns become doubled, giving Black some compensation despite being down a pawn. The engine rates the move as improving Black’s standing by about half a pawn, but it does not erase White’s clear edge – the evaluation remains around +2½ for White. A more precise continuation would have been Ba6, which simply eliminates the immediate danger to the bishop without conceding the same structural weaknesses.

teacher: Black’s …Qb4 tries to pin White’s queen on d2 to the un‑castled king, but the pin is illusory: White can simply capture the queen with Qxb4. After the forced exchange Black recaptures with the c‑pawn and, thanks to the semi‑open c‑file, can activate the rook on c1 with Rc7, leaving Black a pawn down and increasing White’s lead to roughly a pawn. The engine’s top alternative, Qa3, would have kept the queen on a safer square and avoided the material loss. Consequently the move is an inaccuracy, worsening Black’s position by about a pawn.
student: By playing …Qb4 Black tries to pin White’s queen on d2 to the king on e1, but the move simply allows White to capture with Qxb4, after which Black recaptures and White can continue with Rc7, keeping the initiative. The engine shows that this costs Black roughly a pawn, turning an already sizable White edge into a decisive one. A more accurate try would have been …Qa3, which keeps the queen out of the line of fire and preserves the balance. Consequently, the move is marked as an inaccuracy.

teacher: By playing Qxb4 White captures Black’s queen on b4. After the forced …cxb4 the queens are exchanged, leaving a rook‑and‑minor‑piece endgame with an open c‑file for White’s rook on c1 and doubled Black pawns on the b‑file. The exchange does not change the material balance, but it improves White’s pawn structure and the activity of the remaining pieces.
student: By taking on b4 White eliminates Black’s last queen and forces an immediate queen‑exchange that leaves the game in a rook‑and‑minor‑piece ending. After the inevitable …cxb4 the c‑file opens for White’s rook on c1 while Black is left with doubled b‑pawns, giving White a clear structural edge. The engine rates the capture as the best move, improving the evaluation by roughly a sixth of a pawn to a decisive +3.87. In the principal variation Black would reply …cxb4, after which White can continue with Rc7 and keep the initiative.

teacher: By playing 20…cxb4 Black finally eliminates White’s queen, turning the battle into a rook‑and‑minor‑piece ending. The capture opens the c‑file, gives Black a three‑to‑two queenside pawn majority (albeit with doubled b‑pawns), and leaves the evaluation essentially unchanged – the engine’s score drops only about two hundredths of a pawn. White’s rook on c1 now dominates the open c‑file, and the most threatening continuation for White would be 21 Rc7, which would fork the a7 and e7 pawns, but even that does not improve White’s already decisive advantage.
student: By playing …cxb4 Black eliminates White’s queen with his last pawn, turning the game into a rook‑and‑minor‑piece ending where the c‑file opens for both sides’ pieces. The capture also gives Black a three‑pawn queenside majority against White’s two, although it leaves him with doubled b‑pawns. White can reply with Rc7, forking the a7 and e7 pawns, but even after that continuation Black remains the best choice because the engine rates the move as the most accurate way to keep the evaluation essentially unchanged while simplifying the position.

teacher: White’s 21 .Rc7! exploits the open c‑file and launches a fork on the a7‑ and e7‑pawns, preserving the decisive material edge. The move keeps the engine’s assessment at roughly +4 pawns, confirming that White remains clearly ahead in this rook‑and‑minor‑piece ending. Black can only try 21…Re8, which would simply defend the e‑pawn and allow White to capture on a7 on the next move, as the principal variation shows.
student: By playing Rc7 White places his rook on the open c‑file where it simultaneously attacks both Black’s a7 and e7 pawns, creating an immediate fork that forces Black to choose between defending the two targets. The engine rates this as the best continuation, keeping the evaluation at roughly +4 pawns in White’s favour. Black can try Re8 to eliminate the pressure on the e7 pawn, but even after that White remains clearly ahead with a one‑pawn material edge.

teacher: Black’s king step to g7 further thins the pawn shield in front of his monarch, a drawback noted in the move ideas, while doing nothing to the looming danger to the e‑pawn. The engine points out that the more accurate continuation would have been Re8, which directly removes the threat to the pawn on e7. Consequently the evaluation stays virtually unchanged – White remains winning by roughly four pawns – and Black’s position is still a rook‑and‑minor‑piece endgame with White holding a material edge of one pawn.
student: By moving the king to g7 Black steps out of the pawn shield that had protected it, thereby weakening the pawn cover in front of his monarch. The engine still judges White’s position as a decisive +3.9‑pawn advantage, with the evaluation barely changing after the move. Although Kg7 is not a losing choice, the engine would have preferred Re8, which would have removed the immediate threat to the e7 pawn. In this rook‑and‑minor‑piece ending White’s rook already dominates the open c‑file, so the king move does little more than expose the king to further danger.

teacher: By placing the rook on the semi‑open d‑file, Black activates his only heavy piece in this rook‑and‑minor‑piece ending, improving his overall coordination. The engine rates the move as the best, noting a modest swing of about a quarter‑pawn in Black’s favour (the evaluation moves from +3.59 to +3.36 for White). If White tries the most forcing continuation, 23 h6+ +, Black can answer 23…Kf8 and continue with 24 Rxa7 b3, as shown in the principal variation.
student: By playing Rd8 Black finally puts his rook onto the semi‑open d‑file, directly contesting White’s control of the open c‑file in this rook‑and‑minor‑piece ending. The engine rates it as the best continuation, improving Black’s standing by roughly a quarter pawn even though White still enjoys a decisive edge. White can try the checking idea h6+, but after Black’s forced Kf8 White will be unable to capture on a7 without losing material, leaving Black with active chances despite the remaining disadvantage.

teacher: By capturing on d5 Black removes White’s central pawn and opens the d‑file, giving the rook immediate control of that line. In this rook‑and‑minor‑piece ending the exchange does not restore material balance; White remains up a pawn, yet White’s rook on e7 still pins the f‑pawn to the king, limiting Black’s counterplay. The engine marks the capture as the best move, but the evaluation remains around +2.8 pawns for White, so the overall advantage is essentially unchanged. According to the principal variation, White could continue with f4, after which Black might reply Nc6, White Rc7 and Black Nd4.
student: By taking on d5 Black eliminates White’s last central pawn and opens the d‑file for his rook, which now dominates that line in this rook‑and‑minor‑piece ending. The capture also leaves the white rook on e7 pinning the f‑pawn to the black king, so White cannot generate any immediate counterplay along the f‑file. Although White remains clearly better – still about three pawns ahead – the engine rates Rxd5 as the best continuation, keeping the evaluation essentially unchanged at roughly +2.9.

teacher: White’s pawn break e6 looks natural, striking at the f7 pawn and advancing the kingside majority, especially since the rook on e7 pins that pawn to the king. In reality the move allows Black the forcing reply Re5+; after White’s king steps to f1 Black can simply capture on e6, erasing the pawn and cutting White’s advantage by roughly a pawn. The engine therefore tags the move a mistake, pointing out that the quieter f4 would have preserved a much larger edge. The position stays a rook‑and‑minor‑piece ending with White’s rook still pinning f7, but the pawn thrust has back‑fired.
student: White’s 24.e6 tries to strike at Black’s f‑pawn by pushing the kingside pawn majority forward, but it does nothing to stop Black’s immediate checking resource … Re5+. After the check White must step to f1, allowing Black to capture on e6 with his rook and erase most of White’s earlier edge, which drops the evaluation from about +2.9 to roughly +1.6 – a loss of more than a pawn. The engine therefore marks the move as a mistake, noting that the far stronger continuation would have been 24.f4, keeping the pressure without conceding the easy rook exchange. In this rook‑and‑minor‑piece ending White still enjoys a clear advantage, yet the pawn push costs him the initiative.
violations: describes a capture that did not happen

teacher: Black captures the pawn on e6, allowing an exchange of rooks if White recaptures with the rook. After White recaptures, the e‑file is opened and White is left with isolated pawns on f2 and f3, while material remains level. The rook on e6 is temporarily en prise, but the resulting structure gives Black no disadvantage and the evaluation stays essentially unchanged (still about a pawn in White’s favour), confirming the move as the best choice.
student: By playing Rxe6 Black eliminates White’s pawn on e6, opening the e‑file for his own rook while leaving it temporarily en prise. The capture also initiates an exchange that will be answered by fxe6, after which White’s rook on e7 continues to dominate the file but the resulting structure leaves White with isolated f‑pawns (f2 and f3). In this rook‑and‑minor‑piece ending the engine rates the move as the best choice, keeping the evaluation essentially unchanged at roughly a pawn in White’s favour.

teacher: White’s 26.h6+ gives a check and fixes Black’s pawn on h7 to a light square, but the pawn ends up isolated on h6. The move does not address Black’s active rook on e6; the engine notes that the stronger 26.Rxe6 would have captured that rook. After the check Black can simply play Kf6, removing the threat to the rook, and the evaluation drops from roughly +1.2 to +0.9 – a moderate loss of about a third of a pawn. Consequently the move is a good check, but far from the optimal continuation.
student: White’s 26.h6+ checks the black king while fixing Black’s pawn on h7 on a light square, but it also leaves White with an isolated pawn on h6 and allows Black to meet the check by moving the king to f6, removing the immediate danger to the rook on e6. The engine rates the move as “good” yet notes that it costs roughly a third of a pawn compared with the optimal continuation Rxe6, which would have captured the opposing rook outright. After 26…Kf6 White can still win material, but the missed capture reduces White’s advantage significantly.

teacher: White’s king walk to e2 is an inaccuracy because it moves the king away from the centre, allowing Black’s natural …b3 pawn break that “strikes at the pawn on a2.” After the move the engine’s assessment falls from a clear pawn‑plus (+1.12) to only a slight edge (+0.34), a loss of roughly three‑quarters of a pawn. The engine’s preferred reply was Kc2, keeping the king closer to the queenside and better able to meet the …b3 thrust. In this rook‑and‑minor‑piece ending Black’s rook already dominates the open d‑file, so giving up the extra defensive coverage costs White a noticeable amount of material advantage.
student: White’s king step to e2 is an inaccuracy that lets Black seize the initiative with …b3, a pawn break that attacks the a‑pawn and opens lines for the rook on d6. The engine shows the evaluation slipping from roughly a pawn’s advantage to only a modest edge, costing White about three‑quarters of a pawn. A more accurate try would have been Kc2, keeping the king nearer the centre and preserving the larger lead. After Ke2 Black can indeed play …b3, after which White could capture axb3, but the resulting position still leaves Black with active counterplay.

teacher: Black’s 28…Rc6 is a serious blunder; instead of the active pawn break b3, which would have struck at White’s a‑pawn, Black simply shuffled the rook to a square that already controls the open c‑file but does nothing to improve the position. By missing the …b3 idea, Black allows White to keep the initiative and the evaluation jumps from a slight edge for White to a clear advantage of more than two pawns. The engine’s line shows that after the natural reply Rh4, Black could have played b3, forcing axb3 and then Nxb3, but the rook move forfeits that counter‑play and costs Black roughly two pawn‑units.
student: By playing …Rc6 Black merely places his rook on the open c‑file without creating any concrete threats in this rook‑and‑minor‑piece ending. The engine shows that the far stronger continuation would have been the pawn break …b3, striking at White’s a‑pawn and keeping the balance. After …Rc6 White can simply play Rh4, after which Black’s best try b3 does not stop the advance and White emerges with a clear material edge – now about two pawns ahead. In short, the move costs Black roughly two pawns of evaluation and turns an already slight disadvantage into a clearly inferior one.

teacher: Black checks with Rc2+, forking White’s king on e2 and the pawn on a2 and using the open c‑file to create immediate pressure. In practice White can answer with Rd2, after which the rook on d2 is left en prise, and the engine points out that the pawn break b3 would have struck at the a‑pawn more directly. As a result the evaluation slides from a +2.28 advantage for White to about +2.6, a moderate worsening of Black’s position. The move is therefore a good try but not the optimal continuation.
student: Black’s 29…Rc2+ tries to exploit the open c‑file by forking White’s king on e2 and the pawn on a2 with a checking fork. In practice it lets White answer with 30.Rd2, after which the rook on d2 becomes en prise, allowing White to keep the initiative despite the slight worsening of Black’s evaluation – roughly a third of a pawn worse than before. The engine judged that the more accurate continuation would have been the pawn break 29…b3, directly attacking the a2 pawn and preserving Black’s chances. Consequently, while the move is still “good”, it costs Black about three‑tenths of a pawn compared with the optimal line.

teacher: White’s best move was Rd2, sliding the rook onto the open d‑file where it exerts pressure, but the rook is en prise; however, Black’s rook on c2 pins it to the white king on e2, so White cannot move the rook. The move nudges the evaluation up by roughly a tenth of a pawn. Black’s most natural continuation would be Rc6, trying to eliminate the lingering threat on the c‑file.
student: By sliding the rook back to d2 White finally seizes control of the open d‑file in this rook‑and‑minor‑piece ending, even though the rook becomes temporarily en prise because Black’s rook on c2 pins it to the white king on e2. The engine rates the move as the best, improving White’s already sizable advantage by about a tenth of a pawn while keeping the material edge intact. Black can try …Rc6, which would remove the pin but does not erase White’s pressure along the d‑file.

teacher: Black’s capture on d2, although it checks the king and even forks the a‑pawn and the king, is an inaccuracy because White can simply answer Kxd2, eliminating the fork and restoring the material balance. By forcing the exchange, Black gives up the only active idea the rook had on the open d‑file and the evaluation slips from a +2.7 to a decisive +3.3 in White’s favour – roughly a six‑tenths of a pawn worse for Black. The engine’s preferred continuation, Rc6, would have kept the rook safe and avoided the unnecessary trade. Consequently, the move costs Black the initiative without gaining any material.
student: Black’s capture on d2 looks attractive at first glance – it checks the white king while forking the a‑pawn and the king – but White simply answers Kxd2, removing the fork and restoring material equality. In this rook‑and‑minor‑piece ending the exchange does not win anything, and the engine now judges White to be about three pawns ahead, a swing of roughly two‑thirds of a pawn compared with the previous evaluation. The inaccuracy therefore costs Black a significant amount of ground despite being temporarily up four points of material. The engine’s preferred continuation was Rc6, which would have removed the immediate danger to the black rook without allowing the forced trade.

teacher: By moving the rook to a6 White immediately forks the knight on a5 and the pawn on b6, and the pawn is also pinned to the black king on e6, so it cannot legally move. This tactical shot nudges the evaluation up by roughly a fifth of a pawn, keeping White up a pawn with a decisive advantage. Black can reply Kd5, which removes the threat to the knight, but the engine notes that the more accurate continuation would have been the quiet king move Kc2, which would have preserved the advantage even more cleanly.
student: By sliding the rook to a6 White creates a fork on Black’s knight a5 and the pawn b6, while also pinning that pawn to the black king on e6 so it cannot move. The engine rates the move as a slight improvement for White – roughly two‑tenths of a pawn – but notes that the more accurate continuation would have been Kc2. Black can meet the fork with Kd5, which eliminates the immediate danger to the knight, after which White could continue with Ra7 and later bring the king back to c2. In this rook‑and‑minor‑piece ending the move solidifies White’s already decisive edge.

teacher: White’s king walk to d3 is a clear mistake, costing roughly a pawn and dragging the evaluation down from a decisive +4.24 to a still winning but much slimmer +3.21. By stepping away, White allows Black’s immediate pawn break b3, which strikes at the a‑pawn and erodes White’s material edge. The engine’s preferred continuation was Ra7, a move that would have kept the full advantage. In short, Kd3 hands Black the only realistic counter‑play and reduces White’s winning margin by about a pawn.
student: White’s king step to d3 looks natural in this rook‑and‑minor‑piece ending but it actually hands Black the initiative with the pawn break b3, which strikes at the a2 pawn. The engine shows that after Kd3 the evaluation drops by about a pawn, turning a +4.24 advantage into a +3.21 one – a clear mistake. The stronger continuation would have been Ra7, keeping the rook active and preserving the larger edge. Consequently, White’s winning chances are reduced despite still being up a pawn.

teacher: By playing 33…Nc4 Black simply shields the b6 pawn, but the move lets White widen his already decisive edge. The evaluation climbs from a +3.2‑pawn advantage for White to roughly +4.3, a swing of about a pawn in White’s favour. The engine’s preferred continuation, b3, would have broken open the queenside and struck at White’s a‑pawn, keeping the initiative alive. In this rook‑and‑minor‑piece endgame the missed pawn break costs Black roughly a pawn of material value.
student: By playing …Nc4 Black merely eliminates White’s immediate pressure on the b‑pawn, but it does nothing to challenge White’s dominant a‑pawn or to improve his own piece placement in this rook‑and‑minor‑piece ending. The engine shows that the far stronger continuation would have been the pawn break …b3, which strikes directly at White’s a‑pawn and keeps more counterplay for Black. Instead, after …Nc4 White can simply play Ra8, preserving the decisive edge – the evaluation jumps from a +3.2‑pawn advantage for White to about +4.3 pawns, roughly a pawn worse for Black. Consequently the move costs Black about a pawn of standing.

teacher: White’s 34 f4 simply creates an isolated pawn on f4 and costs a little of the winning edge, the engine’s evaluation dropping from +4.29 to +4.06. In a rook‑and‑minor‑piece ending this structural weakness is unnecessary – the engine preferred the more precise 34 Ra8, which would have preserved a larger advantage. Moreover, after the natural Black reply 34…Nd6 the pawn on b6 becomes en prise, a tactical motif that White’s pawn push does nothing to address. Consequently, while the move is still “good” in that White remains clearly ahead, it is a sub‑optimal choice that slightly worsens the position.
student: White pushes f4, creating an isolated pawn but also giving Black the tactical resource …Nd6, after which the b‑pawn becomes vulnerable. The engine rates the move as “good” yet notes that it costs about a quarter of a pawn compared with the optimal Ra8, which would have preserved a larger winning edge. In this rook‑and‑minor‑piece ending the move does not improve White’s chances significantly, though he remains clearly ahead.

teacher: By pushing …b5 Black tries to advance his queenside pawn majority, but the move creates an isolated pawn on b5 in this rook‑and‑minor‑piece ending. The engine shows the evaluation slipping from a decisive White advantage of about +4.0 pawns to roughly +4.6, a loss of half a pawn for Black. A more accurate continuation would have been 34…Nd6, which would have left the b‑pawn vulnerable, whereas after …b5 White can reply 35 Ra8, Black’s only reasonable try is the weakening …b3, and after 36 axb3 White retains the pressure. Thus the pawn push is an inaccuracy, costing Black about a pawn of material value.
student: By pushing …b5 Black tries to advance his queenside pawn majority, but the move leaves him with an isolated pawn on b5 and does nothing to improve his cramped rook‑and‑minor‑piece ending. The engine rates it as an inaccuracy, worsening Black’s standing by roughly half a pawn compared with the more accurate …Nd6, which would have kept the pawn structure intact even though it would leave the b6 pawn vulnerable. In short, the pawn push merely creates new weaknesses without gaining any compensation, allowing White’s already decisive edge to grow further.

teacher: White captures the pawn on h7, turning the h‑file into a semi‑open line for Black and solidifying the already advanced passed pawn on h6. In this rook‑and‑minor‑piece ending the capture is the correct continuation, even though it slightly worsens White’s evaluation (the engine notes a drop of about a quarter pawn). Black’s most accurate reply would be Nf5, which would leave the f7 pawn en prise and allow White to answer with Rh8 followed by the pawn push h7. The move therefore preserves White’s decisive advantage.
student: By taking on h7 White eliminates Black’s last central pawn and instantly creates a passed pawn on h6, preserving the decisive material edge in this rook‑and‑minor‑piece ending. The capture does open the h‑file for Black, but it also leaves Black’s king exposed – after …Nf5 the pawn on f7 would be hanging. Although the engine notes a slight dip of about a quarter of a pawn, White remains clearly ahead with a winning advantage.

teacher: White’s rook slides to h8, a move that keeps the winning edge in this rook‑and‑minor‑piece ending. By occupying the h‑file behind the advanced passed pawn on h6, the rook both backs the pawn’s march and limits Black’s counterplay, preserving White’s decisive material advantage. The engine rates the move as the best choice, and although the evaluation drops only a fraction of a pawn (from +5.56 to +5.29), White remains clearly winning.
student: In this rook‑and‑minor‑piece ending White’s Rh8 simply brings the rook to its most active square while preserving the powerful passed pawn on h6. The engine still judges the position as a decisive White advantage, even though the evaluation slips by about a quarter of a pawn compared with the previous score. Black’s best reply would be …Nf5, after which White can continue with Rb8 and later capture on b5, keeping the winning edge intact.

teacher: By playing 39…Nh4 Black missed the immediate checking move 39…Nd6+, which the engine flags as the far‑better alternative. The knight retreat does nothing to curb White’s advanced h‑pawn in this rook‑and‑minor‑piece ending and lets White’s winning edge swell from roughly five pawns to almost seven. In other words, the move worsened Black’s position by about 1.5 pawns and turned an already decisive advantage into an even larger one.
student: Black’s 39…Nh4 does nothing to stop White’s dangerous passed pawn on h6 in this rook‑and‑minor‑piece ending, so the evaluation slides from a +5.31 to about +6.9 – roughly a two‑pawn swing against Black. The engine shows that the far stronger try was 39…Nd6+, which would have delivered a checking blow. By opting for Nh4 instead, Black allows White to continue with Rb8, after which Black can play …g5 and then …Rb6+ followed by Ke7, leaving White clearly ahead. In short, the move costs Black about one and a half pawns of standing.

teacher: White captures the pawn on d5, initiating an exchange that Black will most likely answer with …Qxd5. After the expected queen recapture the d‑file becomes semi‑open for Black while the e‑file is now semi‑open for White, giving White a modest but tangible activity edge. The engine rates the move as excellent, and the evaluation remains a slight White advantage (about three‑hundredths of a pawn).
student: By playing exd5 White eliminates Black’s central pawn and forces an immediate queen trade. After the inevitable …Qxd5 the d‑file becomes semi‑open for Black while the e‑file opens for White, but the capture simply restores material equality – the engine still rates the position as a slight White edge, with the evaluation changing by only about three hundredths of a pawn. This precise exchange therefore preserves White’s modest advantage without creating any new weaknesses.

teacher: Black develops the king‑side knight to f6, a natural square that finishes development and keeps material equal. The engine rates the move as good and the best choice, although the evaluation nudges a little more in White’s favour (from roughly equal to White being about a third of a pawn ahead). In the principal variation White would continue with Nf3, after which Black can meet it with …Nc6 and later …e6, preserving a balanced opening.
student: Black develops the knight to its natural square f6, completing his development and keeping material balanced. The engine rates it as the best continuation, but White now enjoys a small edge – about three‑tenths of a pawn – because the evaluation shifts from +0.20 for Black to +0.32 in White’s favour. In the principal variation White would continue with Nf3, after which Black can develop further with …Nc6 and later play …e6. Overall the move is solid and follows standard opening principles.

teacher: Black’s 5…e6 pushes the e‑pawn forward, advancing his kingside pawn majority of four pawns against White’s three. Material is still equal and the engine now rates White only a little better (+0.36), meaning the move changed the balance by roughly a tenth of a pawn. Although the engine preferred 5…Nc6, the pawn advance is an excellent continuation in the opening, keeping the position solid and balanced.
student: By playing …e6 Black simply pushes the last pawn of his kingside majority forward, reinforcing the four‑pawn chain against White’s three and keeping material perfectly balanced. The engine rates the move as excellent – it leaves the evaluation virtually unchanged, with White still holding a modest edge of about a third of a pawn. Although the engine preferred 5…Nc6, which would have developed a piece more actively, …e6 does not worsen Black’s position and therefore preserves equality.

teacher: White pushes a3, simply advancing the queenside pawn majority (four pawns against Black’s three).  The move is solid enough to be called good, but it surrenders a little tempo compared with the engine‑preferred Na3, and the evaluation drops from a small plus to a roughly equal position.  After a3 the engine expects Black to develop with Be7, after which White could continue with Be3, followed by …b6 and a checking Bb5+.
student: White pushes a3 to advance his queenside pawn majority, gaining space and giving the four‑pawn chain a little more activity. The engine rates it as a good move but notes that it costs about a third of a pawn compared with the optimal Na3, which would have kept the modest edge. After a3 Black can reply …Be7, after which White could continue with Be3, keeping the balance. In short, the move is solid and keeps material even, yet it relinquishes a small advantage.

teacher: By playing …cxd4 Black captures the pawn on d4, opening the c‑file and leaving White with an isolated queen’s pawn on d4. Although the exchange restores material balance (so after White’s recapture the material is equal), Black is temporarily a pawn up after the capture, and the engine now evaluates White as slightly better (+0.25) and notes that the move cost Black about a tenth of a pawn. The engine considered 7…Ng4 the superior alternative, which would have avoided this small deterioration.
student: By playing …cxd4 Black eliminates White’s pawn on d4 and opens the c‑file, but the capture merely initiates an exchange that will be restored after White’s natural recapture. In doing so White is left with an isolated queen’s pawn on d4, yet the engine still judges the position as slightly better for White – about a quarter of a pawn – because Black has given up the small edge it held before the trade. The engine preferred 7…Ng4, which would have kept the tension without conceding the extra pawn. Consequently, while the move is “good” in that it wins a pawn, it costs Black roughly a tenth of a pawn compared with the optimal continuation.
violations: claims material is won, but the capture is an exchange

teacher: By capturing on d4 White not only eliminates the immediate threat to the bishop on e3 but also opens the c‑file for future play, giving the rooks a potential avenue of activity. The exchange leaves Black with a semi‑open d‑file, while White gains a modest queenside pawn majority (three pawns against Black’s two), even though the resulting pawn on d4 is isolated. The engine rates the move as the best choice, and the evaluation shifts only marginally, keeping White’s slight edge of about a third of a pawn.
student: By playing cxd4 White eliminates Black’s immediate pressure on the e‑file and opens the c‑file while also removing the threat to the bishop on e3. The capture does leave White with an isolated queen’s pawn on d4, but it preserves material equality and nudges the evaluation from a slight edge to about a third of a pawn in White’s favour. With the c‑file now clear, White can continue development such as Nc3 and keep the modest advantage intact.

teacher: White’s knight jumps to c3, the most natural square for the queen’s knight, and the move simply preserves the modest edge White already enjoyed. The engine’s principal variation shows Black replying …Bd6, White meeting it with Bd3, and then both sides comfortably completing development by castling. In short, the move keeps the position balanced while finishing White’s opening setup.
student: White’s knight hops to c3, keeping the modest edge that existed after Black’s …Qd8 and preserving the slight advantage (+0.36 ≈ a third of a pawn). The engine rates it as the best continuation, with the evaluation virtually unchanged. In the principal variation Black would develop with …Bd6, after which White can meet it with Bd3 and both sides castle safely.

teacher: Black’s …h6 simply pushes the kingside pawn majority forward, a quiet but purposeful way to increase space on the side where he already has four pawns against White’s three. With White’s king still stuck in the centre and Black already safely castled, the move does not alter the balance – the engine still rates the position as roughly equal, only a hair better for Black. Moreover, by advancing the h‑pawn Black also gives his bishop on c8 its only safe retreat square, reinforcing the modest but sound setup.
student: By playing …h6 Black expands his four‑pawn majority on the kingside, giving him active space despite White’s king still being in the centre and the bishop on c8 confined to its single safe square. The advance also leaves the position balanced – the engine’s evaluation stays at roughly equal, confirming that Black has not worsened his standing. In the principal variation White would continue with Rg1, after which Black can meet it with Ne7 and keep the pressure. This precise pawn push therefore earns an “excellent” label as the best continuation.

teacher: White’s Ne5 is an excellent maneuver that deprives Black’s bishop on d6 of the key squares f4 and h2, thereby giving the bishop on e3 a safe retreat and curbing the opponent’s piece activity. The engine shows the evaluation slipping only marginally (from –0.35 to –0.41 pawns), so White solves a concrete positional problem without materially worsening the position. The engine’s top choice, Bxf5, would have captured the knight on f5 and likely given White a clearer edge. As it stands, Black remains slightly better, but the move leaves the balance essentially unchanged.
student: By playing Ne5 White removes the f4‑h2 diagonal that Black’s bishop on d6 could otherwise use, thereby limiting its scope while keeping material equal. The engine still judges the position as slightly better for Black – about four‑tenths of a pawn worse for White – but the move leaves the balance essentially unchanged, which is why it is rated “excellent”. Although the engine preferred Bxf5 to capture the active knight on f5, Ne5 does not worsen White’s standing and therefore preserves the modest edge.

teacher: Black’s 16…Rc8 puts the rook on the open c‑file, directly controlling that line while White’s bishop on e3 is confined to its only safe square. The engine’s evaluation remains at about a pawn in Black’s favour, confirming that the move simply preserves the existing advantage. White’s most logical try would be 17.f3, removing the threat to the pawn on g2, after which Black can continue with …Nh5, keeping the pressure.
student: By playing …Rc8 Black puts the rook on the open c‑file, where it dominates that line and leaves White’s bishop on e3 with only one safe retreat while also curbing its activity. The engine rates the move as the best continuation, keeping Black’s clear advantage at roughly a pawn’s worth. White could try f3, which would remove the immediate pressure on the g2 pawn, but even after that Black remains comfortably ahead.

teacher: White’s queen captures the pawn on f5, netting a pawn and giving White a one‑pawn material edge. The engine’s evaluation changes only marginally – Black is still clearly better by about a pawn, but White now enjoys a one‑pawn material edge. Even with Black’s bishop pair, the cramped bishop on b8 and the rook on the open c‑file, the continuation Ba6 … is the line the engine suggests, confirming that Qxf5 is the best move in the position.
student: By taking on f5 White wins a pawn and emerges a pawn ahead, but the engine’s assessment stays roughly the same – Black remains about a pawn better. The capture also leaves Black’s bishop on b8 with only two safe squares while Black still enjoys the bishop pair and an active rook on the open c‑file. Consequently the move is judged excellent because it secures material without worsening White’s position.

teacher: Black meets White’s immediate danger to the e‑7 knight by pulling it back to e7, thereby removing the threat. The retreat also leaves Black’s bishop pair and the rook on c8 fully active on the open c‑file, so the position stays comfortably in Black’s favour. The engine still judges Black to be winning, though the move costs roughly a third of a pawn compared with the previous evaluation. White’s most forcing try would be Nf6+ check, but after Nf6+ the knight is left en prise, so Black remains much better.
student: By retreating the knight to e7 Black eliminates the immediate danger that White’s knight on e2 posed to it, thereby preserving the powerful bishop‑pair and the active rook on c8 while keeping the bishop on a6 pinning White’s other knight to the rook on f1. The engine still judges the position as “much better” for Black – roughly two‑and‑three‑quarters of a pawn ahead – even though White remains a pawn up. If White tries the natural checking idea Nf6+, the knight would be left en prise, allowing Black to capture with gxf6 and continue with …Qd5, maintaining the initiative.

teacher: White’s queen sortie to g4, while attacking the h6 pawn, ignores the far more forcing check Nf6+. By playing Qg4 White attacks the h6 pawn and the position already features the pin of the e‑2 knight by the a6 bishop, which pushes the evaluation from a clear Black edge to a decisive advantage. The engine therefore marks the move a mistake, costing roughly one and a half pawns of value and turning an already inferior position into a winning one for Black. The alternative Nf6+ would have at least forced a reply, even though the checking knight would be left en prise.
student: White’s 22.Qg4 was meant to attack the poorly defended h‑pawn and to get rid of the immediate danger to the queen, but it walks into Black’s tactical shot …f5, which attacks the knight on d7 and leaves that piece vulnerable. The engine shows this costs roughly one and a half pawns, turning an already inferior position into a clearly losing one for White despite being up a pawn in material. A far stronger try would have been 22.Nf6+, delivering check while keeping the knight safe – after the natural reply …f5 the continuation Qf3 – Qxd7 – Bxh6 would have kept more chances. Consequently the move is rightly marked as a mistake.

teacher: By playing …fxg4 Black captures White’s queen, turning the material lead into a decisive advantage. The pawn capture also opens the f‑file for the rook on f8 and eliminates the immediate threats to the g7‑ and h6‑pawns, though it leaves Black with doubled pawns on the g‑file, which explains the slight –0.11‑pawn dip in the evaluation. With opposite‑colour bishops and the bishop on a6 pinning the e2‑knight to the rook on f1, Black’s pieces are well‑coordinated, yet White can try Nxa6 to remove the pin and win the bishop on a6.
student: By playing …fxg4 Black eliminates White’s queen with the pawn, turning the f‑file into a semi‑open line that his rook already exploits while also removing the immediate threats to the g7‑pawn and the h6‑pawn. The capture does leave Black with doubled pawns on the g‑file, but in an opposite‑colour‑bishop ending this structural drawback is outweighed by the active rook and the pin of the e2‑knight by the bishop on a6 against the white rook on f1. The engine rates the move as good and the best continuation, even though it costs Black about a tenth of a pawn compared with the previous evaluation. White could try Nxa6, capturing the bishop on a6, yet Black remains clearly ahead.

teacher: By taking on h3 Black eliminates White’s last pawn on that wing, creating a three‑pawn majority against White’s one and leaving the pawn shield in front of White’s king noticeably weakened. The capture also doubles Black’s own h‑pawns, but Black’s rooks already enjoy strong lines – the f‑rook on the semi‑open f‑file and the c‑rook on the open c‑file – so the structural change does not impair Black’s activity. Although the move costs Black a modest 0.38 pawn of evaluation, the engine still judges the position a decisive Black advantage (about a four‑pawn lead) and rates the move as the correct, good choice.
student: By playing gxh3 Black eliminates White’s last h‑pawn and opens the h‑file, giving the rook on c8 a clearer line while also advancing his three‑pawn majority on that wing. The capture does leave Black with doubled pawns on the h‑file, but the resulting weakness in front of White’s king outweighs this drawback, keeping Black’s decisive material edge intact. The engine rates the move as good and even notes it as the best continuation, though the evaluation slips slightly to about –4.8 pawns because the h‑file becomes semi‑open for White.

teacher: White’s capture on h3 does open the g‑file for him and eliminates the immediate threat to the pawn that had just moved there, but it also leaves White with isolated pawns on f2 and h3 and relinquishes the semi‑open h‑file that could have been useful.  The move therefore deepens Black’s already decisive edge, pushing the evaluation from a Black advantage of about four pawns to roughly five and a half pawns (a loss of about three‑quarters of a pawn for White).  The engine’s preferred continuation, Rc1, would have kept more tension on the position and avoided the further weakening of White’s pawn structure.
student: By playing gxh3 White eliminates the immediate danger to the pawn on h3 but at the cost of creating an isolated pawn on h3 and leaving the h‑file closed, while the g‑file becomes semi‑open for White. The capture also does nothing to stop Black’s active rooks—both the f‑rook and the c‑rook already dominate their respective files—and therefore deepens Black’s decisive edge, worsening White’s evaluation by roughly three‑quarters of a pawn. The engine judged Rc1 to be the superior continuation, keeping more pressure on Black’s pieces without conceding the extra two‑pawn lead that Black already enjoys. Consequently, the move is marked as an inaccuracy.

teacher: White’s 27 Re2 puts a rook on the open e‑file, but it immediately hangs that rook to Black’s rook on f8. Black can simply reply Rxe2, capturing the rook and increasing the already decisive Black advantage by roughly another pawn. The engine’s top choice, Bxh6, would have at least taken a pawn (though the bishop would become en prise) and avoided the loss of the rook. Consequently, Re2 is a clear mistake that deepens White’s material deficit to two points.
student: By playing Re2 White simply places his rook on the open e‑file without any compensation, allowing Black’s rook on c2 to seize the initiative and win the rook outright. The engine shows that this costs roughly a pawn in evaluation, turning an already losing position into one where Black is decisively ahead. A far stronger try would have been Bxh6, even though the bishop would be left en prise, because it at least creates counterplay against Black’s active pieces. After Re2 Black can reply Rxe2, after which White must recapture with the knight, leaving Black with a clear material edge.

teacher: Black tries to create immediate pressure with 28…Qc8, forking White’s pawn on h3 and the knight on a6. In reality the move is an inaccuracy: it worsens Black’s evaluation by almost a pawn because the engine’s top choice, 28…Nxe3, would capture the bishop on e3 and preserve the winning edge. White can answer the fork by 29.Nb4, after which Black could continue …Nxb4 30.axb4 and still threaten Qxh3, but the missed bishop capture costs Black dearly. Even after the slip Black remains winning by roughly five pawns, helped by the semi‑open f‑file that the rook on f8 controls.
student: By playing …Qc8 Black creates a fork on the h‑pawn and the a6‑knight, but the engine shows that this inaccuracy costs roughly a pawn compared with the winning continuation. The stronger try would have been …Nxe3, which simply wins the white bishop on e3 and preserves the larger advantage. After …Qc8 White can reply Nb4, removing the pressure on the knight on b4 and keeping the initiative alive. Although Black remains clearly ahead – up two pawns and still winning by about six pawns – the missed capture leaves the evaluation slipping from a decisive edge to a smaller one.

teacher: Black’s capture on e3 wins a bishop but, as the engine notes, it is an inaccuracy because White can answer fxe3, opening the f‑file and giving White a passed pawn on e3. After that recapture the f‑file becomes fully open, allowing both sides’ heavy pieces to bear down the file toward the opponent’s king and reducing Black’s advantage by roughly three‑quarters of a pawn. The engine’s preferred continuation, Nxb4, would have simply taken the knight on b4 and kept the decisive edge.
student: By playing …Nxe3 Black wins a bishop but immediately hands White the chance to capture with fxe3, opening the f‑file and giving White a passed pawn on e3 while also leaving Black’s own heavy pieces bearing down that same file. The engine rates this as an inaccuracy because it costs roughly three‑quarters of a pawn compared with the superior continuation Nxb4, which would have taken the white knight on b4 and preserved a larger winning edge. After fxe3 Black still enjoys a decisive material lead, yet the newly opened f‑file gives White active counterplay without improving his own position.

teacher: White finally eliminates the invading knight with fxe3, which is the only move that prevents an immediate material loss. By doing so the e‑file becomes semi‑open for Black and the f‑file opens completely, giving Black’s rook on f8 a direct line toward White’s king while White’s own rook on f1 now shares that file. The capture also creates a passed pawn on e3, but the resulting open f‑file allows Black to continue with the forcing continuation Rxf1+ followed by Kxf1, after which Black’s pieces race forward with …a5 and …Nd3, preserving a decisive material edge. Even though it is the best available move, the engine notes that it still worsens White’s position by roughly a fifth of a pawn in an already lost game.
student: By playing fxe3 White eliminates Black’s knight and creates a passed pawn on e3, opening both the f‑file and giving Black a semi‑open file that his rook already dominates. The capture also leaves Black’s rook on f8 bearing down the same line as White’s rook on f1, so the balance of pressure remains roughly equal. Although it is the best continuation available, the engine still judges the position a decisive Black advantage – about four‑and‑three‑quarters of a pawn worse for White than before. Black can reply with Rxf1+, checking the white king and capturing the rook on f1.
violations: calls the position equal at -4.75

teacher: Black finishes the combination with Rxf1+, a checking capture that forces White to recapture with Kxf1. After the forced recapture, the rooks are exchanged and the position becomes an endgame, preserving Black’s decisive material edge. The rook on f1 also seizes control of the open f‑file, and the engine rates the move as the best, leaving the evaluation essentially unchanged at a winning advantage for Black.
student: By playing Rxf1+ Black forces White’s king to capture and immediately trades the rooks, turning the game into an end‑game where Black remains up seven points of material. The capture also leaves Black’s rook dominating the open f‑file, while the engine still evaluates the position as a decisive Black advantage – roughly four‑and‑three‑quarters pawns ahead. After the forced Kxf1 the continuation a5 – Nd5 – Qxh3+ shows how Black can continue to increase pressure without losing the material edge. This precise exchange therefore preserves Black’s winning chances despite the slight swing in the evaluation.

teacher: White calmly captures the rook on f1, removing the immediate danger and steering the game into a pure endgame. The exchange does not alter the balance – the engine still judges Black to have a decisive advantage, the evaluation shifting only by a few hundredths of a pawn. With Black now up two pawns, White’s best‑possible chance is simply to play on in the resulting endgame.
student: By taking the rook on f1 White eliminates Black’s last heavy piece and forces the game into an end‑game where the balance of material is irrelevant. The capture leaves the engine’s assessment virtually unchanged – Black still enjoys a decisive edge of about five pawns – but it is the most accurate continuation available. In the ensuing line Black can try …a5, after which White would continue with Nd5, followed by Qxh3+ and Kg1, yet the overall picture remains clearly unfavorable for White.

teacher: White’s king steps to f2 to meet the queen check, a safe but slightly passive choice. By opting for Kf2 instead of the engine‑recommended Ke1, White lets Black’s winning edge deepen by about a sixth of a pawn, moving the evaluation from roughly a five‑pawn disadvantage to an even larger one. Black can now continue with …a5, after which White’s best reply would be Nd3 and Black can answer with …Qf5+, keeping the pressure. The move is still judged “good” in this middlegame, though it is not the most accurate.
student: White’s king step to f2 does little in this endgame and actually nudges the evaluation a touch deeper into Black’s favour – roughly a sixth of a pawn worse for White than before. The engine judged Ke1 to be the superior try, keeping the king nearer the centre and preserving more pressure. After 32.Kf2 Black can continue with …a5, after which White would have to meet it with Nd3, followed by …Qf5+ and Ndf4, leaving Black clearly ahead. Thus the move is only “good” but not optimal, worsening White’s already losing chances.

teacher: Black’s queen check on f5 keeps the pressure on White’s king by exploiting the open f‑file, but it does so at the price of a modest loss of material value—about half a pawn—from an already decisive advantage. The move obliges White to answer the check, and briefly intensifies the attack, yet the engine judges that the quieter pawn thrust a5 would have retained a larger winning margin. Consequently, while Black remains clearly ahead, Qf5+ is a good move that is nevertheless inferior to the optimal continuation.
student: Black’s queen checks with Qf5+, driving the white king onto f2 and keeping the heavy pieces bearing down the open f‑file in this endgame. The engine still judges the position a decisive Black win, but the evaluation slips by about half a pawn compared with the optimal continuation. A more accurate try would have been a5, which keeps the pressure without conceding the slight loss of ground that follows the check.

teacher: White’s king walk to g3 deepened an already decisive Black advantage, pushing the evaluation from roughly a 4½‑pawn loss to more than a 6‑pawn loss – a swing of about one and a half pawns. The engine had a much safer alternative in Ke1, which would have kept the evaluation at the previous level. After Kg3, Black can continue with a5, and when White replies Nc3 the ensuing exchange axb4 axb4 leaves Black’s material edge even larger. In short, the move unnecessarily worsened White’s position in this endgame.
student: White’s king step to g3 does nothing to improve his already losing stance in this endgame and actually deepens Black’s lead by roughly one and a half pawns. The engine shows that the simple retreat Ke1 would have kept the evaluation around –4½, whereas Kg3 pushes the score down to about –6½. In short, the move costs White a clear edge and leaves him with no realistic chances.

teacher: In this endgame Black simply pushes the a‑pawn to a5, a quiet but precise move that preserves the already decisive material edge. The engine rates it as the best continuation, with the evaluation essentially unchanged (still about six pawns in Black’s favour). White’s most resilient reply would be Na2, removing the threat to the knight on b4, after which Black can continue with Qg6+ and Qd6+, keeping the attack alive and the winning advantage intact.
student: By pushing …a5 Black immediately attacks White’s king, forcing it to retreat with Na2 and allowing Black to continue the attack with checks such as Qg6+. The engine rates this as the best continuation, keeping the decisive –6‑pawn edge virtually intact. After White’s natural reply Na2, Black can keep the pressure with Qg6+, followed by Qd6+ in the principal variation, preserving the winning advantage.

teacher: Black strikes at White’s queenside space with the thematic …d5, a pawn break that attacks the c4 pawn. White can answer calmly with e3, which removes the threat to c4 and keeps the modest edge White already held. The engine rates …d5 as the best move, and the evaluation changes only by a tenth of a pawn, leaving White still slightly better. In the main line White would continue e3, Black …g6, White d4 and Black …Bg7.
student: Black answers with the thematic …d5, a pawn break that strikes directly at White’s pawn on c4 and tries to open lines for his pieces. The engine rates it as the best continuation, keeping the evaluation virtually unchanged – White remains only a fraction of a pawn ahead. White can meet the thrust with e3, which would remove the immediate pressure on the c‑pawn, after which Black could continue with …g6 and later develop the bishop to g7. This precise central break therefore secures material equality while preserving Black’s chances.

teacher: White’s 7.Bc4 is a natural developing move, placing the bishop on an active diagonal, but it is judged slightly inferior to the immediate pawn break 7.d4. The engine notes that 7.d4 would strike at Black’s e5 pawn, whereas after 7…N7b6 the e5 pawn becomes en prise, giving Black an easy way to relieve the pressure. Consequently the move costs White roughly a quarter‑pawn in the evaluation.
student: White’s bishop retreat to c4 does little more than preserve the status quo – it leaves Black’s central pawn untouched and allows Black to continue with …N7b6, after which the e‑pawn becomes vulnerable. The engine rates the move as “good” but notes that it costs White about a quarter of a pawn compared with the optimal continuation d4, which would have struck directly at Black’s e5 pawn. In short, Bc4 keeps material even while giving Black a small edge in the centre.

teacher: Black’s retreat of the b‑knight to b6 is the most sensible continuation, yet it does leave the pawn on e5 hanging. White can answer with Be2, which develops the bishop to e2 and keeps the pressure on the now‑en‑prise pawn. The engine still rates N7b6 as the best move, although the evaluation slips by roughly a tenth of a pawn against Black; the principal line would continue Be2 Bd6 a3 O‑O.
student: Black’s …N7b6 brings a knight into the centre and immediately attacks White’s bishop on c4, forcing it to retreat with Be2. The engine still rates the position as roughly equal, but the move costs Black about a tenth of a pawn because the pawn on e5 becomes en prise. After White’s best reply Be2, Black can continue with …Bd6, keeping the balance despite the temporary weakness.

teacher: White castles, bringing the king to safety and connecting the rooks while Black’s king is still stuck in the centre. The move also leaves the pawn on h7 exposed, giving White a small target to press. Although the engine’s top choice would have been 9.d3, O‑O only nudges the evaluation from +0.16 to +0.23, essentially preserving White’s slight edge. It is therefore a sound, best‑in‑spirit move that keeps the pressure on Black’s uncastled king.
student: By castling, White tucks the king safely away and brings the rook to f1, preserving material equality while Black’s king remains stuck in the centre. The engine notes that this leaves the h‑pawn vulnerable – it can be taken after castling – but the resulting safety more than compensates for any immediate tactical liability. Although the engine preferred the quieter d3, which would have kept the slight edge without exposing the h‑pawn, O‑O still improves White’s standing by about a seventh of a pawn.

teacher: Black’s castling is the natural way to finish development, linking the rooks and putting the king safely on g8, even though it does leave the h‑pawn hanging to White’s queen on c2. The engine rates it as the best move, noting that the evaluation barely shifts – White remains only a fraction of a pawn ahead. In the main line White would likely continue with 10.d3, after which Black can answer 10…Nb4 and keep the balance.
student: By castling, Black tucks the king safely behind the pawn shield and connects the rooks, which is why the engine rates O‑O as the best continuation even though it leaves the h7 pawn temporarily en prise. The evaluation stays virtually unchanged – White remains only a fraction of a pawn ahead – showing that the safety gain more than compensates for the slight exposure to the pawn. In the principal variation White would continue with d3, after which Black can develop the knight to b4 and later push …c5, keeping the balance intact.

teacher: Black develops the dark‑squared bishop to g4, a useful developing move that leaves White’s bishops on e2 and c1 with only one safe square each. The engine’s assessment barely changes, with White’s slight edge slipping from about a quarter pawn to just a fifth of a pawn. Although the engine would have preferred 11…Nd7, which also keeps the evaluation around the same level, …Bg4 is a sound continuation that leaves the balance essentially unchanged.
student: By developing the dark‑squared bishop to g4 Black immediately attacks White’s cramped bishops – the bishop on e2 and the bishop on c1 each have only one safe retreat square. The move leaves material equal and the engine still judges White to be only a fraction of a pawn ahead, so it keeps the balance essentially unchanged. Although the engine preferred Nd7 as the optimal continuation, Bg4 is nevertheless a strong choice that preserves Black’s chances without worsening the position.
