teacher: White’s knight hops to g3, but the move does nothing to ease the cramped situation of the bishops, each of which now has only one safe square. As a result the engine’s assessment slips from a modest +0.21 to roughly +0.05, a loss of about a sixth of a pawn. The engine’s top choice was Rd1, which would have preserved White’s slight edge. Thus Ng3 is a good move, yet it is not the most accurate continuation.
student: White’s knight hops to g3, but it does nothing to relieve the cramped situation of both bishops – each now has only one safe retreat square. By forgoing the more active Rd1, White allows Black to consolidate and erase any edge, which is why the evaluation slides from a slight +0.21 advantage to an almost equal balance. The engine rates Ng3 as a good move, yet it costs about a sixth of a pawn compared with the optimal continuation.

teacher: Black’s 13…Rc8 is a solid, developing move that simply brings the rook to the c‑file, but it does not address the more pressing central tension. The engine rates it as a “good” move yet slightly inferior, costing Black roughly a tenth of a pawn compared with the optimal pawn break 13…c5. In the ensuing line the engine predicts White can continue with h3, Black will answer Bd7, White Bd2 and only then Black finally achieves the desired …c5, indicating that the rook move missed the immediate opportunity to challenge White’s centre.
student: By playing …Rc8 Black simply shuffles a rook to the c‑file without creating any new threats or improving his piece placement. The engine still rates the position as roughly equal, but it notes that the move costs Black about a tenth of a pawn compared with the optimal continuation. A more ambitious try such as …c5 would have challenged White’s cramped bishops – the bishop on e2 already has only one safe square and the bishop on c1 likewise – and could have kept the balance tighter. Consequently, while the move is “good”, it is not the most accurate choice in this middlegame.

teacher: Black retreats the bishop from f8 to e6, putting it on one of the only safe squares available to that piece. The move leaves material level and the evaluation essentially unchanged, so it is judged excellent even though a5 would have nudged the balance a shade in Black’s favour. White can continue with Qb1, after which Black may develop with Nd7, keeping the position roughly equal.
student: By retreating the bishop to e6 Black places it on one of its only two safe squares while White’s bishops remain cramped – each now has just one or two safe retreats. The engine still rates the position as roughly equal, with the evaluation shifting by only about two‑hundredths of a pawn in Black’s favour. Although the move is judged excellent, the engine preferred the more active …a5, which would have increased Black’s chances slightly. In practice, however, Be6 keeps material balanced and leaves the balance essentially unchanged.

teacher: Black’s 19…Qd7 is judged the best continuation, keeping the position essentially equal – the evaluation shifts only a hair in Black’s favour, from +0.15 to +0.14. With Black’s bishop on f8 limited to just two safe squares and the knight on b6 having only one safe square (and White’s bishop on e2 similarly cramped), the queen’s move simply re‑positions without worsening the balance. The engine’s line suggests that after 20 a4 Black can answer 20…Qd8, after which the play remains evenly poised. In short, the move respects the cramped piece placement on both sides and preserves the equality of the middlegame.
student: By retreating the queen to d7 Black preserves the delicate balance of the position – the engine’s evaluation stays at roughly +0.14 for White and remains essentially unchanged. The retreat also leaves the cramped pieces untouched: Black’s bishop on f8 still has only two safe squares while the knight on b6 retains its single safe haven. In the principal variation White can try a4, after which Black would answer with …Qd8, keeping the queens on their respective safe squares and maintaining equality. This quiet, prophylactic move therefore earns the “best” label.

teacher: White’s 22.Rcd1 is a clear mistake, abandoning the only realistic way to equalize. Instead of the pawn break 22.d4, which would have struck at Black’s c5 and e5 pawns, White simply shuffled a rook while Black’s bishops and the b6‑knight already have very few safe squares. Black can now reply with the pawn thrust 22…a4, targeting White’s b3 pawn, and after 23.d4 exd4 24.Bf5 Black gains a clear edge; the evaluation swings from a slight White plus to almost a pawn down. In short, the move costs White about a pawn in evaluation terms.
student: White’s 22.Rcd1 is a clear mistake because it does nothing to challenge Black’s central tension – the engine shows that after the rook shift Black can answer with …a4, striking at White’s b‑pawn and gaining space. The evaluation swings from a slight White edge to a clear Black advantage of roughly a pawn, costing White about a pawn’s worth of standing. The engine’s preferred continuation was the pawn break d4, which would have hit both c5 and e5 while keeping the balance. By playing Rcd1 instead, White missed this dynamic chance and handed Black the initiative.

teacher: Black finally breaks with …a4, a pawn thrust that strikes at White’s b3 pawn and leaves the a3 pawn permanently fixed on a dark square. With both bishops limited to only two safe squares and the knight on b6 confined to a single retreat, opening the a‑file is the most effective way to activate Black’s pieces. The engine rates the move as good; although the evaluation slips slightly from about a pawn to two‑thirds of a pawn, the continuation …axb3 (followed by …Na4) promises to further undermine White’s queenside structure. Overall, …a4 fulfills the only realistic plan for Black in a cramped position.
student: By playing …a4 Black finally opens the centre with a pawn break against White’s b‑pawn, fixing that pawn on a dark square and giving Black active play in an otherwise cramped position where both bishops have very few safe squares. The engine rates it as the best continuation, though the evaluation slips by roughly a third of a pawn because Black’s pieces remain limited. In the principal line White would try Rc1, after which Black can capture on b3, then recapture with Bxb3 and continue with Na4, keeping the initiative alive.

teacher: Black’s 24…Na4 is the engine‑recommended continuation, preserving the roughly pawn‑sized edge that Black already enjoyed. With both of Black’s bishops confined to only two safe squares each, the knight’s redeployment to a4 improves piece coordination without altering the material balance. The move leaves the position essentially unchanged (the evaluation shifts by only a few hundredths of a pawn), and the principal variation shows White’s most natural reply as 25 Rc1, after which Black can continue with …b5 and keep the pressure.
student: By retreating the knight to a4 Black preserves the modest edge that existed before the move – the engine’s evaluation stays at roughly a pawn in Black’s favour. The retreat leaves both of Black’s remaining bishops with only two safe squares each, so White cannot generate any immediate threats. In the principal variation White would continue with Rc1, after which Black can push …b5 and later bring the other knight to b6, keeping the pressure alive. This precise redeployment therefore earns the “best” label.

teacher: By pushing the b‑pawn to b5 Black immediately snatches the a4‑c4 diagonal from White’s bishop on b3, curbing its activity on the queenside. The advance does leave the b5 and c5 pawns technically hanging, yet the resulting pawn structure does not change the balance; Black’s evaluation remains at roughly a pawn’s worth of advantage. The move also brings out the fact that both Black bishops on f8 and g8 have only two safe squares each, underscoring the limited mobility of the minor pieces. Hence 25…b5 is rightly celebrated as an excellent continuation.
student: By pushing …b5 Black not only creates a new target for White’s bishop on b3 but also deprives that bishop of the a4‑c4 diagonal, curbing its activity while leaving both sides with their limited bishops on f8 and g8. The pawn thrust therefore preserves Black’s clear advantage – the engine still evaluates the position at roughly a pawn in Black’s favour – even though it does leave the b5 and c5 pawns temporarily vulnerable. In the principal line White would try to activate his pieces with h4, after which Black can continue with Nab6 and later strike in the centre with c4, keeping the pressure intact.

teacher: Black’s 27…c4 is a precise pawn break that strikes at White’s d‑pawn while simultaneously uncovering the bishop on f8’s line to the a3 pawn. After the forced 28.dxc4, White not only loses the pawn on c4 but is left with an isolated pawn on that square, and Black gains a semi‑open c‑file and an open d‑file for his rooks. The capture also removes the immediate threat to Black’s bishop on b3, allowing the bishop on f8 to become active. The move keeps the evaluation essentially unchanged, but it improves Black’s piece activity and creates long‑term structural advantages.
student: By playing …c4 Black launches a pawn break that attacks White’s d‑pawn and simultaneously uncovers the bishop on f8’s line against the a3 pawn, creating immediate pressure while opening lines for his pieces. If White answers with the natural 28.dxc4, the capture both eliminates the threat to the bishop on b3 and leaves White with an isolated pawn on c4, giving Black a clear target on the queenside. The engine rates the move as excellent and the evaluation stays around –1.15, confirming that Black remains clearly better despite material being equal.

teacher: White’s capture on c4 trades the pawn and restores the material balance, leaving White a pawn ahead. After the expected …bxc4 the b‑ and d‑files open, each side gaining a passed pawn (White on a3, Black on c4), and the exchange also removes the immediate threat to Black’s knight on d5. The move respects the cramped situation of both bishops, each of which has only two safe squares, while Black’s rook on c8 now sits on a semi‑open file. The engine’s principal line …bxc4 2.Bc2 2…Bxa3 3.e4 shows that this capture was indeed the most accurate continuation.
student: By playing dxc4 White opens both the d‑ and b‑files while creating a passed pawn on a3, giving White active play despite the cramped position of his own pieces – each bishop has only two safe squares and Black’s rook already enjoys the semi‑open c‑file. After the forced …bxc4 the material balance is restored, but the resulting structure leaves Black with a passed pawn on c4 and White with a passed pawn on a3, preserving the roughly equal standing that the engine still rates as about a pawn in Black’s favour. The capture therefore neutralises Black’s immediate threats without worsening White’s overall standing, justifying its “best” label.
violations: calls the position equal at -1.14

teacher: By capturing on c4 Black not only removes White’s pawn but also creates an advanced passed pawn on c4 and opens the b‑file for his rooks. The exchange also eliminates the immediate threat to the knight on d5, which accounts for the modest improvement in the engine’s evaluation. White’s most logical continuation would be Bc2, removing the threat to the bishop on c2, after which Black can continue with …Rc6.
student: By playing …bxc4 Black eliminates White’s immediate pressure on the d5‑knight and instantly creates a passed pawn on c4, while also opening the b‑file for his own pieces. The capture leaves material equal but nudges the evaluation in Black’s favour by roughly a tenth of a pawn, confirming it as the best continuation. White can try Bc2 to relieve the tension on the c2‑bishop, yet Black remains comfortably ahead with both sides’ bishops confined to just two safe squares each.

teacher: White’s 29 Bc2 simply eliminates the immediate danger to the bishop on c2, allowing the piece to stay on the board without conceding material. By doing so White preserves the balance of forces and the engine’s evaluation barely improves (about a tenth of a pawn), keeping the position essentially as it was. The move is especially important given Black’s advanced passed pawn on c4 and the fact that both Black’s bishop on g8 and White’s bishop on a1 each have only two safe squares, so any unnecessary loss would be costly. The continuation suggested by the engine (…Qc7 followed by Bf5, Ra8, Red1) shows that Black can keep up pressure, but White’s defensive Bc2 is the most accurate reply.
student: By retreating the bishop to c2 White eliminates the immediate danger that Black’s passed pawn on c4 posed to it, thereby preserving material balance and keeping the position essentially unchanged – the engine still judges Black as about a pawn ahead but with a slight improvement for White after the move. The retreat also respects the cramped situation of both sides’ bishops, which each have only two safe squares. In the principal line Black would continue with …Qc7, after which White can answer Bf5, followed by …Ra8 and Red1, maintaining the tension without worsening the already inferior evaluation.

teacher: By taking on a3 Black eliminates White’s pawn and opens the a‑file, preserving the one‑pawn material edge and leaving the evaluation essentially unchanged at about a pawn’s worth in Black’s favour. The capture also keeps the advanced passed pawn on c4 alive while Black’s bishop on g8 (and White’s bishop on a1) each retain only two safe squares, so the position’s basic balance is maintained. Nevertheless the engine judged Qc7 to be the optimal continuation, a move that would have kept the material edge while improving the queen’s placement.
student: By taking on a3 Black wins a pawn and opens the a‑file, while his own bishop on g8 remains confined to just two safe squares. The capture leaves the engine’s assessment virtually unchanged – Black still enjoys a clear advantage of roughly a pawn – so the position stays favorable for Black despite White’s modest counterplay. Although the engine preferred Qc7 as the optimal continuation, Bxa3 is nevertheless an excellent practical choice that preserves the edge without creating new weaknesses.

teacher: White slides the rook to d1, creating a pin of the d5‑knight against Black’s queen on d7 and removing the immediate danger to the rook on that square. The idea is sound, but it does not neutralise Black’s advanced passed pawn on c4 and leaves White still a pawn down, so the engine now judges Black to be about a pawn and a half better – a moderate worsening of roughly half a pawn for White. The engine’s top choice, 30.e4, would have challenged the centre and kept the evaluation much closer. Hence Rcd1 is a solid, “good” try, but it modestly deteriorates White’s position.
student: White’s rook slides back to d1, pinning Black’s knight on d5 to the queen and simultaneously removing the immediate danger to that piece. The move does not alter the balance – Black remains clearly better by roughly a pawn and even more so after …Qc6, which would give Black active play with the advanced passed pawn on c4. Although it is a good defensive try, the engine rates e4 as the superior continuation, indicating that Rcd1 costs White about half a pawn in evaluation.

teacher: Black’s queen retreats to c7, a quiet move that simply preserves the existing edge. By staying on the c‑file the queen continues to back the advanced passed pawn on c4 while respecting the fact that both bishops have only two safe squares. The evaluation barely shifts (about a two‑hundredth of a pawn), so Black’s material lead remains intact. Although the engine’s top‑choice would have been Qc6, Qc7 still holds the advantage without creating any new weaknesses.
student: By retreating the queen to c7 Black preserves the huge edge – the engine’s assessment stays at roughly a pawn and a half in Black’s favour. The move leaves the position essentially unchanged, with Black still ahead by about one pawn despite White’s limited piece activity. Although the engine preferred Qc6 as the optimal continuation, Qc7 keeps the same balance and therefore earns the “best” label even though it does not improve the score further.

teacher: White’s 32 Bg6 leaves the bishop hanging, so the move actually weakens White’s position. Black can simply answer with 32…Red8, removing the threat to the rook on d8 and preserving the strong passed pawn on c4, which leaves Black about a pawn ahead. The engine indicates that the more accurate 32 h6 – a pawn break against the g7 pawn – would have kept the balance better. Consequently, Bg6, while not a blunder, costs White roughly a fifth of a pawn.
student: White’s retreat Bg6 simply leaves the bishop on g6 hanging, and Black can answer with …Red8, removing the immediate danger to the rook on d8. The engine rates the move as “good” but notes that it costs White roughly a fifth of a pawn, worsening the evaluation by about –0.18 pawns. A more accurate try would have been the pawn break h6, which strikes directly at Black’s g‑pawn and keeps the balance tighter. Consequently, despite being the best available option, the move still hands Black a clear advantage.

teacher: By playing Red8 Black eliminates the immediate threat to the rook on d8, a simple but essential defensive resource. The move also keeps the advanced passed pawn on c4 alive while both bishops remain cramped, leaving Black a full pawn ahead and still evaluated as much better. White’s most logical reply would be Bf5, after which Black can continue with …c3. Although the engine notes a tiny dip of about a tenth of a pawn, the position remains clearly in Black’s favour.
student: By playing …Red8 Black eliminates White’s immediate pressure on the rook that had been threatening it, thereby preserving the valuable piece and keeping the advanced passed pawn on c4 alive. The engine still judges the position as clearly better for Black – about a pawn ahead – but notes a slight dip of roughly a tenth of a pawn compared with the previous evaluation. White could try Bf5, which would remove the threat to the bishop on f5, yet Black remains comfortably ahead.

teacher: White’s 34 Qh3 is a mistake that lets Black’s edge widen from about a pawn to well over a pawn. The queen move merely sidesteps the immediate threat to the queen on h3, but it does nothing about Black’s advanced passed pawn on c4 or the rook on d8 that dominates the open d‑file, and the evaluation drops by roughly a pawn. The engine indicates that the better try was 34 Qf3, which would have removed the threat to the queen on f3 and kept the position only slightly worse for White. Consequently Black is now a full pawn up and enjoys a much more comfortable game.
student: White’s retreat Qh3 merely sidesteps the immediate danger to the queen but does nothing to stop Black’s looming passed pawn on c4 or to relieve the cramped situation of the a‑file bishop. The engine shows that the far stronger try was Qf3, which would have removed the same threat while keeping the queen more flexible and preserving White’s chances. By playing Qh3 White allowed Black to continue with …c3, after which the evaluation slipped by roughly one pawn – Black now enjoys a clear advantage of well over a pawn. In short, the move cost White about a pawn in practical terms.

teacher: Black captures the rook on d1, creating a fork of White’s bishop on a1 and rook on e1 and pinning the latter to the king, but the fork is only superficial because White can simply recapture with Rxd1, removing the threat and restoring the material balance. This exchange costs Black about a pawn of advantage – the evaluation slips from a clear two‑pawn edge to roughly a single pawn – and the engine flags the move as an inaccuracy, preferring the pawn push c3 instead. While Black still retains an advanced passed pawn on c4 and a rook on the open b‑file, the immediate gain from the capture is illusory.
student: By playing Rxd1 Black wins White’s active rook on d1, but the capture merely initiates an exchange that leaves the material balance unchanged – White can simply recapture with Rxd1, restoring equality. The engine rates the move as an inaccuracy because it costs Black roughly a pawn of evaluation, dropping the advantage from “much better” to “clearly better.” A more accurate continuation would have been c3, which keeps the pressure without giving White the chance to equalise. After the forced Rxd1 the game proceeds with lines such as Nbd5 – Ngf5 – Be6, preserving Black’s edge while avoiding the loss of tempo.

teacher: By playing Be6 Black pins the knight on f5 to White’s queen on h3 and removes the immediate threat to the pawn on g7. Although the move keeps the passed pawn on c4 alive, it is not the most accurate continuation: the engine’s top choice, Nxc2, would have captured the bishop on c2 and increased Black’s material advantage. Consequently the evaluation slipped from about a pawn for Black to roughly three‑quarters of a pawn, a loss of roughly a third of a pawn. White can now reply with Ng6+, giving check, but that knight would be left en prise.
student: By playing …Be6 Black both eliminates the immediate danger to the g‑pawn and creates a pin of White’s knight on f5 against the queen on h3. The engine still judges the position as clearly better for Black – roughly a pawn ahead – but the move costs him about a third of a pawn compared with the optimal continuation. The engine preferred 38…Nxc2, which would have captured the white bishop on c2 and preserved more pressure. After …Be6 White can try the checking idea 39.Ng6+, after which Black must reply Nxg6 and then capture hxg6, leaving the knight on g6 vulnerable.

teacher: White’s queen jump to g3 looks tempting, as it threatens an immediate mate with Qxg7# and pins the e‑pawn to Black’s queen on c7. In reality Black can answer with Ned5, which removes the mate threat on g7 and leaves White without compensation, driving the evaluation from a modest Black edge to a much larger advantage, well over a pawn, and even a material loss for White. The engine’s preferred move was Ng6+, a checking sacrifice that, although the knight becomes en prise, would have kept the initiative and avoided the sharp drop in White’s standing.
student: White’s queen retreat to g3 looks tempting because it creates a direct mating idea – Qxg7# – and also pins the e‑pawn to Black’s queen on c7. In practice Black can simply answer …Ned5, which eliminates the immediate danger to the g7 pawn and leaves White without any concrete threats, allowing Black to consolidate his advantage. The engine rates the move as a mistake, worsening White’s evaluation by roughly a pawn and leaving Black up a full pawn in material. A far stronger try would have been 39.Ng6+, checking while keeping the knight active, but that line still avoids the loss incurred by Qg3.

teacher: Black captures the knight on f5, pinning White’s bishop on c2 to the rook on b1, but the exchange is harmless because White can recapture with Nxf5, immediately threatening mate with Qxg7#. By giving up the bishop pair after that recapture, Black gains no material and the evaluation slips by roughly four‑tenths of a pawn. The engine therefore rates the move as only “good” and notes that the stronger continuation would have been Ned5, which would have removed the threat to the g7 pawn. Consequently, Bxf5 modestly worsens Black’s already clear advantage.
student: By playing …Bxf5 Black wins the white knight and immediately pins White’s bishop on c2 to the rook on b1, but the capture merely initiates an exchange that will be met by Nxf5, restoring material balance and leaving Black without the bishop pair. The engine rates the move as good yet not optimal – it costs roughly four‑tenths of a pawn compared with the stronger continuation Ned5, which would have removed the threat to the pawn on g7. After the forced Nxf5 the game continues with ideas such as Qxg7# threats, underscoring how the bishop sacrifice does little to improve Black’s already sizable advantage.

teacher: White eliminates Black’s active bishop on f5, removing the immediate threat to his own bishop and leaving Black without the bishop pair. Nevertheless, the engine points out that the sharper continuation Nxf5 would have both captured the bishop and created a direct mating threat with Qxg7#, a resource White missed, which costs about a third of a pawn. With Black’s passed pawn on c4, the queen pin on e5 and White’s knight on h4 confined to a single safe square, the position now favors Black by a clear margin.
student: By playing Bxf5 White eliminates Black’s active bishop and removes the immediate danger to his own piece, but the capture does not generate any concrete threats. The engine rates it as a moderate worsening for White – roughly a third of a pawn worse than before – because the more forcing continuation Nxf5 would have taken the bishop while also threatening mate with Qxg7#. After the exchange Black remains comfortably ahead, now up a full pawn despite the advanced passed pawn on c4 and the pin on e5. Consequently, although the move is “good”, it is inferior to the best alternative.

teacher: By thrusting the pawn to c3 Black not only creates an advanced passed pawn but also prepares to open the c‑file after the inevitable recapture. If White accepts with Bxc3, the bishop lands on an en‑prise square and Black can simply reply Qxc3, winning a piece and leaving the c‑file fully open for the rook. The move therefore deepens Black’s material advantage—now a full pawn up—and lifts the evaluation by roughly a third of a pawn in Black’s favour. Moreover, White’s queen on g3 already pins the e5‑pawn, leaving the knight on h4 with very few safe squares, so the c‑pawn push compounds White’s difficulties.
student: By pushing …c3 Black creates an advanced passed pawn that will be decisive after White’s forced capture. After the natural reply Bxc3, the bishop lands on a square where it can be taken by the queen and the c‑file opens for Black’s pieces, giving them active play while White’s queen on g3 still pins the e5 pawn to the queen on c7 and the knight on h4 has very few safe squares. The engine rates the move as the best, improving Black’s evaluation by roughly a third of a pawn and leaving Black with a clear material edge. In the principal variation White would take on c3, Black replies Qxc3, then White plays Qf3 and Black continues with Nxf5.
violations: calls the position decisive/winning at -2.09

teacher: White eliminates Black’s advanced c‑pawn with Bxc3, willingly placing the bishop on c3 where it can be taken. After the expected Qxc3 the c‑file opens and the bishops become opposite‑coloured, so White trades the bishop pair without gaining material, which the engine judges as the only move that keeps the evaluation essentially unchanged (a tiny gain of about six‑hundredths of a pawn). The continuation therefore limits Black’s already large advantage while preserving the pin on the e5‑pawn and the cramped squares around Black’s bishop on a3 and White’s knight on h4.
student: By playing Bxc3 White forces Black’s natural reply Qxc3, which opens the c‑file and leaves both sides with opposite‑coloured bishops while restoring material balance. The capture also removes White’s bishop pair, but it does not improve the position because Black remains clearly better – the engine still evaluates the position as about two pawns down for White. Consequently the move keeps the evaluation essentially unchanged, justifying its “best” label.

teacher: Black’s Qxc3 seizes the bishop on c3, converting the material balance into a three‑point lead and pushing the evaluation to roughly two‑and‑a‑third pawns in Black’s favour. By removing White’s bishop the game becomes one of opposite‑coloured bishops, leaving White with only a single safe square for the h4‑knight while Black’s bishop on a3 still enjoys two safe squares. The engine rates the capture as the best move, improving Black’s position by about a third of a pawn.
student: By taking on c3 Black eliminates White’s active bishop and forces the game into an opposite‑colour‑bishop ending, leaving White with only the h4‑knight as its last safe haven while Black enjoys three extra pawns. The capture also curtails White’s piece activity – the knight on h4 has virtually no useful retreats and the bishop on f5 is cramped – whereas Black’s own bishop on a3 remains confined to just two safe squares. The engine rates Qxc3 as the best continuation, improving Black’s evaluation by roughly a third of a pawn even though the overall advantage still exceeds two pawns. In the principal line White would try Qg4, after which Black can continue with …Nd3, keeping the pressure.

teacher: Black’s queen retreat to c4 is a solid try, but it lets White neutralise the pressure on the e‑four bishop: after 43.Qg4 White simply removes the threat, and Black’s advantage shrinks by roughly a quarter‑pawn. The move still leaves Black with the superior material balance and the usual opposite‑colour‑bishop dynamic, while the rook on d8 continues to dominate the open d‑file. Nonetheless, the engine shows that 42…Qc8 would have preserved more of the edge, so Qc4 is good but not optimal.
student: By playing …Qc4 Black keeps the pressure along the queenside while his rook continues to dominate the open d‑file in an opposite‑colour‑bishop ending where the a3‑bishop already has very few safe squares. The engine still judges the position as clearly better for Black – roughly a pawn’s worth – but the evaluation slips by about a quarter pawn compared with the optimal continuation. White can answer with Qg4, which would eliminate the immediate threat to the bishop on e4 and bring the game back into balance. In short, the move is solid and maintains Black’s advantage, yet it is not the most accurate choice.

teacher: White’s 43.Qf3 merely steps the queen away and eliminates the immediate threat to the bishop on e4, but it does nothing to stem Black’s growing lead. The engine now judges the position as a winning one for Black, with the evaluation slipping by roughly two pawns and Black up three pawns of material. The engine’s preferred move, 43.Qg4, would have removed the same threat while keeping the balance more favorable for White. By opting for Qf3 White hands Black a decisive advantage.
student: White’s retreat Qf3 merely sidesteps the immediate danger to the bishop on e4, but it does nothing to relieve the cramped situation created by opposite‑coloured bishops and the limited mobility of White’s knight on h4. The engine shows that the far stronger continuation would have been Qg4, which also eliminates the same threat while keeping more flexibility for the pieces. By playing Qf3 White allowed Black to consolidate with …Na2, after which the evaluation slid from a modest disadvantage to a decisive edge – roughly three pawns in Black’s favour. In short, the move cost White about two pawns of standing and handed Black a clear winning advantage.

teacher: Black’s queen retreat to e6 is a serious blunder: the evaluation collapses from a decisive –3.24 advantage to only about –0.68, a loss of roughly two and a half pawns. By pulling the queen away, Black fails to improve the cramped bishop on a3 (which has only two safe squares) and allows White to activate the a‑file with Ra1, a line the engine’s principal variation continues with. The engine’s preferred move, Na2, would have kept the winning edge. Consequently Black remains clearly better, but the winning chances have evaporated.
student: By playing …Qe6 Black abandoned a decisive edge and allowed White to improve his game with Ra1, after which Black’s pieces become cramped while White can continue with Bb2 and later Rb8. The engine shows that this blunder costs roughly two‑and‑a‑half pawns of value, turning an already winning position into only a modest advantage for Black. The stronger continuation would have been …Na2, keeping the pressure and preserving the larger lead. In short, the queen move dramatically reduced Black’s winning chances.

teacher: Ra7 is a move that eliminates the immediate danger to White’s rook on a7, and it does so while keeping the piece active on the seventh rank. By removing that threat White nudges the evaluation from a slight Black advantage of about half a pawn to roughly a third of a pawn, a modest but meaningful gain given that Black is already up three pawns. The engine’s continuation shows Black’s best reply would be …Nbc6, after which White can retreat the rook to a6, preserving the opposite‑colour‑bishop dynamic and the fact that the knight on h4 has very limited safe squares.
student: By sliding the rook back to a7 White eliminates the immediate danger that Black’s pieces posed to it, thereby preserving the piece and keeping the evaluation modestly in White’s favour (+0.21 pawn). The move also respects the fact that the bishops are of opposite colour and that White’s lone knight on h4 already has very few safe squares, while Black’s rook continues to dominate the open d‑file. In the engine line Black would continue with …Nbc6, after which White can meet it with Ra6, followed by …Qb3 and White’s h6 push, showing how the rook shift neutralises Black’s threats without worsening White’s overall disadvantage.

teacher: White’s 46 g4 is a serious blunder: the pawn thrust shatters the pawn cover in front of his king and hands Black a material lead of three pawns, turning an equal position into a clearly better one for Black. Moreover, the move forfeits the immediate tactical shot Bxd5, which would have captured the knight on d5 and kept the balance. While the pawn does take the f5 square away from Black’s knight on e7, the resulting king‑side weakness far outweighs that modest gain. In the engine line White could have answered a natural …Qb6 with Bxd5, after which Black’s queen would take on a7 but White would still retain enough compensation with Bf7.
student: White’s 46 g4 looks like a modest attempt to restrict Black’s knight on e7 and to loosen the pawn shield in front of his own king, but it fatally overlooks the far more urgent tactical shot Bxd5. By playing g4 instead of capturing the knight on d5, White allows Black to keep the piece and emerges with a three‑pawn material advantage – a swing of about two pawns against an already equal evaluation. The engine therefore marks the move as a blunder, costing White roughly three pawns of value. In short, the pawn push does nothing to improve White’s position while leaving Black comfortably ahead.

teacher: Black’s 46…Bc3 is a clear mistake, costing him about a pawn of evaluation. By moving the bishop to c3, Black gives White the simple plan Nf5, after which Black would have to reply …Bb4 and White can then exchange on d5, relieving the pressure that the opposite‑coloured bishops and the active rook on d8 had created. The engine’s top choice was 46…Qb6, a move that would have preserved the larger advantage. In short, the bishop retreat hands the initiative to White without creating any concrete threats.
student: By playing …Bc3 Black abandoned the far stronger continuation …Qb6, which would have kept the initiative and preserved the three‑pawn material edge. The retreat to c3 does nothing to improve the already opposite‑colour‑bishop situation or to make use of the rook’s control of the open d‑file, so White can simply answer with Nf5, after which Black’s best try Bb4 is met by Bxd5 and then recaptured, leaving Black only about one‑and‑a‑half pawns ahead instead of two. In short, the move costs roughly a pawn in evaluation and hands the game back to White.

teacher: With 47…Bb4 Black keeps the bishops of opposite colours and leaves the rook on d8 in full control of the open d‑file while White’s rook continues to dominate the b‑file. The move nudges the evaluation from a 1.9‑pawn disadvantage for White to roughly a 2‑pawn advantage, a gain of about a tenth of a pawn. The engine, however, judges 47…Ba5 to be marginally stronger, indicating that the bishop could have been placed on a5 for a slightly better score. Nonetheless, the move solidifies Black’s already much‑better position.
student: By playing …Bb4 Black brings his dark‑squared bishop to a more active square while preserving the opposite‑colour‑bishop structure and keeping the rook on d8 dominant on the open d‑file. The engine rates the move as a slight improvement for Black – about a tenth of a pawn – and it leaves Black still clearly ahead in a position where White’s rook dominates the b‑file. Although Ba5 would have been marginally stronger, …Bb4 is an excellent continuation that maintains Black’s sizable advantage.

teacher: By retreating the bishop to d6, Black preserves the opposite‑colour bishop dynamic and leaves the queen’s pin on the g‑pawn untouched, while the rook on d8 continues to dominate the open d‑file. This modest shift nudges the evaluation from roughly –2.3 to –2.5 pawns, keeping Black comfortably ahead by more than two pawns. Although the engine preferred the slightly sharper Bc5, the move to d6 still secures the advantage.
student: By retreating the bishop to d6 Black solidifies his already dominant setup – the queen on e6 still pins White’s g‑pawn and the rook on d8 continues to dominate the open d‑file while the bishops sit on opposite colours. The move nudges the evaluation a shade deeper in Black’s favour (+0.16 pawns), confirming that he remains clearly better despite being down three pawns overall. Although the engine prefers 48…Bc5 as the optimal continuation, Bd6 is an excellent practical choice that preserves the pressure without creating new weaknesses.

teacher: By taking on f5 Black eliminates the immediate danger to the queen on e6 and the pawn on h7, while also forcing an exchange that leaves White with a weakened pawn structure. After the inevitable gxf5, White’s pawn on f5 is fixed on a light square, the g‑file becomes semi‑open for White, and the h‑pawn is left isolated on h5, giving Black a clear target. The capture therefore modestly improves Black’s already decisive position (the engine rates the move a +0.34‑pawn swing), and the resulting pawn weaknesses give Black further chances to press on the open d‑file.
student: By taking on f5 Black eliminates the immediate danger to his queen on e6 and the pawn on h7, while also removing the opponent’s active bishop that was threatening both pieces. After the forced recapture gxf5 the g‑file becomes semi‑open for White but leaves White with an isolated pawn on h5 and a pawn on f5 that is fixed on a light square, giving Black a clear structural edge. The engine rates the capture as the best move, improving Black’s evaluation by about a third of a pawn and preserving a decisive material advantage.

teacher: By capturing on f5 White not only wins a piece but also opens the g‑file, fixing Black’s pawn on f6 on a dark square and immediately targeting the poorly defended g7 pawn. The pawn structure becomes a bit compromised – White now has an isolated h‑pawn and doubled pawns on the f‑file – yet the move still lifts White’s evaluation by roughly a third of a pawn, the only improvement in a position that remains a decisive Black advantage. Black’s most natural reply would be …Qc8, which removes the threat to the queen on c8. Nonetheless, gxf5 is the only move that improves White’s chances, earning the “best” label.
student: By playing gxf5 White eliminates Black’s active knight and opens the g‑file, giving the rook on b7 a useful line while fixing Black’s pawn on f6 on a dark square. The capture also attacks the poorly defended g7 pawn, but it leaves White with an isolated pawn on h5 and doubled pawns on the f‑file, so the resulting structure costs him about a third of a pawn in evaluation. Although Black still enjoys a decisive material edge, the engine rates this as the best continuation, improving White’s standing by roughly three‑tenths of a pawn. Black can answer with …Qc8, removing the immediate threat to the queen on c8.

teacher: Black calmly steps his king back to g8, leaving the powerful rook on d8 untouched on the open d‑file. By doing so he preserves the dominant control of that file and the material edge, which the engine quantifies as a modest gain of roughly a fifth of a pawn, taking the evaluation from –2.02 to –2.21. The move therefore solidifies Black’s already much‑better position; the engine’s continuation shows White could try 52.e4, but Black can answer with …Nc7 and keep the pressure.
student: By slipping the king to g8 Black preserves his three‑pawn material edge and nudges the evaluation a touch deeper into Black’s favour (+0.19 pawns). The move leaves the rooks firmly in their respective files – White’s rook on b7 dominates the open b‑file while Black’s rook on d8 holds the open d‑file – so the balance of forces remains favorable for Black. In the engine line White would try e4, after which Black can continue with …Nc7 and keep the pressure, confirming that Kg8 was indeed the best continuation.

teacher: White’s 52 h6 tries to generate a direct mating idea – the pawn thrust threatens Rxg7# and fixes Black’s h‑pawn on a light square – but it also creates an isolated pawn on h6 and does nothing to counter Black’s active pieces. The move therefore costs White about two‑thirds of a pawn, worsening an already inferior position (the evaluation slides from –2.21 to –2.90). Engine analysis shows that the more precise 52 e4 would have kept the pressure without the structural weakness and would have been the correct continuation. In short, the pawn break is a tempting tactical shot that backfires, leaving White’s position even more precarious.
student: White’s 52.h6 tries to create immediate mating threats by threatening Rxg7#, but it also leaves an isolated pawn on h6 and does nothing to stop Black’s active pieces – the rook on d8 already dominates the open d‑file while Black’s pawn on h7 becomes permanently fixed on a light square. The engine rates the move as an inaccuracy, worsening White’s standing by roughly two‑thirds of a pawn and leaving Black still clearly ahead. A more accurate continuation would have been 52.e4, which keeps the balance without conceding the isolated pawn or allowing the mating idea. Consequently, despite the temporary threat, the position remains heavily in Black’s favour.

teacher: Black’s 52…Bc7 let his advantage shrink dramatically, dropping the evaluation from a clear two‑pawn edge to only about a pawn – a loss of roughly 1.4 pawns, which the engine marks as a mistake. The bishop retreat does not improve the already strong rook on d8 nor does it contest White’s active rook on b7, so the position after the move is less threatening for Black. The engine’s preferred continuation was 52…Nc7, which would have preserved more of Black’s lead. Although Black is still up three pawns, the move has cost him a significant share of his advantage.
student: By playing …Bc7 Black abandoned the more active Nc7, which would have kept the pressure on White’s centre and preserved the larger advantage. The retreat does nothing to improve the already dominant rooks – Black still dominates the open d‑file with the rook on d8 while White’s rook continues to control the b‑file – so the evaluation slipped from roughly three pawns ahead to just under one pawn. In short, the bishop move cost Black about a pawn’s worth of edge.

teacher: By playing Rd7 Black eliminates White’s immediate pressure on the g7 pawn, a concrete tactical nuisance that had been looming. The rook now occupies the open d‑file, matching White’s rook on b7 and allowing Black to retain his material edge – the engine still judges the position as a clear two‑pawn advantage for Black. White’s most natural try would be Ra7, which would remove the threat to the a‑file rook, after which Black can continue with Re7 and later …e4, keeping the initiative.
student: By playing Rd7 Black eliminates White’s immediate pressure on the g‑pawn, thereby preserving the three‑point material edge and keeping the position clearly in Black’s favour. The rook now sits on the open d‑file while White’s rook continues to dominate the b‑file, so the balance of forces remains roughly as before. White could try Ra7, which would remove the threat to the rook on a7, but even after that continuation Black stays comfortably ahead.

teacher: By playing 56…gxh6 Black opened the g‑file, created a passed pawn on h6‑h7 and pushed the kingside pawn majority forward. However the capture also left the g‑file open for White’s heavy pieces, giving them a direct line toward Black’s king, and the engine judges that this worsened Black’s position by about three‑quarters of a pawn (the evaluation slipped from roughly –2.9 to –2.2). The engine’s best move, 56…e4+, would have delivered a discovered check from the bishop on c7 and kept the initiative, so the pawn capture is marked as an inaccuracy.
student: By playing gxh6 Black opens the g‑file but also hands White a semi‑open h‑file that his heavy pieces can immediately exploit, while the newly created passed pawn duo on h6 and h7 does little to offset those factors. The engine rates the capture as an inaccuracy, costing roughly three‑quarters of a pawn compared with the superior checking idea e4+. That pawn push would have delivered a discovered check from the bishop on c7 – even though the pawn would be left en prise – and kept Black’s sizable advantage. Consequently Black remains up four points of material, yet the position is less favorable than it could have been.

teacher: White launches a check with Qg7+, hoping to exploit a fork on the h‑pawn, the king on e7 and the pawn on h7. Black can simply answer Kd6, which uncovers the rook on d7’s line on the queen and forces White to retreat, so the move costs White about half a pawn and leaves Black “much better” (over a pawn ahead). The engine’s preferred continuation,  e4, would have avoided this loss of tempo and kept the evaluation more favorable for White. In short, the check looks attractive but it worsens White’s position and hands Black a comfortable material and positional edge.
student: White’s checking Qg7+ tries to fork Black’s king on e7, the pawn on h6 and the pawn on h7, but it immediately allows …Kd6, which uncovers the rook on d7’s line against the queen. After that Black can continue with Re7, keeping the pressure while White remains down four points of material and the evaluation slips further into Black’s favour. The engine judged the move “good” yet not optimal – the more accurate continuation would have been the pawn push e4, which keeps the balance far tighter. Consequently the position stays clearly worse for White.

teacher: By moving the king to d6 Black clears the seventh rank, allowing the rook on d7 to resume its line against White’s queen on g7. The rook now attacks the queen while still dominating the open d‑file, keeping Black’s four‑pawn material advantage intact. The engine notes the move is a shade less accurate (about a quarter of a pawn), yet Black remains much better, and White’s most forcing try would be Qf8+, a checking fork of the king and the h6 pawn that merely removes the immediate threat to the queen.
student: By moving the king to d6 Black uncovers the rook on d7’s line against White’s queen on g7, creating an immediate tactical pressure that can be exploited later. The engine rates Kd6 as the best continuation, even though it costs Black about a quarter‑pawn in evaluation terms because White could answer with Qf8+, forking the king and the h‑pawn while also removing the threat to the queen. Nevertheless, Black remains clearly better – roughly two pawns ahead – and the position stays favorable despite the slight drop in the score.

teacher: White’s capture on h6 wins a pawn and creates a pin of the f‑pawn against the Black king, but it allows Black to answer with …Qc2, pinning White’s f‑pawn to the king and leaving the White queen on h6 exposed. More importantly, White missed the far stronger Qf8+, a checking fork that would have hit the king on d6 and the pawn on h6, keeping the initiative and winning material. The blunder turned a modest disadvantage into a winning position for Black, who now enjoys a decisive advantage and is up three pawns.
student: By playing Qxh6 White merely wins a pawn but does nothing to stop Black’s looming threats – after the capture Black can reply with …Qc2, pinning the f‑pawn to the king on h2 and leaving White down three pawns in material. The engine shows that the far stronger continuation would have been Qf8+, which checks the king while forking it and the pawn on h6, preserving material balance. Consequently the evaluation slides from a modest disadvantage to a decisive one, costing roughly two pawns of value.

teacher: By moving the king to c5 Black walks straight into a rook check on the c‑file. White can reply with Rc1+, skewering the king and the queen on c6; after the king moves, the queen can be captured, leaving Black without its queen and turning a previously decisive Black advantage into a decisive White one. The engine’s preferred move was Qc2, which would have pinned the f‑pawn to the white king and preserved Black’s material edge. This blunder costs roughly seven pawns and flips the evaluation from a winning Black position to a winning White position.
student: By moving the king to c5 Black walks straight into White’s tactical shot Rc1+, which both checks and skews the black king onto the same line as the queen on c6. After the forced Kb5, White can capture on c6 with Rxc6, turning a decisive –3‑pawn edge for Black into a winning +3‑pawn lead for White—a swing of about seven pawns in evaluation. The engine’s best reply was Qc2, which would have pinned the f‑pawn to the white king and kept the initiative. Consequently, Kc5 cost Black roughly six pawns of value and handed the game to White.

teacher: The move Kh3 is a catastrophic blunder that flips a decisive +3.5‑pawn advantage into a similar winning edge for Black, a swing of about seven pawns. Instead of the forcing check Rc1+, which would have sketched a rook‑c1 check and exposed Black’s queen on c6 behind the king, White simply shuffled the king without creating any threats. With Black’s rook already dominating the open d‑file and the pieces poised, the king move does nothing to stop Black’s counterplay, allowing Black to consolidate a three‑pawn material lead and a decisive advantage.
student: By moving the king to h3 White walks straight into Black’s active rook on d7 that dominates the open d‑file and allows Black to increase his material lead. The engine shows that the correct continuation was Rc1+, which would have delivered a checking blow while skewering the black king on c5 and exposing the queen on c6. After Kh3 Black can simply play …Nc3, after which White’s best try Qf8+ does not stop the counterplay, leaving Black with a decisive edge – roughly three pawns in material. In short, the blunder costs White about seven pawns of evaluation and turns a winning position into a losing one.

teacher: Black’s king steps to a7, moving onto a square adjacent to the open b‑file controlled by White’s rook, while White’s queen on h6 already pins the f‑pawn. As a result White’s heavy pieces now bear down the b‑file toward the Black king, increasing its exposure. The engine preferred Ka6, which would have kept the king a little safer; Ka7 therefore costs about a fifth of a pawn, though Black still retains a decisive winning advantage.
student: By moving the king to a7 Black steps onto the same line as White’s rook on b1, so the white rook now bears down the open b‑file toward the black king. This modestly reduces Black’s edge – the evaluation slips by roughly two‑tenths of a pawn – but it still leaves Black with a decisive material advantage and an active rook on the d‑file while White’s queen on h6 continues to pin the f‑pawn. The engine judged Ka6 to be marginally stronger, yet Ka7 is a good defensive try that keeps the pressure alive.

teacher: By playing …Bb6 Black walks the bishop into a pin: White’s rook on b1 now attacks the bishop and, because the king sits on b7, the bishop cannot legally move because it would expose the king to check. This loss of piece activity costs roughly a pawn, as the engine’s evaluation drops from a decisive –4.64 to –3.58. The engine’s top choice was 63…Nb6, which would have avoided the pin and preserved the larger advantage. After the inaccuracy Black could try Qf8, but White would reply Qc2, and the resulting line is already inferior to the best continuation.
student: By playing …Bb6 Black places the bishop on a square that White’s rook on b1 can immediately pin to the black king on b7, so the piece becomes immobile and loses its activity. This costs roughly a pawn of evaluation – the engine now judges the position about three‑and‑a‑half pawns worse for Black than before. The engine’s preferred continuation was …Nb6, which would have kept more pressure without creating the pin. Consequently, despite being up three pawns in material, Black’s advantage has been reduced by about one pawn.

teacher: White’s Qf3 looks attractive – it pins Black’s queen on c6 to the king on b7 and attacks the bishop on b6 – but it completely overlooks the tactical shot …Nxb1, which captures the rook on b1 and deepens Black’s lead by roughly three pawns. The engine shows that the position deteriorates from a decisive Black advantage to an even larger one (‑3.5 pawns to about ‑7 pawns). The correct move would have been Ra1, simply removing the immediate threat to the rook. As a result, White’s move is a clear blunder that hands Black a winning material edge.
student: White’s queen retreat to f3 looks active – it pins Black’s queen on c6 and even attacks the poorly defended bishop on b6 – but in reality it does nothing to stop Black’s immediate reply …Nxb1, which both eliminates the pin and wins the rook on b1. By allowing that capture White’s evaluation drops by roughly three‑and‑a‑half pawns, turning an already losing position into a clearly decisive disadvantage for Black. The engine’s preferred move was Ra1, which would have removed the threat to the rook on a1 and kept the balance. Consequently, Qf3 is a clear blunder.

teacher: Black answered 1.e4 with the classical 1…e5, a sound developing move that leaves the position essentially equal, White still holding a tiny edge of roughly a third of a pawn. The engine notes that the move kept Black’s evaluation essentially unchanged, only about a hundredth of a pawn worse than the alternative. Nevertheless, the engine’s top choice was 1…c5, which would have given Black a marginally better standing.
student: Black answered 1.e4 with …e5, keeping material equal and leaving White still a hair ahead – the engine’s assessment shifts by only about a hundredth of a pawn. The move does not alter the balance in any way, so it is judged “best” but not the most accurate continuation. In fact, the engine preferred 1…c5, which would have been marginally more precise. After …e5 White can continue with Nf3, after which Black may develop with …Nc6 and later bring the knight to f6.

teacher: White develops the light‑squared bishop to b5, preserving the modest edge that existed after 2…Nc6. The engine rates the move as excellent, noting that the evaluation only slipped from +0.25 to +0.23 – essentially unchanged. Although the engine’s top choice was 3.Bc4, which would have kept a very similar advantage, 3.Bb5 still leaves White slightly better.
student: White develops the dark‑squared bishop to b5, keeping the modest edge that existed before the move. The engine rates it as an excellent continuation, but notes that Bc4 would have been marginally stronger – about two‑hundredths of a pawn more favorable for White. After Bb5 Black can answer with …a6, after which White could continue with Ba4 and later push d4, preserving the slight advantage. In short, the move leaves White’s position essentially unchanged while being solidly sound.

teacher: Black’s 3…Nf6 is a solid developing move, but it lets White keep the slight edge – the evaluation shifts from a modest White advantage of about a quarter pawn to roughly a half‑pawn. The engine notes that the more accurate 3…a6 would have challenged White’s bishop on b5 and kept the pressure lower; by playing …Nf6 Black missed that chance, costing roughly a third of a pawn. In the continuation the engine expects White to castle (O‑O), after which Black could capture on e4, followed by White’s d4 and Black’s …Be7. Overall the move is good, just not the optimal choice.
student: Black’s …Nf6 develops a piece but does not improve his standing – White still enjoys a small edge and the evaluation slips by about a third of a pawn in White’s favour. The engine judged that the more accurate continuation would have been …a6, which would have kept the balance tighter. After …Nf6 White can simply castle, after which Black could try to win material with Nxe4, yet the resulting line leaves White with a modest advantage. In short, the move is good but it costs Black roughly a third of a pawn compared with the optimal reply.

teacher: Black’s Nd6 was an excellent reply because it eliminates the immediate danger to the knight that had just landed on d6, allowing Black to retain the extra pawn. The engine’s evaluation barely changes – White stays only a fraction of a pawn ahead – confirming that Black’s material edge is preserved. White’s rook on e1 now enjoys the semi‑open e‑file, but the most natural continuation would be 6.Nxe5, after which Black can meet the capture with …Be7 and continue with …Bf1 and …O‑O.
student: By playing Nd6 Black eliminates the immediate danger to his knight, allowing it to stay safely on the board while preserving the extra pawn advantage. The engine rates the move as excellent and the best continuation, with the evaluation shifting only marginally from +0.27 to +0.32 in White’s favour – essentially unchanged for Black. If White now tries the natural capture Nxe5, Black can answer with …Be7, keeping the material edge intact.

teacher: Black captures the knight on e5, launching an exchange that White will answer with Rxe5. After the forced recapture the rook on e5 pins Black’s bishop on e7 to the king, limiting Black’s piece activity, yet the trade simply restores material balance and nudges the evaluation a little in Black’s favour (about a tenth of a pawn). This modest improvement, together with the fact that Black’s king is still in the centre while White has already castled and controls the open e‑file, explains why the engine rates Nxe5 as the best move.
student: By taking on e5 Black eliminates White’s active knight and forces an immediate exchange that will be restored after White’s natural recapture with Rxe5. The capture also leaves Black’s king still in the centre while White already enjoys a safe castle and a rook dominating the open e‑file, which explains why the engine rates the position as essentially unchanged – White remains only a fraction of a pawn ahead. In the principal line White would play Rxe5, pinning the bishop on e7 to the king, but even then Black can continue safely with …O‑O and later develop the bishop to f6, keeping the initiative despite the slight disadvantage.

teacher: By playing Rxe5 White not only wins the knight on e5 but also places the rook on the same file as Black’s king, pinning the bishop on e7 because the king on e8 cannot legally move the piece. With the rook now dominating the open e‑file and Black’s king still stuck in the centre while White has already castled, White restores material equality. The engine rates the move as excellent and the evaluation remains a modest White advantage (about +0.25 pawn), showing that the capture compensates Black’s active pieces but does not dramatically swing the balance.
student: By taking on e5 White eliminates Black’s active knight and simultaneously pins the remaining bishop on e7 to the king on e8, so the piece cannot move without exposing the king. The capture also leaves White’s rook on e5 dominating the open e‑file, reinforcing the pressure that already exists with the white king safely castled against Black’s still‑central king. The engine rates the move as excellent, keeping White’s slight edge virtually unchanged at about +0.25 of a pawn.

teacher: By castling, Black both secures the king and brings the rook to f8, ready to meet White’s rook that already dominates the open e‑file. The engine rates the move as the best, leaving the tiny White edge essentially unchanged (White still a fraction of a pawn better). In the principal variation Black would answer White’s forthcoming d4 with …Bf6, after which White could play Re1 and Black would reply …Re8, keeping the balance on the e‑file.
student: By castling, Black tucks the king safely behind the pawn shield and connects the rooks, thereby neutralising White’s slight edge that existed before the move. The engine rates the position virtually unchanged – White remains only about two‑tenths of a pawn ahead – confirming that the castle was indeed the best continuation. In the principal variation White would continue with d4, after which Black can develop the bishop to f6 and later bring the rook back to e8, keeping the balance intact.

teacher: White’s knight jump to d5 nudges the evaluation in White’s favour by roughly two‑tenths of a pawn, capitalising on the fact that the rook on e5 already dominates the open e‑file. Nevertheless, the engine still rates the pawn thrust d4 as the sharper continuation, indicating that Nd5, while solid, is not the absolute optimum. If Black replies with the most accurate move Bd6, White can follow up with Re1, preserving the modest edge gained by the knight’s advance.
student: White’s 10.Nd5 nudges the evaluation up to about a fifth of a pawn in his favour, confirming that the move improves the balance. The engine still prefers 10.d4 as the optimal continuation, but Nd5 is a solid alternative that leaves material unchanged and keeps the rook on e5 active on the open e‑file. In short, the knight hop modestly strengthens White’s position without creating any new weaknesses.

teacher: White’s Re1 eliminates the immediate threat to the rook on e1, but it also leaves the pawn on h2 exposed. The move keeps the evaluation essentially unchanged – White remains only a shade better (about +0.05 pawns) – so it is a solid, maintaining choice. Nevertheless, the engine would have preferred Re2, which removes the same threat while keeping the rook on a more flexible square, a marginally more accurate continuation.
student: White retreats the rook from e2 to e1, eliminating the immediate danger to that piece but leaving the pawn on h2 hanging. The engine still judges the position as only marginally better for White – about two‑tenths of a pawn – and notes that the more accurate continuation would have been Re2, which also leaves the same pawn vulnerable while keeping the rook safer. In practice the move does not worsen White’s standing, so the slight advantage remains essentially unchanged.

teacher: White’s Ne3 is an excellent move because it eliminates the immediate threat to the knight that was on e3, allowing White to keep the slight edge (+0.26 pawns). By placing the knight on a safe square the rook on e1 continues to dominate the open e‑file, even though both bishops on c8 and c1 have no safe squares at the moment. The engine confirms Ne3 as the best continuation; Black’s most natural reply would be …Be7, after which White can proceed with c4, Nc7 and d4 while preserving the modest advantage.
student: By retreating the knight to e3 White eliminates the immediate danger that Black’s pieces posed to it, preserving the material balance and keeping the slight edge intact. With both sides’ bishops confined to their respective dark‑squared complexes – Black’s bishop on c8 lacks safe squares while White’s bishop on c1 does as well – the position remains balanced despite the fact that White’s rook already dominates the open e‑file. The engine rates Ne3 as an excellent continuation, noting that the evaluation stays at roughly +0.25 of a pawn.

teacher: White reinforces the centre with 14.d4, a move that keeps Black’s bishop on c8 without any safe squares while White’s own bishops remain cramped. The engine records a modest swing from a slight White edge to an almost equal balance, but the move is still the best because Black’s most natural reply is the pawn break …d5, striking at the c4 pawn and leading to the line …d5 cxd5 Bb4 Re2. By accepting this break White preserves a roughly equal game despite the small loss in evaluation.
student: White’s advance d4 is the engine‑recommended continuation and leaves the evaluation essentially unchanged – the position remains roughly equal despite Black’s bishop on c8 having few safe squares and both of White’s own bishops being limited to single or two safe squares. By playing d4 White keeps the balance while Black can answer with the thematic …d5 pawn break, striking at the c4 pawn. The move therefore preserves material equality and maintains the slight edge that existed before.

teacher: Black finally strikes in the centre with …d5, a pawn break that attacks White’s pawn on c4 and, after the forced cxd5, opens the c‑file for White while granting Black a semi‑open d‑file. The exchange also leaves White with isolated and doubled pawns on the d‑file, a structural weakness that Black can try to exploit with …Bb4 in the continuation. Although the engine judges the move to have cost Black about a tenth of a pawn (the evaluation shifts from +0.16 to +0.27 in White’s favour), it remains the best move available.
student: Black finally seizes the initiative with …d5, a pawn break that attacks White’s pawn on c4 and forces it to be captured. After the natural reply cxd5, the c‑file becomes semi‑open for White while the d‑file opens for Black, leaving White with isolated and doubled pawns on the d‑file and giving Black active play along the d‑file. The engine rates the move as good and the best available, though it nudges the evaluation in White’s favour by about a tenth of a pawn. In the principal variation White would capture on d5, after which Black can continue with …Bb4, keeping the pressure alive.

teacher: By playing cxd5 White opens the c‑file, giving the side a semi‑open line while simultaneously handing Black a semi‑open d‑file. The capture also pushes White’s queenside pawn majority to four against Black’s three, even though it leaves White with isolated, doubled pawns on d4 and d5. The engine still rates the position as a slight White edge (about a fifth of a pawn) and, with the extra pawn, the move is rightly judged excellent.
student: By playing cxd5 White eliminates Black’s central pawn and opens the c‑file, giving the rook on e1 a useful line while leaving the d‑file semi‑open for Black. The capture also creates an isolated pair of pawns on d4 and d5 but secures a full pawn advantage, which is why the engine rates it as excellent even though the evaluation stays at roughly +0.22. With the bishop on c1 confined to its only safe square and the rook already dominating the open e‑file, the position remains balanced despite the structural weaknesses.

teacher: White retreats the bishop to d2, completing development while leaving the rook on e1 free to dominate the open e‑file. The move simply steps out of the way of Black’s most natural reply …Be6, preserving White’s modest edge. The engine rates it as the clear best, with the evaluation shifting only from +0.52 to +0.60 – essentially unchanged. After …Be6 White can continue with Nc2, after which Black may play Bd6 and White can follow with g3 in the continuation.
student: White’s bishop retreats to d2, keeping the rook on e1 firmly in control of the open e‑file and preserving the modest edge that existed before the move. The engine rates it as the best continuation, nudging the evaluation from +0.52 to about +0.60 – essentially unchanged but with a small gain for White. In the principal variation Black would reply …Be6, after which White can continue with Nc2, followed by Bd6 and g3.

teacher: Black’s 17…Bb7 is a clear mistake, letting White’s advantage swell from a modest edge to almost two pawns. By moving the bishop to b7 Black does nothing to challenge the open e‑file where White’s rook on e1 already exerts pressure, and the engine had a far stronger alternative in 17…Be6. After 17…Bb7 White can continue with Nf5, after which Black might try Bf6 and White can keep the initiative with Qg3, after which Black replies Qd7.
student: By playing …Bb7 Black does nothing to meet White’s active rook on e1 that already dominates the open e‑file, and the bishop simply sits on its square without generating any counterplay. The engine shows this costs Black about a pawn and turns a slight White edge into a clear advantage for White. A far stronger continuation would have been …Be6, which keeps the bishop more flexible and preserves material equality. Consequently the move is rightly marked as a mistake.

teacher: White’s rook lift to c1 does little – the rooks already dominate the open e‑file, and the c‑file will be controlled after the move, and the bishop on d2 is already cramped to only two safe squares. By playing Rac1 White simply gives Black the chance to improve with …Ne6, after which the engine’s continuation shows White could have kept the initiative with Nf5. The missed knight jump would have preserved the earlier +1.7 advantage, whereas Rac1 drops the evaluation by roughly a pawn, turning a clearly better position into only a modest edge.
student: By playing Rac1 White simply shuffles the a‑rook to the c‑file without improving his cramped situation – the bishop on d2 still has only two safe squares and the rook on e1 already dominates the open e‑file. The engine shows that this costs roughly a pawn’s worth of advantage, dropping the evaluation from +1.77 to +0.67. A far stronger continuation would have been Nf5, which keeps more pressure on Black’s pieces while preserving the edge. Consequently the move is rightly marked as a mistake.

teacher: White’s 19.Nf5 is the only move that eliminates Black’s immediate pressure on the d4‑pawn, thereby preserving White’s small but clear edge. By redeploying the knight to f5 the pawn structure stays intact while White’s rooks on the open e‑ and c‑files remain fully active. Black’s most logical try would be 19…Bg5, pinning the bishop on d2 to the c‑file rook, but White can meet it with 20.Bxg5 Qxg5 21.Nd6, keeping the advantage essentially unchanged. This precise defensive maneuver justifies the “!!” rating.
student: By playing Nf5 White eliminates Black’s immediate pressure on the d‑pawn, thereby preserving the modest edge that existed before the move. The engine rates the position as still clearly better for White – roughly a pawn’s worth – and notes that the evaluation improves by about a tenth of a pawn after the move. Black could try …Bg5, pinning the d2‑bishop to the c1‑rook, but White can simply capture with Bxg5 and then continue with Nd6, keeping the initiative. This precise defensive resource therefore justifies the “best” label.

teacher: By playing …Bg5 Black creates a direct pin of White’s bishop on d2 against the rook on c1, a concrete nuisance that limits White’s coordination on the open c‑file. If White accepts the sacrifice with Bxg5, Black simply recaptures with the queen, relinquishing the bishop pair but keeping the material balance, although the pin on the d2 bishop disappears. The move nudges the evaluation a little in Black’s favour (about a tenth of a pawn) and sets the stage for the continuation …Qxg5, …Nd6 and …Rab8 in the principal line.
student: By playing …Bg5 Black creates a pin of White’s bishop on d2 against the rook on c1, forcing an immediate exchange. After White would capture with Bxg5, Black can recapture with the queen and retain material balance while giving up the bishop pair, which nudges the evaluation in Black’s favour by roughly a tenth of a pawn. The engine rates this as the best continuation, improving Black’s standing despite White still being a little better.

teacher: White eliminates Black’s active bishop on g5, initiating an exchange that will most likely be answered by …Qxg5, which restores the material balance but leaves White’s slight edge intact. After the expected recapture Qxg5, White will give up the bishop pair, trading a piece of equal value while keeping the rooks on e1 and c1 dominating the open e‑ and c‑files, a key feature of the position. The engine rates the move as the best continuation, noting that the evaluation remains essentially unchanged at about a pawn’s worth in White’s favour.
student: By taking on g5 White eliminates Black’s active bishop and forces an immediate exchange that leaves both sides without their own bishop pair. After the inevitable …Qxg5 the material balance is restored, but White retains the powerful rooks on the open e‑ and c‑files while Black must give up his bishop for the same reason. The engine rates this as the best continuation, keeping White’s clear advantage of roughly three‑quarters of a pawn.

teacher: Black’s capture on g5 eliminates the immediate danger to his queen while also winning a bishop, so White is forced to give up the bishop pair. The exchange leaves material balanced and the engine’s evaluation barely shifts, keeping White’s advantage at roughly a pawn’s worth. After the capture, White’s most logical try would be Nd6, which leaves the pawn on d4 en prise, as the engine notes. By removing the bishop and neutralising the queen‑target, Black secures the best possible continuation.
student: By playing …Qxg5 Black eliminates White’s active bishop and at the same time removes the immediate danger to his own queen, keeping material even while leaving the position essentially unchanged – the engine still judges White to be about three‑quarters of a pawn ahead. The capture also forces White to give up the bishop pair, which explains why the evaluation stays roughly the same. In the ensuing line White could try Nd6, but that would leave the pawn on d4 hanging, giving Black concrete chances to continue with …Rab8 and later …Qe7.

teacher: White captures the bishop on b7, but the move merely starts an exchange that Black can meet with Qxb7, instantly restoring material balance and, by attacking the pawn on d4, creating a new target for Black. Moreover, the capture leaves the knight on b7 exposed – a danger that the engine‑recommended move Qg3 would have avoided, as it removes the threat to the knight on d6. As a result the evaluation slides from a clear pawn‑plus to only a slight edge, costing White roughly a pawn of value.
student: By playing Nxb7 White wins a bishop but immediately allows Black’s queen to recapture with Qxb7, restoring material balance and erasing most of White’s earlier edge. The capture also attacks the pawn on d5, yet that pawn remains poorly defended – after the forced Qxb7 the pawn on d4 becomes vulnerable while the pawn on d5 is still under attack. The engine rates the move as an inaccuracy, costing roughly a pawn’s worth of evaluation despite White still being up three points of material. A more accurate continuation would have been Qg3, which simply removes the threat to the knight on d6 without giving Black the easy reply Qxb7.

teacher: White calmly plays 24 g3, the engine’s top choice, preserving the modest edge. The move leaves the light‑squared bishop opposite Black’s knight and keeps both rooks on their active open files – White’s on e‑file and Black’s on c‑file. Black can reply with 24…Rxc1, after which White recaptures and the ensuing rook exchanges (Rc8 followed by Rxc8+) lead to a simplified position where White remains slightly better. The evaluation slips only about a tenth of a pawn, confirming that g3 was a sound, quiet continuation.
student: White’s quiet g3 simply preserves the slight edge that existed before the move, keeping material equal and leaving the evaluation at about +0.44 for White. The engine rates it as the best continuation, noting that any other try would allow Black to capture the rook with …Rxc1, after which White can recapture with Rxc1 and then continue with Rc8 followed by an Rxc8+ check. In short, the pawn push maintains White’s modest advantage while respecting the current balance of forces – a light‑squared bishop versus Black’s knight, both sides’ rooks controlling their respective open files.

teacher: Black’s …Rc8 puts his rook on the open c‑file, directly opposing White’s rook on c1 and maintaining control of that line. The engine shows this improves Black’s stance slightly, cutting White’s advantage from about a pawn to just under a pawn. If White answers with Rxc8+, the check is met by …Qxc8, after which the continuation Bh3 g6 is suggested. Although the engine’s top choice was 25…Re8, the rook lift is still a solid, “best‑like” move that secures the file.
student: By playing …Rc8 Black places his rook on the open c‑file, directly contesting White’s rook that already dominates the same line. The engine rates this as a modest improvement for Black – roughly a tenth of a pawn – and it also keeps the balance of material unchanged. Nevertheless, the engine preferred …Re8, which would have kept more flexibility in the ensuing play. In practice White can answer with Rxc8+, after which Black must recapture with the queen and continue with …Bh3 and …g6, but the advantage remains only slight.

teacher: By playing Bh3 White puts the light‑squared bishop on the long diagonal, pinning Black’s knight on e6 to the queen on c8. In this middlegame the bishop‑against‑knight pin limits Black’s piece activity and preserves White’s slight edge, which the engine rates as essentially unchanged at about a half‑pawn advantage. Consequently the move is judged the best continuation.
student: By retreating the bishop to h3 White creates a direct pin of the e‑6 knight against Black’s queen on c8, exploiting the fact that the knight cannot escape while the bishop remains active in this endgame. The engine rates the move as the best continuation, keeping White’s slight edge essentially unchanged at about +0.5 pawn. In the principal variation Black would reply …Qc6, after which White can continue with Kg2 and later bring the bishop back to g4, preserving the pressure.

teacher: Black’s 27…g6 does not block the diagonal of White’s bishop on h3, taking the f5‑square away from it. While this curtails the bishop’s immediate scope, it does nothing to the more critical pin of the e6‑knight to the queen on c8, and White’s advantage widens from a slight edge to about a pawn’s worth. The engine preferred 27…Qc6, which would have kept the evaluation much tighter. Thus g6 is a good move, but it costs Black roughly a tenth of a pawn.
student: By playing …g6 Black tries to take the f5‑square away from White’s bishop on h3, but in doing so he does nothing to relieve the pin that already exists – the bishop still attacks the knight on e6 and leaves the knight vulnerable. The engine rates the move as a slight worsening for Black (about 0.15 pawn) and notes that it costs roughly a third of a pawn compared with the optimal continuation. A more accurate try would have been …Qc6, which keeps the balance without conceding the extra pressure created by the bishop’s pin. Consequently White remains clearly better, now about a pawn ahead.

teacher: White grabs the knight on e6, creating a fork on d5, f7 and the queen and pinning the f‑pawn to the king, but the bishop itself can be taken.
