Black can simply answer Qxe6, which eliminates the fork, captures the bishop and steers the game into a queen‑ending where the material balance is restored, dropping the evaluation by roughly a third of a pawn. Because the queens are exchanged, White’s chances of exploiting the extra material are reduced, making Kg2 the more accurate continuation. Hence the capture is a good try but it costs White a noticeable amount of the earlier edge.
student: White’s capture on e6 wins a knight but immediately allows Black to reply Qxe6, removing the fork and the pin while also taking back the bishop that just attacked the d5‑pawn, the f7‑pawn and the queen. After this forced exchange the game simplifies into a queen ending in which White remains only slightly better – roughly three‑quarters of a pawn instead of the full pawn advantage before the trade. The engine judged Kg2 to be stronger because it would have kept the pressure without giving Black the easy …Qxe6, preserving more of White’s edge. Consequently, Bxe6 costs White about a third of a pawn compared with the optimal continuation.

teacher: White’s king steps to g2, the only move that preserves the tiny edge in this queen‑endgame. Although the move weakens the pawn cover in front of the king, it sidesteps any immediate threats and leaves the evaluation essentially unchanged, with White still a few‑tenths of a pawn better. The engine expects Black’s most natural reply to be 57…h5, after which White can continue 58.h3, then …Kf7 and a checking Qf4+, keeping the initiative.
student: White’s king steps to g2, even though it weakens the pawn shield in front of him, because in this queen‑endgame every square matters and the king must stay active while Black’s pieces remain passive. The engine rates Kg2 as an excellent continuation, keeping White’s slight edge – the evaluation drops by only about six hundredths of a pawn. In the principal variation Black would try …h5, after which White can meet it with h3, then bring the king to f7 and finish with Qf4+, preserving the modest advantage.

teacher: In this queen endgame the pawn structures are locked on opposite colours—White’s pawns sit on dark squares while Black’s are fixed on light—so king safety is paramount. By stepping to h7 Black tucks the king behind its own pawn shield, preserving the balance and keeping the evaluation essentially unchanged, with White still only a hair’s‑breadth better. The move therefore maintains the status quo in a position where any king exposure would immediately swing the tiny edge to White.
student: In this queen‑endgame both sides’ pawns sit on opposite colours – White’s on dark squares and Black’s on light – so the king steps to h7 to keep it safe while remaining central. The engine rates the move as excellent, noting that the evaluation stays virtually the same with White still a hair ahead. If White were to continue with b3, Black can answer Qe7, after which White would have to retreat his king to f3 before Black checks with Qf8+, preserving the balance.

teacher: White strikes with the pawn break a5, directly attacking Black’s b6 pawn. If Black answers bxa5, White recaptures on a5, leaving the a‑file semi‑open for White’s queen while giving Black a semi‑open b‑file and an isolated b4 pawn – a manageable weakness in this queen endgame where White’s pawns sit on dark squares and Black’s on light squares. The engine rates the move as the best, keeping the evaluation at roughly a pawn’s worth in White’s favour. In the principal variation Black would capture, White would recapture, then continue with a6 followed by Qf6, preserving the pressure.
student: White’s a‑pawn thrust a5 strikes directly at Black’s b6 pawn and forces it to be taken, opening the a‑file for White while leaving Black with a semi‑open b‑file. After the inevitable …bxa5, White can recapture with the b‑pawn, but the resulting structure gives White an isolated pawn on b4 that will become a target in this queen ending where both sides’ pawns sit on opposite colours. The engine rates the move as the best continuation, keeping White’s clear advantage of roughly a pawn (+0.73).

teacher: Black captures the pawn on a5, opening the b‑file and removing White’s pawn there. The capture leaves Black with an isolated pawn on a7 (the pawn on a5 is supported by the pawn on a7), and Black is now a pawn up. In this queen‑endgame, with White’s pawns fixed on dark squares and Black’s on light squares, the move is the best available even though it nudges the evaluation a little more in White’s favour, to about a pawn’s worth.
student: By playing …bxa5 Black eliminates White’s pawn on a5 and opens the b‑file for future play, but the capture also leaves both sides with isolated pawns – White on a5 and Black on a7. In this queen ending, where White’s pawns sit on dark squares and Black’s on light, the resulting structure does not improve Black’s standing; the engine still judges White to be about a pawn ahead, and the move actually costs Black roughly a quarter of a pawn in evaluation. Nevertheless it is the best continuation available, as any other try would allow White to keep the extra pawn advantage.

teacher: By playing Qxg7+ White captures the opposing queen with check, simultaneously forking the a7‑pawn, the g6‑pawn and the black king. Black’s only realistic reply is Kxg7, which removes the fork and forces a queen exchange, leaving a winning king‑and‑pawn ending for White; the engine now judges the position a decisive advantage, roughly three pawns ahead. Although the engine’s top choice was the quieter Qf4, the move still improves White’s evaluation by about two pawns, turning the material edge into a clear win.
student: By playing Qxg7+ White not only wins Black’s queen but also creates a fork on the g‑pawn, the a‑pawn and the black king, forcing the only sensible reply Kxg7. After that capture the game simplifies into a pure king‑and‑pawn ending in which White’s dark‑square pawn chain dominates, while Black’s light‑square pawns remain immobile. The engine rates the move as a dramatic improvement – the evaluation jumps from a modest plus to a decisive edge of roughly three pawns – and even flags it as the best continuation despite the alternative Qf4 being marginally stronger. In practice, however, the forced exchange leaves White with a clear material lead and a winning advantage.

teacher: In this pure king‑and‑pawn ending White’s king steps forward to f3, improving its activity in a position where the pawns are locked on opposite colours. The engine judges the move as the best, raising the evaluation by about a pawn and giving White a decisive edge. Black’s most natural reply would be Kf6, after which White can meet it with Kf4 and the continuation proceeds e5+ dxe5+.
student: In this pure king‑and‑pawn ending – with White’s pawns locked on dark squares and Black’s on light – Kf3 nudges the already decisive edge to an even larger one, improving the evaluation by roughly eight‑tenths of a pawn. The engine rates it as the best continuation, rewarding White for keeping the king active while preserving the material balance. After the move Black’s most natural reply would be Kf6, after which White can continue with Kf4 and later meet …e5+ with dxe5+, maintaining the winning pressure.

teacher: White’s Kf4 is the right continuation, keeping the winning edge in this pure king‑and‑pawn ending. By moving the king onto f4 it steps closer to its own dark‑square pawn mass while staying opposite Black’s light‑square pawns, preserving the decisive +4‑pawn advantage (the evaluation only slips a fraction to +4.08). Black’s most natural try would be a6, after which White can continue with f3 and then bring the king back to f7 and e5, maintaining the advantage.
student: In this pure king‑and‑pawn ending, where White’s pawns sit on dark squares while Black’s are locked on light squares, White improves his king’s activity by stepping to f4. The engine rates it as the best continuation, keeping the decisive +4‑pawn edge even though the evaluation slips slightly (about –0.36 pawn). Black’s most natural reply would be …a6, after which White can continue with f3, preserving the winning advantage.

teacher: By pushing …a6 Black creates an isolated pawn on a6 while allowing White’s a‑pawn to become permanently fixed on the dark a5‑square. In this king‑and‑pawn ending, White’s pawns already sit on dark squares and Black’s on light squares, so the new weakness only strengthens White’s positional edge. The engine’s evaluation jumps from a decisive +4.0 pawn advantage for White to about +5.0 pawns, meaning the move cost Black roughly a pawn’s worth of ground. Even though …a6 is the only reasonable try, it still deepens White’s winning prospects.
student: By playing …a6 Black fixes White’s pawn on a5 on a dark square while leaving his own pawn on a6 isolated, which deepens White’s already decisive edge in this king‑and‑pawn ending where both sides’ pawns sit on opposite colours. The engine rates the move as a mistake, worsening Black’s standing by roughly a pawn and pushing the evaluation to about +5 pawns for White. Although it was technically the best continuation available, the resulting structure gives White a clear winning advantage.

teacher: White’s best move is the quiet pawn push f3, which strengthens White's pawn structure in this king and pawn endgame. The engine still sees a decisive winning edge for White – about five pawns – only a shade weaker than before (the evaluation drops by roughly a tenth of a pawn). Black’s most accurate reply would be Kf7, after which White can continue with Ke5, Ke7 and finally push f4, keeping the advantage intact.
student: In this pure king‑and‑pawn ending, where White’s pawns sit on dark squares while Black’s are locked on light squares, White simply reinforces his central pawn with f3, keeping the material balance intact. The engine rates it as the best continuation, even though the evaluation slips by about a tenth of a pawn because Black can answer with …Kf7, after which White would continue Ke5, Ke7 and then play f4 to maintain the pressure. The line shows that White remains decisively ahead, with an advantage of roughly five pawns in a winning endgame.

teacher: Black’s pawn thrust e5+ looks tempting because it forks White’s king on f4 and the pawn on d4, but the pawn can be taken immediately. After White replies dxe5+ the pawn is removed, the check is answered, the d‑file opens for White and a new passed pawn appears on e5, which only strengthens White’s already decisive advantage. The engine rates the move an inaccuracy, noting that the evaluation slips by roughly ‑0.8 pawns; a simple king move such as Kf7 would have kept the material balance and avoided giving White the extra passed pawn.
student: Black’s pawn thrust e5+ looks attractive because it attacks both White’s king on f4 and the pawn on d4, but after the forced dxe5+ the fork disappears and White simply eliminates the attacking pawn while keeping the initiative. The capture also opens the d‑file for White and leaves Black with a semi‑open e‑file, so the material balance remains equal yet the evaluation swings by about three‑quarters of a pawn in White’s favour. In this pure king‑and‑pawn ending – where White’s pawns sit on dark squares and Black’s on light – the engine judged Kf7 to be far stronger, avoiding the costly concession. Consequently, e5+ is an inaccuracy that costs Black roughly a pawn of standing.

teacher: By capturing on e5 with check, White not only eliminates Black’s checking pawn but also opens the d‑file for himself while the e‑file becomes semi‑open for Black. The capture creates a fresh passed pawn on e5 and leaves Black with a passed pawn on d5, yet White’s kingside pawn majority of four against two gives him a clear winning edge in this king‑and‑pawn ending. The engine rates the move as the best, improving White’s already decisive advantage by roughly a quarter of a pawn; the most likely continuation would be 42…Ke6 43.g4 hxg4 44.fxg4.
student: By playing dxe5+ White opens the d‑file while creating a passed pawn on e5, giving the white king a clear line to activate in this pure king‑and‑pawn ending. The capture also leaves Black with a passed pawn on d5, but White’s four‑pawn majority on dark squares remains dominant, which explains why the engine rates the move as the best and even nudges the evaluation up by about a quarter of a pawn. In the principal variation Black would reply Ke6, after which White can continue with g4, preserving the decisive edge.

teacher: Black’s king steps to e6, a move that preserves the already decisive White advantage by centralising and bolstering the d5 pawn against White’s advanced e5 passer. In this pure king‑and‑pawn ending the engine rates the position virtually unchanged – a gain of only about two hundredths of a pawn for Black. White’s most natural reply would be the pawn break g4, striking at the h5 pawn, but Black’s king is already well placed to meet that plan. The engine’s continuation (g4 hxg4 fxg4 d4) shows that Black can hold the position despite White’s material edge.
student: In this pure king‑and‑pawn ending White’s advanced e‑pawn looms while Black’s pieces sit on dark squares, so the king must step forward to protect the h5 pawn. By moving to e6 Black brings his monarch into the line of fire without worsening the already decisive edge for White – the engine still evaluates the position as a winning one for White with roughly six pawns ahead. The most natural continuation would be White’s pawn push g4, after which Black can capture hxg4 and continue with …d4, keeping the balance intact.

teacher: White opens with 1 d4, the engine’s top‑rated move, and it preserves the slight edge White already enjoyed, nudging the evaluation from about +0.23 to +0.30 of a pawn. Material remains equal and the change in the score is only a modest +0.07 pawn. Black’s most natural reply would be 1…Nf6, after which White can continue 2.c4, Black 2…e6 and White 3.Nc3, following the main‑line continuation.
student: White opens with 1.d4!!, the engine’s top choice and the most accurate continuation in this position. The move leaves material equal and keeps White’s slight edge – the evaluation improves by about a seventh of a pawn, confirming that it preserves the modest advantage without creating any new weaknesses. According to the principal variation, Black would reply …Nf6, after which White can continue with c4, followed by …e6 and Nc3, maintaining the balance.

teacher: Black develops the bishop to b4, pinning the knight on c3 to the king on e1 and thus limiting White’s piece coordination. The engine rates it as the best move, with the evaluation shifting only a tenth of a pawn and White still a shade better. In the main line White can try e3, Black answers c5, and after a3 Black can capture on c3, exploiting the pin. The move keeps material equal while curbing White’s development.
student: By playing …Bb4 Black immediately pins White’s knight on c3 to the king on e1, so the knight cannot legally move and thus limits White’s piece coordination. The engine rates the move as good and the best choice, with the evaluation shifting only marginally from +0.24 to +0.34 in White’s favour – a change of about a tenth of a pawn for Black. In the principal variation White would continue with e3, after which Black can answer …c5 and later capture on c3+, keeping the tension alive.

teacher: Black’s castling safely tucks the king away and brings the rook to the f‑file while the bishop on b4 continues to pin the c3‑knight to White’s king, limiting White’s immediate development. The engine rates O‑O as the best continuation, keeping the evaluation essentially unchanged at a roughly equal level. In the principal line White can try Bd2, after which Black can answer with the central break …d5, followed by Nf3 c5, maintaining the balance.
student: By castling, Black tucks the king safely away and connects his rook with the other side, while the bishop on b4 continues to pin White’s knight on c3 to the king. The engine rates this as the best continuation, keeping the evaluation essentially unchanged at roughly equal. In the principal variation White would develop with Bd2, after which Black can answer …d5 and later …c5, preserving the balance.

teacher: Black’s 5…b6 is an excellent quiet move that leaves the position essentially equal, the evaluation moving only a hair from +0.15 to +0.17 in White’s favour. The engine, however, preferred the more active 5…c5, a pawn break that would strike directly at White’s d4 pawn. In the suggested continuation White can play Nf3, Black may answer with d5, then White’s a3 would be met by Bxc3.
student: Black’s …b6 is an excellent quiet move that leaves the balance virtually untouched – the engine still evaluates the position as roughly equal, with only a tiny swing of about two‑hundredths of a pawn against Black. The move does not disturb White’s central pawn structure and keeps material perfectly balanced. Although the engine preferred the more ambitious …c5, which would have struck at White’s d4 pawn, …b6 simply preserves equality without creating any new weaknesses.

teacher: Black’s 6…Bb7 simply develops the queen‑side bishop to a natural diagonal, preserving the balance that the engine had already indicated. The move leaves the position roughly equal, with the evaluation shifting only a hair in Black’s favour (about two‑hundredths of a pawn). White’s most logical continuation would be 7 Nf3, which would eliminate the lingering threat to the pawn on g2.
student: Black’s …Bb7 simply develops the dark‑squared bishop to its natural square, keeping material level and leaving the engine’s assessment virtually unchanged at about +0.15 for White. The move also leaves the balance of forces intact – White can meet it with Nf3, which would remove the lingering pressure on the g2 pawn. In short, the bishop retreat preserves equality while completing development without creating any new weaknesses.

teacher: Black’s …d5 is an excellent pawn break that strikes directly at White’s c4 pawn and simultaneously removes the lingering threat to the bishop on b7. By doing so Black not only frees the bishop but also prepares to complete development with …Bd6 and …Re8 while White’s king is still stuck in the centre. The engine still judges the position roughly equal, but the evaluation nudges a little in Black’s favour (about a seventh of a pawn). In the main line White would continue with a3, after which Black can develop the bishop to d6 and bring the rook to e8.
student: By playing …d5 Black finally strikes at White’s central pawn and simultaneously eliminates the immediate danger to the bishop on b7. The advance also fits naturally with Black having already castled, leaving White’s king still exposed in the centre while Black enjoys a safe kingside setup. The engine rates the move as excellent and the evaluation stays essentially unchanged, confirming that it preserves equality without creating any new weaknesses. In the principal variation White would continue with a3, after which Black can develop the bishop to d6 and later bring the rook to e8.

teacher: White captures the pawn on d5, removing the immediate threat to his own pawn and opening the c‑file for himself while the e‑file becomes semi‑open for Black after the forced …exd5. Because Black can simply recapture, the exchange restores material balance and leaves White’s position a little worse – the evaluation slides from roughly equal to about 0.15 pawn down. The engine therefore preferred the quieter a3, which would have kept the balance without conceding the slight disadvantage. With White’s king still in the centre and Black already castled, the exchange yields no lasting compensation.
student: By playing cxd5 White eliminates Black’s pawn on d5 and opens the c‑file for his pieces, but the capture merely initiates an exchange that will be answered by …exd5, restoring material balance and leaving the evaluation essentially unchanged – the engine even notes a slight dip of about a sixth of a pawn. The move also leaves White’s king still in the centre while Black has already castled, giving Black active play on the queenside. The engine preferred a3, which would have kept the tension without conceding the open c‑file. Consequently, although not a blunder, the move costs White a modest edge compared with the optimal continuation.

teacher: By playing 9…c6 Black steps forward the queenside pawn majority, gaining space on that flank while White’s king is still in the centre and Black has already castled. The engine, however, rates the move as a moderate deterioration for Black—about a third of a pawn—so the evaluation shifts from roughly equal to a roughly equal position. The engine’s preferred continuation was 9…Re8, which would have kept the balance without conceding the small edge.
student: By playing …c6 Black pushes his queenside pawn majority forward, gaining space for the four‑pawn chain against White’s three. The advance does not improve Black’s standing – the engine now judges the position about a third of a pawn worse for Black and prefers the more active Re8 instead. With White’s king still stuck in the centre and Black already castled, the pawn push merely delays any concrete improvement without creating new threats. Consequently the move is “good” but suboptimal compared with the stronger Re8.

teacher: White chose to castle, a solid decision that leaves the position still roughly equal, the evaluation slipping only about a tenth of a pawn. Although the engine rates the move as excellent, it is not the top choice; Ng3 would have kept a marginally better standing for White. In the engine’s line Black would reply Re8, White could continue with Qc2, Black might answer Na6 and White would finally play Ng3. The castling therefore preserves the material balance without changing the overall assessment.
student: White castles kingside, bringing his king to safety and connecting the rooks while keeping material perfectly balanced. The engine rates the move as excellent but notes that it costs about a tenth of a pawn compared with the optimal  Ng3, which would have preserved a slightly larger edge for White. After O‑O Black can continue with …Re8, after which White could answer Qc2 and later bring the knight back to g3, following the suggested continuation in the principal variation. Overall the position remains roughly equal, with no clear advantage gained by the castle.

teacher: Black calmly centralises the rook with …Re8, a simple improvement that leaves the evaluation essentially unchanged – the engine now judges the position to be roughly equal rather than a slight Black edge. The move respects the cramped situation of the bishops: Black's bishop on b7 and White's bishop on f3 each have only two safe squares, while White's bishop on d2 has only one safe square, and it does not worsen that limitation. According to the engine, White’s most testing reply would be 12 Ng3, after which Black can meet it with 12…Bd6, keeping the balance. As the engine’s top choice, …Re8 is rightly judged an excellent move.
student: By retreating the rook to e8 Black immediately improves his piece placement while leaving White’s pieces cramped – both sides’ bishops now have only a single or two safe squares each. The engine rates the move as excellent and notes that it leaves the evaluation essentially unchanged at roughly equal, with Black still holding a slight edge. In the principal variation White would try Ng3, after which Black can continue with …Bd6, keeping the balance intact.

teacher: White’s Re1 simply puts a rook on the e‑file, but that file is already semi‑open for Black and his rook on e8 is the one that actually uses it, so the move does not improve White’s coordination. At the same time White’s bishop on d2 still has no safe squares while Black’s bishop on b7 is limited to only two, leaving White’s pieces cramped and costing roughly a third of a pawn, as the evaluation drops from equality to a slight Black edge. The engine therefore prefers the quieter a3, which would have kept the balance. In the suggested continuation Black can answer with Ne6, after which White’s best try is Nf5, followed by Bf8 (Black) and e4 (White).
student: White’s 13 Re1 simply shuffles the rook to the e‑file, where it already sits with the other rook and does not improve its own cramped situation – both bishops have very few safe squares while Black’s rook on e8 enjoys the semi‑open file. The engine rates the move as “good” but notes that it costs White about a third of a pawn compared with the optimal continuation. A more accurate try would have been 13 a3, which keeps material balanced and avoids giving Black the slight edge after …Ne6. Consequently, Re1 modestly worsens White’s standing despite remaining equal in material.

teacher: White pushes the h‑pawn to h3, expanding the four‑pawn majority on the kingside and depriving Black’s knight on f6 of the g4 square. The engine judges that this concession costs White a little ground – the evaluation slips from a slight Black edge of about half a pawn to roughly six‑tenths of a pawn in Black’s favour. A more precise choice would have been Nce2, which the engine flags as the optimal move and would have kept the balance more favorable for White.
student: White pushes h3 to advance his four‑pawn majority on the kingside and to deprive Black’s knight on f6 of the g4 square. The move does not improve White’s cramped situation – the bishop on d2 still has no safe retreat while Black’s rook already enjoys the semi‑open e‑file – so the evaluation slips from a slight Black edge to roughly a pawn’s advantage. Engine analysis shows that the more accurate continuation would have been Nce2, keeping the tension alive without conceding the extra half‑pawn. Consequently, h3 is a good but suboptimal try that costs White about a tenth of a pawn in the assessment.

teacher: White answered with the quiet pawn move a3, a modest waiting move that leaves material equal and keeps the evaluation at roughly –0.45 pawns, so Black remains only slightly better. It does not relieve the cramped position of White’s bishop on d2, while Black’s bishop on b7 is already confined to two safe squares and the rook on e8 enjoys the semi‑open e‑file. The engine judged Nce2 to be the more accurate continuation, improving the knight’s placement; the suggested line after a3 would be …Bd6 followed by Nce2, gaining a small edge. Nonetheless, a3 does not worsen White’s stance, as reflected by the negligible +0.03‑pawn swing in White’s favour.
student: White’s quiet a3 simply preserves the balance, leaving the position still judged as slightly better for Black – about four‑tenths of a pawn worse for White. The engine notes that the more ambitious Nce2 would have been preferable, but after a3 the evaluation improves by only three hundredths of a pawn, so the move keeps material equal and the slight edge for Black intact. With Black’s bishop on b7 confined to just two safe squares and the rook already exploiting the semi‑open e‑file, White does not create any new threats or weaknesses.

teacher: Re2 is an inaccuracy that costs White roughly a pawn’s worth of evaluation. By sliding the rook to e2 White merely contests the semi‑open e‑file that Black’s rook already exploits, but it does nothing to challenge Black’s central pawn mass or improve the cramped bishop on d2. The engine’s preferred move, f4, would have opened the centre and forced Black to answer with the freeing break …c5, striking at the d4 pawn; by playing the passive rook move White missed this dynamic chance and allowed Black to increase his advantage.
student: White’s 20 Re2 does nothing to meet Black’s looming …c5‑pawn break and simply allows Black to continue with …c5, after which White would have to capture on c5 and then play Bb5, leaving Black clearly ahead by roughly a pawn. The engine rates the move an inaccuracy because it costs White about six‑tenths of a pawn compared with the optimal continuation. A more accurate try would have been 20 f4, which keeps the balance much tighter. After Re2 Black can now strike at the d4 pawn with …c5, exploiting the fact that both sides’ bishops are already cramped – Black’s bishop on b7 has only two safe squares while White’s bishop on d2 has only one.

teacher: Black’s 20…Bd6 is a clear mistake, turning a position that was almost a pawn‑advantage for Black (‑0.98) into an essentially equal one (+0.15). By retreating the bishop, Black forgoes the far more active pawn break c5, which would have struck at White’s d4 pawn and opened lines for the bishop on b7. Instead the bishop move merely shuffles a piece, while Black’s bishop on b7 already has only two safe squares, and White’s bishop on d2 remains cramped and Black’s rook on the semi‑open e‑file loses any immediate prospects. In short, the move costs Black roughly a pawn of evaluation compared with the engine‑recommended 20…c5.
student: By playing …Bd6 Black abandoned the clear edge it enjoyed – the evaluation slipped from about a pawn’s worth to essentially equality, costing roughly a pawn. The move does nothing to address White’s active bishop on d2 or the cramped situation of Black’s own bishop on b7, and it allows White to neutralise Black’s initiative without any compensation. The engine indicates that the far stronger continuation would have been the pawn break …c5, striking at White’s d‑pawn and keeping the pressure alive. Consequently, …Bd6 is a mistake that hands the initiative back to White.

teacher: White’s retreat of the queen to e1 does little to meet Black’s looming pawn break; it places the queen on the semi‑open e‑file that Black already exploits with the rook on e8 and does not improve the cramped bishops—White’s bishop on d2 has no safe squares while Black’s bishop on b7 is already limited. Consequently Black can comfortably play …c5, striking at the d4 pawn and entering the engine‑suggested line c5 dxc5 bxc5 Bb5, which gives Black a clear advantage of about a pawn. The engine even preferred the quieter Be1, which would have kept the position more balanced. As a result, the move costs White roughly a pawn’s worth of evaluation.
student: White’s retreat Qe1 does nothing to relieve the cramped situation – the bishop on d2 still has no safe squares and Black’s bishop on b7 remains limited to just two safe squares while the rook on e8 already enjoys the semi‑open e‑file. By playing Qe1 White allows Black the thematic …c5 break, striking at the pawn on d4 and exploiting the weakened centre, which swings the evaluation sharply in Black’s favour. The engine rates the move an inaccuracy, costing roughly a pawn compared with the best alternative Be1, which would have kept material balance and avoided giving Black the active plan.

teacher: By moving the king to g7 Black missed the more active pawn break c5, which would have struck at White’s d4 pawn and preserved the initiative. The quiet king move does nothing to the central tension, and the engine now sees the position as roughly equal—a loss of about three‑quarters of a pawn for Black. White can simply continue with Qf2, after which Black’s best reply would be Bf8, keeping the balance. Consequently the move is an inaccuracy that costs Black the clear advantage they previously enjoyed.
student: By moving the king to g7 Black steps out of the centre and allows White’s pressure to neutralise the earlier edge, turning a clear pawn‑plus advantage into an almost equal balance. The engine rates the move as an inaccuracy because it missed the more active pawn break c5, which would have struck at White’s d4 pawn and kept Black ahead by roughly a pawn. After Kg7 White can continue with Qf2, after which Black could try Bf8, but the evaluation drops sharply, leaving material even and the game essentially balanced.

teacher: White’s 24.Bc3 is a clear mistake, turning a modest plus for White into a comfortable advantage for Black (the evaluation drops by almost two pawns). The move squanders the tactical shot Nxd6, which would have captured the bishop on d6 and simultaneously forked the pawn on f7 and the rook on e8 – even though the forking knight could be taken, it still wins material. By retreating the bishop, White leaves the d4 pawn vulnerable; Black can reply cxd4, and after White’s natural Bxd4 recapture the material stays level, but Black’s active pieces and the semi‑open e‑file give him a clear advantage. This sequence costs White roughly two pawns of value.
student: By playing Bc3 White simply shuffles a bishop that already has very few safe squares while Black’s rook continues to dominate the semi‑open e‑file. The engine shows this costs roughly two pawns, turning a slight edge into a clear disadvantage. A far stronger try would have been Nxd6, which not only wins the bishop on d6 but also forks the pawn on f7 and the rook on e8, leaving Black with little compensation. After Bc3 Black can reply cxd4, after which White must recapture with the bishop, allowing Black to consolidate his advantage.

teacher: White’s a‑pawn advance fixes Black’s pawn on a5 on a dark square and squeezes the already cramped bishop on a6, which now has very few safe squares. With both Black bishops limited to only two retreat squares each, White curtails Black’s piece activity, even though the engine still judges Black a little better (the move costs White about a tenth of a pawn). Black’s most natural reply would be cxd4, winning the pawn on d4, after which the continuation runs Bxd4 Bb4 Rec2. This is the best move White can play in the position.
student: By pushing a4 White locks Black’s pawn on a5 onto a dark square and further restricts the already cramped bishop on a6, which now has only two safe retreats. The advance also fixes the pawn structure while leaving Black’s bishop on e7 with very few useful squares. Although it is the best continuation available, the engine still judges the position as clearly better for Black – roughly three‑quarters of a pawn worse than before. Black can reply with cxd4, winning the pawn on d4, after which White would recapture with the bishop and continue with Bb4 and Rec2.

teacher: Black’s capture cxd4 seizes the pawn on d4 and, after the inevitable Bxd4, opens the c‑file for Black while leaving White with a semi‑open d‑file. The exchange restores material balance, but because Black already was a pawn up, the net result is a one‑pawn advantage despite the resulting isolated queen’s pawn on d5. White’s most natural recapture, Bxd4, would pin the f6‑knight to the king on g7, limiting Black’s coordination, yet the engine still rates the move as the best continuation, keeping the evaluation essentially unchanged.
student: By playing …cxd4 Black eliminates White’s central pawn and forces the natural reply Bxd4, after which the c‑file opens while the d‑file becomes semi‑open for White. The capture also leaves Black with an isolated queen’s pawn on d5 but does not win material because White can simply recapture with the bishop. With both sides’ bishops limited to just two safe squares each, the exchange keeps the position balanced – the engine still evaluates Black as clearly better by roughly three‑quarters of a pawn. This precise simplification makes cxd4 the best continuation.

teacher: White’s capture on d4 opens the e‑file but, more importantly, it leaves White with an isolated queen’s pawn on d4 and relinquishes the semi‑open d‑file, giving Black the tactical shot … Nf4, which forks the rook on e2 and the bishop on d3. The engine rates the move a mistake, worsening White’s position by roughly a pawn (from a clear Black advantage to a much larger one). The engine’s preferred continuation was Bxd4, which would have captured the pawn while pinning the f6‑knight to the king and eliminating the threat to the bishop on d4. By playing exd4 White missed this resource and allowed Black to obtain a significantly better game.
student: By playing exd4 White opened the e‑file but gave up the semi‑open d‑file that would have allowed the bishop on d3 to become active, leaving an isolated queen’s pawn on d4 and removing the pressure on the bishop on c3. The capture also fixes Black’s pawn on d5 on a light square while Black can immediately reply …Nf4, forking the rook on e2 and the bishop on d3, which explains why the evaluation slid from a modest disadvantage to a clear one‑pawn deficit. The engine indicates that the correct continuation was Bxd4, which would have captured the pawn without creating those tactical liabilities. Consequently, exd4 is a mistake that costs White roughly a pawn in material and positional terms.

teacher: Black’s 26…Nf4 creates a fork, hitting the rook on e2 and the bishop on d3 and exploiting the fact that White’s bishops each have only two safe squares. The move leaves the evaluation essentially unchanged, with Black still much better by well over a pawn. White can meet the threat with 27 Re3, which would both protect the bishop and move the rook out of danger, after which Black can continue 27…Nxd3 28 Rxd3 Qd7, preserving the superior position.
student: By jumping to f4 Black creates an immediate fork, attacking White’s rook on e2 and bishop on d3 at once. The engine rates the move as excellent and the best continuation, keeping Black’s sizable advantage essentially unchanged – still about two pawns ahead. White can meet the threat with Re3, which would remove the pressure on both the bishop and the rook, but even after that line Black remains clearly better.

teacher: White slides the rook to d2, which does eliminate the immediate threat to the bishop on d3 and the rook on that square.  Nevertheless, the engine notes that Re3 would have defended the bishop and rook more effectively, and the inaccuracy costs White about six‑tenths of a pawn, deepening Black’s lead to more than two pawns.  After Rd2 White’s bishop on c3 still has no safe squares while Black’s bishop on a6 is equally cramped, and Black’s rook on e8 continues to control the open e‑file.  Thus Black remains much better.
student: White’s 27.Rd2 simply steps the rook onto d2 to eliminate the immediate danger to both the bishop on d3 and the rook that had just moved there. Although it does stop the attack, the engine points out that the more accurate 27.Re3 would have removed the same threats while keeping the rook on a safer square, thereby preserving material balance. By opting for Rd2 White’s evaluation slipped by roughly half a pawn, leaving Black with a clear advantage of about two‑and‑a‑half pawns.

teacher: Black captures the bishop on d3, creating a fork on White’s rook on c1 and queen on f2, but the fork is short‑lived. White can simply answer with Rxd3, removing the threat, recapturing the knight and restoring material balance, which drags the evaluation from a comfortable –2.47 pawn advantage to about –1.9 pawns for Black. The engine’s preferred move was the quiet Qd7, which would have kept Black’s edge without giving White the easy exchange. Thus the knight capture is an inaccuracy, costing Black roughly half a pawn of the advantage.
student: By playing …Nxd3 Black wins the bishop on d3, but the capture merely initiates an exchange that White can meet with Rxd3, removing the fork and restoring material balance while giving up the bishop pair. The engine rates this as an inaccuracy because it costs Black about half a pawn of evaluation – the position drops from roughly –2.5 to –1.9 pawns. A more accurate continuation would have been …Qd7, which keeps the pressure without allowing the forced trade. After the forced Rxd3, White’s best reply is Bd2, after which Black could continue with Qd7, preserving the advantage.

teacher: By taking on b5 Black eliminates White’s active knight and forces the pawn recapture axb5, which leaves White with isolated and doubled pawns on the b‑file and a pawn fixed on a light square. Although the material balance is restored, those structural weaknesses—combined with White’s bishop on c3 now having only two safe squares—give Black a lasting positional edge. Black also keeps the bishop pair and a rook on the open e‑file, so the evaluation remains at roughly a pawn and two‑thirds in Black’s favour. The natural continuation would be axb5 followed by Qxb5, after which White can try Rce1 and Black can retreat the bishop to f8.
student: By taking on b5 Black eliminates White’s active knight and forces the natural recapture axb5, which leaves White with isolated and doubled b‑pawns while also giving Black a semi‑open a‑file that can be exploited later. The exchange does not change the overall assessment – Black remains about a pawn ahead – but it creates concrete weaknesses in White’s structure without conceding any material. With the bishop pair and the rook on e8 already exerting pressure along the open e‑file, the position stays clearly better for Black.

teacher: White’s 31.Ng3 is a good move in a cramped position where the bishop on c3 is limited to only two safe squares and both sides are fighting for control of the open e‑file.  Nevertheless it nudged the evaluation a little deeper into Black’s favor, slipping from about –1.7 pawns to nearly –2 pawns.  The engine’s top choice, 31.Rce1, would have kept more pressure on the e‑file and avoided the modest loss.  As a result Black remains much better.
student: White’s 31.Ng3 does little to improve his cramped situation – the bishop on c3 still has only two safe squares and Black’s rook already dominates the open e‑file with …Qd7, so the knight shift offers no concrete compensation. The engine rates it as a slight worsening for White (about a quarter‑pawn) and notes that the stronger continuation would have been 31.Rce1, which keeps more pressure on the e‑file. Consequently Black remains clearly better, now about two pawns ahead.

teacher: White’s rook jumps to e5, pinning the d5‑pawn to Black’s queen on b5 and denying the bishop on d6 the squares f4 and g3. The rook is technically en prise, but the pin and the control of the open e‑file offset any immediate danger, leaving the position essentially unchanged – Black remains about a pawn up. The engine rates Re5 as the best move, confirming that White’s active piece placement compensates for the material deficit.
student: By playing Re5 White not only places his rook on the open e‑file but also pins the d5‑pawn to Black’s queen on b5, thereby limiting Black’s bishop on d6. The rook on e5 does become en prise, yet it deprives Black’s pieces of useful squares—f4 and g3—and keeps the pressure on the centre despite White’s cramped bishop on c3. The engine rates the move as excellent and the best continuation, with the evaluation remaining essentially unchanged at about –2 pawns for White. In the principal line Black would reply …Qd3, after which White can continue Ne2, followed by …Rac8 and Nf4.

teacher: Black pushes a4, extending its queenside pawn majority (three pawns against White’s two). The engine judges the move a moderate inaccuracy, costing roughly four‑tenths of a pawn compared with the optimal Qd3, which would have kept a larger advantage. The position remains favorable for Black – the rooks still contest the open e‑file and White’s rook continues to pin the d5 pawn – but the advance missed a more precise continuation.
student: By playing …a4 Black pushes his queenside pawn majority forward, gaining space and preparing to expand on that wing. The advance does not change the fact that White’s rook on e5 still pins the d‑pawn to the queen on b5, so Black cannot immediately exploit the newly created tension. Consequently the engine judges the move as a moderate worsening for Black – roughly a third of a pawn – even though he remains clearly better with about a pawn advantage. The engine preferred Qd3, which would have kept more pressure without conceding the extra pawn.

teacher: White’s 34.Nf5 places the knight on a square where it can be taken, leaving the piece en prise.  Nevertheless it is the best continuation, only slipping White’s standing by roughly a tenth of a pawn (the evaluation moves from about a pawn‑down to a little more than a pawn‑down).  Black can answer with …Bf8, removing the threat to the bishop; White can then continue with Ne7+, Black replies Kh7, and White follows up with Re1, as the engine’s principal variation suggests.
student: White’s knight jumps to f5, but it immediately becomes en prise and Black can answer with …Bf8, removing the threat to the bishop on f8. The engine still rates the move as good – it is the best continuation available even though it costs White roughly a tenth of a pawn in evaluation. After …Bf8 White could try Ne7+, forcing the king to h7 and then Re1, keeping the pressure alive despite Black’s clear advantage.

teacher: Black’s 35…Nh7 is an excellent defensive maneuver, simply pulling the knight back to a safe square and eliminating the immediate danger to it. Although the retreat leaves the pawn on h5 hanging, the move does not alter the balance of forces – Black remains about two pawns ahead and the evaluation stays essentially unchanged. With the knight secure, Black can continue the plan suggested by the engine, for example …Qd7 followed by …Nf6, while White’s best try, 36 Qg3, only removes the threat to the queen without gaining material. The position stays dominated by Black’s extra pawn and active rooks on the open e‑file.
student: By retreating the knight to h7 Black eliminates the immediate danger that White’s queen posed to it, even though the move leaves the pawn on h5 hanging. The retreat preserves Black’s sizable advantage – the engine still evaluates the position as about two pawns better for Black and notes that the move changes the score by only a few hundredths of a pawn. White could try Qg3, which would remove the pressure on the queen, but after …Qd7 Black can continue with Ne3 and Nf6, keeping the edge intact. This precise defensive resource therefore earns an “excellent” label.

teacher: Black’s queen jumps to d3, sharpening the evaluation by about a pawn and pushing the position into a winning‑type advantage. The move, however, leaves the pawn on d5 undefended, and White can answer with Nh4, uncovering a discovered attack by the rook on e5 against the h5 pawn while also eyeing the hanging d5 pawn. The engine’s top choice was Qd7, which would have kept the d5 pawn protected, but even without that the move still leaves Black a pawn up with a decisive edge.
student: By playing …Qd3 Black not only preserves his one‑pawn material edge but also nudges the evaluation from a comfortable –2 pawns to a decisive –3 pawns, a swing of about a pawn in his favour. The engine’s top choice was …Qd7, yet …Qd3 still improves the position and leaves White with no immediate counterplay. If White tries the natural 37.Nh4, it would uncover a discovered attack by the rook on e5 against the pawn on h5, allowing Black to continue with Rxe5 and keep the initiative. In short, the move solidifies Black’s advantage while keeping the pressure alive.

teacher: By playing 37.Rxd5 White wins a pawn but also opens the d‑file, giving Black a semi‑open line for the rook and allowing Black’s pieces to become more active; the evaluation slides from a decisive Black advantage of about three pawns to roughly four, a loss of about a pawn for White. Although the capture creates a passed pawn on d4, Black’s rook on e8 already dominates the open e‑file, so the net effect is unfavorable. The engine points out that the far stronger 37.Nh4 would have uncovered a discovered attack on the h5 pawn with the rook on e5, keeping pressure on Black’s king. Consequently, Rxd5 is a clear mistake, costing White roughly a pawn of value.
student: By playing Rxd5 White simply trades a pawn and opens the d‑file for Black, while also creating a passed pawn on d4 but leaving the material balance unchanged. The engine shows that this costs roughly a pawn in evaluation, pushing Black’s already decisive edge to about four pawns. A far stronger try would have been Nh4, which would have uncovered the rook on e5’s line against the h5 pawn and kept more pressure on Black’s king side. Consequently, the capture is a clear mistake that hands Black an even larger advantage.

teacher: Black’s 37…h4 looks like a pawn‑storm idea, but it simply leaves the pawn on h4 en prise and allows White to answer 38 Qf4, after which the knight on f5 is hanging. By fixing White’s pawn on h3 on a light square the move gains nothing, and the evaluation drops from a decisive –4.3 to –3.3, roughly a pawn of lost ground. The engine’s preferred continuation was 37…Nf6, which would have kept Black’s winning edge.
student: By playing …h4 Black leaves the pawn on h4 hanging and fixes White’s pawn on h3 on a light square, which costs roughly a pawn in evaluation. The engine shows that the far stronger continuation would have been …Nf6, keeping material balanced and preserving the decisive edge. After …h4 White can reply with Qf4, removing the pressure on the queen while also leaving the knight on f5 vulnerable, so Black’s winning chances are reduced by about a pawn.

teacher: By playing Qxh4 White eliminates the pawn that was threatening the queen and nets a pawn, but the capture also leaves the knight on f5 en prise. Black can answer with gxf5, winning the hanging piece and preserving the decisive advantage; the engine’s preferred continuation, Qf4, would have removed the queen’s danger but still leaves the knight on f5 en prise. Consequently the evaluation remains essentially unchanged, still around a three‑pawn disadvantage for White despite the material gain. In a lost position this is an excellent practical try, as it at least secures a pawn and clears the queen’s immediate threat.
student: By playing Qxh4 White eliminates the immediate danger to her queen and wins a pawn, but the capture also leaves the knight on f5 en prise. Black can simply reply gxf5, taking that piece, so the engine’s evaluation stays at roughly a three‑pawn disadvantage for White – essentially unchanged from before the move. The engine preferred Qf4, which would have removed the same queen‑threat while keeping the knight safe, yet the chosen move remains an excellent practical try because it does not worsen White’s already losing position.

teacher: By taking on f5 Black eliminates White’s active knight and preserves the material edge that already gave him a decisive advantage. The capture opens the g‑file, providing Black with a semi‑open line, but it also leaves him with isolated, doubled pawns on f5 and f7 and a slightly weakened pawn shield in front of his king. With the rook on e8 already controlling the open e‑file, Black can meet White’s most natural reply Re1 with a simple exchange on e1, after which the position remains winning for Black. The evaluation stays around –3.25 pawns, confirming the move’s excellent quality.
student: By capturing on f5 Black eliminates White’s active knight and opens the g‑file, giving the rook on e8 a clear line to operate while the white rook continues to dominate the c‑file. The exchange leaves Black with isolated and doubled pawns on the f‑file but also creates a semi‑open g‑file that can be exploited later, which is why the engine rates the move as excellent even though it slightly weakens the pawn shield in front of Black’s king. With the new g‑pawn and the rook activity, Black remains decisively ahead – roughly three pawns – and the position stays a winning one for Black.

teacher: White meets Black’s domination of the open e‑file by bringing the rook to e1, directly contesting that file and relieving the pressure on a bishop that now has only two safe squares. It is the engine’s top choice even though it nudges the evaluation a little deeper into Black’s decisive advantage (about a quarter of a pawn). Black would likely continue with …Bg7, after which White could try Rd7, but Black can simply capture on e1 with the rook, delivering check. Thus the move is the best practical try to hold the position together.
student: By placing the rook on e1 White finally contests the open e‑file, joining Black’s rook that already dominates it and thereby curbing Black’s control of the file. The engine rates Re1 as the best continuation, even though the evaluation slips by about a quarter pawn because Black still enjoys a decisive edge. In the principal variation Black can continue with …Bg7, after which White would have to meet Rd7 and then capture on e1 with check, but the resulting line does not improve White’s chances.

teacher: White’s 40 bxa3 tries to open the b‑file and give White a queenside pawn majority, but it immediately leaves the bishop on c3 en prise. Black can reply 40…Qxc3, winning the bishop (and even leaving the f5‑pawn vulnerable), which pushes the already decisive Black advantage from about three and a third pawns to roughly four and a half pawns. In addition, the capture creates a semi‑open a‑file for Black’s rook on a8 while White is saddled with an isolated pawn on a3. The engine’s preferred continuation was 40 Rde5, which would have avoided the loss of the bishop and the material deficit.
student: By playing bxa3 White opens the a‑file and leaves the bishop on c3 hanging, while also creating an isolated pawn on a3 and giving Black’s rook on a8 a useful semi‑open line. The capture does nothing to stop Black’s active pieces – the queen can simply take the bishop with Qxc3, after which the pawn on f5 becomes vulnerable – and it actually deepens White’s disadvantage by about a pawn. The engine indicates that the far stronger continuation would have been Rde5, keeping the balance instead of handing Black a clear edge. Consequently the move costs White roughly one pawn in evaluation.

teacher: By capturing on c3 Black eliminates White’s active bishop and nudges the evaluation a shade deeper in Black’s favor, turning a decisive –4.48 into –4.68. The trade does leave the pawn on f5 en prise, giving White a tactical target. White’s most forcing reply would be Rxe8, after which Black can simply recapture with Rxe8 and keep the material edge. The resulting position leaves Black up a full bishop with solid control of both the e‑ and a‑files.
student: By taking on c3 Black eliminates White’s active bishop and secures a four‑pawn material edge, nudging the evaluation from a decisive –4.48 to an even sharper –4.68 in Black’s favour. The capture does leave the pawn on f5 hanging, but with both sides’ rooks already contesting the open e‑file the resulting structure gives Black enough compensation. White could try Rxe8, pinning the bishop on f8 to the king, yet after …Rxe8 …Kh2 …Qc2 Black remains clearly ahead. This precise exchange therefore earns the “best” label.

teacher: White captures the black rook on e8, pinning the bishop on f8 to the king and taking command of the open e‑file. The move initiates an exchange—Black’s recapture restores material balance, so White ends up merely a pawn ahead. Even though it is the best move available, the engine judges the resulting position slightly worse for White, deepening Black’s decisive advantage by about a fifth of a pawn.
student: By playing Rxe8 White eliminates Black’s active rook on e8 and simultaneously pins the remaining bishop on f8 to the black king on g8, leaving that piece unable to move without exposing the king. The capture initiates an exchange that will be answered by …Rxf5, after which Black can continue with Qe1+ forcing a queen trade, but even this line leaves Black clearly ahead – the engine still evaluates the position as a decisive Black advantage, now about four‑and‑a‑half pawns in Black’s favour. Although it is the best continuation available, the move costs White roughly two‑tenths of a pawn compared with the previous evaluation.

teacher: By capturing the pawn on f5, White reduces Black's material lead and nudges the evaluation in his favour by roughly a sixth of a pawn, though Black still enjoys a decisive advantage. According to the engine, Black’s most natural reply would be Re6, after which White can continue with Re5, leading to a sequence of trades.
student: By taking on f5 White eliminates Black’s last central pawn and nudges the evaluation in his favour by about a sixth of a pawn, even though Black still enjoys a decisive material edge. The capture also leaves White with a rook on f5 while Black’s rook continues to dominate the open e‑file, so the engine rates it as the best continuation. In the principal line Black would reply …Re6, after which White can continue Re5, keeping the pressure alive despite the ongoing disadvantage.

teacher: Black launches a tactical strike with Qe1+, forking White’s king on g1 and queen on h4. The idea looks tempting, but White can meet the check by taking the queen (Qxe1), after which Black’s rook on the open e‑file recaptures with check, leaving Black only a fraction of a pawn worse (the evaluation slips from about –5 to –4.8). Thus the move is merely a good try; the engine judged Re6 to be superior, preserving a larger winning edge. The position remains winning for Black, but the fork costs a small amount of the advantage.
student: Black’s queen jumps to e1 with check, forking White’s king on g1 and queen on h4 while also taking full advantage of the open e‑file that his rook already dominates. In practice White can simply capture the queen with Qxe1, after which Black recaptures with the rook and continues the attack, but the engine judges the move as a slight inaccuracy – about a sixth of a pawn worse than the optimal continuation. The engine preferred Re6, which would have kept more pressure without allowing the immediate exchange. Nonetheless, the fork still wins material and leaves Black clearly ahead.

teacher: White continues with the natural developing move Nf3, bringing a piece into the game, attacking the e5 pawn and preparing to castle. The engine rates it as the best continuation, nudging the evaluation from +0.28 to +0.31 – essentially unchanged. Black’s most logical reply would be …Nc6, which removes the threat to the pawn on e5. The move therefore preserves White’s slight edge.
student: White develops the knight to its natural square f3, keeping the modest edge that existed after 1.e4 e5. The engine rates this as the best continuation, and the evaluation barely improves from +0.28 to +0.31 – essentially unchanged in practical terms. Black’s most accurate reply would be …Nc6, which simply eliminates the pressure on the e‑pawn. In the principal variation White can continue with Bb5, followed by …a6 and Ba4.

teacher: Black’s castling is the only move that preserves the balance, and it immediately eliminates the pressure on the f‑pawn – the rook now shields the king and the threat to f2 disappears. The engine rates it as the best move, keeping the evaluation at a modest White edge (+0.22) and keeping Black’s standing essentially unchanged, with only a few hundredths of a pawn shift. In the principal variation Black would continue with …d5, after which White’s natural exd5 is met by …Qxd5, but the castling itself already neutralises White’s slight initiative.
student: By castling, Black eliminates White’s immediate pressure on the f‑pawn and brings the king safely into the game while also connecting the rooks. The engine rates this as the best continuation, keeping the evaluation virtually unchanged – White remains only a fraction of a pawn ahead. In the principal variation White would continue with d5, after which Black can capture on d5 and recapture with the queen, preserving material equality.

teacher: With 6…d5 Black launches a central pawn break that directly attacks White’s e4 pawn and, after the ensuing exchange, opens the d‑file for Black’s pieces. After the expected 7.exd5 Black can recapture with the queen, leaving White with doubled pawns on the d‑file and a semi‑open d‑file for Black while the e‑file becomes semi‑open for White. The move also exploits the bishop on c5, which already pins the f2‑pawn to the king, making the e4 pawn harder to defend. The engine rates it as the best continuation, keeping the evaluation essentially equal.
student: Black’s …d5 is a timely pawn break that strikes directly at White’s e‑pawn and opens the d‑file for his pieces while leaving material perfectly balanced. After the natural capture exd5, the d‑file becomes semi‑open for Black and White ends up with doubled pawns on that file, giving Black active play along the open line. The move also preserves the pin of the f2‑pawn by the bishop on c5, so Black remains well‑placed despite the slight drop in the engine’s assessment from +0.14 to +0.09. In short, …d5 keeps the balance and prepares concrete chances without conceding any advantage.

teacher: White develops the light‑squared bishop to the natural square c4, keeping material level and leaving the engine’s assessment essentially unchanged at roughly equal (+0.20). The move does not relieve the existing pin of the f‑pawn by Black’s bishop on c5, but it nevertheless is the best continuation, improving White’s standing by only a small fraction of a pawn. Black’s most accurate reply would be 8…Qd8, which would remove the queen’s exposure on d5. According to the principal variation the game could continue 9 b4 Bd6 Re1.
student: White’s retreat Bc4 simply preserves the balance, keeping the engine’s assessment at roughly +0.20 for White and leaving material perfectly equal. By moving back to c4 White sidesteps any immediate danger while Black’s bishop on c5 continues to pin the f‑pawn to the white king. The engine rates this as the best continuation, with Black’s most natural reply being …Qd8, which would remove the pressure on the queen.

teacher: White advances the queenside pawn majority with b4, giving him four pawns against Black’s three on that flank. The move leaves the evaluation essentially unchanged at roughly equal and maintains the mutual pins – White’s bishop on c4 still pins the f‑pawn to Black’s king, while Black’s bishop on c5 pins White’s f‑pawn to his own king. Black’s most natural reply would be …Bd6, which would remove the pressure on the bishop that could appear on d6. The engine’s continuation (Bd6 Re1 h6 a4) shows both sides keeping the balance while the queenside tension grows.
student: By playing b4 White expands his queenside pawn majority, turning a four‑pawn versus three‑pawn structure into a more active one while keeping material perfectly balanced. The advance also respects the pin created by Black’s bishop on c5, which now attacks the f2‑pawn and cannot be moved without losing its own safety. Black’s most natural reply would be …Bd6, simply removing the immediate pressure on the bishop, after which White can continue with Re1 and later push a4 to consolidate the newly gained space. This subtle but precise pawn thrust therefore preserves equality and secures long‑term chances.

teacher: Black pushes 10…h6, advancing a pawn of its kingside pawn majority. The move does not address the pin on the f7‑pawn created by White’s bishop on c4, and it leaves Black’s bishop on d6 confined to its only safe square, so the engine judges the position to be still roughly equal but about a tenth of a pawn better for White. It notes that the stronger continuation would have been 10…e4, a central pawn break striking at White’s d3 pawn. Thus, while 10…h6 is a decent waiting move, it slightly worsens Black’s standing compared with the optimal plan.
student: By playing …h6 Black simply pushes the last pawn of his kingside majority, gaining space for the four‑pawn chain against White’s three. The advance does little to relieve the pin on the f7‑pawn created by White’s bishop on c4 and leaves the bishop on d6 with its single safe retreat, so the engine judges it a slight inaccuracy – about a sixth of a pawn worse than the optimal continuation. The engine preferred the central break …e4, which would have struck at White’s d3 pawn and kept more pressure on the centre. After …h6 White can continue with Nbd2, after which Black might try …a6, followed by a4 and Re8.

teacher: The move a6 is a quiet, prophylactic pawn push that leaves Black’s cramped pieces untouched – the bishop on d6 still has only one safe square and White’s bishop on c4 continues to pin the f‑pawn. It is the engine’s top choice and costs Black only about a tenth of a pawn, so the position remains essentially equal with a slight edge to White. By playing on the flank, Black preserves the current tension without creating new weaknesses.
student: Black’s …a6 simply reinforces the centre and keeps the pawn structure solid while the white bishop on c4 continues to pin the f‑pawn to the black king. The engine rates it as the best continuation, even though White now enjoys a small edge – about a tenth of a pawn more favourable for White. In the principal line White can try a4, after which Black would answer with Re8, followed by Re1 and Qe7. Overall the move is sound but costs Black a modest amount of evaluation advantage.

teacher: White advances his queenside pawn majority with a4, while the evaluation stays essentially unchanged (only a few hundredths of a pawn worse). By keeping the bishop on c4 pinning the f7‑pawn, Black’s natural reply Re8 would leave that pawn en prise, so Black cannot easily relieve the pressure. The move also respects the cramped position of Black’s bishop on d6, which has only one safe square, and does not create any new weaknesses for White’s own bishops. The engine rates a4 as an excellent, best move, with the continuation Re8 – Re1 – Rb8 – a5.
student: By playing a4 White expands his queenside pawn majority, turning a three‑pawn versus Black’s four into a solid four‑pawn majority and giving the side more space on that flank. The advance also leaves the f7‑pawn pinned by White’s bishop on c4, so even if Black replies with …Re8 the pawn would be left en prise. With both sides’ bishops limited—Black’s d6‑bishop having only one safe square and White’s c1‑bishop just two—the extra pawn activity compensates for any slight drop in the engine’s assessment, keeping the position roughly equal. This precise pawn push therefore earns the “excellent” label as the best continuation.

teacher: White’s 13.Qc2 is a solid, “good” move that simply redeploys the queen while keeping the bishop on c4’s pin on the f‑pawn intact. However, it allows Black to answer with …Be6, which eliminates the pressure on f7 and therefore improves Black’s standing, costing White roughly a tenth of a pawn. The engine judged that 13.Re1 would have been stronger, keeping more tension on the e‑file. Consequently the position remains roughly equal, but the queen move is a slight step back compared with the optimal continuation.
student: White’s retreat Qc2 does little more than preserve the status quo – it simply re‑positions the queen while leaving Black’s bishop on d6 still cramped and the pin on the f7‑pawn untouched. The engine rates the move as “good” but notes that it costs White about a tenth of a pawn compared with the optimal continuation Re1, which would have kept the balance. After Qc2 Black can meet the pressure by playing …Be6, removing the immediate threat to the f7‑pawn. In short, the move is solid but not the most accurate choice in this middlegame.

teacher: Black’s 13…Bf5 places the bishop on the f‑file, pinning White’s pawn on d3 to the queen on c2. While the pin creates a tactical nuisance, it does nothing to the more acute pressure on Black’s pawn on f7, which remains pinned by White’s bishop on c4; the engine noted that the alternative 13…Be6 would have removed that threat. As a result Black’s position is now a little worse – roughly a fifth of a pawn down – though the overall balance of the game remains roughly equal.
student: By playing …Bf5 Black creates a pin of the d‑pawn against White’s queen on c2, but the move also leaves the more urgent problem that the pawn on f7 remains under attack by White’s bishop on c4. The engine judged Be6 – which would have removed the threat to f7 – as superior, and after …Bf5 the evaluation slipped by about a fifth of a pawn in Black’s favour. Thus the move is still “good” in that it does not lose material, yet it costs Black a small edge compared with the optimal continuation.

teacher: By playing …Rxe6 Black eliminates the bishop that was menacing the f7 pawn, thereby removing White’s immediate pressure and keeping material level. The capture also forces White to give up the bishop pair, while Black’s remaining bishop on d6 is left with only two safe squares, limiting its scope. The engine rates the move as excellent, with the evaluation staying roughly equal at about a tenth of a pawn in Black’s favour. In the principal continuation White would try Re1, after which Black can continue with …Qd7, …Bb2 and …Nxe4.
student: By playing Rxe6 Black eliminates White’s active bishop and simultaneously removes the immediate danger to the pawn on f7. The capture also leaves material level while keeping the engine’s assessment essentially unchanged at roughly equal. With Black’s own bishop on d6 confined to just two safe squares, this exchange preserves the balance without creating any new weaknesses. Consequently the move is judged excellent and is indeed the best continuation.

teacher: Black captures the knight on e4, but the exchange is forced to be undone by White’s d‑pawn: after 17.dxe4 the d‑file opens and White’s pawn on e4 is fixed on a light square, while the e‑file – previously semi‑open for White’s rook on e1 – is no longer available to him. This leaves Black’s bishop on d6 with only two safe squares and, despite being up three points of material, the position is evaluated slightly worse for Black, with White still a shade better. The engine therefore judged 16…Qd7 as the superior alternative, preserving the e‑file pressure without conceding the exchange.
student: By playing …Nxe4 Black wins a piece and opens the d‑file after White’s forced dxe4, but the capture also fixes White’s pawn on e4 on a light square and closes the e‑file that White had been exploiting. This exchange does not restore material equality – the engine still evaluates the position as slightly better for White – because the newly opened d‑file gives White active play while Black’s bishop on d6 remains cramped with only two safe squares. The engine preferred Qd7, which would have kept the balance without conceding the open file. Consequently, the move costs Black about a sixth of a pawn in evaluation.
violations: claims material is won, but the capture is an exchange

teacher: Black’s 17…a5 is an excellent pawn break that directly attacks White’s b‑pawn and, as a side‑effect, leaves White’s a‑pawn permanently lodged on a light square. By striking at b4 and fixing the white pawn structure on light squares, Black respects the opposite‑colour pawn complexes that already dominate the position, while his own pawns remain on dark squares. The engine’s evaluation barely changes (White stays a shade better), showing that the move maintains the balance even though Qf6 would have been marginally stronger.
student: By playing …a5 Black finally breaks open the centre with a pawn thrust against White’s b‑pawn, fixing that pawn on a light square and giving Black active counterplay while his own pawns remain locked on dark squares. The move does not alter the overall balance – the engine still judges White to be a hair better, about two‑tenths of a pawn – but it creates concrete threats such as the potential …Nb8 after White’s natural reply b5. Although the engine preferred the quieter Qf6, …a5 is an excellent practical try because it keeps material even and preserves Black’s chances without worsening the position.

teacher: By pushing the b‑pawn to b5 White solidifies a light‑square pawn chain and further cramps Black’s dark‑squared bishop, which is already hemmed in by its own pawns. The advance also forces Black’s only sensible reply, Nb8, to protect the knight, after which White can continue with Be3 and bring the rook to d1. The engine rates the move as the best, improving White’s standing by roughly a seventh of a pawn.
student: By pushing b5 White immediately attacks Black’s dark‑squared bishop, which is cramped behind its own pawns and therefore vulnerable. The engine rates the move as the best, improving White’s standing from a slight edge to about a third of a pawn. Black can meet the pressure with Nb8, removing the immediate threat to the knight, after which White would continue with Be3, keeping the initiative alive. This subtle infiltration exploits the opposite‑colour pawn structure – White’s pawns sit on light squares while Black’s are locked on dark – and leaves Black’s bishop exposed.

teacher: Black’s retreat Nd7 places the knight on a natural, flexible square. The dark‑squared bishop remains hemmed in by Black’s own pawn chain. The engine’s evaluation stays virtually the same – White remains only a fraction of a pawn better – confirming that the move perfectly preserves Black’s chances in a position where both sides have fixed pawn structures.
student: By retreating the knight to d7 Black simply preserves the balance of the position, leaving White’s slight edge virtually unchanged at about half a pawn. The move does not alter the fact that Black’s dark‑squared bishop remains cramped behind its own pawns while White’s pawns sit on light squares, so the overall structure stays roughly the same. In the engine’s continuation White would continue with Rad1, after which Black can meet it with …Qe7 and keep the tension alive. This quiet redeployment therefore earns the “excellent” label as the best move in the position.

teacher: Black’s queen retreats to e7, a safe square that fits the locked pawn structure—White’s pawns are fixed on light squares, Black’s on dark squares, and the dark‑squared bishop is already cramped by its own pawns. The engine rates the move as excellent and the evaluation shifts only marginally, leaving White with a slight edge, less than a pawn. In the continuation the engine suggests White could try g3 while Black can answer with …b6 and later …Nf6, preserving the solid balance.
student: By retreating the queen to e7 Black simply preserves the balance of the position, leaving White’s slight edge virtually unchanged at about +0.47 pawn. The move does not alter the fact that Black’s dark‑squared bishop remains cramped behind its own pawns while White’s pawns sit on light squares, so the overall structure stays roughly the same. With material still equal and the engine’s evaluation essentially flat, Qe7 is rightly judged an excellent continuation.

teacher: By playing b6 Black both fixes White’s pawn on b5 to a light square and eliminates the immediate threat to the knight on c5. The move also preserves Black’s dark‑square pawn structure while the rook on d6 continues to dominate the open d‑file, keeping the position solid. The engine rates the move as excellent and the evaluation remains a small edge for Black (about –0.28 of a pawn), essentially unchanged by the move.
student: By playing …b6 Black fixes White’s pawn on b5 on a light square and eliminates the immediate danger to the knight on c5. The move leaves material equal and keeps Black’s slight edge – the engine still evaluates the position at about –0.28 pawn. With both sides’ pawns locked on opposite colours and Black’s rook already dominating the open d‑file, the position remains balanced but Black retains a modest advantage.

teacher: Black captures the rook on d6, instantly eliminating the threat to his queen and preserving the slight edge that Black already enjoyed. The capture does leave the f‑pawn exposed, but White’s queen on c4 pins that pawn to the Black king, so the material gain is safe. The engine rates the move as excellent, and the most plausible continuation is White’s rook to d1, after which Black can retreat the queen to e7 and keep the advantage.
student: By taking on d6 Black eliminates White’s active rook and at the same time removes the immediate danger to his own queen, which was under attack by the white rook. The capture does leave the pawn on f7 hanging – it is pinned by White’s queen on c4 so it cannot be moved without exposing the black king – but this concession is acceptable because the material balance remains equal and Black stays only marginally better. The engine rates the move as excellent and the evaluation barely changes, confirming that Black has preserved his slight edge despite the temporary weakness on the f‑file.

teacher: White’s 29.Rd1 is a quiet, improving move that simply brings the rook to the d‑file, leaving the evaluation essentially unchanged (the score improves by only a few hundredths of a pawn). By keeping the queen on c4, White preserves the pin on the f7‑pawn, which still cannot move because the king sits on g8. Black’s most accurate reply would be …Qe6, which would both defend the pawn on f7 and remove the immediate pressure of the pin, yet the position would remain only marginally better for Black. For these reasons the engine correctly rates Rd1 as the best continuation.
student: By sliding the rook to d1 White immediately attacks Black’s queen on d6, forcing it to retreat with …Qe6. After that reply the queen will be removed from any immediate danger while the pin on the f‑pawn remains intact, so material stays equal and the engine still judges the position only marginally in Black’s favour. The move therefore preserves White’s slight edge without worsening the already balanced game.

teacher: Black’s queen retreats to e6, eliminating the immediate danger to the f‑pawn and shielding the queen itself, thereby removing the threat to the pawn on f7. By doing so the position slips from a small Black edge to an almost equal balance, with both sides still locked into opposite‑colour pawn structures—White’s pawns fixed on light squares and Black’s on dark squares, while White’s rook dominates the open d‑file. The engine rates Qe6 as the only excellent continuation, confirming it as the best move in the position.
student: By playing …Qe6 Black eliminates White’s immediate pressure on both the f‑pawn and the queen itself, thereby neutralising any danger that White might have posed. The move also leaves material even while keeping the engine’s assessment essentially unchanged – the position slips from a slight Black edge to near equality. With White’s pawns locked on light squares and the rook on d1 dominating the open d‑file, Black can now meet White’s most natural continuation with …Rc8, after which the game proceeds along lines such as Ng4 and c6. This precise defensive resource therefore earns the “excellent” label.

teacher: White’s pawn thrust to h4 fixes Black’s pawn on h5 on a light square, but at the same time it loosens the pawn shield in front of his own king. The resulting imbalance leaves White’s position slightly worse – the engine drops the evaluation to about a fifth of a pawn in Black’s favour. A more accurate continuation would have been Rxc5, which captures the knight on c5 (though the rook would then be en prise), and the engine rates that line as clearly superior.
student: White’s 31.h4 fixes Black’s pawn on h5 on a light square and weakens the pawn shield in front of his own king, so the evaluation slips to a small Black edge. The engine judged that the more accurate continuation would have been Rxc5, which wins the knight but leaves the rook on c5 hanging. By opting for h4 instead, White gives up the immediate tactical gain without improving his position.

teacher: Black’s 31…g6 is an excellent defensive try that neutralises White’s knight by removing the f5 square from its reach.
