By doing so the pawn advance also prepares to meet the natural 32 Rxc5 with …bxc5, after which the rook on c5 is captured and White would recapture with the queen, leading to a queen trade after …Qd6. The move improves the evaluation from a slight Black edge (‑0.22) to a roughly equal balance (‑0.14), even though the engine’s top‑ranking alternative was 31…Rc8.
student: By playing …g6 Black removes the f5‑square from White’s knight on e3, curbing its activity and keeping the balance of the position. The engine still rates the move as excellent because it leaves the evaluation essentially unchanged – the slight edge that existed before the move disappears after the natural continuation Rxc5, which would capture the knight but leave the rook on c5 hanging. In other words, the move neutralises White’s pressure without conceding any material or positional advantage.

teacher: By playing 34…bxc5 Black finally wins the rook on c5, converting an equal position into a material edge of roughly two pawns. The capture also opens the b‑file for Black, though it leaves him with isolated and doubled pawns on a5, c5 and c7. White could try the tactical shot 35 Qxe6, capturing the Black queen on e6; Black can simply recapture with 35…fxe6, after which the engine line continues Kf3 Kh6. The move is therefore judged excellent, as it secures the material gain while keeping the evaluation essentially unchanged.
student: By playing …bxc5 Black wins the white rook on c5, turning his side into a two‑pawn material advantage while opening the b‑file for future play. The capture does leave Black with isolated and doubled pawns on a5, c5 and c7, but the resulting structure gives him active counterplay in an otherwise balanced position where White’s pawns sit on light squares and Black’s on dark. If White replies with the natural Qxe6, Black can recapture with …fxe6 and continue with Kf3, keeping the initiative despite the structural weaknesses. This precise exchange therefore justifies the “best” label.

teacher: White’s capture on c5 merely wins a pawn, but it relinquishes a clear tactical opportunity. By playing Qxe6 instead, White could have taken the enemy queen and simultaneously forked the e‑5 pawn, the f‑7 pawn and the rook on c8, a sequence the engine rates as slightly better. As a result, after Qxc5 Black remains a pawn up and the evaluation slips to a slight edge for Black (about a fifth of a pawn).
student: By playing Qxc5 White simply wins a pawn, but the engine shows that this costs him about two‑tenths of a pawn because Black now enjoys a small edge. The capture does not improve White’s cramped light‑square pawn structure while Black’s dark‑square pawn chain remains solid. A more accurate continuation would have been Qxe6, which both removes the opponent’s queen and creates a fork on e5, f7 and rook c8, keeping the balance. Consequently, although the move is still classified as good, it is inferior to the optimal queen sacrifice.

teacher: White’s knight jumps to d5, a square that lies outside the reach of both White’s light‑square pawn chain and Black’s dark‑square pawn chain, thereby improving piece placement without altering the material balance. The move respects the existing pawn structure and neutralises any immediate threats from Black’s rook on the open d‑file, keeping the evaluation essentially unchanged at a slight Black edge. The engine confirms Nd5 as the best continuation; Black’s most natural reply would be Rd7, after which White can continue with Qb3, maintaining the balance.
student: White’s knight jumps to d5, directly contesting Black’s control of the open d‑file and keeping the position balanced despite being a pawn down. The engine rates it as the best continuation, with the evaluation barely shifting from –0.50 to –0.48 in Black’s favour. In the principal variation Black would reply …Rd7, after which White can continue with Qb3, preserving the slight edge for White.

teacher: White’s 38 f3 is a serious blunder. By pushing the pawn to f3 White does nothing to meet Black’s looming pawn break f5, which strikes at the e4 pawn and, after the forced exchanges, leaves Black a pawn up and turns a slight Black edge into a clear advantage of more than two pawns. The engine had preferred 38 Qb3, which would have kept the balance. Consequently the evaluation swung from a modest Black edge to Black being much better.
student: White’s quiet f3 does nothing to challenge Black’s dominant rook on the open d‑file or to stop the natural …f5 pawn break that would strike at the e4 pawn. By allowing this thrust, White hands Black the initiative and the evaluation drops sharply – the engine now judges Black about two pawns ahead instead of a slight edge for Black. The blunder costs roughly two pawns in material and leaves Black clearly better. The engine’s preferred continuation was Qb3, which would have kept more pressure on Black’s queenside.

teacher: By playing …fxe4 Black eliminates White’s pawn on e4, opens the f‑file and weakens the pawn shield in front of White’s king, leaving White with an isolated pawn on e4. The capture also creates an isolated pawn on e5 for Black, but the open f‑file and the rook on d7 already controlling the d‑file give Black active chances, and the material balance is restored without any loss. The engine rates the move as the best, improving Black’s already decisive advantage by roughly a half‑pawn.
student: By playing …fxe4 Black eliminates White’s pawn on e4 and opens the f‑file, while simultaneously leaving both sides with isolated pawns that weaken the pawn shield around White’s king. The capture also gives Black a clear line for his queen – after White’s most natural reply Qa3, Black can continue with …Qe2 and then check with Rf7+, exploiting the newly opened file and the pressure along it. This exchange improves Black’s evaluation by about four‑tenths of a pawn, confirming why the engine rates the move as the best possible continuation.

teacher: White eliminates Black’s pressure on the e‑pawn by playing fxe4, which opens the f‑file for his pieces and fixes Black’s pawn on e5 on a dark square. At the same time the capture leaves White with an isolated pawn on e4 and removes the semi‑open e‑file that could have offered counterplay. It is the most accurate continuation, but the position remains decisively Black‑favoured, with the engine now judging Black about 3.8 pawns ahead – a small further deterioration for White compared with the previous evaluation.
student: By playing fxe4 White eliminates Black’s immediate pressure on the e‑pawn and opens the f‑file, while the capture also fixes Black’s pawn on e5 on a dark square. The trade does leave White with an isolated pawn on e4, but it is still the best continuation because any alternative would allow Black to increase his lead further. With Black’s rook already dominating the open d‑file, the engine judges the position as a decisive Black advantage that has grown marginally after the capture.

teacher: The rook lift to f7 brings Black’s heavy piece onto the open f‑file and checks the white king, taking full advantage of the fixed light‑square pawn structure that White has built.  The evaluation stays virtually unchanged, with Black still ahead by about three‑and‑a‑half pawns and the winning advantage intact.  Yet the engine judges Qa3 to be the most accurate continuation – after …Ke2 Black could answer Qa3, after which White would play Qc6 and then Black would capture on a4 (Qxa4), keeping the pressure even sharper.
student: By playing Rf7+ Black checks the white king while his rook now dominates the open f‑file, increasing pressure on White’s position. The engine still judges the position as a decisive Black advantage, with the evaluation virtually unchanged at about –3.9 pawns. Although the move keeps the winning edge, the engine preferred Qa3 as the optimal continuation. In practice the check leaves White’s king exposed and does not alter the overall assessment.

teacher: Black’s queen check on b1 looks active, but it fails to address the immediate danger to the rook and therefore lets White improve, costing Black roughly a pawn of winning material. The engine rates the move a clear mistake, with the evaluation sliding from a decisive –4.63 to –3.47, and points out that the far stronger continuation would have been Rd7+, which both checks the king and eliminates the threat to the rook on d7. In the resulting position White’s light‑square pawn structure remains solid while Black’s dark‑square pawns and the rook on the open f‑file are left under‑utilised.
student: Black’s checking move Qb1+ looks natural but it lets White sidestep with Ke2 and allows Black to lose about a pawn of evaluation – the engine now judges the position as roughly three‑and‑a‑half pawns worse for Black than before. The engine preferred Rd7+, which would have both removed the immediate danger to the rook on d7 and delivered a check, preserving Black’s decisive edge. By opting for the check instead, Black missed that defensive resource and the advantage slipped by roughly one pawn.

teacher: White’s queen retreat to c5 leaves the a‑pawn hanging. The position was already a decisive Black advantage and the move pushes the evaluation from roughly –3.4 to –4.1 pawns, a moderate worsening of about three‑quarters of a pawn. Black can now answer with Qb2+ – Kd3 – Qb1+ – Ke2, keeping the initiative and exploiting the now‑undefended a4 pawn while the rook on f7 continues to dominate the open f‑file.
student: White’s queen retreat to c5 does little more than leave the a‑pawn hanging – it simply allows Black to continue with …Qb2+, checking and forcing the king back, after which Black can repeat the same checking sequence. The engine rates the move as an inaccuracy because it deepens Black’s already decisive edge by roughly three‑quarters of a pawn, leaving Black up one pawn and still winning decisively. Although Qc5 was technically the best continuation available, it fails to improve White’s cramped light‑square pawn structure or challenge Black’s dominant rook on the open f‑file.

teacher: Black’s 45…Qa2+ is a forcing check that forks the white king on e2 and the pawn on a4, tightening the already decisive edge and nudging the evaluation a little further in Black’s favour. The move also exploits the fact that White’s pawns are fixed on light squares while Black’s pieces, especially the rook on f7, dominate the open f‑file. The engine, however, rates Qb2+ as the optimal checking continuation, which would keep the pressure while preserving a marginally stronger position.
student: Black’s queen jumps to a2 with check, forking White’s king on e2 and the pawn on a4 while also exploiting the fact that White’s pawns sit on light squares and Black’s own pawns are locked on dark squares. The engine rates the move as a slight improvement – about two‑tenths of a pawn – but it still leaves Black with a decisive advantage of roughly four pawns. Although the engine preferred the alternative Qb2+, which would have kept the same fork without moving the queen, the chosen move remains an excellent way to increase pressure in this clearly winning endgame.

teacher: White steps his king to d3, staying on the same colour complex as his light‑squared pawn chain and away from the open f‑file that Black’s rook on f7 controls. The move is only a little inferior to the engine’s preferred Kd1; Black can now reply with Rd7+ giving check, and the evaluation slides from a –4.3 to about a –4.6 pawn disadvantage. Although the position remains a decisive Black advantage, Kd3 is still a decent try that keeps the king relatively safe without creating new weaknesses.
student: White’s king step to d3 does little more than keep it safe and leaves Black’s decisive edge essentially unchanged – the evaluation slips by about a third of a pawn in Black’s favour. The engine judged Kd1 to be stronger, as it would have kept the king nearer the centre and avoided giving Black the immediate checking resource …Rd7+. After that check White could try Nd5, but Black can continue with …Qb1+, keeping the pressure alive. In short, Kd3 is a good defensive try but costs White a small amount of ground against an already winning position for Black.

teacher: White meets Black’s check with Ke2, the only move that keeps the material balance and avoids a more immediate disaster. By stepping onto e2 the pawn on e4 becomes en prise, and this move concludes the forcing sequence that began with Black’s Qa2+ fork of the king and the a‑pawn, which forced White to Kd1 and was followed by Black’s Qb1+ check. The engine rates the move as good—the evaluation stays around a four‑pawn disadvantage for White, so the position remains a decisive Black advantage.
student: White’s king steps to e2, the engine’s top choice, but it leaves the e‑pawn hanging. Black can reply with …Qa2+, forking the king on e2 and the a‑pawn while also delivering check, after which White must retreat to Kd1 before repeating the sequence with …Qb1+. The position remains a decisive Black advantage, about four pawns ahead, so the move does not improve White’s standing – in fact it costs roughly a tenth of a pawn compared with the previous evaluation.

teacher: White’s queen jump to c4 tries to fork Black’s queen on e4 and rook on f7, but it leaves both the queen on c4 and the knight on e3 hanging. Black can answer with Qf3+, forking the king, the knight and the pawn on g3 while also removing the pressure on the rook, which wins material and pushes the evaluation from a decisive Black edge to an even larger one (about 2.9 pawns worse for White). The engine’s preferred move was Qd5, which would have kept the same fork idea without allowing the immediate check, though it still leaves the queen and knight en prise. By playing Qc4 White dramatically worsened the position, dropping the assessment by roughly 2.9 pawns.
student: White’s 48.Qc4 tries to fork Black’s queen on e4 and rook on f7, but it also leaves both the queen on c4 and the knight on e3 hanging. After the move Black can reply with …Qf3+, checking the king, removing the threat to the rook and attacking the white knight, which forces a forced sequence that deepens Black’s lead by roughly three pawns. The engine shows that the correct continuation was 48.Qd5, which would have created the same fork while keeping the pieces defended, so the blunder costs White about two‑and‑a‑half pawns in evaluation.

teacher: With 48…Qf3+ Black unleashes a powerful queen fork, checking the king on e2 while simultaneously attacking White’s knight on e3 and the pawn on g3. The move also eliminates the immediate danger to the rook on f7, which already dominates the open f‑file. This precise check deepens Black’s already decisive edge, nudging the evaluation from a six‑pawn advantage to about six and a third pawns in Black’s favour. White’s most natural reply would be 49 Kd3, after which Black can continue with 49…Rd7+, White replies 50 Kc2, and then Black plays 50…Qxe3, preserving the winning material lead.
student: Black’s queen jumps to f3 with a checking fork that hits White’s king on e2, the knight on e3 and the pawn on g3 at once. The move also eliminates the immediate danger to the rook on f7, preserving Black’s two‑pawn material edge while keeping the pressure on White’s king. The engine rates it as the best continuation, improving Black’s already decisive advantage by roughly a tenth of a pawn. In the principal line White would have to retreat the king to d3, after which Black can continue with …Rd7+ and then capture on e3, cementing the win.

teacher: Black meets 1.e4 with 1…c5, entering the Sicilian Defence and immediately contesting White’s central pawn. The move leaves the evaluation essentially unchanged, with White still only a hair’s‑breadth better (about a quarter of a pawn). In the main line the game would likely continue 2.Nf3 d6 3.d4 cxd4, a dynamic continuation that keeps the balance. This reply is therefore judged excellent, as it preserves Black’s chances while adhering to well‑established theory.
student: Black’s reply …c5 is an excellent way to contest White’s centre and keep material balanced, leaving the engine’s assessment virtually unchanged – White remains only a fraction of a pawn ahead. The engine rates it as the best continuation, with the most likely line continuing 2.Nf3 d6 3.d4 cxd4. By playing …c5 Black preserves equality while preparing to meet White’s natural development with …d6 in the ensuing game.

teacher: Black captures the pawn on d4, gaining a pawn that is recaptured by White with Nxd4, so the material balance is restored and the exchange is completed. After the recapture the c‑file becomes semi‑open for Black while the d‑file is semi‑open for White, giving each side a modest line‑opening benefit. The engine rates the capture as the best move, noting that the evaluation shifts by only about a tenth of a pawn in Black’s favour. In the principal line White would reply Nxd4, after which Black can continue with …Nf6.
student: By playing …cxd4 Black eliminates White’s central pawn and forces the natural reply Nxd4, which opens the c‑file for Black while giving White a semi‑open d‑file. The capture therefore initiates an exchange that leaves the material balance unchanged – Black remains a pawn ahead but the engine still judges White to be only marginally better. This precise simplification is why the move earns the “best” label, with the evaluation improving by about a tenth of a pawn in Black’s favour.

teacher: Black brings the knight to its natural f6 square, completing development while leaving material perfectly balanced. The engine rates the move as good, noting that it keeps Black’s evaluation essentially unchanged – White still holds a slight edge of about a third of a pawn, now edging to roughly two‑fifths of a pawn. White’s most accurate reply would be Nc3, which removes the lingering threat to the pawn on e4.
student: Black’s …Nf6 develops the knight and immediately attacks White’s e‑pawn, forcing it to retreat with Nc3. After that reply White can continue with a6, after which Black may play …e6, keeping material equal while the engine still judges White to be a little better – roughly +0.4 of a pawn. The move therefore preserves Black’s chances without worsening his position, justifying its “good” label.

teacher: Black meets White’s last development with the quiet pawn push a6. The engine rates a6 as the best continuation and it leaves the evaluation virtually unchanged, with White still a little better (about +0.30 of a pawn). No material is altered and the balance of the position is maintained. In the principal variation White would continue with Bg5, Black replying Nbd7, then Be3 and h6.
student: Black’s …a6 is judged the best continuation, keeping the balance virtually untouched – White remains only a fraction of a pawn ahead. The engine rates it as an improvement of about two‑hundredths of a pawn for Black, and after the move the position stays roughly equal in material. In the principal variation White would continue with Bg5, Black replies Nbd7, then White plays Be3 and Black can answer h6.

teacher: White’s queen retreat to d3 gives up the modest edge it enjoyed, dropping the evaluation from a slight plus to essentially equal. The engine points out that 6 Bg5 would have been preferable, preserving the advantage rather than allowing Black to neutralise it. After 6 Qd3 Black can answer with …g6, after which White would have to play Be2 and Black can continue …Bg7 and …O‑O, leading to a roughly balanced position. In short, the move cost White about a third of a pawn and missed the more accurate bishop sortie.
student: White’s queen retreat to d3 does little more than preserve the status quo – it leaves material unchanged and nudges the evaluation back to near equality, costing about a third of a pawn compared with the engine‑preferred Bg5. The engine judged that Bg5 would have been stronger, keeping White’s slight edge instead of surrendering it. In short, Qd3 is a good move but not the most accurate continuation in this opening.

teacher: White’s queen sidesteps to g3, a perfectly legal move but one that lets Black seize the initiative. After 7.Qg3 the engine evaluates the position as a small edge for Black (about a quarter‑pawn), whereas the more accurate 7.a4 would have kept the balance. Black can now continue with …b5, after which White would have to meet it with b4, and the ensuing play (…e5, Nb3) leaves Black a little better. In short, the move is acceptable but it costs White roughly a third of a pawn in evaluation.
student: White’s queen retreat to g3 does little more than shuffle the pieces and leaves Black with a small edge – the evaluation slides from a tiny plus for White to a slight minus for Black, about a third of a pawn worse. The engine judged a4 to be the stronger continuation, keeping material even while preserving equality. After Qg3 the most likely reply would be …b5, after which White could try b4, followed by …e5 and Nb3 in the principal variation. In short, the move costs White roughly a third of a pawn compared with the optimal line.

teacher: White’s 8 Bd3 simply finishes development, putting the bishop on a natural diagonal. The move nudges the assessment from a barely equal position to a slight edge of about a third of a pawn, so it does improve White’s standing. Nevertheless, the engine points out that the more ambitious 8 f4 would have been preferable and could have yielded a larger advantage. The material balance remains unchanged and White now has a slight edge.
student: White’s bishop retreat to d3 nudges the evaluation from a barely balanced position to a modest edge for White – about a sixth of a pawn more. The engine still prefers the more ambitious f4, but Bd3 is a solid choice that keeps material even and preserves White’s slight advantage. In the principal variation Black would reply …Nh5, after which White can continue with Qf3, keeping the initiative.

teacher: Black’s 8…Nc6 is judged an excellent move because it leaves the evaluation virtually unchanged, with White still a hair better (+0.36). The engine’s top choice was 8…Nh5, but the knight move does not alter the material balance. White can capture on c6, and Black would recapture with the bishop, after which the line could continue with Be3 and Qa5. Thus Black does not improve the position, leaving White still slightly better.
student: Black’s …Nc6 simply develops a piece and leaves material equal, so White remains only marginally better – roughly a third of a pawn. The engine rates it as an excellent move because it does not worsen Black’s standing, but it is not the top choice; …Nh5 would have been preferable. After …Nc6 White can capture with Nxc6, after which Black recaptures Bxc6 and the game proceeds with Be3 followed by Qa5. In short, the move keeps the balance while giving White a small edge.

teacher: White captures the black knight on c6, starting an exchange that compels Black to recapture with the bishop. By forcing …Bxc6 the threat to Black’s queen on d8 disappears, yet the material balance is restored after the exchange. The engine rates the move as the best, nudging White’s evaluation upward by about a tenth of a pawn.
student: By playing Nxc6 White eliminates Black’s active knight and forces an immediate exchange that leaves the material balance unchanged – after Black’s natural reply Bxc6 the queens remain on their original squares while White retains a small edge. The engine rates this as the best continuation, improving White’s evaluation by about a tenth of a pawn even though the position remains only marginally better for White. In the principal variation Black would capture with Bxc6, removing the threat to the queen on d8 and restoring material equality, but the resulting position still favours White.

teacher: By playing Bxc6 Black eliminates the immediate threat to the queen on d8 while recapturing the knight, thereby restoring material balance. This exchange lifts Black’s standing by roughly a sixth of a pawn, narrowing White’s earlier edge from about a half‑pawn to a third‑pawn. The engine judges the capture as the best continuation, and the line would likely proceed with White developing Be3, after which Black can answer with Qa5, continuing the fight for the centre.
student: By playing …Bxc6 Black eliminates White’s active knight and at the same time removes the immediate danger to the queen on d8. The capture restores material balance while nudging the evaluation in Black’s favour by roughly a sixth of a pawn, which is why the engine rates it as the best continuation. In the principal line White would continue with Be3, after which Black can answer Qa5, keeping the pressure alive.

teacher: By playing 13 f4 White weakens the pawn cover in front of his king, as the move ideas point out. This concession turns a roughly equal position into a slight Black advantage (the evaluation shifts from +0.13 to –0.31, about a half‑pawn swing). The engine preferred 13 Rad1, which would have kept the balance. With Black’s king still in the centre and White’s bishop on d3 limited to only two safe squares, the pawn push offers little compensation.
student: By playing f4 White loosens the pawn shield in front of his king, a drawback that already exists because Black’s king remains in the centre and White’s bishop on d3 is cramped to just two safe squares. The engine rates the move as “good” but notes it costs about four‑tenths of a pawn, turning an essentially equal position into a slight edge for Black. A more accurate continuation would have been Rad1, which keeps the king safer and preserves the balance. Consequently, although not a blunder, f4 modestly worsens White’s standing.

teacher: By capturing on f5 Black eliminates White’s advanced pawn and restores material balance, leaving the position roughly equal. The exchange also opens the e‑file, giving Black a new line of activity, while the resulting isolated queen’s pawn on d6 is a structural concession. White’s bishop on d3 is now confined to only two safe squares and the rook on f1, which had been using a semi‑open f‑file, loses its immediate prospects. Overall, the move equalises the material and improves Black’s chances despite the slight weakening of the pawn structure.
student: By taking on f5 Black eliminates White’s central pawn and opens the e‑file, but the capture also leaves Black with an isolated queen’s pawn on d6. The engine rates it as the best continuation, even though the evaluation slips by about a tenth of a pawn because the material edge disappears after White can recapture. After the forced …exf5 the game proceeds with lines such as Re8, Rad1 and …d5, keeping the position balanced despite Black being temporarily down a pawn.

teacher: White finally eliminates Black’s pawn on f5 with exf5, opening the e‑file and giving up the semi‑open f‑file that White had enjoyed. The capture is the engine’s top choice and keeps the material balance level, but the evaluation slips only a tenth of a pawn, leaving Black a little better. In practice the move clears the central file for White’s pieces while the position remains roughly equal.
student: By taking on f5 White eliminates Black’s pawn and opens the e‑file, while the capture removes the semi‑open f‑file that had been available to White. The exchange leaves material even and the engine still rates the position as roughly equal, with Black only a fraction of a pawn ahead. Consequently the move is judged good and is indeed the best continuation in this middlegame.

teacher: By playing …d5 Black accepts an isolated queen’s pawn on d5 and leaves White’s bishop on d3 with essentially only one safe square. This also allows White the tactical idea Ne2, after which the pawn on b2 becomes en prise (the engine’s line continues Bxb2). The move is still playable, but it costs Black roughly a third of a pawn compared with the engine‑recommended Re8, turning a slight Black edge into an equal position.
student: By pushing …d5 Black creates an isolated queen’s pawn and leaves White’s bishop on d3 with virtually no useful retreats, but the pawn thrust also allows White to answer with Ne2, after which the b‑pawn becomes hanging. The engine therefore rates the move as a moderate worsening for Black – about a third of a pawn – because it gives White active counterplay while the evaluation slides back to equality. In contrast, the stronger continuation would have been Re8, keeping material balanced without conceding the isolated pawn or the vulnerable b‑pawn. Consequently, despite being “good”, the move costs Black roughly three‑quarters of a pawn in practical terms.

teacher: By playing Rae1 White tried to contest the open e‑file, but the move immediately allows Black to capture on e1, after which the Black rook on e1 pins the remaining White rook on f1 to the king on g1. The move worsens White's position by roughly half a pawn, turning a slight Black edge into a clear one (about –0.8 pawns). The engine’s best reply was Rad1, which would have kept the rook off the e‑file and avoided the pin. In the principal variation Black would capture on e1, White would recapture, and the game would continue with Nf4 and Qg3.
student: White’s 17.Rae1 puts his rook on the open e‑file, but it immediately allows Black to capture with …Rxe1, after which White must recapture and Black can continue with Nf4 and Qg3, leaving Black clearly better – roughly a pawn’s worth. The engine rates this as a moderate worsening for White (about ‑0.47 pawn) compared with the optimal 17.Rad1, which would have kept the rook more safely defended. In addition, White’s bishop on d3 already has only one safe square, so the new placement does not improve its prospects. Consequently, while the move is still “good”, it costs White a significant amount of positional ground.

teacher: White’s 19.Ne2 is a clear mistake: by moving the knight the pawn on b2 becomes en prise, giving Black an immediate target. In addition, the move permits Black to answer with …d4, which uncovers the queen on g5’s discovered attack on the bishop on c5 and swings the evaluation from a modest –0.76 to a much larger –2.35 (about two pawns). The engine indicates that the far‑better try was 19.Qf3. Consequently White’s position deteriorated by roughly one and a half pawns.
student: By playing Ne2 White leaves the b‑pawn hanging and allows Black to answer with …d4, uncovering a discovered attack by the queen on g5 against the bishop on c5. This concession pushes the evaluation from a modest Black edge to a clear advantage of roughly two pawns, as reflected in the swing of about one and a half pawns. The engine’s preferred continuation was Qf3, which would have kept material equal and avoided giving Black such active play. Consequently, Ne2 is a mistake that costs White a significant amount of ground.

teacher: By playing …d4 Black uncovers the queen on g5, delivering a discovered attack on White’s bishop on c5 and stripping that piece of the e3 and f2 squares. The pawn becomes isolated on d4, but the material balance stays level and Black’s sizable advantage (roughly two pawns) is preserved. White’s most natural reply, 20 Bd6, would simply remove the bishop from the attack, after which Black can continue with …Re3 and later …Rd8, keeping the pressure. The move also dovetails with Black’s control of the open e‑file while White’s bishop on d3 remains cramped.
student: By playing …d4 Black not only opens the way for the queen on g5 to strike at White’s bishop on c5 but also deprives that bishop of the e‑3 and f2 squares it had been eyeing. The pawn thrust therefore creates a concrete tactical pressure while leaving Black’s material balance untouched, so the engine still judges the position as clearly better for Black – roughly two pawns ahead. White could try Bd6 to eliminate the immediate danger, yet even after that continuation Black remains comfortably ahead.

teacher: Black’s 20…a5 is a mistake because it does nothing to counter White’s strong reply Bd6; White can simply answer with Bd6, which neutralises Black’s ideas and leaves Black’s pieces unchanged. By opting for a flank pawn push instead of the engine‑recommended Re3, Black lets the evaluation slide from a decisive –3.37 to a still winning but smaller –2.34, roughly a pawn’s worth of advantage. The move therefore costs Black about a pawn of positional value while the e‑file contest between the rooks remains as before.
student: By playing …a5 Black allowed White’s bishop to retreat to d6, removing the immediate pressure on that piece and giving White active counterplay. The engine shows this costs roughly a pawn of evaluation, dropping the score from a decisive –3.37 to about –2.34. A far stronger continuation would have been …Re3, keeping the rook on the open e‑file and preserving Black’s large advantage. Consequently the move is rightly marked as a mistake.

teacher: White’s 21.Bc4 does create a pin of the f‑pawn against the king, but it completely overlooks the immediate danger to the bishop on b4. Black can simply reply …axb4, winning the bishop on b4 and turning a modest Black edge into a decisive one (about a pawn‑and‑a‑half in Black’s favour). The engine’s top choice, 21.Bd6, would have removed the threat to the bishop on d6 and kept the material balance. As played, the move cost White roughly a pawn and handed Black a winning advantage.
student: White’s 21 Bc4 tries to pin the f‑pawn to Black’s king, but it does nothing to meet the real danger that Black already poses – the rook on e8 dominates the open e‑file and can simply capture the bishop on b4 with …axb4. The engine shows this costs roughly a pawn, turning an already inferior position into a clearly losing one. A far stronger try would have been 21 Bd6, which eliminates the immediate threat to the bishop on d6 and keeps material balanced. By playing Bc4 White allowed Black to win the bishop and consolidate a decisive edge.

teacher: By playing 21…axb4 Black finally eliminates White’s active bishop on b4, winning the piece and increasing his material lead to three pawns. The capture also opens the a‑file for Black, though it leaves isolated and doubled pawns on b4 and b7. White’s most forcing reply is the natural Bxf7+ fork, checking the king and attacking the rook on e8; Black can meet it with Kh7 and, after Bxe8 Rxe8, retain the decisive material advantage. The engine rates the move as good – the evaluation drops only a little because of the new pawn weaknesses, but Black remains clearly winning.
student: By taking on b4 Black eliminates White’s active bishop and opens the a‑file, giving Black a semi‑open line while leaving him with isolated and doubled pawns on the b‑file. The capture also removes White’s bishop pair, but it costs Black about a sixth of a pawn in evaluation because White can reply Bxf7+, checking the king and simultaneously forking the rook on e8 and the king on g8. Nevertheless, the engine rates axb4 as the best continuation, preserving Black’s decisive material edge.

teacher: White finally wins the rook on e8, but the capture merely initiates an exchange that Black will answer with Rxe8, restoring material balance. Because the bishop is exchanged, White’s position actually slips a little further—about a third of a pawn—while the pawn on a2 becomes vulnerable. The move is nevertheless the best available, as it at least forces the exchange and leaves Black’s bishop pair and the semi‑open a‑file as the only remaining assets for the side that is already winning.
student: By taking on e8 White eliminates Black’s active rook and forces an immediate exchange that will be met by …Rxe8, restoring material balance while leaving the a‑pawn hanging. The capture also exploits the queen on h3 pinning the h5‑knight to the king, but it does not improve White’s overall standing – the engine still judges Black to be decisively better despite being down three pawns. Consequently the move costs roughly a third of a pawn in evaluation, yet it remains the best continuation available.

teacher: Black’s 24…Re3!! places the rook on the open e‑file while pinning White’s knight on g3 to the queen on h3, a concrete tactical idea that leaves White unable to move the knight without losing the queen. The only plausible reply is the forced 25.Rxe3, after which Black recaptures with the d‑pawn and continues with …c3 and …Qd5, keeping the initiative. The move leaves the evaluation unchanged at a decisive –3.5‑pawn advantage, confirming it as the correct continuation in a position where Black already enjoys the bishop pair and White’s queen is pinning Black’s own knight on h5.
student: By playing Re3 Black not only places his rook on the open e‑file but also pins White’s knight on g3 to the queen on h3, while simultaneously keeping the pressure on the white queen that already pins the black knight on h5 to the king. The engine rates this as the best continuation, and the evaluation remains a decisive –3½ pawn advantage for Black. If White were to capture with Rxe3, Black can simply recapture with dxe3, preserving the pin and the material balance. This precise rook lift therefore consolidates Black’s winning position without altering the score.

teacher: White’s king steps to h1 to address the threat from Black’s queen on e3, escaping the immediate danger but leaving the king on a square where the bishop on c6 now pins the g‑pawn and the queen on e3 continues to pin the knight on g3 to the queen on h3. The move is the only reasonable reply and is indeed the engine’s best choice, yet it still worsens White’s standing, pushing the evaluation from a decisive Black edge of about four and three‑quarters pawns to roughly five‑and‑a‑third pawns. In other words, Kh1 is a necessary inaccuracy that costs White about half a pawn in an already lost position.
student: White’s retreat Kh1 does nothing to relieve the pressure created by Black’s queen on e3 pinning the knight on g3 and the bishop on c6 pinning the g‑pawn, so the evaluation slips further into Black’s favor – roughly half a pawn worse for White. The engine still rates Kh1 as the best continuation, but it leaves Black with a decisive edge that grows from about four‑and‑three‑quarters pawns to just under five pawns. In short, the move merely preserves the existing disadvantage without improving White’s chances.

teacher: Black’s 26…Be5 abandons the bishop on c6 that was pinning White’s g‑pawn to the king, and by doing so it allows White to play the forcing 27 Qh4, after which the pawn on g2 is left en prise. This concession reduces Black’s winning edge from a decisive –5.3‑pawn advantage to about –4.0, a swing of roughly a pawn in White’s favour. The engine’s preferred continuation was 26…Bh6, which would have kept the pin and preserved the larger advantage. Consequently the bishop move is a clear mistake.
student: By playing …Be5 Black not only gives up the small edge it already enjoyed but also allows White’s queen on h3 to become active, as the engine notes that after the natural reply Qh4 the pawn on g2 would be left en prise. The evaluation therefore drops by roughly a pawn, turning a decisive –5‑pawn advantage into only about –4. This loss of momentum makes the move a clear mistake. The engine’s preferred continuation was Bh6, which would have kept the larger lead without conceding the pin‑targeted piece.

teacher: White’s Qh4 pins the black knight on h5 to the king on h7, a concrete tactical resource that limits Black’s defensive options even though the move leaves the g‑pawn hanging. Black’s strongest reply would be Bxg3, after which White can recapture with the pawn (hxg3), continue with Qxg3 and then generate checking chances with Qe7+. The engine shows the position slipping by roughly a third of a pawn, but no other move improves White’s situation, so Qh4 is the correct choice despite the modest loss of ground.
student: White’s queen jumps to h4, pinning Black’s knight on h5 to the king and leaving the pawn on g2 permanently en prise because it is also pinned by Black’s bishop on c6. The engine still judges the position as decisively better for Black – roughly four‑and‑a‑half pawns ahead – but this move is objectively the best available, costing White about a third of a pawn in evaluation. Black can reply with …Bxg3, after which White would recapture hxg3 and continue with Qxg3 followed by Qe7+, keeping the pressure alive despite the material balance remaining equal.

teacher: White finally eliminates the bishop’s attack on the g‑pawn (and the pin on g2) by playing hxg3, thereby forcing an exchange that restores material balance. After the inevitable …Qxg3 the h‑file opens, the Black queen simultaneously forks the g‑pawn and White’s queen on h4 and even threatens the immediate mate Qxg2#, leaving White with an isolated g‑pawn and a still‑decisive Black advantage. The move is the best available, but it still worsens White’s standing by about a fifth of a pawn, keeping Black firmly winning.
student: By playing hxg3 White eliminates the immediate danger to the queen on h4 and forces Black’s best reply Qxg3, which both captures the bishop and opens the h‑file. After the forced queen recapture the h‑file becomes open, allowing White’s heavy pieces to bear down on Black’s king while the isolated pawn on g2 remains vulnerable. Although the capture does not win material, it creates concrete threats – the queen on g3 would fork the pawn on g2 and the queen on h4, and after the inevitable …Qxg3 White could continue with checks such as Qe7+, keeping pressure on Black’s king. The engine rates the move as good, noting that it costs White about a fifth of a pawn in evaluation but still leaves Black with a decisive advantage.

teacher: Black’s queen capture on g3 is the decisive blow, forking White’s pawn on g2 and the queen on h4 while also threatening the immediate mate Qxg2#. Even though the queen on g3 is itself left en prise, White cannot exploit this because the queen also threatens immediate mate with Qxg2# and the g‑pawn is pinned by Black’s bishop on c6. The move leaves Black’s material edge intact (up a pawn) and the engine’s evaluation remains essentially unchanged at a winning –4.3 pawn advantage. Thus 28…Qxg3!! both consolidates the material lead and forces White into a hopeless defensive scramble.
student: By taking on g3 Black not only wins a pawn but also creates a fork on White’s pawn g2 and queen h4, while simultaneously threatening the immediate mate Qxg2#. The capture leaves both the queen on g3 and the pawn on d4 hanging, yet the engine still judges the position as a decisive Black advantage – roughly four‑and‑a‑half pawns ahead. White’s most natural reply would be Qh2, which would remove the mating idea but leave the white queen vulnerable, after which Black can continue with …Kg7 and keep the pressure. This precise queen sacrifice therefore preserves the winning edge without any loss in evaluation.

teacher: White’s check on e7 creates a fork of the b‑pawn and Black’s king, but it does nothing to stem Black’s overwhelming pressure. After the natural reply …Ng7 Black threatens an immediate mate with Qxg2#, and although the knight on g7 becomes a target, White remains down a pawn and the evaluation slips to about –4½ pawns. The engine’s preferred move was 29.Qh2, which would have eliminated the danger to the g‑pawn (even though the queen would then be en prise). By opting for the check, White’s position worsened by roughly a tenth of a pawn.
student: White’s checking queen on e7 does create a fork on the b‑pawn and the black king, but it also leaves the white queen vulnerable – Black can answer with …Ng7, which both attacks the g2‑pawn and threatens immediate mate on g2. The engine rates the move as “good” yet notes that it costs roughly a tenth of a pawn compared with the optimal continuation Qh2, which would have removed the danger to the g2‑pawn without allowing the mating idea. After 29.Qe7+ Black can indeed play …Ng7, after which White must meet the ensuing threats while still being down a pawn in an already losing position.

teacher: Black’s retreat Ne3 is a clear inaccuracy: instead of the winning Bxg2 capture, which would have taken the pawn on g2, Black allows White to answer with Rf8, moving the white rook from f1 to f8 and ending its control of the open f‑file. This concession shrinks Black’s lead from a decisive –5.28 to about –3.6, a loss of roughly a pawn and a half. The knight on e3 is also less active than the bishop that could have seized the pawn.
student: By playing …Ne3 Black missed the simple capture Bxg2, which would have taken the pawn on g2 and preserved a larger edge. The engine now evaluates the position as about a pawn worse for Black – roughly a six‑pawn swing in White’s favour – even though Black remains clearly ahead. White can simply meet the move with Rf8, removing the pressure on the rook that was created by the previous move. In short, the knight retreat costs Black a decisive amount of ground despite still being up one pawn.

teacher: Black improves the safety of his king by stepping to h6, moving out of the open f‑file that White’s rook on f7 dominates. The move leaves the evaluation essentially unchanged, preserving Black’s decisive material edge of one pawn. In the engine line White would try Qf2, after which Black can continue with the forcing sequence Qxg2+ followed by Nxg2, showing that the king on h6 remains well‑protected while Black’s attack persists.
student: By moving to h6 Black brings his king onto the sixth rank, directly contesting White’s rook that dominates the open f‑file and keeping the pressure on White’s position. The engine rates the move as excellent and the evaluation remains a decisive –4½ pawn advantage for Black, essentially unchanged from before. In the principal variation White would try Qf2, after which Black can capture on g2 with check and then recapture, preserving the material edge.

teacher: By playing 33…Qxg2+ Black eliminates White’s g‑pawn with check, compelling the forced reply 34.Qxg2, which captures the queen on g2. After the inevitable …Nxg2 the queens are exchanged, maintaining Black’s material advantage (still up two pawns) and leaving Black with a passed pawn on g6, while the pawn shield in front of White’s king is weakened. The move therefore keeps the decisive –4.4‑pawn advantage essentially unchanged, confirming Black’s winning position.
student: By playing Qxg2+ Black eliminates the immediate danger to his queen and forces White’s only sensible reply Qxg2. After the forced recapture the g‑file becomes semi‑open for White while Black retains a passed pawn on g6 and a weakened pawn shield around White’s king, which together keep the decisive edge that was already present. The engine rates the move as good and the evaluation stays at roughly –4½ pawns, confirming that Black remains clearly ahead.

teacher: White finally eliminates Black’s queen with Qxg2, but the gain is only apparent: Black can answer Nxg2, removing the threat to the g‑pawn and restoring material balance, so the position stays a decisive Black advantage (about ‑4½ pawns). The exchange leads directly into a rook‑and‑minor‑piece ending, where White’s only concrete asset is the rook on f7 that dominates the open f‑file. Consequently, the move is judged good—it is the best continuation, yet it leaves the evaluation essentially unchanged.
student: By taking on g2 White eliminates Black’s queen and forces an immediate queen‑exchange that leaves the game in a rook‑and‑minor‑piece ending. After the inevitable …Nxg2 the queens disappear, and White retains his rook on the open f‑file while Black’s king must scramble to meet the threats created by the newly placed knight. The engine rates the capture as good – it keeps the evaluation essentially unchanged at a decisive Black advantage – but it does not alter the overall outcome.

teacher: By playing Nxg2 Black eliminates White’s queen, turning the game into a rook‑and‑minor‑piece ending in which Black is now up a queen while still retaining his knight. The capture also removes the only immediate threat to Black’s pawn on g6. With the queen gone the evaluation stays at a decisive Black advantage, essentially unchanged from the previous position. White’s active rook on f7 continues to control the open f‑file, but it cannot compensate for the material loss.
student: By taking on g2 Black eliminates White’s queen and instantly converts the game into a rook‑and‑minor‑piece ending, leaving Black with a two‑pawn material edge. The capture also removes the immediate danger to the pawn on g6, preserving Black’s decisive advantage. With the white king still confined to g1 while Black’s pieces dominate the board, the engine rates the move as excellent and the evaluation remains at roughly –4½ pawns.

teacher: White’s king steps to f2, the only move that keeps the rook on f7 dominant over the open f‑file in this rook‑and‑minor‑piece ending. By improving the king’s placement the evaluation nudges in White’s favour by about a tenth of a pawn, even though Black still enjoys a decisive four‑pawn lead. The engine’s continuation shows Black could try Nh4, after which White would reply Ke2, followed by …​.
student: In this rook‑and‑minor‑piece ending, where Black already enjoys a decisive edge, White’s king steps to f2, getting out of the pawn mass and keeping the rook active on the open f‑file. The engine rates Kf2 as the best continuation, improving White’s standing by roughly a tenth of a pawn even though Black remains clearly ahead. After the move Black can continue with …Nh4, after which White would head for Ke2 and later bring the rook into the fight.

teacher: By pushing …g5 Black creates a passed pawn and advances the lone kingside pawn majority, but the pawn is left isolated on g5. In this rook‑and‑minor‑piece ending White’s rook on f7 already dominates the open f‑file, and the pawn push allows White to answer with c3, a pawn break that forks the b4 and d4 pawns and eliminates the threat to the c‑pawn. The engine judges the move only “good”, noting that it costs Black about half a pawn compared with the optimal Nf5, yet Black still remains winning by roughly four pawns.
student: By pushing …g5 Black creates a passed pawn on the g‑file but does so while leaving that pawn isolated, which costs about half a pawn in evaluation. The engine preferred 36…Nf5, keeping the pressure without conceding the extra pawn. After …g5 White can answer with the pawn break c3, forking the b4 and d4 pawns and removing the threat to the newly placed g‑pawn, after which Black’s best continuation would be Kg6 followed by Rf8 and Nf5. Thus the move is still winning, yet it is not the most accurate choice.

teacher: Black’s …Nf5 eliminates White’s threat to the pawn on d4, solidifying the material edge even though the knight lands en prise. The engine still judges the position a decisive Black win, but the evaluation slips by about a sixth of a pawn compared with the previous move. White’s most logical try would be the pawn break c3, striking at both b4 and d4, yet Black remains comfortably ahead.
student: By playing …Nf5 Black eliminates White’s immediate pressure on the d‑pawn, but the knight lands on a square that can be taken. The engine still judges the position as a decisive Black win, even though the evaluation slips by about a sixth of a pawn compared with the previous score. In this rook‑and‑minor‑piece ending White’s rook already dominates the open f‑file, so the most natural continuation would be the pawn break c3, striking at both the b4 and d4 pawns.

teacher: White’s retreat of the rook to f1 looks logical in a rook‑and‑minor‑piece ending, since the rook now controls the open f‑file, but it walks straight into Black’s decisive resource. After 39.Rf1 Black can play …Bb5+, a checking skewer that forces the white king away and then captures the rook on f1, increasing Black’s material lead (now up a rook in addition to its existing advantage). The engine’s preferred move, 39.c3, would have struck at the b4 and d4 pawns, keeping material balance and offering White a fighting chance. Instead, the rook move worsened White’s already losing position by roughly two pawns.
student: White’s 39.Rf1 looks active, placing the rook on the open f‑file in this rook‑and‑minor‑piece ending, but it completely overlooks Black’s tactical resource … Bb5+. After the bishop checks with …Bb5+, White’s king on d3 is skewered by the bishop and the rook on f1 becomes vulnerable, allowing Black to win material. The engine shows that the correct continuation was the pawn break c3, which would have struck at Black’s b4 and d4 pawns and kept the balance. By playing Rf1 instead, White’s evaluation slid from a decisive –4.9 to an even larger –7.3, worsening the position by roughly two pawns.

teacher: Black’s 39…g4 is a serious blunder that turns a clearly winning position into a much tighter one, costing roughly two and a half pawns of advantage. The pawn push does create an advanced passed pawn on the g‑file, but it also leaves that pawn isolated and fails to address the more powerful tactical possibilities in the position. The engine indicates that the winning continuation was 39…Bb5+, a checking move that would have skewered White’s king on d3 and the rook on f1, preserving Black’s material edge. By opting for g4, Black forfeits this decisive resource and allows White to cling to the game with the rook controlling the open f‑file.
student: By pushing …g4 Black creates a passed pawn but leaves it isolated on the g‑file, allowing White’s rook to dominate the open f‑file in this rook‑and‑minor‑piece ending. The engine shows that the far stronger continuation was Bb5+, which would have delivered a checking skewer of the white king on d3 while exposing the rook on f1. After …g4 the evaluation drops by roughly two and a half pawns, turning a decisive –7.3 advantage into only about –4½. In short, the pawn advance costs Black a large part of its winning edge.

teacher: White slides the rook to e1, keeping it on the open e‑file in this rook‑and‑minor‑piece ending where Black’s advanced g‑pawn is a constant menace. The engine rates the move as good but it does not improve White’s situation; Black still enjoys a decisive advantage of roughly five pawns. The engine’s preferred move was Rc1, which would have been more accurate, while Black could reply with Nh4, after which the pawn on d4 becomes en prise. In short, Re1 is a solid try that leaves the decisive Black edge essentially unchanged.
student: White’s rook slides to e1, seizing control of the open e‑file in this rook‑and‑minor‑piece ending where Black already enjoys a decisive edge thanks to the advanced passed pawn on g4. The move does not alter the balance – the engine still judges Black winning by roughly four and three‑quarters of a pawn and even notes that after …Nh4 the pawn on d4 would become en prise. Nevertheless, the engine preferred Rc1, which would have been marginally more accurate, so Re1 is a solid but suboptimal choice.

teacher: White’s Re7 is a serious blunder because it simply leaves the rook hanging; Black can reply Nxe7, capturing the rook and converting the position into a minor‑piece endgame where Black is already up two pawns and has an advanced passed pawn on g3. The move therefore worsens the evaluation from a Black advantage of about four pawns to nearly eight, and after the forced Nxe7 the pawn on d4 becomes en prise. The engine’s preferred move was c3, a pawn break that would have struck at both Black’s b4 and d4 pawns and kept material balance.
student: White’s 41 Re7 looks active – it sits on the open e‑file – but it immediately hangs the rook. Black can reply with …Nxe7, capturing the rook and turning the game into a minor‑piece ending while leaving the pawn on d4 undefended, which pushes the evaluation down by roughly three pawns to a decisive Black advantage. The engine indicates that the correct continuation was the pawn break 41 c3, striking at both b4 and d4 and keeping the rook safe. By playing Re7 instead, White handed Black a clear winning edge.

teacher: By capturing the rook on e7 Black not only wins a full rook but also forces the game into a minor‑piece ending, leaving the pawn on d4 hanging. This exchange deepens an already decisive advantage—from roughly seven‑and‑a‑half pawns to more than eight—thanks in part to Black’s advanced passed pawn on g3. The modest improvement of about half a pawn further cements Black’s winning prospects in the simplified position.
student: By taking on e7 Black eliminates White’s last heavy piece and converts the game into a pure minor‑piece ending, leaving Black with a decisive material edge – roughly seven pawns ahead. The capture also leaves the pawn on d4 hanging, but Black already enjoys an advanced passed pawn on g3 that can be exploited later. The engine rates the move as the best possible, improving the evaluation by about half a pawn while preserving a winning advantage. In the principal line White would try to bring his king closer with Ke2, after which Black can continue Kg5 and keep the pressure.

teacher: Black answers White’s 1.d4 with the natural developing move Nf6, bringing the knight to its usual square and keeping the balance of the position. The engine rates it as the best continuation, with the evaluation shifting only a few hundredths of a pawn in Black’s favour (about 0.04 pawns). In the principal variation the game would likely continue 2.e3 e6 3.Be2 c5, preserving the roughly equal standing.
student: Black’s reply …Nf6 develops the knight to its natural square and leaves material perfectly balanced, so the engine still judges the position as roughly equal with a tiny edge for White. The engine rates it as the best continuation, noting that the evaluation changes by only about four‑hundredths of a pawn in Black’s favour. In the principal variation White would likely play e3, after which Black can meet it with …e6 and continue with …c5, keeping the balance intact.

teacher: White’s 3 Bg5 develops a piece but it lets Black equalise a little more, the evaluation slipping from a modest +0.40 to about +0.25 – a loss of roughly a‑quarter pawn. The engine judged the pawn thrust 3 c4 to be superior, keeping a clearer edge for White. In the line the engine suggests, Black could reply …Bb7, after which White might capture on f6 and follow up with d5, but the bishop move itself does not achieve as much as the preferred c4.
student: White develops the bishop to g5, keeping material equal but allowing Black’s …Bb7 and then the exchange on f6 that reduces White’s edge from roughly +0.40 to about +0.25 – a loss of about a sixth of a pawn. The engine judged the more accurate continuation c4, which would have preserved a larger advantage. After Bg5 the evaluation slipped by –0.15 pawns, so while the move is still “good”, it is not the optimal choice in this position.

teacher: Black’s 3…Bb7 completes the queenside fianchetto, placing the bishop on the long diagonal behind the b‑pawn and finishing development without altering the material balance. The engine rates the move as the best in the position, noting that it leaves the evaluation essentially unchanged – White’s slight edge shrinks from +0.25 to +0.22, a gain of only about three‑hundredths of a pawn for Black. In the suggested continuation White could play e3, Black e6, White c4 and Black Bb4+, but the move itself already secures a solid setup and preserves equality.
student: Black’s …Bb7 simply develops the dark‑squared bishop to its natural square, keeping material equal and leaving White still only marginally better – the engine’s assessment shifts by only three hundredths of a pawn in Black’s favour. The move therefore preserves the balance without creating any new weaknesses, which is why it is judged the best continuation. In the principal variation White would continue with e3, after which Black can answer …e6 and later bring the bishop back to b4+, maintaining the equilibrium.

teacher: Black develops the f‑bishop to the natural square e7, bringing the piece into play. The engine rates this as the best continuation, leaving the evaluation essentially unchanged at roughly +0.15 for White—a shift of only about +0.05 pawns for Black. By playing Be7 Black preserves the balance that existed after White’s 5.e3.
student: Black’s …Be7 simply develops the dark‑squared bishop to its natural square, keeping material level and leaving the engine’s assessment virtually unchanged at about +0.15 for White. The move therefore preserves equality while completing development without creating any new weaknesses. According to the principal variation, White would continue with Bd3, after which Black can answer …c5 and later bring the knight to c6, maintaining the balance.

teacher: White’s a4 simply preserves the modest edge, leaving the evaluation at about +0.22. With Black’s king still in the centre while White has already castled, the move does not change the balance of the position. The engine, however, judged Bf4 to be the optimal continuation, but a4 costs nothing – the assessment remains essentially unchanged.
student: White’s 8 a4 simply reinforces the queenside and leaves Black’s king still stuck in the centre while White has already castled, so the position remains roughly equal with a slight edge for White. The engine rates the move as “best” but notes that it does not improve White’s standing – the evaluation stays at about +0.22 pawns. A more ambitious continuation would have been 8 Bf4, which the engine flags as the optimal choice. In practice, however, a4 keeps material even and preserves White’s modest advantage without creating any new threats.

teacher: Black meets White’s pin on the e‑7 bishop head‑on by jumping the knight to e4, immediately attacking the g5 bishop that is doing the pinning. By doing so Black not only forces White to decide how to resolve the pin, but also prepares to answer the natural Bxe7‑fork with …Qxe7, neutralising White’s tactical shot. The engine rates the move as the best continuation and notes that the evaluation stays essentially equal, confirming that the knight jump both relieves the pressure and keeps the balance of the position.
student: By playing …Ne4 Black immediately attacks White’s bishop on e7, which was pinned by the bishop on g5 to the queen on d8. The knight jump forces White to capture with Bxe7, after which Black recaptures with the queen and continues with …Rc1‑c5, keeping material balanced while preserving the slight edge that existed before the exchange. The engine rates the move as excellent and the best continuation, noting that the evaluation remains roughly equal despite the tactical threat. In short, Ne4 creates an immediate counter‑play without conceding any advantage.

teacher: White’s bishop capture on e7 is a striking fork of Black’s queen on d8 and rook on f8, and it wins the opponent’s bishop outright. Black can answer simply with Qxe7, which both removes the fork and captures the intruding bishop, so the material balance is restored; after the recapture White no longer has the bishop pair, while Black retains his lone bishop, leaving the position roughly equal. The engine rates the move as the best continuation, and the evaluation stays essentially unchanged at roughly equal. In the main line Black would recapture with the queen, after which White can continue with Rc1, keeping the position balanced.
student: By playing Bxe7 White eliminates Black’s active bishop and simultaneously creates a fork on the queen on d8 and the rook on f8. The capture forces an immediate queen recapture Qxe7, which both removes the fork and restores material balance, leaving White without the bishop pair but with a clear tactical edge. After the forced line Qxe7 – Rc1 – Rac8 – c4, the engine still evaluates the position as roughly equal, confirming that the trade‑off was worth it despite giving up the bishop pair. This precise sacrifice therefore earns the “best” label.

teacher: By taking on e7 Black eliminates the immediate danger to both the rook on f8 and the queen on e7, while also capturing the bishop. The capture restores material balance and leaves the position essentially equal, with the engine’s evaluation shifting only a few hundredths of a pawn. In the ensuing line White can continue with Qc2, after which Black may press with …f5, but the exchange has already neutralised White’s initiative.
student: By playing Qxe7 Black eliminates White’s active bishop on e7, thereby removing the immediate threat to both the rook on f8 and the queen that had just arrived there. The capture also leaves material perfectly balanced – the engine still evaluates the position as roughly equal, with only a tiny swing of about six‑hundredths of a pawn in Black’s favour. Consequently the move is judged excellent, preserving equality while neutralising White’s most potent piece advantage.

teacher: Black’s rook retreat to f6 turns a modest edge for Black (about half a pawn) into a small advantage for White (just over half a pawn), a swing of roughly a pawn. The move does nothing to improve Black’s cramped bishop on b7, which already has only two safe squares, and it allows White to unleash the pawn break b4, hitting the a5 pawn and opening lines. Engine analysis shows that the far stronger continuation would have been g5, keeping the balance and avoiding the b‑pawn thrust. Consequently, Rf6 is a clear mistake, costing Black about a pawn in evaluation.
student: By playing …Rf6 Black does nothing to relieve the cramped bishop on b7, which already has only two safe squares, and allows White to seize the initiative with the pawn break b4, striking at the a‑pawn. The engine shows that this concession flips the evaluation from a slight Black edge to a small White advantage – roughly a pawn’s worth – making the move a clear mistake. The stronger continuation would have been …g5, keeping the balance, whereas after …Rf6 White can immediately play b4, gaining space and activity.

teacher: White pushes b4, a pawn break that strikes at Black’s pawn on a5. If Black captures with axb4, the a‑file becomes semi‑open for Black while the b‑file becomes semi‑open for White, leaving White with an isolated a4 pawn and Black with doubled b‑pawns – a trade‑off that justifies the slight dip in the engine’s assessment (about a sixth of a pawn). The move also takes advantage of Black’s bishop on b7, which is limited to only two safe squares, and keeps White’s modest edge in the position.
student: White launches the thematic pawn break b4, directly challenging Black’s a‑pawn and opening lines that can be exploited later. If Black replies axb4, the a‑file becomes semi‑open for Black while the b‑file opens for White, leaving Black with doubled b‑pawns and an isolated a‑pawn on a4. The engine rates the move as good and the best continuation, even though it costs White about a sixth of a pawn in evaluation. Black’s bishop on b7 remains cramped to just two safe squares.

teacher: White captures the pawn on b4, opening the c‑file for his pieces. Black would most naturally answer Qxb4, keeping material equality and leaving White with a semi‑open c‑file while Black’s bishop on b7 is confined to only two safe squares and the a‑file remains the main line for Black’s rook. The engine rates the move as good; it trims White’s edge from about +0.62 to +0.51, but White still retains a slight advantage.
student: By playing cxb4 White eliminates Black’s pawn on b4 and forces the natural reply Qxb4, after which the c‑file becomes semi‑open for White while the material balance is restored. The capture also leaves Black’s bishop on b7 with only two safe squares and limits the activity of Black’s rook on the semi‑open a‑file. Although the engine notes that the evaluation slips by roughly a tenth of a pawn, it remains the best continuation because it creates concrete chances without worsening White’s standing.

teacher: White’s 17.Reb1 is a sensible‑looking rook redeployment, but it misses the more forcing pawn break a5 that the engine prefers. By moving the rook to b1 White does not contest Black’s semi‑open a‑file or the pressure on the b6 pawn, and the evaluation slides from a slight plus to a virtually equal position with Black a pawn ahead. Black can then answer with …Qd6, eliminating the queen‑target and solidifying the position. In contrast, a5 would have struck at b6, generating immediate counterplay that White’s move fails to achieve.
student: White’s 17 Reb1 does little more than shuffle the rook and leaves the evaluation essentially unchanged – the engine still judges the position as roughly equal but with Black a pawn ahead. The move therefore costs White about half a pawn compared with the optimal continuation. The engine preferred the pawn break a5, which would have struck at Black’s b‑pawn and kept the initiative. After Reb1 Black can simply answer with …Qd6, removing the pressure on the queen and preserving the extra pawn.

teacher: White’s 18.Qb2 is an inaccuracy that lets Black seize the initiative. By moving the queen White missed the more forcing pawn break a5, which would have struck at the b6 pawn and challenged Black’s semi‑open a‑file, and the evaluation drops from a roughly equal standing to Black being about a pawn better. The move also leaves Black’s rook on a8 comfortably using the a‑file while the bishop on b7 and White’s knight on d2 remain cramped, so the engine rates a5 as the superior continuation.
student: White’s retreat Qb2 does nothing to relieve the cramped situation – Black’s bishop on b7 still has only two safe squares and the rook on a8 already enjoys the semi‑open a‑file while White’s knight on d2 is limited to just one. The engine shows that this inaccuracy costs White roughly three‑quarters of a pawn, turning an almost equal balance into a clear Black advantage. A far stronger try would have been the pawn break a5, striking directly at Black’s b6 pawn and keeping the tension alive. By playing Qb2 White missed that chance and handed Black the initiative.

teacher: White captures the knight on e4, forking Black’s queen on d6 and rook on f6, but the fork is only temporary because Black can simply recapture with the f‑pawn. After the forced …fxe4 the threat disappears, the material balance is restored and Black’s pawn sits firmly on e4 while the f‑file becomes semi‑open for him, leaving White about a pawn worse (the evaluation drops from roughly equal to a clear –0.6). The capture also eliminates the immediate danger to White’s pawn on f2. Even though the position is now slightly inferior, Nxe4 was still the only move that avoids a larger loss, and the engine confirms it as the best continuation.
student: White’s Nxe4 creates a fork on Black’s queen d6 and rook f6, but after the forced …fxe4 the knight disappears and the material balance is restored, leaving Black with a semi‑open f‑file and a pawn on e4 that becomes fixed on a light square. The capture also eliminates the immediate danger to White’s pawn on f2, yet it costs White about half a pawn in evaluation, turning an essentially equal position into one where Black is clearly better. Nevertheless, the engine rates Nxe4 as the best continuation, even though it does not win material outright.

teacher: Ne5 is a precise centralising move that eliminates the immediate danger to the knight, taking advantage of White’s dark‑square pawn mass while Black’s light‑squared bishop is cramped by its own pawns. By doing so White narrows Black’s lead from about half a pawn to roughly a third of a pawn, a modest but meaningful swing in White’s favour. Black can answer with Bxf1, capturing the bishop on f1, yet the engine still rates Ne5 as the best continuation, showing that White’s compensation outweighs the material loss.
student: By playing Ne5 White eliminates the immediate danger to his knight and nudges the evaluation in his favour, improving it by roughly a quarter‑pawn despite Black still being a pawn ahead. The engine’s continuation shows that Black can capture on f1 with Bxf1, after which White recaptures with Rxf1, keeping the balance as tight as possible while Black’s light‑squared bishop remains cramped behind its own pawns. This subtle defensive resource therefore earns the “best” label for the move.

teacher: Black eliminates White’s bishop on f1, initiating an exchange that White must meet with Rxf1. By giving up the only active piece of its “bad” light‑squared bishop, Black restores material balance while keeping the slight edge it already held (the evaluation shifts only from –0.33 to –0.37). The forced rook recapture also removes the immediate pressure on the g2 pawn, leaving Black with a clean, slightly better position. This is why the capture is judged the best move.
student: By taking on f1 Black eliminates White’s active bishop and forces an immediate exchange that will be met by Rxf1, removing the threat to the pawn on g2. The capture does not win material outright – after the forced recapture the material balance remains equal – but it neutralises White’s piece activity while leaving Black with a slight edge (the engine still evaluates the position at about –0.37 for Black). With both sides’ pawns locked on opposite colours, Black’s light‑squared bishop was already cramped by its own pawns, so this simplification preserves the modest advantage without worsening Black’s standing.

teacher: White’s subtle h3 eliminates the immediate danger to the pawn that Black’s rook on h6 was creating, a quiet prophylactic move that leaves the evaluation essentially unchanged – White improves by about a four‑hundredth of a pawn despite being a pawn down. The engine rates it as the best continuation; Black’s most natural reply, Nxe5, would capture the knight on e5 but would also leave the pawn on b6 undefended, giving White chances to generate counterplay. In a position where White’s pawns sit on dark squares and Black’s on light, the move preserves the balance while keeping Black’s semi‑open a‑file pressure in check.
student: By playing h3 White eliminates the immediate danger to the pawn that had just moved onto h3, thereby preserving the structure and keeping the position as balanced as possible despite being a pawn down. The engine rates it as the best continuation, noting that the evaluation shifts by only about four‑hundredths of a pawn in White’s favour while Black remains a little better. If Black were to answer with Nxe5, the capture would win the knight but leave the b6 pawn hanging, giving White counterplay after dxe5. This subtle defensive resource therefore neutralises Black’s pressure without worsening White’s already slight disadvantage.

teacher: Black’s 25…Rg6 keeps the pressure on while respecting the fixed pawn structure – White’s pawns sit on dark squares and Black’s on light, and the rook on a6 already exploits the semi‑open a‑file. By redeploying the second rook to g6 Black improves piece coordination without disturbing the pawn layout, and the engine still judges the position clearly better for Black, roughly a pawn’s worth. The move is the engine’s top choice; the tiny dip in the evaluation (about a fifth of a pawn) simply reflects that it does not increase the advantage further, but it remains a good continuation.
student: By sliding the rook to g6 Black brings another heavy piece onto the board while preserving the pressure along the semi‑open a‑file that his other rook already dominates. The move leaves White’s pawns locked on dark squares and Black’s own pawns fixed on light squares, so the balance of the position stays roughly as it was before – Black remains clearly better by about a pawn. Although the engine notes a slight dip in the evaluation (from –0.93 to –0.74), Rg6 is still the best continuation because it keeps the initiative without creating new weaknesses.

teacher: White’s rook retreat to c2 does nothing to alter the static pawn structure – White’s pawns remain fixed on dark squares while Black’s pawns sit on light squares and Black’s rook already dominates the semi‑open a‑file. Consequently the position slips from a modest Black advantage to a clear one, roughly a pawn down, and the engine points out that the far‑more accurate continuation would have been Qc3. After Rc2 Black can simply play h6 and later expand with c5, a plan that the principal variation shows further consolidates Black’s edge.
student: White’s 26.Rc2 does nothing to challenge Black’s active rook on the semi‑open a‑file and simply shuffles a rook without improving his cramped dark‑square pawn structure. The engine shows that this inaccuracy costs roughly three‑quarters of a pawn, turning an already inferior position into one where Black is clearly better by more than a pawn. A far stronger try would have been 26.Qc3, which keeps the queen active and could have at least reduced Black’s advantage. After 26.Rc2 Black can continue with …h6, after which White might try Rac1 but Black remains comfortably ahead.

teacher: By retreating the rook to a8, Black squandered a clear advantage and let the position slip to equality; the engine’s evaluation drops from a comfortable –1.6 pawns to essentially level. The move gives White the simple reply Rb1, after which the a‑pawn becomes en prise, allowing White to neutralise Black’s earlier superiority. The engine’s preferred move, h6, would have kept the advantage, but Ra8 handed the initiative to White and cost roughly a pawn‑worth of evaluation.
student: By playing Ra8 Black abandoned the initiative that was already in his favour – the evaluation slipped from a clear advantage of about a pawn to an almost level balance. The move does nothing to exploit the semi‑open a‑file or to improve Black’s cramped pawn structure, whereas the engine‑recommended h6 would have kept the pressure and preserved the edge. White can now answer with Rb1, after which the pawn on a4 becomes en prise, giving White active counterplay. In short, Ra8 costs Black roughly one and a half pawns of value.

teacher: White’s 27 Rb1 is the only move that preserves the balance, keeping the evaluation essentially unchanged even though Black is a pawn up. By shifting the rook onto the b‑file White does not directly contest the semi‑open a‑file that Black’s rook on a8 exploits, and although the a4 pawn becomes a target, Black would have to meet the move with …Rb8 to protect the file, after which White can continue with a5 and later Qc3. The engine therefore rates the move as the best, gaining roughly a sixth of a pawn in the assessment.
student: By sliding the rook to b1 White immediately contests the semi‑open a‑file that Black’s rook already occupies, while also eyeing the a‑pawn and preparing to push a5. The move does leave the a4 pawn hanging, but it neutralises Black’s active rook on the file and keeps the balance, as reflected by the engine’s assessment staying essentially equal despite Black being a pawn ahead. In the principal variation Black would reply …Rb8, after which White can continue with a5, followed by …b5 and Qc3, preserving the equilibrium. This precise rook lift therefore earns the “best” label.

teacher: By capturing the pawn on b6 White not only wins a pawn but also opens the b‑file for his rook and instantly creates a passed pawn on a4. With White’s pawns fixed on dark squares and Black’s pawn mass on light squares, the newly opened b‑file gives White active play while Black’s rook on a8 is left on a semi‑open a‑file. Black’s most dangerous continuation would be Qf3, forking the g2‑ and h3‑pawns and threatening Qxg2#, but White can meet it with g3, after which the line continues Rf8 Kh2, leaving the position still roughly equal.
