teacher: White’s bishop jump to g5 checks the king and simultaneously forks the black king on h4 and the pawn on e3, exploiting the fact that Black’s advanced e‑pawn is already hanging. The move is the best continuation, but it nevertheless worsens White’s evaluation by almost a pawn, dropping it from a decisive +11.9 to about +11.0. After the forced king move (the engine’s line continues with …Kh5), White can keep the initiative with g4+ and later capture the e‑pawn, preserving the winning material edge.
student: White’s bishop jump to g5 checks the black king while forking the pawn on e3, exploiting the fact that Black’s e‑pawn is already vulnerable. In this minor‑piece ending the fork does win material – White would continue with g4+, forcing Kg6 and then Bxe3 – but it also costs about a pawn of evaluation, dropping the score from roughly +12 to +10. The engine therefore marks the move as an inaccuracy despite being the best available.

teacher: By pushing the g‑pawn with check, White both creates a new passed pawn on g4 and eliminates the immediate danger to it, while the black king is forced onto g6. After the king move, White can simply capture the advanced e‑pawn (Bxe3) and continue with h4, exploiting Black’s remaining hanging f3 pawn. The engine rewards the idea with a jump of roughly a pawn in the evaluation, confirming that g4+ is the decisive continuation.
student: By playing g4+ White creates a passed pawn on the fourth rank while delivering a check that also eliminates Black’s immediate pressure on the pawn. The move not only secures a new passed pawn but also weakens the pawn shield around his own king, which explains why the engine rates it as the best continuation and even improves the evaluation by about a pawn. In this minor‑piece ending both sides have vulnerable passed pawns—Black’s e‑pawn and f‑pawn—so the extra pawn gives White a clear edge.

teacher: Black’s king step to h7 does nothing to halt White’s overwhelming attack; the engine still sees a forced mate in 20 before the move and, after Kh7, a decisive advantage of roughly +11.2 pawns for White. The move therefore leaves Black in a hopeless position, whereas the engine’s top‑choice Kg7 would have been the only move that could at least keep the defence alive. In this minor‑piece ending with Black’s lone passed pawn on f3, the king retreat to h7 merely walks into the inevitable collapse.
student: By moving the king to h7 Black steps into White’s mating net and immediately allows the forced win that was already looming – the engine now evaluates the position as a decisive White advantage of about eleven pawns. The move does nothing to stop the inevitable mate, whereas the alternative Kg7 would have kept the king out of the line of fire. In this minor‑piece ending with an advanced passed pawn on f3, the loss of the king costs Black roughly ten pawns of material and turns a losing game into a clearly winning one for White.

teacher: Black’s king step to g6 keeps the king out of White’s immediate mating net, inching toward the lone Black pawn. Nevertheless, White can simply capture the advanced passed pawn with Kxf3, after which the material balance swings dramatically in White’s favour. The engine now rates the position as a decisive +10.94‑pawn advantage for White, a far cry from the forced mate that loomed before Black’s move.
student: By moving the king to g6 Black steps out of White’s immediate mating net – the engine had already judged the position a forced mate in nineteen moves for White and now evaluates Kg6 as the best defence, turning the evaluation from “mating in 19” to a decisive +10‑pawn advantage for White. In this minor‑piece ending Black still retains his advanced passed pawn on f3, but the king’s retreat removes any immediate danger. If White continues with the natural Kxf3 capture, Black can answer Kf7 and keep the king active while the pawn remains safe. The move therefore neutralises White’s attack without worsening Black’s overall disadvantage.

teacher: White captures the pawn on f3, opening the f‑file and giving the king more scope in this minor‑piece ending. The capture preserves White’s huge material lead (up eight points) and nudges the engine’s assessment from a decisive +10.9‑pawn advantage to an even larger +11.2‑pawn advantage. With the f‑file now open, White can continue with the plan shown in the principal variation (Kf4‑Kg6‑h4). The move is rightly judged as the best, earning a !!.
student: By taking on f3 White eliminates Black’s last pawn and opens the f‑file for his king, which fits naturally in this minor‑piece ending where the king can become active while the bishop and knight remain well placed. The capture also leaves White with an eight‑point material lead, nudging the evaluation from roughly +10.9 to about +11.2 – a modest but clear improvement. In the engine line Black would reply Kh7, after which White can continue with Kf4, keeping the initiative alive.

teacher: Black’s 57…Kf7 is a catastrophic blunder; instead of the only safe king move Kh7 it steps straight into a forced mating net. After 57…Kf7 White can play h4, and the engine’s continuation (e.g. 58…Ke6 59 Kf4 Kd5) leads to a forced mate in 18 moves. The position collapses from a decisive material advantage for White (+11 pawns) to an inevitable checkmate. By choosing Kh7 Black would have at least avoided the immediate loss.
student: By moving the king to f7 Black walks straight into White’s mating net. The engine shows that the correct defence was Kh7, which would have kept the king out of the line and avoided the forced mate. After Kf7 White can continue with h4, forcing the black king to e6, then Kf4 and finally Kd5, leading to a mate in eighteen moves. In this minor‑piece ending the blunder turns an already losing position for Black into an immediate loss.

teacher: By pushing the h‑pawn White creates a passed pawn on h4 and expands the two‑pawn kingside majority that Black cannot contest. The new pawn structure, with hanging pawns on g4 and h4, shortens the forced mate from 18 moves to 17. In this minor‑piece ending the pawn advance is decisive, and the engine confirms it as the best move.
student: By pushing h4 White creates a passed pawn on the h‑file while advancing his two‑pawn majority on the kingside, turning an already forced mate into a mate even sooner – the engine’s evaluation improves from 18 to 17 moves. The advance also leaves both g4 and h4 hanging, but Black’s king cannot intervene without exposing further weaknesses. In this minor‑piece ending White remains up eight points of material and the mating net stays intact.

teacher: Kg6 is a mistake because it shortens White’s forced mate from 17 moves to 16. By moving onto g6 Black steps into the line of White’s king, allowing White to continue with Kf4 (and then Kf5) and bring the mate home one move earlier. The engine’s preferred move was Ke6, which would have kept the mate at 17. In this minor‑piece ending, with White’s hanging g‑ and h‑pawns, the king move does nothing to improve Black’s situation.
student: By moving the king to g6 Black walks straight into White’s mating net – the evaluation slips from a forced mate in 17 to one in 16, meaning the attack becomes even more urgent. The engine shows that the correct defence would have been Ke6, which would have kept the mate at roughly 17 moves instead of the immediate loss of tempo. After Kg6 White can continue with Kf4, forcing the black king to retreat again, and then the sequence Kf7‑Kf5‑Ke7 drives the opponent closer to victory. In this minor‑piece ending, where White already has hanging g4 and h4 pawns, the mistake costs Black an extra move and accelerates the inevitable mate.

teacher: White pushes the h‑pawn with check, creating an advanced passed pawn and exploiting the two‑pawn majority on the kingside. The move forces the black king to move and shortens the forced mate from 16 to 15 moves. Although the engine would have preferred the quieter Kf4, h5+ still guarantees the same winning outcome while actively advancing the pawn majority.
student: By pushing h5+ White creates a passed pawn and forces Black’s king to step away, shortening the forced win from mate in sixteen to mate in fifteen. The check also advances White’s two‑pawn majority on the kingside while keeping the decisive advantage of being up eight points of material. Although the engine prefers the quieter Kf4, which would have kept the same mating net, the check still improves the evaluation by about a turn.

teacher: Black’s king steps to f7, the best defence that leaves the evaluation unchanged – White still has a forced mate in 15. By moving onto the f‑file Black keeps the king as close as possible to White’s advanced passed pawn on h5 in this minor‑piece ending. The line then continues, for example,  g5 ! Kf8   Kf4  Ke7, and the mate proceeds in the prescribed fifteen moves.
student: Black’s king steps to f7, the only square that keeps the game alive – any other try would allow White to finish with a forced mate in fifteen moves. In this minor‑piece ending White already enjoys an advanced passed pawn on h5 and a clear winning edge, so the move merely delays the inevitable rather than creating new threats. The engine rates Kf7 as the best continuation, but the evaluation remains a forced mate for White in fifteen moves.

teacher: By pushing g‑pawn White creates a passed pawn on g5 and establishes a two‑pawn majority on the kingside in this minor‑piece ending. The advance also leaves White with hanging pawns on g5 and h5, but Black is reduced to a lone king, so the pawn mass will be decisive. The engine still sees a forced mate in 15, confirming that the move preserves the winning line and is indeed the best continuation.
student: By pushing g5 White creates a passed pawn on the seventh rank while also advancing his two‑pawn majority on the kingside, turning the h‑pawn into a hanging pawn that can be taken later. The engine confirms this as the best continuation, preserving the forced mate in fifteen moves even though both sides have hanging pawns. Black’s most natural reply would be Ke6, after which White can continue with Nc5+ and keep the attack alive.

teacher: White’s 1.e4 is the strongest reply, preserving the modest edge of roughly a third of a pawn. The engine notes that the move keeps White’s evaluation essentially unchanged, confirming that it is the best continuation. In the principal variation Black would answer with 1…c5, after which White can continue 2.Nf3 d6 3.c3.
student: White opens with e4, keeping the modest edge that existed before the game and even nudging it up to roughly three‑tenths of a pawn. The engine rates this as the best continuation, noting that Black’s most natural reply would be …c5, after which White can develop with Nf3 and later bring the centre into play with c3. In short, the move preserves White’s slight advantage while preparing to activate his pieces in the ensuing position.

teacher: Black’s …d5 looks like an aggressive pawn break against White’s e‑pawn, but it allows the simple reply exd5. After White captures, Black must recapture with the queen, leaving White with a semi‑open e‑file, a semi‑open d‑file for Black, and doubled pawns on d‑file – a structural concession that pushes the evaluation from a slight White edge to almost a full pawn advantage. The engine judged …e5 to be the correct move; …e5 would have avoided the concession and kept the material balance, whereas …d5 cost Black roughly half a pawn in the eyes of the engine.
student: Black’s …d5 was intended as a pawn break against White’s e‑pawn, but after the natural capture exd5 the d‑file becomes semi‑open for Black while White gains a semi‑open e‑file and ends up with doubled pawns on that file. This structural concession lets White increase his advantage to roughly a pawn’s worth, which is why the engine marks the move an inaccuracy and rates it about half a pawn worse for Black. The engine’s preferred continuation was the central thrust …e5, which would have kept the balance without conceding those extra open lines. Consequently, Black’s position slipped from a slight edge for White to a clear one.

teacher: White correctly captures the pawn on d5, initiating an exchange that Black will almost certainly meet with …Qxd5. After the queen recaptures, the d‑file becomes semi‑open for Black while the e‑file opens for White, preserving White’s modest but clear edge that the engine values at about a pawn. The capture does not win material outright—Black regains the pawn—but it removes the central pawn and keeps White’s slight advantage essentially unchanged.
student: By playing exd5 White eliminates Black’s central pawn and forces an immediate queen trade. After the inevitable …Qxd5 the d‑file becomes semi‑open for Black while the e‑file opens for White, but the capture simply restores material equality – the engine still evaluates White as clearly better by roughly a pawn. The resulting position leaves White with a clear edge in the centre without any loss of advantage.

teacher: White develops the bishop to b5, pinning the knight on c6 to the king on e8. The move leaves White’s clear advantage essentially unchanged, even nudging the evaluation up by about a tenth of a pawn. By fixing the knight, White preserves the pressure and can continue with the natural central break d4, as the engine’s continuation suggests. This is rightly judged the best move in the position.
student: By playing Bb5 White immediately pins the black knight on c6 to the king on e8, so the piece cannot legally move and therefore limits Black’s coordination. The engine rates the move as the best continuation, keeping White’s clear advantage at roughly a pawn’s worth. In the principal variation Black would reply …Bd7, after which White can continue with d4, preserving the pressure.

teacher: White’s 8 b4 is a clear mistake: the pawn on b4 is left en prise, so Black can simply capture with 8…Qxb4, capturing the pawn on b4 and winning a pawn. After that capture the b‑file becomes semi‑open for White and White is left with an isolated a‑pawn, turning a previously clear +0.85 advantage into a roughly –0.73 disadvantage (about a pawn). The engine’s preferred move was 8 d4, which would have kept the balance. Even though Black’s king is still in the centre, White’s premature pawn push squandered the opening edge.
student: By pushing b4 White creates a hanging pawn that can be taken immediately – Black’s best reply would be Qxb4, which both eliminates the threat to the queen and wins the pawn. After the capture White is left with an isolated a‑pawn and a semi‑open b‑file, whereas before the move the evaluation was roughly a pawn in White’s favour. The engine therefore labels the move a mistake, costing about one and a half pawns compared with the correct continuation d4, which would have kept material equal and preserved White’s advantage.

teacher: Black tried 8…Qh5, mainly to shield the f7‑pawn and the queen, but the move leaves the queen far from the centre while Black’s king is still uncastled and White has already secured his king. By playing it Black also gives up the obvious 8…Qxb4, which would have captured the pawn on b4 and removed the threat to the queen. The slip flips the evaluation from a clear Black advantage (about a pawn) to a White edge of roughly the same magnitude, making the move a clear mistake that costs Black about a pawn.
student: By playing …Qh5 Black merely sidesteps the immediate danger to the f‑pawn and the queen, but it does nothing to meet White’s pressure on the queenside. The engine shows that the far stronger continuation would have been …Qxb4, which both eliminates the threat to the queen on b4 and wins the pawn on b4, keeping material balanced. After …Qh5 White can simply castle, after which the evaluation swings to a clear advantage for White – roughly a pawn’s worth. In short, the move costs Black about a pawn’s worth of standing.

teacher: White seizes the moment with the pawn break b5, striking at Black’s a‑pawn and expanding the queenside majority of four pawns against three. The push also removes the immediate threat to the b‑pawn, but it costs a little ground: the engine rates Be2 as the optimal continuation, which would have kept White’s edge a bit larger. After 9.b5 the position is still only slightly better for White (about a half‑pawn), with Black’s king still in the centre while White has already castled. Black could answer with …Na5, which removes the threat to the knight on a5.
student: White pushes b5, a pawn break that strikes directly at Black’s a‑pawn and expands his queenside majority (four pawns versus three). The advance also eliminates the immediate danger to the pawn on b5, but it does not improve White’s standing – the engine’s evaluation slips from roughly +0.66 to +0.56, a loss of about a tenth of a pawn. Although the position remains favourable for White with his king already safely castled, the engine judged Be2 to be stronger because it would keep more pressure without conceding the small drop in score. teacher: White chose 11 d4, advancing the queenside pawn majority. Although the move gains space, it costs White almost a pawn of evaluation, shrinking the lead from about a pawn to a slight edge and earning an “inaccuracy” label. Even with Black’s king still in the centre and the f8‑bishop lacking safe squares, the pawn push fails to exploit those factors.
student: White’s advance d4 looks natural – it pushes the queenside pawn majority forward and leaves Black’s king stuck in the centre while the bishop on f8 remains without safe squares. In practice, however, the move costs roughly a pawn of evaluation, shrinking White’s advantage from about a pawn to just a small edge. The engine judged Rb1 to be the superior continuation, keeping more pressure on Black’s cramped king and avoiding the loss of momentum that occurred after d4. Consequently, the pawn push is an inaccuracy that reduces White’s lead.

teacher: Black’s 11…Bg4, which merely pins the f‑knight to the queen, turns out to be a costly mistake, worsening the evaluation by roughly a pawn. With the king still stuck in the centre and the f8‑bishop lacking any safe squares, the pin does little to improve Black’s position; White can simply meet it with 12 Bf4, after which Black’s best continuation would be to capture on f3, allowing White to recapture and retain the initiative. The engine shows that the far stronger 11…Na5 would have kept the balance, whereas the bishop move lets White consolidate and enjoy a clear advantage.
student: By playing …Bg4 Black tries to pin the f‑knight to the queen on d1, but the move does nothing to relieve the cramped situation of his own pieces – especially since his king remains in the centre and the bishop on f8 already has no safe squares. The engine shows that this costs Black roughly a pawn’s worth of evaluation, turning a slight White edge into a clear one. A far stronger try would have been …Na5, which keeps the king safer and avoids giving White the easy Bxf3 continuation. Consequently, …Bg4 is a mistake that hands White a comfortable lead.

teacher: White’s bishop retreats to f4, completing development while leaving Black’s king stranded in the centre and the cramped bishop on f8 without a safe haven. The move preserves White’s clear edge – the engine’s evaluation nudges from +1.35 to +1.44 – and forces Black to confront the awkward pin on the f‑knight. If Black replies with the natural …Bxf3, the bishop does fork the queen on d1 and the pawn on g2, but White can simply recapture, after which Black’s best continuation is …e6, after which White can continue with Rb1, leaving White’s positional superiority intact.
student: By retreating the bishop to f4 White eliminates Black’s active pin on the f‑file – the bishop on g4 now attacks both the queen on d1 and the white knight on f3, but that knight cannot be taken because it is defended by the other knight on f3. The engine rates this as the best continuation, keeping White’s clear advantage of roughly a pawn (+1.4 pawns). If Black were to capture with …Bxf3, White could recapture with gxf3 and continue with ideas such as e6 and Rb1, preserving the edge.

teacher: White’s 13.Qxf3 does eliminate the bishop, but it walks straight into Black’s queen on h5, which simultaneously forks the g2‑pawn and the bishop on f4 and also attacks the pawn on f7. That queen pressure costs White about a pawn, pulling the evaluation down from a comfortable +1.6 to a modest +0.55. The engine’s preferred continuation, 13.gxf3, would have captured the bishop while keeping the queen safe and avoiding the fork. Hence the capture is a clear mistake that hands Black a concrete tactical resource and erodes White’s advantage.
student: White’s capture Qxf3 looks tempting because it eliminates the immediate danger to the queen and the pawn on g2, but it merely initiates an exchange that leaves Black with the bishop pair after the inevitable …Qxf3. By allowing this forced queen trade White forfeits the larger advantage – the evaluation drops from about +1.6 to +0.5, roughly a pawn’s worth. The engine’s preferred continuation was gxf3, which would have removed the same threats without giving Black the chance to equalise. Consequently, the move costs White a clear edge.

teacher: Black’s queen takes on f3, winning the white queen and forking the pawn on g2 and the bishop on f4, but the queen itself becomes a target. White can simply recapture with gxf3, eliminating the fork, opening the g‑file and giving Black a slight pawn‑majority edge on the kingside. Although the capture restores material balance, the resulting queen exchange leaves Black with a modestly worse position (White’s advantage rises to about a pawn). The move is nevertheless the best available, even if it costs Black a little in the evaluation.
student: By playing Qxf3 Black not only wins White’s queen but also creates a fork on the g‑pawn and the bishop on f4, forcing White to capture with gxf3. The resulting exchange leaves Black with a four‑to‑three pawn majority on the kingside while the g‑file becomes semi‑open for White, which explains why the engine still judges White to be about a pawn ahead even though Black was temporarily up nine points of material. Although the move costs Black roughly a sixth of a pawn in evaluation terms, it remains the best continuation because any other try would allow White to retain the extra queen.

teacher: Black’s 16…e6 is the engine’s top choice, a quiet pawn push that bolsters the kingside majority of four pawns against White’s three. The move leaves material unchanged and even nudges the evaluation a few tenths in Black’s favour, while White still enjoys the bishop pair and Black’s knight on a5 is limited to a single safe square. The engine foresees White replying with Bd2, after which Black can bring the rook to a8 and later improve the bishop to e7, maintaining the slight advantage for White.
student: By playing …e6 Black pushes his last pawn forward, strengthening the four‑pawn majority on the kingside and keeping material perfectly balanced. The engine rates it as the best continuation, noting that the evaluation shifts only marginally from +0.33 to +0.26 in White’s favour – essentially unchanged for Black. With the knight on a5 confined to its single safe square and White still enjoying the bishop pair, this modest advance preserves Black’s chances without worsening the position.

teacher: By jumping to a4 White lifts the knight and uncovers a discovered attack from the bishop on d2 against Black’s only‑move‑able knight on a5. The move also leaves the rook on b1 active on the semi‑open b‑file, and White’s evaluation barely improves, staying a hair better (+0.08 pawns). Engines, however, prefer Ne2, which creates the same discovered attack while keeping the knight more flexible; after Na4 Black can answer with Ra8, removing the threat to the a5‑knight. Nonetheless, the position remains essentially unchanged, with White still holding a slight edge.
student: By playing Na4 White uncovers the bishop on d2’s line against Black’s knight on a5, exploiting the fact that the knight now has only one safe retreat while White already enjoys the bishop pair and a semi‑open b‑file with the rook on b1. The engine rates the move as keeping White’s slight edge essentially unchanged – the evaluation improves from +0.29 to +0.37 – but it notes that Ne2 would have achieved the same discovery more directly. Black can meet the idea most comfortably with Ra8, which would remove the pressure on the a5‑knight. In short, Na4 is a solid continuation that preserves White’s modest advantage without creating new weaknesses.

teacher: By pulling the rook back to a8 Black eliminates the only real danger to the knight on a5, which otherwise had just a single safe square. The move also re‑establishes the rook on the semi‑open a‑file, preserving Black’s piece activity while the material balance stays level. The engine rates the move as excellent, the evaluation shifting only marginally in White’s favour (about a few hundredths of a pawn). In the principal line White can try Nb6, after which Black would reply Ra7, keeping the position roughly equal.
student: By sliding the rook from a7 to a8 Black eliminates White’s immediate pressure on the a‑file and thereby protects the lone safe haven for the a5‑knight. The move also makes full use of the semi‑open a‑file that now belongs to Black’s rook, while White still enjoys the bishop pair. The engine rates it as an excellent continuation, keeping the evaluation virtually unchanged with White remaining only marginally better. In the principal line White would try Nb6, after which Black can meet it with Ra7 and continue with …c4 followed by Rd8.

teacher: White sharpens his queenside majority by playing c4, a move that both expands the three‑pawn majority against Black’s two and removes the d5 square from the Black knight on f6. With the bishop pair in hand and Black’s knight on a5 cramped to a single safe retreat, the pawn push consolidates White’s slight edge, which the engine rates as a modest increase. Black can answer with the thematic …c5 pawn break against the d4 pawn, but White remains a little better.
student: By pushing c4 White expands his queenside pawn majority to three versus Black’s two and simultaneously deprives the Black knight on f6 of the useful d5‑square. The advance also leaves Black’s knight on a5 with only one safe retreat while preserving White’s bishop pair in an endgame where Black’s rook already enjoys the semi‑open a‑file. The engine rates the move as the best, keeping White’s slight edge essentially unchanged at about +0.4 pawn. Black could try the thematic …c5 pawn break, striking at White’s d4 pawn, but White remains comfortably ahead.

teacher: White’s 22 Be3 simply neutralises the immediate threat to the d4‑pawn, but in doing so it relinquishes the modest edge that White enjoyed. The inaccuracy cost White about two‑thirds of a pawn; a more precise 22 Rfd1 would have kept the rook on the semi‑open d‑file and preserved the advantage.
student: White’s retreat Be3 does eliminate the immediate danger to the d‑pawn, but it allows Black the thematic …c5 break that strikes at that pawn and erases White’s earlier edge. The engine rates the move an inaccuracy, dropping the evaluation by roughly two‑thirds of a pawn despite material being equal. A more accurate continuation would have been Rfd1, keeping pressure on Black’s queenside while preserving the advantage. After …c5, White could answer with d5, after which Black can capture on d5 and the game proceeds into a balanced endgame.

teacher: Black’s retreat Nd7 not only leaves the h7 pawn en prise to White’s bishop on d3, but also gives up the far more demanding pawn break c5, which would have struck at White’s d4 pawn. By allowing the bishop to target h7, Black gives White a clear advantage and the evaluation jumps from roughly equal to White being about a pawn better. In engine terms the move costs roughly three‑quarters of a pawn compared with the preferred 1…c5, which would have created active counterplay on the queenside. Even though the rook on d8 still enjoys the semi‑open d‑file, that advantage is outweighed by the new tactical liability.
student: By playing Nd7 Black leaves the h‑pawn hanging and does nothing to challenge White’s central pawn chain, allowing White to consolidate his advantage. The engine rates the move an inaccuracy, costing Black roughly three‑quarters of a pawn compared with the more active …c5 pawn break that would have struck at White’s d4 pawn. After Nd7 White can continue with Rfd1, after which Black could try Nxb6 but White simply recaptures with Rxb6, leaving Black still worse.

student: By playing cxd5 White eliminates Black’s pawn on d5, opening the c‑file and leaving Black with isolated pawns on d5 and b7 while also giving White a temporary edge in the centre. student: By playing …cxd5 Black opens the c‑file while creating a passed pawn on d5, giving him a two‑pawn majority on the queenside despite leaving isolated b7 and d5 pawns. Consequently the rook shift is an excellent, precise way to maximise activity in this equal endgame.
student: By playing Rfd1 White brings his rook onto the semi‑open d‑file, directly contesting Black’s rook that already occupies the a‑file and complementing the bishop pair that gives him a clear spatial edge. The engine rates the move as excellent and the best continuation, keeping the evaluation essentially unchanged at roughly equal despite being down a pawn. In the principal variation Black would try …d4, after which White can capture with Rxd4, then recapture with Rxd4 and finally develop the knight to c8, preserving the balance.

student: By playing Rxa2 Black wins a pawn and opens the a‑file while creating a passed pawn on b7, but the capture also allows White to give check with Nxe7+, attacking the poorly defended knight on c5 and capturing the bishop on e7. This sequence turns a modest White edge into a decisive one – the evaluation jumps from +0.42 to +5.79 in White’s favour, a swing of about five pawns for Black. student: White opens with 1.d4, keeping material level and leaving the engine’s assessment virtually unchanged at about +0.16 for White. Although the engine prefers 1.e4 as the optimal continuation, 1.d4 is still an excellent choice because it maintains equality without any immediate drawback.

teacher: Black’s …Nf6 is an excellent developing move that leaves the position essentially unchanged, with White still holding a very slight edge (the engine now scores the position at +0.21, i.e. less than a pawn). The engine, however, rates 1…d5 as the superior alternative; by striking at White’s centre Black could have improved the evaluation by about a fifth of a pawn. In practice the knight move keeps material level and the balance of the opening, but it forfeits the more ambitious central break that would have reduced White's edge by about a fifth of a pawn.
student: Black’s reply …Nf6 simply develops the knight to its natural square and leaves material perfectly balanced, so the engine still rates the position as roughly equal with White a shade better. The engine preferred the more ambitious …d5, which would have challenged White’s centre and kept the balance tighter. By opting for Nf6 Black missed that chance but the move does not worsen his standing – the evaluation shifts by only about five‑hundredths of a pawn in White’s favour.

teacher: Black meets White’s early c4 with the natural …e6, a solid developing move that keeps material level and the position essentially balanced. The engine still judges the position roughly equal, with White only a few‑tenths of a pawn better. In the expected continuation the game would go 3.Nf3 Be7 4.Nc3 d5, showing Black’s plan to finish development and contest the centre.
student: Black’s …e6 is an excellent reply that leaves material perfectly balanced and keeps the engine’s assessment virtually unchanged – White remains only a fraction of a pawn ahead. The engine rates it as the best continuation, with the most likely line continuing 3.Nf3 Be7 4.Nc3 d5. By playing …e6 Black preserves equality while giving himself the option to develop the bishop later.

teacher: White’s 8.b4 is an attempt to launch a queenside pawn break against Black’s c5 pawn, but with the king still in the centre while Black has already castled the thrust is premature. Black can simply reply 8…cxd4, recapturing the pawn on d4 and erasing White’s modest edge, which drops the evaluation from about a pawn’s worth to a roughly equal standing. The engine judged the move an inaccuracy, costing White roughly three‑quarters of a pawn, and preferred the central break 8.d5, which would have struck at Black’s e6 pawn and kept the advantage.
student: White’s 8 b4 tries to strike at Black’s pawn on c5, but it does nothing to address the fact that his own king is still stuck in the centre while Black has already castled. The engine shows that this concession costs roughly two‑thirds of a pawn, turning a clear +0.7 advantage into an almost equal standing. A more accurate continuation would have been 8 d5, which attacks Black’s e6 pawn and keeps the initiative. After 8 b4 Black can simply capture on d4 with …cxd4, after which White recaptures Nxd4 and the game proceeds without any lasting edge for White.

teacher: White develops the bishop to b2, putting it on the long diagonal from b2 to g7.  Although the evaluation drops a little to about +0.22, the engine still rates Bb2 as the best continuation, with White’s king still in the centre while Black has already castled.  Black’s most accurate reply would be Ne5, after which White can answer Be2 and later bring the king to safety by castling.
student: White develops the dark‑squared bishop to b2, keeping material equal and preserving the slight edge that existed before the move. The engine rates it as the best continuation, though the evaluation slips by about a tenth of a pawn because White’s king remains in the centre while Black has already castled. In the principal variation Black would continue with Ne5, after which White can meet it with Be2 and later castle safely.

teacher: Black answered with 11…b6, a quiet pawn move that simply reinforces the queenside but does nothing to alleviate the fact that the bishop on e7 has no safe squares. The move is solid, yet it allows White to retain a small edge – the evaluation shifts to White being about six‑tenths of a pawn better. The engine’s top choice was the more aggressive 11…a5, a pawn break that would strike at White’s b4 pawn and generate immediate counter‑play. By opting for b6 instead, Black missed that more active possibility and the position slipped to a slight White advantage.
student: By playing …b6 Black does nothing to relieve the cramped situation – his bishop on e7 remains without safe squares and White’s king is still stuck in the centre. The engine rates the move as a moderate worsening for Black, turning an essentially equal position into one where White is about half a pawn ahead. A more accurate continuation would have been the pawn break a5, which strikes directly at White’s b‑pawn and keeps the balance. Consequently, …b6 is a good but suboptimal choice that costs Black about a third of a pawn.

teacher: White’s checking capture on e7 forces Black’s queen to recapture, trading the knight for the bishop and leaving Black without the bishop pair. The exchange restores material balance, so White’s slight edge (about a quarter‑pawn) is essentially unchanged, while the loss of the bishop pair gives Black a lingering structural drawback. Because the king is still in the centre and Black has already castled, the move also keeps White’s initiative. The engine rates the move “excellent” and confirms that the only sensible reply is Qxe7, after which the position remains only marginally better for White.
student: White’s capture Nxe7+ forces an immediate queen trade and leaves Black with a bishop that can be taken later, thereby eliminating the opponent’s bishop‑pair advantage. After the forced …Qxe7 the material balance is restored, but Black has surrendered the bishop pair, leaving White with the bishop pair and a slight edge – the engine’s evaluation stays at roughly +0.27 for White. The move also keeps White’s king safe while Black enjoys the safety of having already castled, making it an excellent continuation.

teacher: White’s retreat of the bishop to d3 does little to meet Black’s looming pawn break; after the move Black can play …e5, striking at the pawn on f4 and nudging the evaluation into Black’s favor. The engine’s preferred continuation was 16 g3, which would have reinforced f4 and kept the position roughly equal. By allowing …e5, White’s position slipped by about half a pawn, turning a marginally better stance into a slight Black edge. This inaccuracy costs White a modest but tangible advantage.
student: White’s retreat Bd3 does nothing to meet Black’s looming …e5 pawn break, which would strike directly at the f‑pawn and give Black active counterplay. The engine rates the move an inaccuracy, dropping the evaluation by about half a pawn even though White still enjoys the bishop pair. A more accurate continuation would have been g3, keeping the balance without allowing the central thrust. Consequently Black now holds a slight edge.

teacher: By jumping to f4 Black immediately creates a fork on g2 and d3, hitting both the pawn that shields the king and the bishop on d3 while also removing the earlier threat to the knight itself. The fork is especially potent because White’s bishop on b2 is already limited to only two safe squares, making it hard for White to defend both targets. White’s most accurate reply would be Qf3, which would simultaneously protect the bishop and the g‑pawn, after which Black can continue with …a6 and later capture on d3. The move leaves the evaluation essentially unchanged, keeping Black a shade better.
student: By playing …Nf4 Black not only eliminates White’s immediate pressure on the knight but also creates a fork, attacking both the pawn on g2 and the bishop on d3 at once. The move leaves material equal and the engine still judges Black to be a shade better – roughly half a pawn ahead. White can meet the threat most simply with Qf3, which would remove the forked pieces while keeping the position balanced. This precise tactical resource therefore earns the “best” label.

teacher: White retreats the bishop to c2, thereby removing the immediate threat to the bishop on d3.  While the move is safe and keeps the bishop pair intact—especially important since the bishop on b2 has only two safe squares—it is a modest inaccuracy: the engine notes that Qf3 would have simultaneously defended the bishop on d3 and the pawn on g2, preserving White’s standing.  By choosing Bc2 the evaluation slides from a slight Black edge to a clearer one, roughly a pawn’s worth, and now Black can consider the pawn break …b5, striking at White’s pawn on c4.
student: White retreats the bishop to c2, eliminating the immediate danger that had been aimed at it. The move does not address Black’s looming …b5 pawn thrust against the c‑pawn, so the evaluation slips from a slight Black edge to roughly a pawn’s advantage – a loss of about 0.18 pawn for White. The engine judged Qf3 to be superior because it would have removed the threats to both the d3‑bishop and the g2‑pawn while keeping more pressure on Black’s centre. Consequently, Bc2 is a good defensive try but costs White a modest amount of ground.

teacher: White captures the pawn on d5, starting an exchange that opens the d‑file and leaves the e‑file semi‑open for White. After Black’s forced N6xd5 the knight lands on d5 and is left en prise, while Black gains a passed pawn on e5 and a bishop on b7 that has only one safe square, which together explain why the evaluation slips further into Black’s favor (about a third of a pawn worse for White) even though White remains a pawn up. Nevertheless, exd5 restores material balance and makes use of the newly opened lines, so it is rightly judged as the best (good) continuation.
student: By playing exd5 White eliminates Black’s central pawn and opens the d‑file while giving White a semi‑open e‑file after the forced recapture N6xd5. The capture also leaves Black with a passed pawn on e5, but it does not win material because Black can simply recapture with N6xd5, restoring the balance. Although this exchange costs White about a third of a pawn in evaluation terms, it remains the best continuation available, keeping the bishop pair active against Black’s cramped bishop on b7.

teacher: Black captures the pawn on d5 with the knight from b6, starting an exchange that leaves the knight temporarily en prise. After White recaptures with cxd5 the c‑file opens, giving Black’s rook on c8 a useful semi‑open line while White is left with an isolated queen’s pawn on d5. The engine rates the move as good – it costs Black only a small fraction of a pawn, but the resulting structural weakness for White and the active c‑file keep Black comfortably better.
student: By taking on d5 Black eliminates White’s central pawn and forces an immediate trade that leaves White with an isolated queen’s pawn on d5. The capture also opens the c‑file, giving Black’s rook on c8 a useful line while the bishop on b7 remains confined to its single safe square. Although the knight on d5 becomes en prise, White can simply recapture with cxd5, restoring material equality but leaving Black still ahead in the evaluation. This exchange therefore preserves Black’s sizable advantage without worsening it further.

teacher: Black’s queen swoops into c2, taking the bishop and simultaneously forking White’s remaining bishop on b2 and the pawn on f5, thereby eliminating the immediate threats to those pieces. After White is forced to recapture, the queens are exchanged and the bishops become opposite‑coloured, leaving material equal while Black retains a comfortable advantage despite the slight dip in the engine’s evaluation. The sacrifice costs Black only about a seventh of a pawn, yet it preserves a comfortable advantage in a position where White’s passed d‑pawn is the only real counter‑play.
student: By playing …Qxc2 Black eliminates White’s active bishop on c2 while forking the bishop on b2 and the pawn on f5, forcing the natural reply Qxc2. After this forced exchange the game heads into a queenside attack with opposite‑coloured bishops – a long‑term structural asset that compensates for the slight drop in evaluation. The engine rates the capture as good, noting that it costs Black about a sixth of a pawn compared with the previous position but still leaves him clearly better by roughly one and a half pawns.

teacher: Black forces a check with Qxd1+, the queen simultaneously forking White’s king on g1 and the advanced pawn on d5. White can only answer Rxd1, which simply removes the queen and restores the material balance, so Black does not lose any material and the advantage (about two pawns) actually improves slightly. The move therefore eliminates White’s queen, leaves the passed pawn on d5 under attack, and is rightly judged the best continuation in a position with opposite‑coloured bishops.
student: By playing Qxd1+ Black not only wins White’s queen but also delivers a checking fork that attacks both the white king on g1 and the advanced passed pawn on d5. The capture forces the natural reply Rxd1, which eliminates the immediate danger to the pawn while restoring material balance, leaving Black still up nine points of material with a clear positional edge. The engine rates the move as the best possible, improving Black’s evaluation by about a tenth of a pawn even though the material advantage remains unchanged. In the principal line White would take on d1, after which Black can continue with …f6, followed by …d6 and …Rfd8.

teacher: By playing Rxd1 White eliminates Black’s queen and simultaneously removes the direct threat to the advanced passed pawn on d5. The capture neutralises Black’s immediate pressure, yet the engine still judges the position as roughly two pawns better for Black, so White’s evaluation remains essentially unchanged. Black’s most natural reply would be f6, which would shore up the pawn on e5.
student: By playing Rxd1 White eliminates Black’s queen and simultaneously removes the immediate danger to the advanced passed pawn on d5. The capture restores material balance while leaving the position with opposite‑coloured bishops and a bishop on b7 that has very few safe squares, so the engine still judges Black as clearly better—about two pawns ahead. Black can try …f6, which would defend the e5 pawn, but even after that continuation White remains the best choice in this endgame.

teacher: By pushing h4 White loosens the pawn shield that guards his king, and the move also gives Black the tactical shot Nd5, which immediately attacks the advanced d6 pawn that is only thinly defended.  The engine shows that this costs White roughly a third of a pawn, deepening Black’s already sizable advantage (now about ‑2.6 pawns).  In contrast, the stronger continuation Rfd2 would have kept the d‑pawn better protected and avoided the weakening of the king’s shelter.  After h4, Black can continue Nd5, followed by White’s forced h5 and Black’s Ne3, keeping the pressure on the passed pawn.
student: By pushing h4 White loosens the pawn shield in front of his king, a concession that Black can immediately exploit with …Nd5, attacking the advanced passed pawn on d6 and further weakening White’s defensive structure. The engine rates the move as “good” but notes it costs roughly a third of a pawn compared with the optimal continuation Rfd2, which would have kept the king more secure. In the resulting line Black can continue …Nd5, after which White may try to defend with h5, followed by …Ne3 and Rd3, leaving Black clearly ahead.

teacher: By playing …Bxf3 Black eliminates White’s knight on f3, and after the forced Rxf3 the game simplifies into a rook‑and‑minor‑piece ending. The capture does not gain material—White simply recaptures—but it still pushes the evaluation from a clear advantage to a winning one, improving Black’s score by roughly three‑quarters of a pawn and temporarily leaving him up three pawns before White’s recapture. The engine, however, notes that the sharper …Nd5 would have struck at White’s advanced passed pawn on d6, a target that is only loosely defended. After White’s recapture, the g‑pawn on g2 becomes en prise, yet despite the material being equal, Black’s opposite‑colour bishops give him a decisive edge.
student: By taking on f3 Black eliminates White’s active knight and forces the natural reply Rxf3, turning the game into a rook‑and‑minor‑piece ending where Black remains three points ahead. The capture also leaves the white pawn on g2 hanging, giving Black concrete chances to win material. Although the engine prefers the more aggressive Nd5, which would attack the poorly defended d6 pawn, Bxf3 still improves Black’s standing by about three‑quarters of a pawn and secures a decisive edge despite White’s advanced passed pawn on d6 and opposite‑colour bishops.
violations: claims material is won, but the capture is an exchange

teacher: White eliminates Black’s active bishop on f3, converting the position into a rook‑and‑minor‑piece ending and removing the immediate threat to the rook on d1. Although the capture allows Black to fork the bishop on b2 and the pawn on g2 with a rook move, Black’s most forcing reply would be 27…Rc2, forking the bishop on b2 and the pawn on g2, after which White can continue 28.Rxf4 and the game proceeds with 28…exf4 29.Bc1. The engine’s evaluation stays at a decisive Black advantage (about three‑and‑a‑half pawns) and the change in material is negligible, confirming that Rxf3 was the correct, excellent move.
student: By taking on f3 White eliminates Black’s active bishop and forces the game into a rook‑and‑minor‑piece ending while also removing the immediate danger to his own rook on d1. The capture does leave the pawn on g2 hanging, but with White’s passed pawn on d6 already marching forward and his light‑square pawn structure intact, the material balance remains equal. Black can reply with …Rc2, forking the bishop on b2 and the pawn on g2, yet even that continuation leaves Black with a decisive edge – the engine still evaluates the position as about three pawns ahead for Black. Thus Rxf3 is the correct choice, keeping the evaluation essentially unchanged despite the slight loss in material.

teacher: Black’s 27…Rc2!! creates a powerful fork, attacking White’s bishop on b2 and the pawn on g2, and thereby nudges the already decisive advantage a little higher. White’s most natural reply would be 28 Rxf4, which captures the knight but leaves the rook on f4 en prise; after 28…exf4 Black regains the piece and can continue with …Rc5, keeping the winning edge in this rook‑and‑minor‑piece ending where White’s passed pawn on d6 is still far from promotion. The engine rates the move as a slight improvement (+0.13 pawn) and confirms it as the best continuation.
student: By playing Rc2 Black not only places his rook on the critical c‑file but also creates a fork, attacking White’s bishop on b2 and the pawn on g2 at once. The engine rates this as the best continuation, improving Black’s already decisive edge by roughly a tenth of a pawn. If White tries to eliminate the threat with Rxf4, the rook on f4 would be left en prise, allowing Black to recapture with exf4 and keep the initiative. In this rook‑and‑minor‑piece ending, where White’s passed pawn sits on d6 and all pawns are fixed on light squares, the fork consolidates Black’s winning chances.

teacher: Black’s 28…Rc5 merely sidesteps the immediate danger to the rook, “removing the threat to the rook on c5”, but it does so at the cost of a huge swing in the evaluation – the position falls from a decisive –3.6‑pawn edge to only a slight –0.5‑pawn advantage. The engine’s preferred move, Ne2+, would have both eliminated the threat to the rook on c2 and delivered a check, preserving Black’s winning chances. After the blunder White can play a4, securing the b5 pawn and maintaining the pressure, while Black’s pieces become passive. In short, the move squandered about three pawns of advantage and turned a winning endgame into a barely better one.
student: By playing Rc5 Black merely sidesteps the immediate danger to the rook, but in doing so he allows White’s advanced passed pawn on d6 to march forward with a4, which eliminates the pressure on the b‑pawn. The engine shows that the far stronger continuation would have been Ne2+, a checking move that also removes the threat to the rook on c2 while keeping the initiative alive. After Rc5 the evaluation drops sharply – roughly three pawns – turning a decisive advantage into only a slight edge for Black. In short, the move costs Black about three pawns of value.

teacher: White’s move Rfd2 ignores the most urgent danger in this rook‑and‑minor‑piece ending: the b5 pawn is hanging. Black can simply reply Rxb5, winning the pawn and pushing the evaluation from a slight Black edge to a clear advantage of more than a pawn. The engine’s top choice, a4, would have removed that threat by allowing axb5 after a capture, keeping material equal. As a result the move costs White roughly a pawn of material and strategic chances.
student: White’s 29.Rfd2 does nothing to meet Black’s looming …Rxb5 capture that would win the b‑pawn, so the evaluation slides from a slight Black edge to a clear one‑pawn disadvantage. The engine shows that the far stronger try was 29.a4, which would have removed the threat to the b5 pawn and kept material balanced. By playing Rfd2 instead, White allows Black to seize the pawn with …Rxb5, after which the continuation Bc3 e4 Re1 leaves Black comfortably ahead. This mistake costs roughly a pawn in practical terms.

teacher: White’s 30 a4 simply creates an isolated pawn on a4, a fact that the engine notes without improving White’s standing; Black is still about a pawn ahead and the evaluation stays unchanged. In this rook‑and‑minor‑piece ending, where White’s dark‑squared bishop faces Black’s knight and White already has an advanced passed pawn on d6, the engine preferred the more active 30 g3. Black can comfortably answer with …Rb3, removing the threat to the rook on b3.
student: White pushes a4, leaving an isolated pawn on a4 in this rook‑and‑minor‑piece ending where his dark‑squared bishop meets Black’s lone knight. The engine rates the move as essentially neutral – it does not improve White’s standing and leaves Black still about two pawns ahead. A more accurate try would have been g3, which would have kept the balance, but after a4 Black can simply meet the threat by playing Rb3, removing the danger to the rook on b3.

teacher: By playing …Rxd6 Black captures the pawn on d6 and opens the d‑file, instantly removing the threat to the knight on d3. The capture also eliminates White’s pressure along the file, turning Black’s existing two‑pawn material edge into a decisive advantage in this rook‑and‑minor‑piece ending. The engine rates the move as improving the evaluation by roughly a third of a pawn, confirming it as the clear best continuation.
student: By playing Rxd6 Black eliminates White’s pawn on d6, opens the d‑file and at the same time removes the immediate danger to the knight that was pinned by White’s rook on d1. The capture also leaves Black with a two‑pawn material edge in this rook‑and‑minor‑piece ending, nudging the evaluation from a comfortable –2.9 to a decisive –3.2. In the engine line White would try h5, after which Black can continue with Rd7, keeping the pressure and preserving the winning advantage.

teacher: White’s 33 .Be1 simply shuffles the dark‑squared bishop to a passive square, leaving the rook‑and‑minor‑piece ending unchanged and allowing Black’s advantage to grow. In this position the white rook on d1 already pins Black’s knight on d3 to the rook on d6, but the bishop retreat does nothing to challenge Black’s active pieces or improve White’s pawn structure. The engine shows that the more precise 33 .h5 is the best move, while Be1 pushes the score to about –4 pawns, a loss of roughly three‑quarters of a pawn. Consequently the move is rightly marked as an inaccuracy.
student: White’s retreat Be1 does nothing to improve his cramped situation in this rook‑and‑minor‑piece ending – the bishop simply sits on an inactive square while Black’s knight remains pinned by the rook on d1. The engine shows that the pawn push h5 would have been far more effective, keeping the balance tighter and avoiding the loss of about three‑quarters of a pawn. Consequently the evaluation slides from a decisive Black edge of roughly three pawns to almost four pawns, confirming Be1 as an inaccuracy.

teacher: White’s rook jumps to c7, forking the a‑ and g‑pawns and pinning the g‑pawn to Black’s king. Black can simply reply …a5, which removes the fork on a7 and leaves Black with a decisive material edge; the engine even preferred 35 Ra8 instead. Consequently the move worsens White’s position by about a sixth of a pawn, with the evaluation slipping from a –3.9 to –4.05 pawn disadvantage. In this rook‑and‑minor‑piece ending White still has a bishop versus a knight and a rook on d1 pinning the knight on d3, but the rook move does not improve the overall situation.
student: White’s rook jumps to c7, forking the a‑pawn and the g‑pawn while also pinning the latter to the black king on h7. The idea looks tempting in this rook‑and‑minor‑piece ending, but it does not stop Black’s natural …a5, which would simply remove the forked pawn and keep the pressure alive. Consequently the evaluation slips by about a sixth of a pawn, leaving Black with a decisive advantage. The engine judged Ra8 as the superior try, keeping more active counterplay.

teacher: Black pushes …a6, advancing his queenside pawn majority and eliminating the immediate danger to the a‑pawn. The engine judges the move as slightly inferior – about two‑tenths of a pawn – because the more forcing …a5 would have removed the threat to the a‑pawn and created a pawn break striking at the pawn on b6. Nevertheless, the position remains a rook‑and‑minor‑piece ending with Black’s knight versus White’s bishop, and Black still holds a decisive material advantage.
student: By playing a6 Black both pushes his queenside pawn majority forward and eliminates the immediate danger to the a‑pawn, keeping the two‑pawn versus one‑pawn edge in this rook‑and‑minor‑piece ending. The engine still judges the position as winning for Black – roughly three‑and‑a‑half pawns ahead – but notes that the move costs about two‑tenths of a pawn compared with the optimal continuation. The best alternative would have been a5, which also defends the a‑pawn while preserving the same material balance without worsening the evaluation. In practice, however, the chosen move leaves Black’s winning chances intact.

teacher: White’s 38 Ra1 is a clear mistake: by moving the rook away, the bishop on e1 is left unprotected and Black can simply capture it with …Nxe1, a reply the engine predicts would deepen Black’s winning edge to roughly four pawns. The move does nothing to improve the already decisive rook‑and‑minor‑piece ending, where White’s rook on b7 already pins the g7 pawn to the king. The engine had instead recommended 38 Bg3, which would have kept the bishop safe and avoided the material loss that now costs White about two pawns.
student: By playing Ra1 White simply abandons his last piece in this rook‑and‑minor‑piece ending, allowing Black’s natural reply Nxe1 which wins the bishop on e1. The engine shows that the correct continuation would have been Bg3, keeping the bishop safe and preserving material balance. After Ra1 the evaluation drops by about a pawn, leaving Black with a decisive advantage of roughly four pawns. In short, the move costs White a valuable piece and deepens an already losing position.

teacher: By capturing the knight on e1 White eliminates the last Black minor piece, turning the contest into a pure rook ending and simultaneously removing the immediate threat to the pawn on g2. The resulting rook endgame leaves White’s rook on b7 still pinning the g‑pawn to the black king on h7 and exploiting the semi‑open b‑file, but Black remains up two pawns and clearly ahead. The engine rates the move as the best available, even though it costs White about a tenth of a pawn and leaves the evaluation at a decisive Black advantage.
student: By playing Rxe1 White eliminates Black’s active knight and steers the game into a pure rook ending while also removing the immediate danger to the pawn on g2. The capture does not change the overall balance – Black still enjoys a decisive edge – but it is the best continuation available in this position. With the white rook now on e1 and the other rook on b7 pinning the g‑pawn, White can continue with ideas such as Rd2 followed by Rxe5, keeping the pressure alive despite the material deficit.

teacher: Black’s 39…Rd4 simply shuffles the rook to a more active central square, preserving the decisive –5‑pawn edge (the evaluation barely changes, staying around a five‑pawn advantage). The move respects the fact that White’s rook on b7 pins the g‑pawn to the black king, so Black does not disturb that tension. In the engine’s view the only slightly sharper try would have been 39…Rd2, but 39…Rd4 is still strong enough that White’s best continuation would be 40 Rf7, forking the f6‑ and g7‑pawns, after which Black can continue with …Rxh4 and keep the winning march.
student: By playing Rd4 Black simply preserves his two‑pawn material edge in this rook ending, leaving the engine’s assessment virtually unchanged at about –4.9 pawns. The move does not alter the fact that White’s rook on b7 still pins the g‑pawn to the black king and controls the semi‑open b‑file, so White can continue with Rf7, forking the f6‑ and g7‑pawns. Although the engine prefers Rd2 as the optimal continuation, Rd4 keeps the position decisively better for Black.

teacher: By taking the pawn on h4 Black not only eliminates a target but also widens his material lead to three pawns, nudging the evaluation a quarter‑pawn further in Black’s favour and preserving a decisive edge. The capture leaves the h‑file semi‑open for White, yet White’s rook is committed to the b‑file and cannot exploit it immediately; the most threatening reply would be 41 Rf7, forking the f6 and g7 pawns, but Black can answer with …Kh6 and continue the winning rook‑endgame.
student: By taking on h4 Black eliminates White’s last central pawn, turning the game into a pure rook ending where Black is already up three pawns. The capture also leaves the h‑file semi‑open for White, but it does not affect the pin of the g7‑pawn by White’s rook on b7, so Black remains decisively better. The engine rates Rxh4 as the best continuation, improving the evaluation by roughly a quarter of a pawn while preserving the winning edge. White could try Rf7, forking the f6‑ and g7‑pawns, yet Black can meet that with Kh6 and keep the initiative.

teacher: White opens with 1.e4, which the engine flags as the best move (!!). The move nudges the evaluation from a roughly equal position to a slight White edge of less than a pawn, improving the score by roughly six hundredths of a pawn. According to the engine’s principal variation, Black would most naturally answer with 1…c5, after which White can continue with Nf3, d6 and Nc3.
student: White opens with e4, keeping material perfectly balanced and nudging the engine’s assessment from a tiny edge for Black to a modest advantage for White – about six‑hundredths of a pawn. The engine rates this as the best continuation, confirming that it preserves equality while giving White a slight edge. In the principal variation Black would reply …c5, after which White can develop with Nf3, followed by …d6 and Nc3.

teacher: By retreating the bishop to a4, White eliminates the pawn’s attack on the piece and keeps the position balanced, with the engine’s evaluation barely improving to a modest plus. The move is judged the best continuation, preserving material equality and leaving White’s slight edge intact. Black’s most logical reply would be …Nf6, after which White can seize the centre with 5.d4, leading to the natural exchange Nxd4 Nxd4. This quiet maneuver therefore maintains White’s small advantage without creating any new weaknesses.
student: White’s Ba4 simply eliminates the immediate danger to the bishop that had been hanging on a4, thereby preserving the modest edge that existed before the move. The engine rates it as the best continuation, and the evaluation stays at roughly +0.4 pawn, confirming that White has not lost any ground despite Black’s active setup. In the principal variation Black would reply …Nf6, after which White can continue with d4, keeping the pressure while maintaining the slight advantage.

teacher: White castles, putting the king safely on g1 and bringing the rook to f1 while the evaluation stays essentially the same, a slight edge for White (+0.35). The engine, however, preferred the pawn break d4, which would have struck at Black’s e5 pawn and opened sharper chances. After d4, Black could answer with Nxe4, capturing the pawn on e4, so White’s castling, though solid, missed the more aggressive option.
student: White castles kingside, bringing his king to safety and connecting the rooks while keeping material equal. The engine’s numbers show that this modestly improves White’s standing – the evaluation shifts from +0.29 to +0.35, an increase of about six‑hundredths of a pawn. Nevertheless, the engine preferred the more ambitious pawn break d4, which would strike directly at Black’s e5 pawn and give White a clearer edge. After O‑O Black can reply with Nxe4, winning the pawn on e4.

teacher: By taking on e4 Black wins a pawn, but the capture also opens the e‑file for White, giving the newly castled king a semi‑open line. The engine still judges the position as slightly better for White (about a half‑pawn), because White can answer with the pawn break d4, striking at the e5 pawn and generating central pressure. The suggested continuation is 5…Nxe4 6.d4 b5 7.Bb3 d5, indicating Black will have to seek counter‑play on the queenside. Overall it is the best move, though it costs Black a little in the evaluation.
student: By taking on e4 Black wins a pawn and opens the e‑file for White, but the capture also leaves the e5 pawn vulnerable to a central thrust such as d4, which strikes at that pawn. The engine rates the move as good – it is the best continuation despite the slight swing in the evaluation, with White still holding a modest edge of about half a pawn. In the principal variation White can answer with d4, after which Black may continue …b5 and later …d5.

teacher: By capturing on e5 White eliminates Black’s central pawn and creates a semi‑open d‑file for his own pieces while granting Black a half‑open e‑file. The exchange also bolsters White’s kingside pawn majority – four pawns now face Black’s three – and leaves Black’s king still in the centre whereas White has already castled, preserving a small but tangible edge. The engine still rates White slightly better, though the move costs about two‑tenths of a pawn compared with the previous evaluation.
student: By playing dxe5 White eliminates Black’s central pawn and opens the d‑file, giving White a semi‑open line that can be used later. The capture also strengthens White’s kingside pawn majority—four pawns against three—and leaves Black with a semi‑open e‑file. Although the engine notes a slight dip in White’s edge (about two‑tenths of a pawn), it remains the best continuation because Black’s king is still stuck in the centre while White has already castled. The suggested follow‑up …Be6 would keep the balance, after which White could continue with c3, followed by …Bc5 and Nbd2.

teacher: Black finally strikes with the pawn break d4, attacking White’s pawn on c3 and preparing to open the d‑file. After the natural reply Nxd4, Black can recapture, leaving the d‑file open and making the e5 pawn vulnerable, while White’s bishop on c1 still has no safe squares. The move leaves the evaluation essentially unchanged, keeping White only a fraction of a pawn ahead, and is therefore rightly judged as an excellent choice.
student: By playing …d4 Black finally opens the d‑file and strikes directly at White’s pawn on c3, immediately challenging the central tension. After the natural reply Nxd4, the pawn on e5 becomes en prise, giving Black active counterplay. The engine rates the move as excellent because it neutralises White’s slight edge – the evaluation shifts by only about a seventh of a pawn – even though Black’s king remains in the centre and White’s bishop on c1 has no safe squares. In short, …d4 creates concrete threats while opening lines that can be exploited later.

teacher: By playing …dxc3 Black wins a pawn and opens the d‑file, but the capture also leaves Black with doubled c‑pawns while his king is still in the centre. This structural concession allows White to continue with Nxc5, capturing the knight on c5 and leaving the material balance only marginally in Black’s favour. The engine rates the move good, yet notes that 12…d3 would have preserved the pawn structure and kept the evaluation essentially equal. As a result, after …dxc3 the position is slightly better for White (+0.48) despite Black’s extra pawn.
student: By playing …dxc3 Black wins a pawn and opens the d‑file, but the capture also makes the c‑file semi‑open for White and leaves Black with doubled pawns on that file. The engine rates the move as “good” yet notes it costs Black about a third of a pawn, turning an essentially equal position into one where White is a little better. In addition, the move does nothing to stop White’s natural continuation Nxc5, which would simply recapture the knight on c5. The engine’s preferred alternative was the quieter …d3, which would have kept the balance without creating those structural weaknesses.

teacher: By placing the bishop on e4 White creates a direct pin of the knight on c6 against the rook on a8, adding new tactical pressure that Black must answer. The move leaves the evaluation essentially unchanged, preserving White’s slight edge even though Black is a pawn up, and it does so while White’s king is safely castled and Black’s king remains in the centre. Black’s most natural reply would be Qxd1, exchanging queens, but it does not create any additional pins; after the forced exchange White’s position stays solid. Consequently, Be4 is an excellent continuation that maximises the pin and limits Black’s counterplay.
student: By playing Be4 White places the bishop on an active diagonal that immediately pins Black’s knight on c6 to the rook on a8, curbing its activity and limiting any immediate counterplay. The pin also leaves Black’s pieces cramped – the queen on d1 would be forced to give up the rook on f1 after White recaptures with Rxd1, and the queen on d1 would then attack the poorly defended pawn on f2. With Black’s king still stuck in the centre and the bishop on c5 already pinning the f‑pawn, White preserves his slight edge without worsening the position. The engine rates the move as excellent and the best continuation, keeping the evaluation at roughly +0.5 pawn for White.

teacher: Black’s 16…Bc4 was intended to eliminate the immediate threat to the bishop on c5, but in doing so it does not affect the pin on the f‑pawn and lets White seize the initiative, driving the evaluation from a slight White edge to a clear advantage of more than a pawn. The engine marks the move as a mistake, costing Black roughly a pawn’s worth of standing, and points out that 16…Bd5 would have been far more resilient. As a result White now enjoys a comfortable lead despite material being equal.
student: By playing …Bc4 Black merely steps the bishop away and eliminates the immediate danger to it on c5, but this concession lets White’s advantage swell from a modest edge to roughly a pawn‑and‑a‑half in White’s favour. The engine shows that the far stronger continuation would have been …Bd5, which keeps the pressure on White’s pieces while preserving the pin on the f‑pawn. After …Bc4 White can continue with Be3, after which Black may try …f5, leading to an exchange on f6 and then Rhe8, as the principal variation suggests. In short, the retreat costs Black about a pawn of evaluation and hands White a clear positional lead.

teacher: White captures the knight on d4, but the move merely starts an exchange that Black can answer with Qxd4. That queen recapture would fork the bishop on e4 and the pawn on e5 while also pinning the f‑pawn to the king, wiping out most of White’s earlier +2‑pawn lead and leaving a clear but much smaller advantage of about a pawn (+1.46). The engine’s preferred continuation, 18.Qa5, would have kept the larger edge, so the capture is judged an inaccuracy that cost roughly three‑quarters of a pawn.
student: White’s capture on d4 merely initiates an exchange that Black can answer with Qxd4, forking the bishop on e4 and the pawn on e5 while also pinning the f‑pawn to the king. This concession costs White roughly three‑quarters of a pawn, as the evaluation drops from +2.2 to +1.5 – a clear inaccuracy compared with the engine‑recommended Qa5. The move does not improve White’s standing despite being up three points of material, because it allows Black to neutralise the advantage without losing any material.

teacher: Black’s 18…Bxd4 captures the knight and creates a fork on White’s queen on c3 and the pawn on e5 while pinning the f‑pawn to the king, but it is an inaccuracy because the engine preferred 18…Qxd4. The queen capture would have hit the bishop on e4 as well as the pawn on e5, a stronger double attack that keeps the same pin on f2, and would have preserved White’s advantage at roughly a pawn instead of letting it grow to almost two pawns. By opting for the bishop, Black’s evaluation slipped from a modest White edge of about a pawn to a clear lead of nearly two pawns, a loss of roughly half a pawn. In the optimal line after the queen capture White could answer with Qa5, leaving the b‑pawn vulnerable, a possibility that disappears after the bishop move.
student: By playing …Bxd4 Black wins the white knight but immediately walks into White’s tactical shot Qa5, which both eliminates the fork on e5 and leaves the b‑pawn hanging. The engine rates the capture as an inaccuracy because it costs Black roughly half a pawn compared with the superior alternative …Qxd4, which would have kept material equal while preserving the same threats. After …Bxd4 White can reply Qa5, after which Black must recapture with the queen, allowing White to continue with Qe6 and then exchange on d8, leaving Black still worse despite the material balance.

teacher: White retreats the queen to f3 to eliminate the immediate threat against it, but the move leaves the b‑pawn undefended.  The position remains roughly the same, with Black’s bishop on d4 still pinning the f‑pawn and the rook on d8 dominating the open d‑file, and White’s advantage slips by about a tenth of a pawn.  The engine preferred 19. Qa5, which also removes the queen‑threat while keeping the b2 pawn under the same pressure, and would have preserved a slightly larger edge.
student: White retreats the queen to f3, eliminating the immediate danger that had been hovering around it. The drawback is that the pawn on b2 becomes hanging – Black can capture it with …c5 and then win material after White’s forced Rfd1. Although the engine still judges White “much better” (+1.88 pawns), the move costs roughly a tenth of a pawn compared with the optimal continuation Qa5, which would have kept the same pressure without creating the new target. Consequently, while not a blunder, Qf3 is a sub‑optimal choice that slightly reduces White’s advantage.

teacher: Black finally snatches the rook on f1, but the capture is a fatal blunder because it lets White answer with Bf5, pinning the queen on d7 and threatening immediate mate with Qa8#. The engine’s evaluation jumps from a modest +1.88 for White before the move to a decisive +4.77 afterwards – a swing of almost three pawns from Black’s point of view. The position could have been saved by the quiet king move Kb8, which would have kept material balance and avoided the mating net. Thus the material gain costs Black a winning chance and turns a slight White edge into a crushing defeat.
student: By playing …Bxf1 Black wins a rook but immediately walks into White’s tactical shot Bf5, which pins the queen on d7 to the king and threatens an immediate mate with Qa8#. The engine shows that this blunder costs roughly three pawns in evaluation, turning a modest White edge into a decisive one despite Black still being up five points of material. The correct continuation would have been Kb8, keeping the king out of the mating net and preserving Black’s chances. Consequently, the capture not only loses material but also hands White a winning advantage.

teacher: Black’s capture on d8 eliminates the bishop that was eyeing the c7 pawn and, in doing so, strips White of the bishop‑pair advantage. After the exchange Black retains the bishop pair and a rook that dominates the open d‑file, while White’s only realistic reply is 23 Bc6, which simply moves the bishop to c6. The engine rates the move as the best available, but the position remains a decisive White advantage, the move costing Black roughly a tenth of a pawn.
student: By playing Rxd8 Black eliminates White’s active bishop and at the same time removes the immediate danger to the pawn on c7. The capture also leaves Black with the bishop pair while his rook now dominates the open d‑file, giving him some counterplay despite being down material. Although the engine still judges White to be decisively ahead, this exchange costs Black roughly a tenth of a pawn compared with the previous evaluation. White can continue with Bc6, which would remove the pressure on the bishop that remains on c6.

teacher: White retreats the bishop to f5, eliminating the immediate danger to that piece, but this gives Black the tactical shot …Bxb2, where the bishop on b2 would fork the rook on a1 and the pawn on e5. After that capture White could try Rd1, but the engine shows the sequence costs White about half a pawn, dropping the evaluation from roughly +5.3 to +4.8. The engine’s preferred continuation was Bc6, which would have removed the threat to the bishop on c6. Hence Bf5 is an inaccuracy that modestly weakens White’s winning position.
student: White’s retreat Bf5 merely sidesteps the immediate danger to the bishop, but it does nothing to relieve the pin that Black’s bishop on d4 exerts against the f‑pawn or to stop Black’s looming tactical shot. After …Bxb2 the fork on a1 and e5 wins material, so White’s evaluation drops by roughly half a pawn despite still being up six points in material. The engine judged Bc6 to be superior because it would have removed the same threat while keeping the bishop more flexible, whereas after Bf5 Black can capture on b2 with the bishop and then continue with …Rxd1+, forcing a forced exchange and losing material. Consequently, the move costs White about half a pawn of advantage.

teacher: Black’s 23…Bxb2 seizes the pawn on b2 while simultaneously forking White’s rook on a1 and the pawn on e5, exploiting the bishop pair and the semi‑open b‑file. The capture also leaves White with an isolated a‑pawn and gives Black a passed pawn on c7, but the engine still evaluates White as decisively better (+5 ≈ a pawn), and the move actually costs Black about a third of a pawn in relative terms. White can meet the threat by playing 24 Rd1, which removes the bishop’s attack on the rook and, after the forced exchanges, leaves the a2 pawn en prise. Thus, although the move is the best available, it only marginally worsens Black’s already inferior position.
student: By playing …Bxb2 Black wins the pawn on b2 while simultaneously creating a fork on White’s rook a1 and the pawn e5, exploiting the semi‑open b‑file that will become available after the capture. The exchange also leaves White with an isolated a‑pawn and gives Black a passed pawn on c7, but it does not improve Black’s overall standing – the engine still judges White to be decisively ahead, roughly three pawns in material. Nevertheless, this is the best continuation available, as any alternative would allow White to increase his lead further.

teacher: Instead of the winning check Rxd1+ that would have captured White’s rook on d1, Black chose Re8, merely removing the immediate threat to the rook on e8. By forgoing the check‑capture, Black missed the chance to improve the material balance and the position. The engine now scores the game at roughly +6 pawns for White, about a pawn more than before, reflecting a clear deterioration for Black. Hence the move is a mistake, costing Black roughly a pawn of material.
student: By playing Re8 Black merely sidesteps the immediate danger to the rook, but it does nothing to challenge White’s dominant presence on the open d‑file and therefore allows White to keep the initiative. The engine shows that the far stronger continuation would have been Rxd1+, a checking capture that wins the white rook outright. After Re8 White can continue with g4, after which Black must meet it with …g6, allowing White to consolidate his material edge and the evaluation climbs further in White’s favour.
