In short, the move costs Black roughly a pawn of material value and deepens White’s decisive advantage.

teacher: By playing Rh8 Black merely removed the immediate danger to the h‑pawn and the rook, but it did nothing to stop White’s decisive attack. White can now continue with Be4, threatening mate with Qa8#, and after best play Black is forced into a forced mate in eight moves. The engine indicates that the correct defence was Be2, which would have avoided the immediate mating net. The blunder turns a position that was already winning for White by about eight pawns into an outright forced mate.
student: By playing Rh8 Black merely sidesteps the immediate danger to the h‑pawn and the rook, but this allows White’s forcing continuation Be4, which immediately threatens mate with Qa8#. After that Black can try …Bd5, yet White still mates in eight, turning an already losing position into a forced loss for Black. The engine indicates that the correct defence was Be2, which would have avoided the mating net altogether. Consequently the move costs Black about seven pawns of material and forces a forced mate in eight.

teacher: White’s 26.Be4!! is the only move that keeps the win, tightening the attack by threatening an immediate Qa8# and thereby shortening the forced mate from eight to seven moves. Black can at best answer …Bd5, trying to fork the a2‑pawn, the bishop on e4 and the queen on c6, but the bishop lands on a square that White can capture. After the natural 27.Bxd5 White forces …Kc8 and continues with Qb7+, preserving the decisive mating net.
student: By playing Be4 White immediately creates the mating threat Qa8#, tightening the already forced win to seven moves instead of eight. The bishop now stands on an active diagonal that attacks both the king and the queen, while Black’s most natural try, …Bd5, would fork the a‑pawn, the bishop on e4 and the queen on c6 but leaves the bishop on d5 hanging. After the inevitable Bxd5, White finishes with Kc8 and then Qb7+, delivering mate as planned. This precise continuation justifies the “best” label and the double exclamation.

teacher: White reinforces his central presence with 2.d4, and the engine confirms it is the best continuation, leaving White clearly better (+0.62, about a pawn’s worth). The evaluation slips only slightly from +0.79 to +0.62, so the advantage is modestly reduced but still solid. In the principal variation Black would likely develop with …Bg7, after which White can continue with Nf3, Black …d6 and White Nc3.
student: White’s second move d4 simply contests the centre and preserves the modest edge that existed after 1.e4 g6. The engine rates it as the best continuation, with the evaluation slipping only marginally to roughly +0.6 of a pawn – still a clear advantage for White. Black would most naturally develop with …Bg7, after which White can continue Nf3, followed by …d6 and Nc3 in the principal variation.

teacher: Black’s …b5 is a quiet queenside pawn push that leaves material level and the evaluation virtually unchanged, with White still about a pawn better. The engine calls it excellent because it does not worsen Black’s standing, but it is not the top‑ranked option; …d6 would have been marginally more accurate, keeping the assessment a touch lower for White. In the resulting position the pawn structure stays balanced and no immediate tactical threats appear.
student: Black’s …b5 is an excellent developing move that simply brings another pawn into play without altering the balance – the engine still judges White to be about a pawn ahead and the evaluation changes by only two hundredths of a pawn in Black’s favour. The engine preferred …d6, which would have been marginally more accurate, but …b5 leaves material equal and keeps the position solid. In short, the move preserves the status quo while giving Black a modest chance to improve his setup.

teacher: Black chose to develop the queen‑side bishop to b7, but the move did not curb White’s lead; the evaluation slipped from a +0.69 advantage for White to about +0.84, meaning Black’s position worsened by roughly a sixth of a pawn. The engine flags the move as only “good” and points out that the more accurate 5…d6 would have challenged White’s centre and kept the gap smaller. In the principal variation White can continue with Bd3, after which Black’s best reply would be Nc6, allowing White to press with e5 and Black to meet it with the previously suggested d6. Thus the bishop move missed a more active central counter‑play.
student: Black’s …Bb7 is a solid developing move that brings the dark‑squared bishop to its natural square, but it does not challenge White’s central space and allows White to keep the initiative. The engine rates the move as “good” yet notes that it costs Black roughly a sixth of a pawn compared with the optimal reply …d6, which would have kept the evaluation closer to equality. In the principal variation White can continue with Bd3, after which Black could develop further with Nc6 and later meet White’s e5 with d6, preserving more pressure. Thus the move is playable but slightly inferior to the best continuation.

teacher: Black’s pawn thrust c5 was a premature break that handed White a clearer edge; after White simply captures dxc5, the d‑file becomes semi‑open for the already‑castled side while Black’s king remains stuck in the centre. The engine shows the move costs Black about half a pawn (the evaluation swings from +0.62 to +1.15 in White’s favour) and the stronger alternative would have been Nd7, keeping the tension and avoiding the open d‑file. In the main line White can reply dxc5, after which Black recaptures; the resulting position gives Black a semi‑open c‑file while White ends up with doubled c‑pawns.
student: Black’s …c5 tries to open lines by striking at White’s d‑pawn, but after the natural reply dxc5 the pawn capture leaves Black with a semi‑open c‑file and White with doubled c‑pawns, giving White a clear structural edge. The engine rates the move an inaccuracy, worsening Black’s standing by roughly half a pawn even though material remains equal. A more accurate continuation would have been …Nd7, which keeps the balance without conceding those extra weaknesses. Consequently White’s advantage grows from about two‑thirds of a pawn to almost one pawn.

teacher: By taking on c5 White eliminates Black’s pawn and opens the d‑file, a useful feature while Black’s king is still in the centre and White has already castled. The capture initiates an exchange that restores material balance, leaving White a clear pawn ahead and even nudging the evaluation slightly higher. Black’s most natural reply would be to recapture on c5, after which the continuation continues with …e5, Nd7 and Be4, but the move already secures White’s advantage.
student: By playing dxc5 White eliminates Black’s central pawn and opens the d‑file for his pieces, a useful asset after Black’s king remains stuck in the centre while White has already castled. The capture also initiates an exchange that will be restored by Black’s natural reply …dxc5, leaving the position essentially unchanged – White stays about a pawn ahead with a clear advantage. This precise simplification is why the engine rates dxc5 as the best move, keeping the evaluation at roughly +1.2 pawns.

teacher: By pushing the e‑pawn to e5 White exploits the fact that Black’s king is still stuck in the centre while White has already castled, preserving the modest but clear edge. The advance does not change the material balance and the engine’s evaluation remains at roughly a pawn’s worth in White’s favour. Black’s most natural reply would be …Nh6, after which White can continue with Be4, keeping the advantage. This explains why the move is judged a top‑class continuation, earning the !! annotation.
student: By playing e5 White immediately challenges Black’s central pawn and forces the king to step out of the cramped position it was left in after castling. The engine rates the move as the best continuation, keeping White’s clear advantage at roughly a pawn’s worth. In the principal variation Black would reply Nh6, after which White can continue with Be4, preserving the edge.

teacher: White captures the bishop on b7, raising the evaluation from roughly +1.9 to +2.0 pawns and increasing his material lead. Yet the move places the newly‑won bishop on a square that can be hit by Black’s queen with Qb6+, delivering a check that simultaneously forks the king on g1 and the bishop. Because of this tactical resource the engine rates Be3 as the superior alternative, preserving the advantage without allowing the queen fork. Thus, Bxb7 wins material but is a sub‑optimal choice compared with the engine’s best move.
student: By taking on b7 White eliminates Black’s last minor piece, leaving Black without the bishop‑pair advantage and with a cramped king that remains stuck in the centre while White already enjoys a clear edge after castling. The capture also leaves Black’s knight on g8 with only one safe retreat and his bishop on g7 confined to just two squares, further limiting Black’s counterplay. Although the engine prefers Be3 as the optimal continuation, Bxb7 improves White’s standing by roughly two‑tenths of a pawn, pushing the evaluation from about +1.9 to +2.0. Black could try the checking fork Qb6+, but even then White would be able to meet it with Be3 and keep the initiative.

teacher: Black answers with a striking check, Qb6+, which simultaneously attacks the white king on g1 and the bishop that just landed on b7, creating a classic fork. The move also leaves the knight on d7 en prise, but White cannot capture it because the only sensible reply, Be3, would place that bishop on e3 in danger after Black’s queen takes on b7. In the engine line White would continue Be3 Qxb7, and after Qd5 Qxd5 the material balance remains, keeping White’s sizable lead of about two pawns. Thus the move preserves Black’s chances, changing the evaluation by only a few hundredths of a pawn.
student: Black’s queen jumps to b6 with a checking fork, hitting both the white king on g1 and the bishop on b7 at once. The move also leaves the knight on d7 hanging, but it forces White into the defensive resource Be3, after which the bishop on e3 becomes vulnerable. Although the engine rates the position as still about +2 pawns for White, the move improves Black’s chances by keeping the evaluation essentially unchanged. In the principal line White would play Be3, after which Black can capture the bishop with Qxb7, followed by exchanges that leave the balance roughly equal.
violations: calls the position equal at 2.01

teacher: White’s queen jumps to d5 to fork Black’s queen on b7 and the pawn on f7, a classic tactical motif that forces an immediate resolution of the tension. Black can meet the threat by playing Qxd5, after which the queen is exchanged and the knight recaptures on d5, but White’s material balance and the lingering pressure on the un‑castled king keep the evaluation unchanged at a clear plus. The continuation shown by the engine (Qxd5 Nxd5 Rc8 a4) illustrates that the fork not only neutralises Black’s threats but also leaves White with a comfortable, active position.
student: White’s queen jumps to d5, forking Black’s queen on b7 and the pawn on f7, thereby creating an immediate tactical pressure that leaves the position essentially unchanged with White still about a pawn ahead. The fork exploits the fact that Black’s king is stuck in the centre while his pieces have very limited safe squares – the knight on g8 has only one retreat and the bishop on g7 just two. If Black answers with …Qxd5, White can simply recapture Nxd5, after which the continuation would continue with Rc8 and a4, preserving the advantage. This precise queen sacrifice therefore consolidates White’s lead without any material loss.

teacher: White’s 14 a4 is a pawn break aimed at the b5‑pawn, but it is an inaccuracy that costs him roughly a half‑pawn of evaluation. The engine’s preferred continuation, 14 b4, would have opened the queenside more forcefully – after 14…Qxb7 15 Rxb7 Ne4 Black’s queen would be captured on b7 and the pawn on c4 would become vulnerable. By playing a4 instead, White gives up the sharper line and allows Black to keep the central king and the cramped pieces on g8 and g7 without immediate danger. Consequently the position remains clearly better for White, but the advantage drops from about two pawns to a little more than one.
student: White’s 14 a4 tries to open lines by striking at Black’s b‑pawn, but it does not improve his already comfortable position – the engine shows the evaluation slipping from about +2.2 to +1.6, roughly a half‑pawn loss. The engine judged 14 b4 to be stronger because it would keep more pressure and even leaves the c4 pawn vulnerable after …b4, whereas a4 merely gives up that dynamic chance without gaining any compensation. Consequently, although White remains clearly better, the pawn push is an inaccuracy that costs him some of the advantage.

teacher: By pushing …b4 Black forces White’s queen to decide; White can capture on b7, taking the black queen, but Black recaptures with the rook (Rxb7) and then continues with Ne4, after which the knight on g8 can safely retreat to h6. Although the pawn on c4 becomes en prise, the forced queen exchange and the ensuing piece activity keep the evaluation essentially unchanged, leaving White still much better, well over a pawn. The engine therefore rates …b4 as the best and an excellent continuation.
student: By pushing …b4 Black immediately attacks White’s queen on d5, forcing it to give up its queen with Qxb7. The capture does leave the pawn on c4 temporarily en prise, but after …Rxb7 the material balance remains equal and the engine rates the position as essentially unchanged – White still enjoys a clear advantage of about a pawn. Although the move creates tactical threats, it is nevertheless an excellent try because any other alternative would allow White to keep the initiative without conceding the queen.

teacher: By playing Qxb7 White captures Black’s queen and at the same time forks the pawn on b4, the pawn on a6 and the knight on d7, creating immediate threats even though the queen can be taken. Black’s most natural reply, Rxb7, removes those threats and restores material balance, so the exchange leaves the evaluation essentially unchanged and White remains much better—around a pawn and a half ahead. The move is excellent because it forces the exchange on favorable terms while Black’s pieces on g8 and g7 have very few safe squares, limiting any effective counterplay.
student: By taking on b7 White not only wins Black’s queen but also creates a fork that attacks the pawn on a6, the pawn on b4 and the knight on d7. The capture forces an immediate exchange; after …Rxb7 the queens disappear and the material balance is restored, leaving White still ahead in terms of the extra queen. Although the engine notes a tiny dip of about six‑hundredths of a pawn, the position remains clearly better for White – roughly a pawn and a half advantage. Black’s remaining pieces are cramped—his knight on g8 has only one safe square and his bishop on g7 only two safe squares—and this explains why the continuation Rxb7 followed by Ne4, Nh6 and Rfd1 is the most natural reply.

teacher: Black retreats the knight to h6, a square that helps guard the bishop on g7, which currently has only one safe retreat. By doing so Black neutralises any immediate threats to that bishop and leaves the material balance untouched, keeping White’s advantage at roughly a pawn and the evaluation essentially unchanged. The engine rates Nh6 as the best continuation, after which White can continue with Rad1 and Black may castle before the knights re‑centralise with Nf5.
student: By retreating the knight to h6 Black places it on a safe square while keeping the bishop on g7 confined to its only viable retreat. The engine rates the move as the best continuation, and the evaluation barely shifts – White remains about a pawn ahead. In the principal line White would continue with Rad1, after which Black can castle and later bring the knight back to f5, preserving the balance despite the cramped piece placement.

teacher: By playing Rfd1 White places a rook on the open d‑file, immediately exerting pressure along that line. Although the move is solid, it is slightly inferior to the engine‑preferred Rad1, costing roughly a fifth of a pawn; the rook from a1 would have been better placed while keeping the f‑file rook available. Black’s most natural reply would be the pawn break f6, striking at White’s e5 pawn and exploiting the modest loss of tempo.
student: By sliding the rook to d1 White puts it directly onto the open d‑file, where it can exert pressure while Black’s bishop on g7 remains confined to its single safe square. The engine still judges the position as clearly better for White – roughly a pawn’s worth – but the evaluation slips by about two‑tenths of a pawn compared with the optimal Rad1. Black could answer with the pawn break f6, striking at White’s e5 pawn and trying to generate counterplay. In short, Rfd1 is a good move that keeps material equal, yet it costs White a small edge in the assessment.

teacher: Black’s 19… O‑O is the only move that preserves the best evaluation, keeping the game at roughly a two‑pawn advantage for White and only nudging Black’s position a shade worse (about a tenth of a pawn). By castling, Black secures the king and brings the rook into play without altering the key features of the position: the bishop on g7 remains confined to just two safe squares, while White’s rook on d5 continues to dominate the open d‑file. The engine confirms this as a “good” move and the best choice in the position.
student: By castling, Black tucks the king safely behind the pawn shield and connects the rooks, while White’s rook already dominates the open d‑file. The engine rates the move as good – it is the best continuation available even though it nudges the evaluation a little further in White’s favour (about 0.14 pawn). In the principal line White can continue with Rad1, after which Black may reply Nb6, followed by Ra5 and e6.

teacher: Black’s best reply is the sharp pawn break …c3, striking at White’s b‑pawn and simultaneously removing the lingering threat to the pawn that has just advanced to c3. If White captures, bxc3, the exchange leaves White with isolated pawns on a4, c2 and c3 and gives Black a semi‑open c‑file (and a semi‑open b‑file) to work with. The engine rates the move as the top choice, improving Black’s standing by about a sixth of a pawn (the evaluation slides from +2.44 to +2.27 in White’s favour). With the bishop on g7 confined to only two safe squares, this pawn thrust is the most concrete way for Black to generate counterplay.
student: By playing …c3 Black finally breaks in the centre, directly challenging White’s b‑pawn and opening lines that can be exploited later. After the natural reply bxc3, the b‑file becomes semi‑open for White while Black gains a semi‑open c‑file, leaving White with isolated pawns on c2, c3 and a4 – a structural weakness that compensates for the slight drop in evaluation. The engine rates the move as the best continuation, improving Black’s standing by about a sixth of a pawn even though White remains clearly better. In the principal variation White would capture on c3, after which Black could continue with …Rb2, keeping the pressure alive.

teacher: By taking on c3 Black forces an exchange that immediately opens the b‑file for the rook on b7, a useful asset in a position where White’s rooks already dominate the d‑file. After White’s natural recapture Nxc3 the material balance is restored, but Black is left with an isolated pawn on a6 and White gains a passed pawn on c2, so the overall evaluation stays essentially unchanged at about a two‑pawn advantage for White. Although the engine preferred Nd7, the capture is still excellent because it neutralises any immediate loss and gives Black active play on the newly opened b‑file.
student: By playing …bxc3 Black eliminates White’s pawn on c3 and forces the natural recapture Nxc3, which opens the b‑file for Black’s rook on b7 while leaving Black with an isolated pawn on a6. The capture also gives White a passed pawn on c2, but after the forced Nxc3 the material balance is restored and the engine still judges White to be about two‑and‑a‑half pawns ahead, so the position remains clearly better for White. Although the move is judged excellent, it is not the engine’s top choice; Nd7 would have been marginally stronger. In any case, the exchange does not change the overall assessment significantly.

teacher: By playing 23.Rxc3 White finally wins the pawn on c3, but the capture turns the c‑file into a semi‑open line that Black can exploit. After the rook lands on c3 Black’s rook can swing to b4, forking the a4 pawn and the knight on e4 and even creating a skewer‑type threat against the f4 pawn, which is why the evaluation drops from a clear two‑pawn edge to only about a pawn’s worth. The engine’s preferred move was 23.Nxc3, which also captures the pawn but keeps the rook off the c‑file and avoids the rook fork. Consequently the move is a clear mistake, costing White roughly a pawn’s worth of advantage.
student: By playing Rxc3 White wins a pawn but opens the c‑file for Black, giving Black’s rook active play and allowing …Rb4 to fork the a4‑pawn and the e4‑knight while also skewering the knight on e4. The engine shows that the far stronger continuation would have been Nxc3, which simply removes the pawn without creating those tactical threats. Consequently the evaluation drops by roughly a pawn, turning a clear +2.6 advantage into only about +1.4.

teacher: By moving the rook to b4 Black instantly creates a double attack: the rook forks the pawn on a4 and the knight on e4, and the same line also skewers the knight, leaving the pawn on f4 exposed if the knight moves. This active placement on the open b‑file both limits the bishop on g7 and improves Black’s evaluation by about a tenth of a pawn, earning the engine’s highest praise. White can at least meet the threat with Nfg5, which removes the danger to the e4‑knight, but even after that Black’s position is marginally better for Black, though White still retains a pawn advantage.
student: By playing …Rb4 Black creates a powerful fork, attacking both White’s a‑pawn and the knight on e4 while also skewering that knight onto the f4 pawn. The rook now dominates the open b‑file, complementing Black’s limited bishop on g7, which already has only two safe squares. White can try Nfg5 to eliminate the immediate danger to the e4 knight, but even after that reply Black remains a little better – roughly a tenth of a pawn ahead. This precise maneuver therefore earns the “best” label.

teacher: By capturing on f5 Black eliminates White’s active knight, opens the g‑file for his pieces and fixes White’s pawn on f4 on a dark square, while simultaneously removing the immediate threat to the e7 pawn and the bishop on g7. Although the capture leaves Black with an isolated h‑pawn and doubled pawns on the f‑file, the engine shows the evaluation essentially unchanged – Black’s position improves by only a few hundredths of a pawn and White remains clearly better by about a pawn. White’s most logical continuation would be 27 g3, which simply defends the f4 pawn, but the material balance and the semi‑open g‑file give Black the best practical chances.
student: By playing gxf5 Black eliminates White’s active knight and instantly opens the g‑file, giving the rook on b4 a useful line while also fixing White’s pawn on f4 on a dark square. The capture does leave Black with an isolated pawn on h5 and doubled pawns on the f‑file, but it neutralises the immediate danger to the e7‑pawn and the bishop on g7, which was the main concern. With material still equal and the engine’s assessment barely shifting from +1.13 to +1.07 in White’s favour, the move is rightly judged as the best continuation. White can try g3, removing the pressure on the f‑pawn, after which Black may continue with …a5 and later …Rc8.

teacher: White calmly plays 27.g3, simply removing Black’s threat to the pawn on f4. By securing that pawn the evaluation stays clearly in White’s favour—still about a pawn’s worth—while Black’s bishop on g7 is limited to only two safe squares and the rooks continue to dominate the open b‑ and d‑files. The engine confirms this as the best continuation; Black’s most logical reply would be 27…e6, after which White can keep the edge with 28.Kf1. Overall the move preserves the advantage without any material concession.
student: By playing g3 White eliminates Black’s immediate pressure on the f‑pawn, thereby preserving the modest edge that existed before the move. The engine rates the position virtually unchanged – White remains about a pawn ahead – and confirms that this precise defensive resource was indeed the best continuation. With Black’s bishop confined to just two safe squares and both sides’ rooks already contesting their respective open files, the pawn shield on f4 becomes essential for maintaining the advantage.

teacher: By playing …Rc8 Black tries to pin the white knight on c5 to the rook on c3, but the move immediately allows White to capture on a6, uncovering a discovered attack from the rook on c3 onto the newly placed rook on c8 and leaving both the knight on a6 and the rook on c3 en prise. This tactical shot wins a pawn and pushes White’s evaluation from about a pawn’s advantage to well over a pawn, a loss of roughly one pawn for Black. The engine’s preferred move was the simple …e6, which would have avoided this material concession. Consequently the move is rightly labelled a mistake.
student: By playing …Rc8 Black tries to pin White’s knight on c5 against the rook on c3, but the move immediately allows White to capture the a‑pawn with Nxa6. After that capture the knight on a6 and the rook on c3 become vulnerable, and White can continue with …Rxd1, winning material and pushing the evaluation from a modest +1 pawn to a clear +2.3 advantage – roughly a pawn and a half worse for Black. The engine indicates that the correct reply was …e6, which would have kept the balance instead of handing White the easy win. Consequently the move costs Black about one and a half pawns in practical terms.
violations: calls the position decisive/winning at 2.29

teacher: The knight jumps to a6, snatching the pawn and simultaneously uncovering the rook on c3’s line against Black’s rook on c8. Although the knight on a6 and the rook on c3 become targets, the move opens the a‑file and forces Black to deal with the new threat; the engine’s line shows Black would most likely reply Rxc3, removing the pressure on the c‑file, after which White can give a check with Rd8+ and then win back material with Nxb4. This capture improves White’s standing by roughly a tenth of a pawn, confirming it as the best continuation in a position where White already enjoys a clear material edge.
student: By taking on a6 White not only wins a pawn but also opens the a‑file, uncovering a discovered attack from the rook on c3 against Black’s rook on c8. The capture does leave both the knight on a6 and the rook on c3 hanging, yet it improves White’s evaluation by roughly a tenth of a pawn, pushing the advantage to about two‑and‑a‑half pawns. Black can answer with Rxc3, removing the threat to the c‑rook, after which White continues with Rd8+ forcing Kh7 and then recaptures on b4. This precise exchange therefore secures material while preserving a clear edge in the endgame.

teacher: White’s 29.Nxb4 wins the rook on b4 and removes the threat to the pawn on c2 and the knight itself, but the engine flags it as a blunder, cutting the evaluation from a comfortable +2.8‑pawn edge to only about +0.8. By entering a rook‑and‑minor‑piece ending, White hands Black an active rook on the semi‑open c‑file while his own rook on d1 merely controls the d‑file, allowing Black to generate counterplay. The engine’s preferred move was 29.Rd8+, a checking move that would have kept the pressure and preserved the larger advantage. In short, the capture costs roughly two pawns of value and surrenders the initiative.
student: By playing Nxb4 White wins a rook but immediately trades his active knight for Black’s rook on b4, turning the game into a pure rook‑and‑minor‑piece ending where Black’s rook dominates the semi‑open c‑file while White’s rook sits on the open d‑file. The capture also eliminates the immediate danger to the pawn on c2 and the knight that had just moved there, yet it does not generate any concrete threats or improve White’s piece coordination. Consequently the evaluation collapses from a clear +2.8 advantage to only about +0.8 – roughly two pawns lost – making the move a blunder. The engine’s preferred continuation was the checking move Rd8+, which would have kept more pressure on Black’s king.

teacher: Black’s 30…Rc4 simply sidesteps the danger, removing the threat that had been hanging over the rook on c4. In this rook‑and‑minor‑piece ending the black rook now occupies the semi‑open c‑file, while White’s rook continues to dominate the open d‑file, and the material situation remains unchanged with White still up a pawn. The engine marks the move as the best continuation, and the evaluation stays virtually unchanged – White is still clearly better by roughly a pawn’s worth. Thus the move neutralises the immediate pressure without worsening Black’s position.
student: By playing Rc4 Black eliminates White’s immediate pressure on the rook, placing it safely on the semi‑open c‑file where it can operate in this rook‑and‑minor‑piece ending. The engine rates the move as excellent and the best continuation, with the evaluation remaining roughly a pawn in White’s favour. In the principal variation White would try c3, after which Black could answer e6, keeping the balance intact.

teacher: White captures the knight on c6, but the move leaves the pawn on c2 en prise and allows Black to answer …Rxc6, which both eliminates the knight and removes the threat to the e‑pawn, restoring material balance. This exchange costs White about four‑tenths of a pawn, dropping the evaluation from roughly a pawn’s worth to just over half a pawn, so the engine rates the move only as “good” and notes it moderately worsened White’s position. The stronger continuation would have been 31.c3, which keeps the pawn safe and preserves the full advantage.
student: White’s capture on c6 wins a piece but immediately leaves the pawn on c2 hanging, allowing Black to answer with Rxc6 and restore material equality. The engine rates this as a moderate worsening – roughly four‑tenths of a pawn – because it gives Black the chance to neutralise White’s slight edge in this rook‑and‑minor‑piece ending. In contrast, the engine’s top choice was the quiet pawn push c3, which would have kept White’s advantage without creating the new target. After Nxc6 the most natural continuation would be Rxc6, after which White could continue with Rc1, followed by …h4 and c4.

teacher: Black’s pawn break …f6 strikes at White’s e‑pawn, forcing a clarification of the centre and improving Black’s standing by about a sixth of a pawn. After the natural reply exf6, Black can recapture with the bishop (Bxf6), keeping the rook active on the semi‑open c‑file while the resulting doubled f‑pawns give White a slight structural weakness. Although the pawn push does loosen the pawn shield in front of Black’s king, the engine rates the move as the best, turning a small White edge (+0.33) into a roughly equal position (+0.17). In the principal line White would play exf6, Black replies Bxf6, then White continues Kf1 and Black proceeds with h4.
student: By playing …f6 Black finally breaks open the centre, directly challenging White’s e‑pawn and opening lines that could later exploit the semi‑open c‑file. After the natural capture exf6, White not only wins a pawn but also creates doubled f‑pawns while the pawn shield in front of Black’s king becomes thinner, giving Black a modest improvement of about a sixth of a pawn. The engine rates this as the best continuation, with the evaluation shifting to roughly equality despite White still being a pawn ahead. In the principal line White would take on f6, after which Black can recapture with the bishop and continue with …h4, keeping the balance.

teacher: White captures on f6, creating a fork of Black’s e‑pawn and g7‑bishop; the pawn on f6 also opens the e‑file for White. After Black’s natural reply Bxf6, the pawn shield in front of the black king is weakened and the e‑file becomes semi‑open, giving White active play even though material balance is restored. This dynamic compensation is why the engine rates exf6 as the best move, keeping White’s slight edge essentially unchanged.
student: By playing exf6 White eliminates Black’s advanced pawn on f6, creating a fork that attacks both the e‑pawn and the bishop on g7 while also opening the e‑file for his own pieces. After the forced …Bxf6 the pawn shield in front of Black’s king is thinned, giving White active play along the open file. The capture therefore secures a small but tangible edge – the engine rates it as the best move, improving White’s standing by about a tenth of a pawn even though the material balance remains unchanged.

teacher: By pushing …h4 Black finally creates a pawn break against White’s pawn on g3, opening the kingside. If White captures with gxh4, the g‑file becomes open for Black and the h‑file turns semi‑open, while White is left with isolated pawns on h2, f4 and the new h4 pawn, giving Black clear targets and limiting the cramped bishop on e1. The move also lets Black’s rook on c6 keep exploiting the semi‑open c‑file, and the engine rates it as the best move, improving Black’s evaluation from a slight White edge to roughly equal.
student: By pushing …h4 Black finally creates a pawn break against White’s g‑pawn, immediately challenging the centre in this rook‑and‑minor‑piece ending. After the natural capture gxh4 the g‑file opens for Black while the h‑file becomes semi‑open, giving the rook on c6 active play along the semi‑open c‑file. The exchange also leaves White with isolated pawns on h2, f4 and h4, weakening their structure. Although White remains a pawn ahead, the engine rates the move as the best, improving Black’s standing by about a fifth of a pawn.

teacher: By moving the rook to a6 Black does seize the open a‑file, a sensible plan in this rook‑and‑minor‑piece ending, but the move lets White immediately capture the pawn on h4. After 35…Ra6 White can play gxh4, after which Black’s rook will have to linger on the a‑file while White is already a pawn up and enjoys a small advantage. The engine rates Kf7 as the better alternative, keeping the king active and preserving material. Thus Ra6 costs Black roughly a fifth of a pawn, leaving White slightly better.
student: By playing Ra6 Black places his rook on the open a‑file, but the move does not improve his standing in this rook‑and‑minor‑piece ending where White’s bishop on e1 already has very few safe squares. The engine shows that White can simply capture the pawn on h4 with gxh4, gaining a pawn and leaving Black a little worse – about a fifth of a pawn down. A more accurate try would have been Kf7, which keeps the king active and avoids giving White the easy exchange. Consequently the evaluation shifts to a slight edge for White.

teacher: Black’s 36…Ra2+ is a checking skewer that forces White to interpose, but it yields no tangible gain. White can meet the check with 37.Rd2, after which the pawn on c3 is left en prise, while Black has already passed up the far stronger 36…hxg3 that would have captured the g‑pawn and improved his material. As a result the engine’s assessment slides from a roughly equal balance to White being a little better – about a sixth of a pawn – reflecting the slight worsening of Black’s position. The move is therefore a decent try, but not the optimal continuation.
student: Black’s 36…Ra2+ checks the white king while also creating a skewer that threatens to expose the pawn on h2 if White steps away. In practice the move lets White keep the extra pawn – the evaluation shifts from a tiny edge for White to about a third of a pawn in White’s favour – and even allows White to continue with Rd2, after which the pawn on c3 becomes vulnerable. The engine judged hxg3, capturing the pawn on g3, as the superior continuation because it would have eliminated White’s central pressure without conceding the material deficit. Consequently, Ra2+ is a good checking move but costs Black roughly a sixth of a pawn compared with the optimal capture.

teacher: White’s best‑move Rd2 simply consolidates the tiny edge, keeping the evaluation at roughly +0.3 pawns and preserving the one‑pawn material advantage. The rook’s placement does leave the c3 pawn en prise; while the rook on a2 is pinned to the king on e2 and cannot capture it, Black’s bishop on f6 can take the pawn. In the most likely continuation Black would play …Ra4 to relieve the pressure on the a‑file, yet White still retains the slight advantage in this rook‑and‑minor‑piece ending.
student: By playing Rd2 White places his rook directly behind Black’s rook on a2, so that the black rook cannot attack it without exposing the white king on e2. The move also leaves the pawn on c3 hanging, but because the bishop on e1 now has only one safe square this does not create any immediate tactical problems. Black can try Ra4, which would remove the pressure on the a‑file, yet even after that continuation White remains a little better – roughly three‑quarters of a pawn. This subtle defensive resource preserves White’s slight edge in an otherwise balanced rook‑and‑minor‑piece ending.

teacher: Black’s 37…Ra1 simply eliminates the immediate danger to the rook on a1, but it is inferior to the engine‑recommended 37…Ra4, which would have removed the same threat to the rook on a4. After Ra1 White can meet it with Rc2, protecting the pawn on c3, and the evaluation slides from a modest White edge of about a quarter pawn to roughly a half‑pawn. The position remains a rook‑and‑minor‑piece ending, with White’s bishop cramped on e1 and his rook dominating the open d‑file.
student: By playing Ra1 Black eliminates the immediate danger to his rook, but the engine judges that the more accurate continuation would have been Ra4, which also shields the rook while keeping the pressure on White’s pieces. Consequently the evaluation slips from a slight White edge to an even larger one – roughly two‑tenths of a pawn worse for Black. In this rook‑and‑minor‑piece ending White still enjoys a modest advantage thanks to the bishop on e1 being confined to its only safe square and the white rook dominating the open d‑file. White can now answer with Rc2, removing the threat to the pawn on c3.

teacher: Black answers with 38…Ra2+, a checking skewer that lines the rook up against White’s king on e2 and the pawn on h2, exploiting the fact that White’s bishop is limited to only two safe squares. The move leaves the material balance essentially unchanged, preserving White’s slight edge of about a quarter of a pawn. Nevertheless, the engine prefers 38…hxg3, which wins a pawn outright; the most accurate defensive try for White after the check would be 39.Rd2, but that would leave the pawn on c3 vulnerable.
student: Black’s rook jump to a2 checks the white king while also creating a skewer that forces the king to step away from the h‑pawn, which becomes vulnerable once the king moves. The engine rates the move as keeping the evaluation essentially unchanged – White remains only a fraction of a pawn ahead – but notes that the more accurate continuation would have been hxg3, capturing the pawn on g3. After the check White can reply with Rd2, after which the pawn on c3 would be left en prise, giving Black a concrete target in this rook‑and‑minor‑piece ending.

teacher: White’s 41 Rd7 simply steps the rook out of danger, removing the threat to the piece on d7 while keeping it active on the open d‑file. By doing so White also preserves the pawn on c3, which the engine‑suggested 41 Rd2 would have left en prise. The move nudges the evaluation from roughly equal to a slight edge for White, who is now a pawn up. Black’s most natural reply would be 41…hxg3, capturing the g‑pawn, but this does not change the modest advantage.
student: By playing Rd7 White eliminates Black’s immediate pressure on the rook, simply removing the threat that had been hanging over it. The move also leaves the rook firmly on the open d‑file in this rook‑and‑minor‑piece ending, where White’s bishop on e1 already has very few safe squares. Although the engine prefers Rd2, which would have removed the same threat while leaving the c3 pawn vulnerable, the chosen move keeps White’s slight edge – the evaluation improves by about five hundredths of a pawn. Black can reply with hxg3, after which White recaptures and continues with Kf8 followed by Bd2.

student: Black’s rook jump to a2 checks the white king while also creating a skewer that forces the king to step away from the h‑pawn, which becomes vulnerable once the king moves. The engine rates the move as excellent because it keeps the balance virtually unchanged – White remains only a fraction of a pawn ahead – even though the more accurate continuation would have been hxg3, winning the pawn on g3. After the check White can reply with Rd2, after which the pawn on c3 would be left en prise, but Ra2+ already secures the most active defensive resource in this rook‑and‑minor‑piece ending.

Black’s most natural reply would be hxg3, capturing the pawn on g3, but even that does not change the evaluation appreciably.
student: By playing Rd2 White places his rook directly behind Black’s rook on a2, so that any capture on g3 would simply recapture with the same piece, leaving the position essentially unchanged in terms of material. The engine rates the move as excellent because it preserves White’s slight edge – the evaluation drops by only about three‑hundredths of a pawn – while keeping the rooks active in this rook‑and‑minor‑piece ending where Black’s rook already pins the white rook to the king. If Black does reply hxg3, White can continue with hxg3 and later bring the king to d3, maintaining the pressure.

Although the move keeps the evaluation essentially unchanged, the engine’s top choice was Ke3, which would have been marginally more accurate. In practice, however, c5 keeps the game level while securing a passed pawn for White.

teacher: White’s king steps to d3, a solid centralizing move that leaves the position essentially equal – the engine’s evaluation shifts only by a few hundredths of a pawn. The drawback is that the bishop on d2 becomes hanging; Black can reply Rxc5, winning the advanced pawn on c5 (and removing the rook’s target), while the bishop on d2 remains under attack. Although Ke3 would have kept the bishop safe and is therefore the engine’s top choice, Kd3 is still an excellent move that preserves White’s material edge without worsening the overall balance.
student: White’s king steps to d3, but in doing so leaves the bishop on d2 hanging. student: Black’s king steps to c6, keeping the material balance and leaving the evaluation exactly equal in this bishop‑ending where White’s pawns sit on dark squares and Black’s on light squares. The engine notes that the more ambitious pawn break e5 would strike at White’s f4 pawn, but after Kc6 White can simply retreat the bishop with Ba7, removing any immediate pressure. teacher: White’s pawn break f5 strikes at Black’s e‑pawn while uncovering the bishop on g3, which now eyes the enemy bishop on c7. The advance also pushes the kingside pawn majority forward, even though it leaves an isolated pawn on f5. Black could capture the bishop on g3, and White would recapture with fxe6; the material edge remains and the position stays roughly equal, with White now a pawn up.
student: White’s pawn thrust f5 is an excellent way to activate his last king‑side pawn and to strike at Black’s e6 pawn while also uncovering the bishop on g3’s line against Black’s bishop on c7. By advancing the two‑pawn majority against Black’s single pawn, White creates immediate pressure in this bishop ending. The engine rates the move as keeping the balance essentially unchanged – the evaluation slips only about three hundredths of a pawn – but it remains the best continuation because any other try would allow Black to capture the bishop on g3.

teacher: By playing …Bxg3 Black eliminates White’s last bishop, turning a roughly equal bishop‑ending into a material advantage (a bishop for a pawn) and leaving Black up two points. The engine rates the capture as the best move, with the evaluation essentially unchanged at equality, confirming its precision. White’s most natural reply would be fxe6, which removes the threat to the e‑pawn and captures the pawn on e6, after which Black can continue with …Bd6 and advance the king. This continuation shows Black comfortably preserving the material edge.
student: By taking on g3 Black eliminates White’s last bishop and emerges with a two‑pawn material edge in this pure bishop ending. The capture leaves the balance essentially unchanged – the engine still evaluates the position as roughly equal – but it secures a clear advantage that can be exploited later. White’s most natural reply would be fxe6, which both removes the threat to the pawn on e6 and wins the pawn, after which Black can continue with …Bd6 and keep the initiative. This precise exchange therefore justifies the “best” label.

teacher: White’s capture on e6 creates a passed pawn deep in Black’s position and opens the f‑file, while the e‑file becomes semi‑open for Black. In this bishop endgame the new e‑pawn not only removes the immediate threat to itself but also gives White a two‑pawn majority on the kingside (h2 and e6) against none for Black. Black’s most accurate reply would be …Bd6, which simply eliminates the danger to the bishop on d6; White can then push e7, after which Black would have to capture on e7. Although the exchange leaves White a pawn down, the engine’s evaluation stays equal, showing that the dynamic chances generated by the passed pawn fully compensate for the material deficit.
student: By playing fxe6 White eliminates Black’s immediate pressure on the e‑file and creates a passed pawn on e6, giving him a two‑pawn majority on the kingside in this bishop ending. The capture also opens the f‑file while removing the threat to the pawn that had just arrived on e6, so the engine rates it as the best continuation even though Black remains a pawn ahead. Black can answer with …Bd6, which would simply remove the lingering danger to the bishop on d6, after which the game continues with e7 and the exchange on e7.

teacher: Black’s bishop steps back to d6, eliminating the direct threat to it. In this bishop‑ending White’s advanced passed pawn on e6 is the only real danger, and by retreating the bishop Black preserves the one‑pawn material edge while keeping the evaluation essentially equal. Should White push e7, the pawn would be left en prise and Black can answer Bxe7, regaining the pawn without trouble.
student: By retreating the bishop to d6 Black eliminates White’s immediate pressure on that piece, preserving the extra pawn in this bishop‑only ending where White’s only active asset is the far‑advanced passed pawn on e6. The engine rates Bd6 as the best continuation, and after any sensible reply such as e7 the pawn on e7 would be left en prise, allowing Black to capture it with Bxe7. Consequently the evaluation remains roughly equal, confirming that the move neutralises White’s threats without conceding anything.

teacher: White drives his far‑advanced passed pawn to e7, deliberately leaving it en prise. If Black captures with Bxe7, the resulting position is a stalemate, so Black cannot take without conceding a draw. By creating this stalemate threat White neutralises Black’s extra pawn and keeps the evaluation essentially equal, which is why the engine rates e7 as the best move.
student: By pushing e7 White creates an advanced passed pawn that can be taken by Black’s bishop with check, and after the forced Bxe7 the e‑file opens for White’s king to march forward. In this bishop ending the pawn on e7 becomes en prise, but it also forces the bishop to capture, leaving Black down a pawn and giving White a clear route to activate his pieces. The engine rates the move as the best possible, keeping the evaluation at equality despite being a pawn down. If Black replies Bxe7, the resulting stalemate leaves the balance unchanged.

teacher: By capturing on e7 Black not only wins a pawn but also creates a stalemate net for White, which is why the engine still evaluates the position as essentially equal despite the material gain. With only the white king on h3 and a lone pawn on h2 left, Black’s extra piece is offset by the drawing chances that the stalemate threat provides, making Bxe7 the only move that preserves the balance while netting material.
student: By taking on e7 Black not only wins a pawn but also forces a forced mate – the bishop lands on e7 and immediately attacks White’s king, which has no safe squares. The capture opens the e‑file for Black’s pieces while leaving the material balance untouched, so the engine still evaluates the position as roughly equal despite Black being up two pawns. This precise combination makes Bxe7 the clear best continuation in this bishop ending.

teacher: Black answered 1.Nf3 with the natural developing move Nf6, bringing a piece into play and preparing to meet White’s central ideas.  However, the engine rates the pawn thrust c5 as the superior reply; c5 would have nudged the evaluation a few hundredths of a pawn in Black’s favour.  After Nf6 the position remains almost unchanged, with White still holding a slight edge (about +0.26 pawns).  In short, the move is sound but gives up the tiny advantage that the more active c5 would have secured.
student: Black develops the knight to its natural square f6, completing his opening setup and leaving material equal while the engine’s assessment stays at roughly +0.26 for White – essentially unchanged from the previous position. The move therefore preserves the status quo without creating any new weaknesses. Nevertheless, the engine rates …c5 as the optimal continuation, which would have nudged the evaluation in Black’s favour by about two‑hundredths of a pawn. In short, 1…Nf6 is solid but not the most accurate choice.

teacher: Black’s 2…b6 leaves the balance exactly where it was, with White still a hair’s‑breadth better (about a quarter of a pawn). The engine judges the move as solid but not the most accurate; it would have preferred 2…e6, which keeps the evaluation unchanged while developing a piece more directly. In practice, …b6 does not create any new threats or structural changes, so the position remains essentially equal in material and evaluation.
student: Black’s …b6 simply reinforces the centre and leaves material equal, so the engine still judges White to be a shade better – roughly a quarter‑pawn advantage. The move does not alter the balance in any way, which is why it earns only a modest “best” label rather than the more precise “best”. After …b6 White can continue with Bg5, after which Black could answer …Bb7 and later play …e6, but the position remains essentially unchanged.

teacher: White chooses 4 g3, a solid move that nudges the evaluation from +0.22 to +0.41 – roughly a fifth of a pawn in White’s favour. student: White’s quiet g3 simply preserves the slight edge that existed after Black’s …Bb7‑pinning of the f3‑knight to the rook on h1. The engine rates it as a modest improvement – roughly a fifth of a pawn – and notes that the more ambitious Bf4 would have been preferable. teacher: White’s 5 Bg2 is the engine’s top choice, preserving the modest edge of roughly a pawn’s worth. student: Black’s …Be4 does little more than place a bishop on an arbitrary square and leaves White still a shade ahead – the evaluation slides from +0.31 to about +0.64, roughly a third of a pawn worse for Black. The engine points out that the far stronger continuation would have been the pawn break …c5, which strikes directly at White’s d4 pawn and keeps the balance tighter. After …Be4 White can simply meet the thrust with Qd1, removing the immediate pressure on the queen. In short, the move is good but it costs Black a modest edge compared with the optimal central break.

teacher: By playing cxd5 White eliminates Black’s pawn on d5, removing the threat to the pawn and turning the c‑file into a semi‑open line for White’s pieces. student: By playing cxd5 White eliminates Black’s pawn on d5 and opens the c‑file, giving White a semi‑open line while removing the immediate threat to the pawn that had just arrived there. With material still equal and the engine’s assessment barely shifting from +0.86 to +0.77, the move preserves White’s clear advantage without creating any new weaknesses.

teacher: White’s 13 Re1 is a solid, “good” move that simply brings the rook to the centre, but it does not improve on the already‑slightly‑better position – the evaluation drops from about +0.86 to +0.56, a loss of roughly a third of a pawn. student: White’s Re1 simply brings the rook to the seventh rank, keeping material equal but leaving the evaluation slip by roughly a third of a pawn. student: White’s 14.e4 tries to push the kingside pawn majority and deprive Black’s knight on f6 of the d5‑square, but it does nothing to stop Black’s active pieces. student: By taking on d5 Black eliminates White’s central pawn and forces the natural recapture exd5, after which the e‑file opens and Black can continue with …Rxe1+ followed by Qxe1 and Bxd4, exploiting the newly opened line while keeping the queenside pawn majority intact. student: By taking on d5 Black eliminates White’s active knight and secures a clear material edge, leaving Black a pawn ahead. student: By playing exd5 White eliminates Black’s active bishop and opens the e‑file, giving both sides a rook control of that line while leaving White with an isolated queen’s pawn on d5. student: By playing Be3 White eliminates Black’s immediate pressure on the f‑pawn, thereby preserving the balance despite being down a pawn. student: By playing Rd1 White does nothing to improve his cramped bishop on g2 or to challenge Black’s dominant rook on the open e‑file, and the engine now judges the position as clearly better for Black – about a pawn down and even with Black a pawn ahead. student: By retreating the bishop to f1 White preserves the valuable bishop pair while Black’s bishop on f6 remains confined to its single safe square. student: White’s king steps back to g2, keeping it out of Black’s rook’s line while preserving its activity in this rook‑and‑minor‑piece ending. student: White’s bishop retreats to c4, keeping the pieces coordinated in this rook‑and‑minor‑piece ending where Black’s rook dominates the open e‑file while White’s rook works the semi‑open c‑file. The engine rates the move as essentially unchanged – Black remains about two pawns ahead – but it does not improve the position enough to justify the slight loss of ground that would have been avoided by the more ambitious …c5. In fact, after the check White can answer Kf3, after which Black could continue with …d5, preserving the advantage. Thus the move is solid and keeps Black’s lead, yet it misses the sharper continuation offered by …c5.

teacher: White’s king steps to f3, the only move that preserves the balance in this rook‑and‑minor‑piece ending. The engine’s numbers show the position remains essentially unchanged – Black is still about two pawns better – while the white rook continues to exploit the semi‑open d‑file. In the principal variation Black could try …c5, after which White would keep up the pressure with Rd7 and Black would reply Rd4, maintaining the same level of disadvantage.
student: In this rook‑and‑minor‑piece ending White’s king steps to f3, keeping it active while the rook continues to dominate the semi‑open d‑file. The engine rates Kf3 as the best continuation, noting that the evaluation stays essentially unchanged – Black remains about two pawns ahead. If Black were to reply with …c5, White could answer Rd7, after which Black would continue with Rd4 and White would follow up with Rc7, preserving the balance despite being down material.

teacher: Black’s bishop retreat to c5 creates an immediate mating threat, as the move threatens Rf2#. Nevertheless, the sacrifice of tempo costs Black about a third of a pawn – the evaluation slips from a clear –2.18 advantage to –1.77 – and the engine flags the pawn push c5 as the superior alternative. If White answers correctly, the pawn break g4 strikes at the f5 pawn, blunting Black’s attack.
student: By playing …Bc5 Black immediately creates an immediate mating threat with Rf2#, but the engine judges that this costs about four‑tenths of a pawn compared with the more accurate …c5. After …Bc5 White can answer with the pawn break g4, striking at the f5 pawn and opening lines for his pieces while the black king remains under pressure. The move still leaves Black clearly ahead in material – up two pawns – yet it is not the optimal continuation.

teacher: Rd7 looks tempting, for it attacks both c7 and f7 and even pins the f‑pawn to the black king, exploiting the semi‑open d‑file in this rook‑and‑minor‑piece ending. However, it fatally overlooks Black’s immediate resource: after 91…Rf2# White is checkmated, turning an already worse position into a forced loss. The engine shows that the correct continuation would have been the pawn break g4, striking at the f5 pawn and keeping any mate at bay.
student: White’s 91.Rd7 tries to fork the c‑pawn and the f‑pawn while also pinning the latter to Black’s king on g7, but the move completely overlooks the immediate mating threat. After Rd7 Black can reply with …Rf2#, delivering a forced mate in one. The engine shows that the correct continuation was 91.g4, a pawn break aimed at the f5 pawn, which would have avoided the loss. Consequently the evaluation swings from a clear Black advantage of about two pawns to an inevitable mate.

teacher: Black ends the game with Rf2#, delivering immediate checkmate. White’s king on f3 is completely immobilised – the rook on d7 pins the pawn on f7, so the king cannot interpose or capture, and the rook on f2 covers the only escape squares. The move simply converts the already‑forced mate‑in‑one into a finished game, leaving Black up two points of material but, more importantly, securing the win.
student: Black finishes the game with Rf2#, delivering immediate checkmate because the white king on f3 cannot escape while the rook on d7 continues to pin the f‑pawn to the black king on g7. The engine’s evaluation changes from “Black has a forced mate in one” to an outright win, confirming that the move converts the previously existing mating net into a decisive finish. In this rook‑and‑minor‑piece ending, where White’s rook already pins the f‑pawn, the simple rook lift to f2 forces the inevitable mate without any defensive resource left for White.

teacher: Black answered 1.d4 with the natural 1…Nf6, developing a piece and leaving the score essentially level – the engine still sees White only a hair ahead (about 0.18 of a pawn). The move is perfectly sound, but the engine’s top choice is the central break 2…d5, which would have contested White’s centre and given Black a small edge (roughly a tenth of a pawn). Consequently, Nf6 is a solid continuation, though slightly less ambitious than the preferred …d5.
student: Black’s …Nf6 simply develops the knight to its natural square and leaves material perfectly balanced, with the engine still judging the position as roughly equal – the evaluation shifts by only about a seventh of a pawn in White’s favour. The move therefore keeps the balance intact without creating any new weaknesses. Although the engine would have preferred the more aggressive …d5, which it rates as the best continuation, …Nf6 is nevertheless a sound choice that preserves equality.

teacher: White develops the queen‑knight to c3, keeping the modest plus of about a third of a pawn that existed before the move. The evaluation is essentially unchanged, remaining at roughly +0.37 for White. Although the engine preferred  Nf3 — which would keep the knight more flexible and let White meet Black’s natural …d5 break (striking at the c4 pawn) with Nf3 and then Qb3 — the move to c3 is still a sound developing choice that preserves White’s slight edge.
student: White develops the knight to its natural square on c3, keeping the modest edge that existed after 2…g6. The engine rates the move as “best” but notes that it changes the evaluation by only about two‑hundredths of a pawn, leaving White still slightly better. Black’s most logical reply would be the pawn break …d5, striking at White’s pawn on c4 and challenging the centre.

teacher: Black’s 5…Bg4 creates a pin of the f3‑knight against the queen on d1, but the maneuver does not justify the concession of time: White’s evaluation rises from a slight edge to a clear advantage of about a pawn. The engine rates the move only “good” and notes that castling with 5…O‑O would have been preferable, keeping the balance more even. In the principal line White can meet the pin with 6 Be2, after which Black’s best continuation would be to castle and only then consider exchanges on f3. Consequently the bishop sortie costs Black roughly a quarter‑pawn in the assessment.
student: By playing …Bg4 Black places his bishop on an active diagonal that immediately attacks White’s knight on f3 and pins it to the queen on d1. The pin does create some pressure, but it also allows White to improve with Be2, after which Black would have to decide whether to castle or meet the ensuing threats. The engine rates the move as “good” yet notes that it costs Black roughly a fifth of a pawn compared with the optimal castling choice, leaving White still a little better. In short, the bishop move is solid but not the most accurate continuation in this opening.

teacher: White’s 6.Be2 is judged the best continuation, preserving the modest but clear advantage of roughly a pawn. By developing the bishop to e2 the engine’s evaluation nudges from +0.62 to +0.71, essentially unchanged for White. In the principal variation Black would castle, after which White can continue with Be3 and later Qc2, keeping the edge.
student: White’s bishop retreats to e2, keeping the modest edge that existed after 5.Nf3 Bg4 and nudging it up by roughly a tenth of a pawn. The engine rates this as the best continuation, with Black most likely castling long (…O‑O) and then developing …Be3, followed by White’s natural Nbd7 and Qc2. By preserving the slight advantage without altering material, Be2 maintains White’s clear superiority in the opening.

teacher: Black’s Bxf3 wins the knight on f3 and, by landing on that square, pins White’s bishop on e2 to the queen on d1. White can simply recapture with Bxf3, which removes the threat to the pawn on g2 and restores material balance, but Black has given up the bishop pair, so the engine’s evaluation stays almost unchanged with White still a little better. The move is nevertheless rated excellent for the piece win, even though the engine prefers the quieter castling move O‑O.
student: By playing …Bxf3 Black eliminates White’s active knight and forces an immediate exchange that leaves the material balance essentially unchanged – Black remains up three points but the engine still judges White to be about a pawn ahead. The capture also creates a pin of White’s bishop on e2 against the queen on d1, yet after the forced recapture Bxf3 the bishop pair disappears for both sides. Although the position stays roughly equal in material, the engine rates the move as excellent because it neutralises White’s pressure without worsening Black’s standing.

teacher: White’s Bxf3 eliminates the threat to the g2 pawn and forces Black to give up the bishop pair, leaving White with the two bishops against bishop and knight. Material stays equal and the evaluation remains about a pawn in White’s favour, showing the move kept the advantage essentially unchanged. Black’s best reply would be the pawn break e5, striking at the d4 pawn, after which the line continues dxe5 dxe5 Qxd8+. Thus the capture is the excellent, best move, preserving White’s slight edge.
student: By taking on f3 White eliminates Black’s active bishop and simultaneously removes the immediate danger to the g‑pawn, preserving material equality while keeping the bishop pair that underpins his advantage. The engine rates the capture as an excellent continuation, with the evaluation barely slipping from +0.77 to +0.69 – essentially unchanged in practical terms. Black can now try the thematic …e5 pawn break, striking at White’s d4 pawn, but even after that line White remains clearly better.

teacher: White advances the d‑pawn to d5, keeping his light‑square pawn chain intact and retaining the bishop pair. The move is good, but it relinquishes the more precise dxe5, which would have captured the e5 pawn and preserved a larger advantage. As a result the evaluation slips from about a pawn’s worth to a little less than a pawn, a loss of roughly a fifth of a pawn. In the engine’s continuation Black can reply with …h5, after which White could press on with c5.
student: White’s 8.d5 simply pushes the centre while preserving the light‑square pawn chain and the bishop pair, but it does nothing to address Black’s central tension. The engine points out that the more accurate continuation would have been 8.dxe5, which captures the pawn on e5 and keeps White’s advantage larger. By opting for d5 instead, White’s edge shrinks from roughly two‑thirds of a pawn to just under half a pawn – a loss of about 0.21 pawn.

teacher: White’s 9 h4 leaves the position essentially unchanged, with the light‑square pawn chain still intact and the bishop pair preserved, so White remains only a hair’s‑breadth better. The engine judged the pawn break 9 c5 – striking at Black’s d6 pawn – to be the sharper try; by opting for h4 White gave up that immediate pressure, though the cost is only about two‑hundredths of a pawn. In the continuation the engine expects Black to develop with …Nbd7, after which White could play g3 and the game would carry on along the line Nbd7 – g3 – Bh6 – Bxh6.
student: White’s quiet h4 simply reinforces the light‑square pawn chain while leaving the position essentially unchanged – the engine still rates White as a shade better, about three‑tenths of a pawn. The move does not create any immediate threats and therefore keeps the slight edge intact. Nevertheless, the engine points out that the more ambitious pawn break c5 would have struck directly at Black’s d6 pawn, offering White a clearer chance to improve his standing. By opting for h4 instead, White missed that dynamic opportunity but remains comfortably ahead.

teacher: White’s quiet 10 g3 simply reinforces White’s dark‑square pawn chain on the kingside and keeps the bishop pair intact, a subtle but consistent improvement that nudges the evaluation from a modest edge to about a half‑pawn in White’s favour. The move also prepares to meet Black’s most natural try …Bh6 with Bxh6, after which a …Rxh6 can be answered by Bg2, preserving the bishops while the pawn structure remains fixed on opposite colours. This small but precise strengthening is why the engine rates g3 as the best move, rewarding White with a slight increase in the advantage.
student: White’s quiet g3 is judged the best continuation, nudging the evaluation up by roughly a fifth of a pawn to about +0.60. By fixing the pawn structure – White’s pawns remain on light squares while Black’s sit on dark squares – and preserving the bishop pair, the move solidifies White’s slight edge without creating any new weaknesses. The engine predicts that Black would most naturally answer with …Bh6, after which White can capture on h6, then recapture with Rxh6 and continue with Bg2, keeping the modest advantage intact.

teacher: White eliminates Black’s dark‑square bishop with Bxh6, initiating an exchange that forces Black to recapture with the rook. Although the material balance will be restored after Rxh6, the line leaves White a little better – the evaluation climbs to roughly a pawn’s worth – and it fits the position where White’s pawns sit on light squares while Black’s are fixed on dark squares. The capture also keeps White’s bishop pair intact for the moment, preserving the slight edge before the inevitable trade. The engine rates the move as the best, and the expected continuation is Rxh6 followed by Qd2, Rh8, O‑O.
student: By taking on h6 White eliminates Black’s active bishop and forces an immediate trade that leaves the material balance essentially unchanged – after Black’s natural …Rxh6 the bishops will be exchanged and White will have given up the bishop pair but still retains a clear edge. The capture also preserves White’s advantage of being up three points of material while keeping the pawn structure locked on opposite colours. Consequently the engine rates Bxh6 as the best continuation, nudging the evaluation from a slight plus to roughly a pawn’s worth in White’s favour.

teacher: By taking on h6 Black eliminates one of White’s bishops, thereby removing White’s bishop‑pair advantage that it previously enjoyed. The capture restores material equality, but the evaluation still favours White by about a pawn, reflecting the slightly worse standing for Black (‑0.11 pawns). With White’s pawns locked on light squares and Black’s on dark squares, the position remains balanced, and the engine’s continuation would see White playing Qd2, Black replying Rh8, followed by O‑O and …a4.
student: By taking on h6 Black eliminates White’s active bishop and forces a trade that leaves material equal while conceding the bishop pair to White. The capture also fits the opposite‑colour pawn structure – White’s pawns sit on light squares and Black’s on dark – so the exchange does not disturb those long‑term dynamics. Although it costs Black a small fraction of a pawn in the engine’s eyes, Rxh6 remains the best continuation because it neutralises White’s piece advantage without creating new weaknesses.

teacher: Black’s 13…Rh8 simply removes the looming threat to the rook on h8, preserving the material balance in a position where White’s pawns are fixed on light squares and Black’s on dark squares. By retreating the rook, Black neutralises White’s immediate pressure without altering the overall assessment, which still favours White by about a pawn. The engine’s continuation shows White can safely castle, followed by a4 and a bishop lift to h3, while Black’s king steps to f8, keeping the game balanced.
student: By playing Rh8 Black eliminates White’s immediate pressure on the rook that had just been captured on h6, thereby preserving material equality and keeping the position solid. The engine rates the move as excellent, noting that it leaves the evaluation virtually unchanged – White remains about a pawn ahead. In the principal line White would castle, after which Black can continue with …a4, followed by …Bh3 and Kf8, maintaining the balance.

teacher: White decided to castle queenside, moving the king to c1. Although the king is now safe behind the pawn chain, the engine shows the move costs about half a pawn, reducing White’s edge from roughly a pawn’s worth to less than that. With Black’s king still in the centre and White’s pawns fixed on light squares, Black can answer …Nc5, forcing White’s king to step back to b1 and giving Black active counterplay. The engine judged short castling (O‑O) to be the better choice, which would have kept the larger advantage.
student: By castling long White finally brings his king to safety and connects the rooks, but the move also leaves Black’s king still exposed in the centre while White’s own pawns remain locked on light squares. The engine rates the position after O‑O‑O as only “slightly” better for White – roughly half a pawn down compared with the optimal continuation. In other words, although the move is solid, it costs White about four‑tenths of a pawn in evaluation. The engine’s preferred reply was simply O‑O, which would have kept the same material balance without conceding the slight disadvantage.

teacher: Black’s queen retreat to e7 leaves the king stranded in the centre while White has already castled, and it does nothing to improve Black’s safety. The engine points out that the far‑safer Kf8 would have been the correct move; after Qe7 White can continue with Rde1, after which Black would have to shuffle the king to d8 and White’s bishop can head to h3. As a result the evaluation slides from a slight White edge to a clearer advantage of roughly a pawn, costing Black about a quarter pawn. Material remains equal and both sides’ pawn structures stay fixed on opposite colour complexes.
student: By retreating the queen to e7 Black does little more than keep the pieces safely placed, but it also leaves the king exposed in the middle while White already enjoys a clear edge thanks to his solidly‑fixed light‑square pawn chain and a safe castle. The engine rates Kf8 as the superior try, which would have kept the evaluation around +0.5 for White instead of the current +0.75. After 15…Qe7 White can continue with Rde1, after which Black’s best reply is Kd8, followed by Bh3 and Ng4 according to the principal variation. In short, the move costs Black roughly a quarter of a pawn in practical terms.

teacher: Black pushes …c6 to launch a pawn break against White’s d5 pawn and to deprive the knight on c3 of the b5‑square. While the idea is sound, the engine judges that it costs Black roughly half a pawn, leaving White clearly better (+1.1 pawn) compared with the position before the move. A more accurate continuation would have been the king move Kd8, which keeps the king safer while still un‑castled. Consequently, …c6 is a good try but it moderately worsens Black’s standing.
student: Black’s …c6 tries to open lines by striking at White’s d5 pawn and taking the b5 square away from the knight on c3, but it does little to improve his cramped central setup or to challenge White’s already‑castled king. The engine rates the move as “good” yet notes that it costs Black roughly four‑tenths of a pawn, leaving White with a clear advantage of about a pawn. A more accurate try would have been …Kd8, which keeps the king safer and avoids giving White the chance to increase the pressure. After …c6 White can continue with Rhf1, after which Black might reply a4, followed by Rd1 and Rg8.

teacher: By playing …bxc6 Black eliminates White’s pawn on c6, turning the b‑file into a semi‑open line that can be used for counter‑play. The capture also deprives the White knight on c3 of the b5 and d5 squares, and although it leaves Black with an isolated pawn on a5, material is level and the evaluation remains essentially unchanged, preserving the balance. With Black’s king still in the centre while White has already castled, the exchange is a safe way to neutralise White’s slight edge.
student: By playing …bxc6 Black eliminates White’s pawn on c6, opening the b‑file but leaving the c‑file closed and creating an isolated pawn on a5. The capture also deprives White’s knight on c3 of the useful squares b5 and d5, curbing its activity. Although Black’s king remains in the centre while White has already castled, the engine rates the move as the best choice, keeping the evaluation essentially unchanged at a slight edge for White. In the principal variation White would continue with Rd1, after which Black can meet it with …Rb8 and later bring the king to f8.

teacher: With Rd1 White finally occupies the semi‑open d‑file, a natural way to exploit the fact that Black’s king is still stuck in the centre while White has already castled. The rook now eyes the d‑file and prepares to double on it – the engine’s line shows Black’s best reply would be Rd8, after which White can continue Rhf1 and increase the pressure with exf4 gxf4. The move lifts White’s edge from a slight advantage to roughly a half‑pawn, confirming it as the best choice in the position.
student: By sliding the rook to d1 White immediately occupies the semi‑open d‑file, a line that Black’s king must now navigate while his own king is safely castled. The engine rates this as the best continuation, nudging the evaluation up by roughly a tenth of a pawn and preserving White’s slight edge. In the principal variation Black would reply …Rd8, after which White can continue with Rhf1, keeping the pressure along the newly opened file.

teacher: Black’s retreat Kf8 is the only move that preserves the balance, keeping the evaluation essentially unchanged (the engine now sees White only a hair better, about 0.22 of a pawn). By stepping back to a safer square the king sidesteps any immediate threats while the position remains level in material, and White’s rook on d1 continues to enjoy the semi‑open d‑file. The engine’s line shows White could try b3, Black replying Kg7, after which White might play Rhf1 and Black can meet it with exf4. This precise king move therefore earns the “excellent” label as the best continuation in the position.
student: Black’s king steps to f8, the engine’s top choice and an excellent defensive maneuver that leaves material even while keeping the balance virtually untouched – the evaluation shifts by only about five‑hundredths of a pawn in White’s favour. By moving onto f8 Black also readies the natural …Kg7 reply suggested by the principal variation, after which White can continue with b3, Black replies Kg7, then White plays Rhf1 and Black captures on f4, preserving equality. The move therefore neutralises any immediate threats without conceding any advantage.

teacher: By playing gxf4 White eliminates the pawn that was threatening the f‑pawn and opens the g‑file, giving White a semi‑open line for future piece activity. The capture, however, leaves the h‑pawn isolated and en prise, so Black can reply Qxh4 to win that pawn and push the evaluation to a slight Black edge (about a third of a pawn). Even though the position worsens a bit, the move was still the best choice because it removes the immediate threat on f4 while the d‑file already remains semi‑open for the rook on d1.
student: By playing gxf4 White eliminates Black’s immediate pressure on the f‑file and opens the g‑file, giving the rook on d1 a useful semi‑open line while also removing the threat to the pawn that had just arrived on f4. The capture does leave the h‑pawn hanging, but it is still the best continuation because any other try would allow Black to seize the initiative. Black can reply with Qxh4, winning the pawn on h4, yet even after this exchange White remains a little worse – the engine rates the move as good but notes a modest swing in evaluation to about a quarter of a pawn against White.

teacher: By capturing on h4 Black wins a pawn and instantly creates a passed pawn on h5, preserving the slight edge the engine already assigned to Black. Although the move leaves the h‑file semi‑open for White, the material gain keeps the evaluation essentially unchanged at about –0.32 of a pawn. White can answer with Rf3, which would remove the immediate threat to the bishop on h3, after which the engine’s line continues Kg7, Qe3, Qe7.
