After 28.Rbe1 Black can reply 28…hxg4, after which White can win the pinned knight with 29.Rxe4, but the position remains only “much better” for White rather than maximally exploiting the advantage.
student: White’s 28.Rbe1 creates a pin of Black’s knight on e4 against the rook on e8, but it also leaves the b‑pawn hanging. The engine rates the move as a moderate worsening – roughly four‑tenths of a pawn – because Black can reply …hxg4, winning the g‑pawn and forcing a sequence that costs White material. A more accurate continuation would have been 28.fxg6, which both attacks the poorly defended h5 pawn and eliminates the dangerous bishop on g6. Consequently, while the rook lift does generate a tactical threat, it forfeits the larger advantage that could have been achieved with the capture.

teacher: White captures the knight on e4, turning his rook into a fork that attacks both the pawn on c4 and Black’s rook on e8. Black is compelled to recapture, most naturally with Qxe4, which removes the fork but restores the material balance, leaving White still up two pawns and pushing the evaluation to about +2.8. The engine’s continuation (Qxe4 gxf3 Ne1) shows that even Black’s best try cannot erase White’s clear advantage, confirming the move as an excellent choice.
student: By playing Rxe4 White eliminates Black’s active knight on e4 while simultaneously forking the pawn on c4 and the black rook on e8, exploiting the fact that both sides’ rooks already dominate the open e‑file. The capture forces an immediate exchange—after Black would recapture with Rxe4—the material balance is restored but White’s evaluation improves by roughly four‑tenths of a pawn, taking the advantage to about three‑quarters of a pawn. This precise fork therefore justifies the engine’s “best” label and the double exclamation.

teacher: By taking on g4 White eliminates the pawn that was threatening both the knight on f3 and the pawn on h3, and the capture also secures an extra pawn, nudging the evaluation up by roughly a third of a pawn. With the queen now on g4 White creates a latent threat to the g7 pawn that would materialise after Black’s most logical reply, Bh5, which paradoxically would leave that pawn hanging while removing the bishop’s own danger. The move therefore consolidates White’s material lead and improves the position without creating any new weaknesses.
student: By taking on g4 White eliminates the immediate danger to both the knight on f3 and the pawn on h3, thereby preserving the material edge that already leaves him three pawns ahead. The capture also nudges the evaluation up by roughly a third of a pawn, confirming it as the strongest continuation. Black’s most natural reply would be …Bh5, but that move would leave the pawn on g7 hanging, allowing White to win it with Qxg7 and keep the advantage. With White’s rook on e4 dominating the open e‑file while Black’s rooks sit on the semi‑open h‑ and d‑files, the position remains clearly in White’s favour.

teacher: Black’s bishop moves to h5, removing the immediate threat to it, but the retreat leaves the g7 pawn hanging. White can exploit this by playing Qxg7, which both captures the pawn and eliminates the danger to the queen; Black can then reply …Qd8 and later …Rxe3, keeping the material balance essentially unchanged. The engine judges Bh5 as the best move, with the evaluation remaining at roughly a three‑pawn advantage for White, so the move merely preserves Black’s already inferior position.
student: By playing …Bh5 Black finally finds a safe haven for his bishop, even though it leaves the pawn on g7 hanging. The retreat also keeps the rook on h8 active on the semi‑open h‑file while White’s rook continues to dominate the open e‑file. If White replies with the natural Qxg7, Black can meet it with …Qd8 and later capture on e3, preserving the balance despite being down three points of material. This precise maneuver therefore neutralises White’s immediate threats without worsening Black’s position.

teacher: By capturing on g7 White eliminates the pawn that was threatening the queen, opens the g‑file and leaves Black with an isolated pawn on f7 while a passed pawn on h3 is created. The move also takes advantage of Black’s cramped bishop on h5, whose only safe square is limited, and of the rook on h8 now occupying a semi‑open file. The engine rates Qxg7 as the best continuation, keeping White’s decisive +3‑pawn advantage essentially unchanged. Black’s most natural reply would be Rdd8, removing the threat to the rook on h8, after which White can continue with Re3 and later bring the queen back to e5.
student: By taking on g7 White eliminates the immediate danger to her queen and opens the g‑file, while also creating a passed pawn on h3 that will become a key asset in the ensuing play. The capture leaves Black with an isolated pawn on f7 and forces the rook on h8 to retreat to d8, after which White can continue with Re3 and keep the pressure. With the queen now active on g7 and the open file giving White’s pieces easy lines, the engine rates the position as a decisive +3‑pawn advantage, confirming that Qxg7 was indeed the best continuation.

teacher: White’s 32 Rd4 tries to exploit Black’s cramped pieces by forking the pawn on c4 and the queen on d8, while also seizing control of the open d‑file. In practice, however, Black can meet the fork with …Qb8, which removes the threat to the queen and leaves White a little worse – the evaluation slips from a decisive three‑pawn edge to about two‑and‑a‑half pawns, a loss of roughly 0.4 pawn. The engine therefore rates Re3 as the superior move, which would have preserved more of White’s advantage. In the principal line Black’s …Qb8 would be followed by White’s Rh4, Black’s …Rg8, and then White can capture on g8.
student: White’s Rd4 creates a fork, attacking both the pawn on c4 and Black’s queen on d8 while also seizing control of the open d‑file. The engine rates it as good but not optimal – Re3 would have kept more pressure without giving Black the simple defensive resource …Qb8 that eliminates the immediate danger to the queen. After the natural reply …Qb8, White can continue with Rh4, after which Black may play Rg8 and then capture on g8, leaving White still ahead in material despite the modest drop in evaluation.

teacher: Black’s 32…Rxd4 looks active, grabbing the white rook and opening the d‑file, but it merely hands the rook to White’s queen. After 33.Qxd4 White recaptures and, with the queen on d4, forks the c4 pawn and the a7 pawn, turning the material balance into a decisive advantage for White. The engine’s preferred 32…Qb8 would have removed the threat to the queen on b8 and kept Black’s position more tenable. By opting for the exchange, Black worsened the evaluation by roughly two pawns.
student: By playing Rxd4 Black merely trades a rook for White’s rook, allowing White to recapture with Qxd4 and fork the c‑pawn and the a7‑pawn while also removing the immediate danger to the queen on d8. The engine shows that this exchange costs Black roughly two pawns of evaluation, turning a +2.8 advantage for White into a decisive +4.5 lead – a clear mistake. The stronger continuation would have been Qb8, which simply eliminates the queen‑threat without giving White the tactical shot. Consequently Black remains up a pawn but is now down about three pawns in overall assessment.

teacher: By taking on d4 White not only wins the rook but also places the queen on a powerful square that simultaneously attacks the pawn on c4 and the pawn on a7, a classic fork. This capture lifts White’s already decisive edge from about four‑and‑a‑half pawns to roughly four‑and‑three‑quarters of a pawn. Black’s most resilient try would be Qc8, which would at least remove the threat to the c4 pawn, after which White can continue with Qf4 and keep the initiative. The move fully exploits Black’s cramped bishop on h5 and the semi‑open h‑file, cementing White’s winning material advantage.
student: By playing Qxd4 White not only wins the rook but also creates a powerful fork, attacking both the c‑pawn and the a7 pawn at once. The capture nudges the evaluation up by roughly a tenth of a pawn, confirming it as the best continuation. Black’s most natural reply would be …Qc8, which simply eliminates the immediate danger to the c4 pawn, after which White can continue with Qf4 and keep the initiative. With Black’s bishop on h5 confined to its single safe square and the h‑file already contested, the position remains decisively in White’s favour.

teacher: By moving the queen to g8 Black lines the queen on the semi‑open g‑file, joining the rook on the h‑file, so they now bear down on White’s king on h1. This placement fits the position’s constraints—Black’s bishop on h5 has only one safe square and the rook on h8 already uses the h‑file—so the queen’s move reinforces Black’s limited activity. Although the engine prefers 33…Qc8, which would have removed the threat to the c4 pawn, 33…Qg8 keeps the evaluation essentially unchanged, preserving Black’s chances in a clearly losing position.
student: By retreating the queen to g8 Black places it directly behind the white king along the open g‑file, where its heavy pieces can now bear down on White’s monarch. The move also leaves the bishop on h5 with only one safe square and keeps the rook on h8 active on the semi‑open h‑file, so Black does not lose any immediate tactical chances. Although the engine prefers Qc8, which would eliminate the threat to the pawn on c4, the chosen move still preserves the same level of disadvantage – White remains about four pawns ahead and the evaluation changes by only three hundredths of a pawn. Consequently, Qg8 is an excellent defensive resource that maintains Black’s position as well as possible in this losing endgame.

teacher: White’s 35.Rg1 does stop the immediate danger to the knight on g2, but it leaves the rook on h8 free to swing to h3, where it both pins the knight on h2 to the king on h1 and can capture the pawn on h3. That infiltration costs White roughly a pawn‑and‑a‑half, shrinking the evaluation from a decisive +4.2 to a comfortable +2.7. The engine’s preferred move, 35.Rf2, would have removed the same threat while keeping the h‑file under tighter control. Consequently, Rg1 is a clear mistake that hands Black active counter‑play on the semi‑open h‑file.
student: White’s 35.Rg1 was intended to shield both the knight on g2 and the rook that had just moved there, but it does nothing to stop Black’s active rook on the semi‑open h‑file or to meet the immediate danger posed by …Rxh3. By playing Rg1 instead of the engine‑recommended Rf2, White missed the chance to eliminate the pin on the h‑pawn and allowed Black to capture on h3 with Rxh3, after which the evaluation fell from a decisive +4.2 to a comfortable +2.7 – roughly a loss of about one and a half pawns. The move therefore costs White a clear edge in the game.

teacher: Black’s queen slides back to b8, both protecting the a‑pawn and the queen itself while creating the direct mating threat Qxh2#. Because the rook on h3 pins the white knight on h2, that threat is immediate. White can at least blunt it with Qf2, which would remove the danger to the knight. The move leaves White still winning by roughly three pawns—a decisive edge—but it is the best Black could play, worsening the position by only a small fraction of a pawn.
student: By retreating the queen to b8 Black both eliminates the immediate danger to the a‑pawn and the queen itself, while also keeping the powerful mating idea Qxh2#. The move does not change the overall balance – White still enjoys a clear material edge and an evaluation that has slipped by roughly a sixth of a pawn for Black – but it is the best continuation available in this position. White can answer with Qf2, which would remove the pressure on the h‑knight, after which Black could continue with …Bh5 and later …Bd1 as suggested by the engine’s principal variation.

teacher: Black’s …Bf3 looks tempting, pinning the rook on g2 to the king and threatening the immediate mate Qxh2#. In reality the bishop move hangs the pawn on c4 and allows White to reply Nxf3, which captures the bishop and simultaneously removes the rook‑pin and the mating idea. The engine’s best move was Bf1, which would have simply saved the bishop without creating new weaknesses. By playing …Bf3 Black’s evaluation dropped from a modest +2.6 for White to a decisive +5.3, a loss of roughly two and a half pawns and a winning advantage for White.
student: By playing …Bf3 Black creates a pin on the g‑file and even threatens an immediate mate with Qxh2#, but the move also leaves the pawn on c4 undefended and allows White to capture the bishop. After the natural reply Nxf3, the bishop disappears and White’s evaluation jumps from a modest +2.6 to a decisive +5.3 – roughly three pawns in White’s favour. The engine indicates that the correct defence was …Bf1, which would have removed the threat to the bishop without conceding the material loss. Consequently the move costs Black about two and a half pawns and turns a clearly inferior position into a losing one.

teacher: Black’s 39…Rxf3 looks tempting, but it simply hangs the rook: after the capture the rook on f3 is en prise and White can reply 40 Nxf3, removing the threat to the f‑pawn and winning the rook back. The engine already judged the position a decisive White advantage (+5.54) and after the blunder it jumps to an even larger lead (+7.55), a swing of about two pawns. The move therefore fails to gain any material, as the expected exchange restores the balance while costing Black a whole rook. The engine’s preferred move was 39…Rh8, which would have avoided this material loss.
student: By playing Rxf3 Black not only loses the active rook but also leaves it hanging – White can simply answer with Nxf3, which both eliminates the remaining pressure on the f‑pawn and wins the rook. This exchange turns a already losing position for Black into one that is even more clearly in White’s favour, as reflected by the evaluation swing from +5.54 to +7.55. The engine indicates that the correct defence would have been Rh8, keeping the rook safe and avoiding the costly exchange. Consequently, the capture costs Black roughly two pawns of value.

teacher: Black’s queen hops to h8 delivering a check, so the heavy piece now bears down the open h‑file toward White’s king. White can meet the check with Rh2, immediately threatening mate by Rxh8#, while Black can keep the queen active with …Qe8 as the engine’s continuation suggests. The move is judged the best possible for Black, nudging the evaluation in Black’s favour by about a tenth of a pawn, but White still retains a decisive winning edge.
student: Black’s Qh8+ not only checks the white king but also forces it onto the h‑file where Black’s queen and rook already dominate that line, increasing pressure on White’s cramped king. The engine rates the move as the best continuation, improving Black’s standing by roughly a tenth of a pawn even though White still enjoys a decisive material edge. White can try Rh2, which would threaten an immediate mate on xh8, yet Black remains able to meet the threat with …Qe8 and keep the initiative.

teacher: White finishes the combination with Rg8!!, putting the rook on the open g‑file and, crucially, pinning Black’s queen on b8 to the king on a8 so the queen cannot move. The move leaves the evaluation essentially unchanged at a decisive +7.97‑pawn advantage, confirming White’s winning position. According to the engine, Black’s best reply would be b5, after which White can capture on b8 with check, forcing Kxb8 and then continue with Kg2.
student: By sliding the rook to g8 White not only occupies the open g‑file but also creates an immediate pin of Black’s queen on b8 against the king on a8, so the queen cannot move without exposing the king. The engine rates this as the best continuation, and the evaluation remains at roughly +8 pawns – a decisive edge for White. In the principal variation Black would try …b5, after which White can capture the queen with check (Rxb8+) and then bring the king to g2, preserving the winning advantage.

teacher: White captures the queen with Rxb8+, delivering check and compelling Black to recapture with the king. Although the rook is given up and White remains materially ahead, the trade steers the game into an endgame where White’s remaining forces keep a decisive advantage (the engine still evaluates the position at roughly +8 pawns). The move is judged excellent and is the engine’s top choice, changing the evaluation by only a few hundredths of a pawn. After the forced Kxb8, White can continue with checks such as Qb6+ and Qc6+ to maintain the pressure.
student: White’s capture Rxb8+ forces Black to reply Kxb8, after which the game simplifies into an end‑game with no queens remaining. The check does not win material because Black can simply take back, but it nevertheless preserves White’s decisive edge – the engine still evaluates the position at roughly +8½ pawns. By forcing this forced trade, White keeps the initiative and maintains the winning advantage.

teacher: With Qb6+ White delivers a checking fork, hitting both the black king on b8 and the pawn on a6. Black would be forced to move, for example Ka8, after which White can capture a6 with check and then, after the king returns to b8, take the b5 pawn, preserving the winning material edge. The evaluation rises from a decisive +8.28 to +8.55, a modest gain of about a quarter pawn. Consequently the engine correctly rates the move as the best, marked with a brilliant !!.
student: White’s Qb6+ delivers a checking fork that attacks both Black’s king on b8 and the pawn on a6, forcing the black king to retreat. After the forced Ka8, White can continue with Qxa6+, winning the a‑pawn and then capture on b5 with another check, preserving the decisive material edge. The engine rates the move as the best, improving the evaluation by roughly a quarter of a pawn while keeping White clearly ahead in this winning endgame.

teacher: By moving the queen to d6 White lines her heavy pieces along the open d‑file, increasing the pressure on Black’s king in this endgame. However, the engine judges Kg2 to be the superior continuation, and the queen shift costs White about two‑thirds of a pawn, reducing the winning advantage from +8.6 to +8.0. Consequently the move is marked as an inaccuracy.
student: White’s queen retreat to d6 does create pressure along the open d‑file, but it allows Black to improve his king placement with …Kb7 and then continue with …a5, after which White would have to step to g2 before launching Qe5. The engine rates Kg2 as the superior continuation, keeping the evaluation at roughly +8 pawns instead of dropping by about two‑thirds of a pawn. In short, Qd6 modestly weakens White’s winning edge in this endgame.

teacher: Black pushes …b4 as a pawn break against White’s c3 pawn, but in this endgame it immediately allows White the forcing reply Qxa6+, a checking capture that also forks the c4 pawn and the black king. That tactical shot wins the a6 pawn and leaves White’s decisive material advantage even larger, nudging the evaluation from roughly +8.8 pawns to about +9.1 pawns (a loss of about a third of a pawn for Black). The engine judged Kb7 to be the correct alternative, keeping the king safe and avoiding the queen‑fork. Consequently, …b4 is only a good move, not the best, and it slightly worsens Black’s position.
student: Black’s …b4 tries to open lines by striking at White’s pawn on c3, but it immediately allows White to play Qxa6+, forking the black king on a8 and the pawn on c4. After the forced Kb8, White can continue Kg2 and then push f6, keeping the initiative while the engine still judges White to be winning by roughly nine pawns. The move therefore costs Black about a third of a pawn in evaluation terms, making it a good but sub‑optimal choice. The engine preferred Kb7, which would have avoided the fork and kept the balance more favorable for Black.

teacher: White’s queen leap to c7 creates a fork on the c4‑pawn and the f7‑pawn, keeping the initiative and guaranteeing a forced mate in eight moves. The engine, however, notes that the sharper continuation would be Qxa6+, which checks the king on a8 and simultaneously attacks the c4‑pawn, thus winning even more quickly. Black can only try to blunt the pressure with …f6, removing the immediate threat to the f‑pawn, but White’s follow‑up (Kg2, then exploiting the b‑pawn) still leads to an inevitable checkmate.
student: By playing Qc7 White creates a fork, attacking both Black’s c‑pawn and the f‑pawn while also eyeing the black king on a8. The engine shows that this forces a forced mate in eight, turning a previously decisive material edge into an immediate win. Although the engine preferred Qxa6+, which would have captured the a‑pawn with check and kept more pressure, the fork still wins by forcing the sequence …f6 – Kg2 – b3 – axb3. In short, the move converts a winning position into a forced mate.

teacher: Black’s 48…bxc3 is a serious blunder: instead of the defensive …f6, which would have removed the threat to the f‑pawn, Black captures on c3, opening the b‑file but leaving both sides with isolated pawns and, more importantly, allowing White’s forced mate to shrink from eight moves to four. The capture merely exchanges a pawn—White’s pawn on c3 is taken and the material balance is restored—yet it does nothing to stop the impending checkmate. As a result the evaluation swings dramatically in White’s favour, turning an already lost position into a forced mate in four.
student: By playing …bxc3 Black merely trades a pawn for the white pawn on c3, opening the b‑file but leaving both sides with isolated pawns – White’s a‑ and c‑pawns versus Black’s c4 and a6. The capture does not stop White’s looming mating net; after the forced continuation White can continue Kg2 and then a5, delivering mate in four. In contrast, the engine‑recommended …f6 would have removed the immediate danger to the f‑pawn and kept the game alive. Consequently the move costs Black about three moves of life, turning a forced mate in eight into a forced mate in four.

teacher: White’s 49.Nc6 finishes the game instantly: the knight jump creates the direct mating threat Qc8#, turning a forced mate in four into a forced mate in one. Even if Black tries the only plausible defence f6, White simply answers with Qa7# and the king on a8 has no escape. The move therefore exploits the end‑game’s cramped layout to deliver the quickest possible win.
student: White’s knight jump to c6 creates an immediate mating threat with Qc8#, turning a forced mate‑in‑four into a forced mate‑in‑one. The engine notes that the more accurate continuation would have been bxc3, which both eliminates Black’s pawn on c3 and removes the danger to that pawn, but the knight move still forces the win. After Nc6 Black can try f6, which merely shields the pawn on f6 while White already holds the decisive mate.

teacher: White’s pawn push to a3 only creates the threat of Qc8# and fixes Black’s a‑pawn on a light square, leaving White with an isolated pawn on a3.  In fact the engine shows that White could have delivered an immediate checkmate with Qa7#, a move that was available before the pawn move.  After a3 Black can answer with …f6, removing the threat to the f‑pawn, and White will still mate on the next move with Qa7#, so the move forfeits the instant win but does not change the fact that White still has a forced mate in one.
student: White’s a3 simply reinforces the already‑existing mating net, fixing Black’s a‑pawn on a light square and threatening the immediate Qc8# while leaving White with an isolated pawn on a3. The engine still evaluates the position as a forced mate in one, but notes that the more accurate continuation would have been Qa7#, which delivers the same win without any concession. After a3 Black can try …f6, removing the danger to the f‑pawn, yet even this reply cannot escape the inevitable mate.

teacher: Black meets the inevitable threat with 51…f6, the only move that removes the immediate danger to the pawn on f6 and leaves that pawn isolated, while White’s pawn on f5 becomes fixed on a light square. Even though the move does not alter the evaluation – White still has a forced mate in one – it is the best defence available in this endgame. White can now finish the game with Qa7#, delivering checkmate.
student: By playing …f6 Black fixes White’s pawn on f5 on a light square and eliminates the immediate danger to his own pawn, but the resulting isolated pawn on f6 does not change the fact that White can finish the game with Qa7#, delivering mate in one. The engine rates this as the best continuation, yet the evaluation remains a forced mate for White because the position is already hopeless for Black. In short, the move merely delays the inevitable loss.

teacher: White ends the game with a queen‑check on b8, delivering mate along the open b‑file in this pure endgame where White’s pawns sit on dark squares and Black’s on light squares. Nevertheless the engine flags the move as a mistake because the even more direct finishing move Qa7# also mates, so White missed the optimal finishing move. The position was already winning for White—up a huge material margin—but the best move would have been Qa7#, not Qb8#.
student: White’s queen retreat to b8 delivers immediate checkmate, converting the previous one‑move win into a forced loss for Black. The engine had preferred Qa7#, which would have delivered the same mate but with a slightly better continuation. By playing Qb8 instead, White allows Black to reply …f6 and then capture the queen, ending the game immediately.

teacher: White’s 3.Nd5 places the knight on an active central square, yet it does nothing about the bishop on b4 that pins the d‑pawn to the king. Black can simply meet it with …a5, removing the threat to the bishop and leaving the balance roughly equal; the engine even preferred 3.g3, which would have kept a small edge for White. Consequently the move is “good” but costs White about a sixth of a pawn compared with the optimal continuation.
student: White’s 3.Nd5 does little more than shuffle a knight and leaves Black’s bishop on b4 still pinning the d‑pawn, so the engine judges it a slight inaccuracy – about a sixth of a pawn worse for White. The engine preferred 3.g3, which would have kept the balance without creating any new weaknesses. After 3.Nd5 Black can answer with …a5, removing the pressure on the bishop and preserving the pin, after which the game proceeds along the suggested line a5 – a3 – Be7 – Nf3. In short, the move is good but not optimal compared with the alternative.

teacher: Black meets the immediate danger by playing Bc5, which removes the threat to the bishop on c5.  The engine rates the move as good, but it does cost Black a little – the evaluation slides from a roughly equal position to White being a bit better, about a sixth of a pawn.  White can answer with e3, eliminating the threat to the f2 pawn, and the suggested continuation would follow …Nd7, Qc2, …Ngf6.
student: By playing …Bc5 Black eliminates White’s immediate pressure on the bishop, thereby neutralising the tactical danger that had been looming over it. The engine still rates the position as slightly better for White – about three‑tenths of a pawn – but the move is judged good and is indeed the best continuation available. White can now answer with e3, which would remove the threat to the pawn on f2, after which Black could continue with …Nd7 and later develop the knight to g6 according to the principal variation.

teacher: White’s 8.Nc3 is an excellent move because it eliminates the immediate danger to the knight on c3, allowing the piece to remain safely on the board. By doing so, White preserves the balance of the position, with the engine’s evaluation staying around a small plus for White (about +0.13 pawn). The move is judged the best continuation, keeping the game essentially equal.
student: White’s retreat Nc3 simply eliminates the immediate danger to the knight that had been hanging on c3, thereby preserving material equality and keeping the balance at roughly +0.13 for White. The engine rates it as an excellent continuation, noting that the evaluation changes by only about a seventh of a pawn in Black’s favour. In the principal line Black would reply …Nd7, after which White can develop with Be2, followed by …Ngf6 and Qc2, maintaining the equilibrium.

teacher: By sliding the rook to e8 Black completes a simple but sound re‑routing, keeping the material balance and leaving the evaluation essentially unchanged – White still enjoys a tiny edge of about a third of a pawn. Although the engine preferred the prophylactic pawn move h6, Re8 is still excellent because it does not worsen Black’s cramped bishop situation (the c8‑bishop has no safe squares while White’s bishops are similarly restricted) and it preserves the king’s safety. White can now try the thematic pawn break b4, striking at the a5 pawn, but Black’s position remains solid, as the continuation Bb8 – Rb1 – axb4 illustrates.
student: By playing …Re8 Black simply re‑anchors his rook to the eighth rank, keeping material equal and leaving White’s slight edge virtually untouched – the engine still judges White about +0.38 of a pawn ahead. The move does not improve Black’s cramped situation with the bishop on c8 having no safe squares and both White bishops confined to very few retreats. Nevertheless it is an excellent defensive resource that preserves the balance without creating new weaknesses.

teacher: White’s pawn break b4 attacks the a5 pawn and immediately curtails Black’s bishop on a7, which now has only two safe squares, while also taking the c5‑square away from the knight on d7. The move therefore improves White’s spatial control without altering the modest edge – the engine’s evaluation stays at roughly a third of a pawn in White’s favour. Black’s most natural reply would be Bb8, simply removing the threat to the a5 pawn, after which White can continue with Bd2 and recapture on a5 if the pawn is taken.
student: White’s 13 b4 is an excellent pawn break that strikes directly at Black’s a‑pawn and deprives the black bishop on a7 of any useful squares while also taking the c5 square away from Black’s knight on d7. The thrust leaves Black’s bishop on c8 with virtually no safe retreats, underscoring how cramped Black’s pieces have become in this position. Black can answer most naturally with …Bb8, which would simply remove the immediate pressure on the a5 pawn, but even after that continuation White remains only marginally better – roughly three‑tenths of a pawn.

teacher: By playing Nd4 White eliminates the immediate threat to his knight, maintaining material equality. The move also highlights how cramped Black’s bishop on a7 has become, with only two safe squares, while White’s bishop on b2 still enjoys its single safe haven. The engine rates the move as a slight improvement, lifting White’s advantage to about a pawn. If Black were to reply cxd5, White can continue with Ndb5, maintaining the initiative.
student: By playing Nd4 White eliminates the immediate danger to his knight and nudges the evaluation up by roughly a tenth of a pawn. The engine rates this as the best continuation, noting that Black’s bishop on a7 is already cramped with only two safe squares while White’s own bishop on b2 has just one. If Black replies cxd5, White can recapture with Ndb5, after which the line continues d4 – Nxd4, preserving the modest edge.

teacher: Capturing on b4 is the only move that turns the a‑file into a useful line for Black’s rook on a8, exploiting the semi‑open file that already existed. By removing the pawn on b4 the capture also eliminates the threat to White’s knight on c3 and initiates an exchange that leaves Black a pawn ahead, though the evaluation change is only a few hundredths of a pawn, confirming that Black has neutralised White’s earlier edge without creating any new problems.
student: By playing …axb4 Black eliminates White’s pawn on b4 and opens the a‑file, giving the rook on a8 a clear line of activity while also removing the immediate danger to the knight on c3. The capture initiates an exchange that will be answered by White’s forced Rxa1+, after which Black can continue with …Bxa1 and then play cxd5, keeping the pressure on White’s position despite being down a pawn overall. Although the engine still judges White to be about a pawn ahead, the move improves Black’s chances without worsening his standing, making it the best continuation.

teacher: The capture axb4 not only wins the pawn on b4 but also opens the a‑file, uncovering a discovered attack from White’s rook on a1 against Black’s rook on a8 and eliminating the pawn that was threatening the knight on c3. This precise idea leaves the evaluation essentially unchanged at about a pawn’s worth, confirming White’s clear edge. Black’s most forcing reply would be Rxa1+ (check and capture), after which White simply recaptures with Bxa1, preserving the material balance and the advantage.
student: By playing axb4 White eliminates Black’s pawn on b4 and simultaneously opens the a‑file, uncovering a discovered attack from the rook on a1 against Black’s rook on a8. The capture also removes the immediate danger to the knight on c3 while closing the b‑file that had been semi‑open for White. Although material remains equal, the engine still judges White to be about a pawn ahead, with the position essentially unchanged after the move. Black’s most forcing reply would be Rxa1+, checking the king and winning the rook on a1, but even then White retains the advantage.

teacher: Black grabs the rook on a1 with a checking capture, compelling White to recapture with the bishop. After the forced Bxa1 the bishop is cramped on a1, and the black rook that delivered the check has been exchanged. The exchange restores material balance, so the evaluation stays essentially unchanged (still about a pawn in White’s favour), but the move is objectively the best continuation.
student: Black’s Rxa1+ forces the white bishop to capture and immediately leaves that piece cramped – after the forced Bxa1 the bishop will have very few useful squares. The exchange also removes White’s active rook from the board while Black retains his own rook on the open a‑file, giving him a clear long‑term asset despite the engine still judging White as slightly better. By forcing this sequence Black keeps the position balanced in terms of material, with the evaluation barely shifting (+0.03 pawns for Black). This precise checking sacrifice therefore earns the “best” label.

teacher: By taking on a1 White eliminates Black’s rook and secures the only safe square for the bishop, but the material balance is now level, leaving only the positional advantage that already gave White about a pawn’s worth of evaluation. The capture leaves the position essentially unchanged in evaluation, with White still clearly better. Black’s most accurate reply would be …cxd5, after which the sequence cxd5 Nxd5 Nxd5 Rxd5 continues, but White remains the better side.
student: By taking on a1 White eliminates Black’s active rook and preserves the valuable bishop pair, leaving material completely equal. The capture also leaves the white bishop on a1 with only one safe square, so it does not create any new weaknesses. Black can reply cxd5, winning the pawn on d5, but after White recaptures Nxd5 the ensuing exchange forces a sequence that keeps White’s modest edge – roughly a pawn’s worth – as reflected by the unchanged evaluation. This precise simplification makes Bxa1 an excellent continuation.

teacher: Black’s 19…Nh4 is a quiet redeployment that leaves the material balance untouched and the evaluation still about a pawn in White’s favour. The engine rates it as a good move, but it is marginally inferior to the immediate 19…cxd5, which would have captured White’s pawn on d5 and given Black a clearer chance to level the game. In the line the engine proposes, White could reply 20.dxc6, after which Black would continue …bxc6 and …Nd7, but the knight‑move itself does not worsen Black’s position, keeping the score essentially unchanged.
student: Black’s …Nh4 simply shuffles the knight to an active square while leaving White’s clear edge virtually untouched – the engine still judges White about a pawn ahead and the move even nudges the score in Black’s favour by just six‑hundredths of a pawn. The position remains characterised by White’s bishop pair and the fact that White’s bishop on a1 has only one safe retreat. Although the engine preferred the more aggressive …cxd5, which would have captured the pawn on d5, the chosen move does not worsen Black’s standing and keeps material perfectly balanced.

teacher: White removes Black’s pawn on c6 with dxc6, starting an exchange that will be restored by the expected …bxc6; after dxc6 White is temporarily up a pawn, but the recapture will restore material balance. The capture, however, opens the d‑file, giving White’s rook on d4 a clear semi‑open lane to operate on—a crucial asset in a position where White already enjoys the bishop pair. Although the b‑file becomes semi‑open for Black, the immediate increase in activity for the d‑file more than compensates, and the evaluation stays at a comfortable +1.6‑pawn edge. Hence the move rightly earns the “!!” as the best choice.
student: By playing dxc6 White eliminates Black’s pawn on c6 and forces the natural reply bxc6, after which the b‑file becomes semi‑open for Black while the d‑file opens for White. The capture also leaves White with the bishop pair and a rook that already enjoys the semi‑open d‑file, preserving the pressure despite the a1‑bishop having no safe squares. The engine rates it as the best continuation, keeping White’s advantage at roughly +1.6 pawns.

teacher: By taking on c6 Black opens the b‑file, giving the rook a potential line of attack while also depriving White’s knight on c3 of the b5 and d5 squares. The capture removes the pawn that had kept the c‑file semi‑open for Black, yet the material balance stays level and the evaluation remains roughly a pawn in White’s favour. Black’s best follow‑up would be to meet White’s likely …b5 pawn break with …Rb8, keeping the newly opened b‑file active.
student: By playing …bxc6 Black eliminates White’s pawn on c6, turning the b‑file into a semi‑open line that can be used later while the c‑file ceases to be a useful avenue for Black. The capture also deprives White’s knight on c3 of the b5 and d5 squares it had been eyeing, curbing its activity. Although material remains equal, the engine still judges White to be about a pawn ahead, so the move does not improve Black’s standing but is nevertheless the best continuation available. White could try the pawn break b5, striking at the newly placed pawn on c6, yet Black’s position stays solid despite the slight disadvantage.

teacher: White pushes b5, a pawn break that directly attacks Black’s pawn on c6 and tries to pry open the queenside for his bishop pair. The engine notes a very small dip of roughly a tenth of a pawn, but White still enjoys a comfortable plus‑one‑and‑a‑half pawn edge. The rook on d4 already benefits from the semi‑open d‑file.
student: White’s 22 b5 is a timely pawn break that strikes directly at Black’s pawn on c6, trying to open lines while preserving the valuable bishop pair and the semi‑open d‑file for his rook. Although the engine notes a slight dip in the evaluation (about a tenth of a pawn), White remains clearly better – roughly +1½ pawns – and the move is rightly judged as good. The continuation suggested by the engine would see Black reply …Rb8, after which White can continue with Rd1, keeping the pressure alive.

teacher: By sliding the rook to b8 Black immediately occupies the semi‑open b‑file, a line that is especially useful now that White’s bishop on a1 has no safe squares and the b‑pawn is advanced to b5. The move leaves the evaluation essentially unchanged, keeping White’s modest lead of about a pawn, and the engine marks it as the best continuation. White’s most natural reply would be Qa3, pinning the d6‑pawn to the queen on e7, after which Black can answer with …c5, preserving the pressure on the b‑file.
student: By sliding the rook from a9 to b8 Black finally makes use of the semi‑open b‑file, keeping material equal and leaving the engine’s assessment virtually unchanged – White remains about a pawn ahead. The move also respects the fact that White’s bishop on a1 has no safe squares, so the rook does not create any new weaknesses. If White now tries Qa3, pinning the d6‑pawn to the queen on e7, Black can answer with …c5 as shown in the principal variation, preserving the balance. This subtle redeployment therefore earns the “best” label.

teacher: Black’s 23…Bd7 was a mis‑step; although it removes the immediate threat to the pawn on c6, it does not prevent White from capturing it with bxc6, winning a pawn. The engine’s preferred continuation, Nd7, would have kept the pawn defended and avoided the loss, a difference of roughly a pawn in the evaluation. After the capture White’s bishop pair and the semi‑open b‑file for Black’s rook give White a clear edge, as reflected by the jump from a modest +1 pawn to a comfortable +2 pawns.
student: By playing …Bd7 Black merely sidesteps the immediate danger to the pawn on c6, but it does nothing to stop White’s natural capture bxc6. After that exchange Black would recapture with the bishop and then lose material, as the engine line shows White can continue Rxd6 followed by Ra8. The mistake therefore costs roughly a pawn in evaluation, turning an already slight White edge into a clear advantage. The engine’s preferred move was …Nd7, which would have kept the balance without allowing the pawn grab.

teacher: White captures the pawn on c6, opening the b‑file but allowing Black to recapture with the bishop; this exchange restores material equality, gives Black a semi‑open c‑file and leaves White with an isolated pawn on c4. Although it was the only reasonable continuation, the move still reduced White’s edge from a clear two‑pawn advantage to about a pawn, a moderate inaccuracy worth roughly half a pawn. In the engine’s line Black would answer Bxc6, after which White can continue with Rxd6, followed by Black’s …Rc8 and White’s …Qd1.
student: By playing bxc6 White eliminates Black’s pawn on c6 and opens the b‑file, but the capture also leaves an isolated pawn on c4 and gives Black a semi‑open c‑file, which together cost White roughly two‑thirds of a pawn in evaluation. The engine still rates the move as the best available, yet it is marked as an inaccuracy because the resulting structure weakens White’s position. After the forced …Bxc6 the game would continue Rxd6, Rc8, Qd1, etc., keeping White’s advantage at about a pawn’s worth.

teacher: By taking on d6 White not only wins a pawn but also opens the d‑file, giving the rook on d6 immediate activity and turning the pawn on c4 into a passed pawn. The capture therefore consolidates White’s material edge while improving piece placement, leaving the position still clearly better for White (about a pawn’s worth). Black’s most natural reply would be …Rc8, which would simply remove the lingering threat to the bishop on c6 without altering the overall assessment.
student: By taking on d6 White eliminates Black’s last central pawn and opens the d‑file, while also creating a passed pawn on c4 that can become a long‑term asset. The capture leaves White still a clear pawn ahead and keeps the evaluation essentially unchanged at roughly +1½ pawns. Black could try …Rc8 to remove the pressure on the bishop on c6, but even after that continuation White remains comfortably better.

teacher: White’s bishop captures the knight on f6, delivering a fork that simultaneously attacks the knight on h4, the queen on e7 and the pawn on g7. Black can only answer with Qxf6, which eliminates the immediate threats but also forces the exchange that costs White the bishop pair; after the recapture the queen no longer attacks the h4‑knight or the g7‑pawn. Even though material balance is restored, White remains up four points and retains active rooks on the open d‑ and b‑files, so the evaluation stays at a strong plus and the move is rightly judged excellent.
student: By playing Bxf6 White eliminates Black’s active knight on f6 while simultaneously creating a fork on the knight on h4, the queen on e7 and the pawn on g7. The capture forces an immediate queen recapture, after which White retains the bishop pair but concedes the bishop that was just taken, leaving the position essentially unchanged – the engine still evaluates it as about two pawns ahead. In the principal line Black would reply Qxf6, removing the threats to the g‑pawn, the h‑knight and the newly placed bishop, yet White remains clearly better.

teacher: Black eliminates White’s dangerous bishop on f6, which was threatening the pawn on g7, the knight on h4 and the queen itself, by playing Qxf6. The capture removes that threat and leaves White down a bishop, while the rook on d6 continues to pin the e‑6 bishop to the queen on f6. The material balance and the evaluation remain essentially unchanged, with White still about a pawn ahead, so the engine rates the move as excellent and the best continuation. The position now features Black’s queen on f6, a rook on b8 controlling the open b‑file and White’s rook on d6 dominating the open d‑file.
student: By taking on f6 Black eliminates White’s active bishop and simultaneously neutralises the immediate threats to the g‑pawn, the knight on h4 and the queen itself. The capture also leaves White without the bishop pair, while Black retains control of the open b‑file with his rook on b8 and the pin created by the white rook on d6 against the e6‑bishop. Although the engine still judges White about two pawns ahead, the move keeps the balance essentially unchanged – the evaluation shifts by only a few hundredths of a pawn in Black’s favour. Consequently it is rightly marked as an excellent continuation.

teacher: Black’s 28…Qg5 tries to create an immediate danger by threatening the crushing Qxg2#, but White can meet it calmly with Qxe4, which both eliminates the mate threat and captures the pawn on e4, leaving Black a pawn down and turning a +2‑pawn advantage for White into a decisive one. The engine rates this as a mistake, noting that the move worsened Black’s position by roughly a pawn. In contrast, 28…Nf5 would have forked White’s queen on d4 and rook on d6, preserving material and keeping the balance.
student: Black’s 28…Qg5 looks tempting because it creates an immediate mating idea – White can capture on g2 with check, forcing mate if Black does not answer. In reality the engine shows that this simply hands White a larger edge, turning a +2‑pawn advantage into a decisive +3‑pawn lead for White. The stronger continuation would have been 28…Nf5, which forks White’s queen on d4 and rook on d6 and keeps the pressure alive. By playing Qg5 Black missed that tactical shot and allowed White to consolidate comfortably.

teacher: White’s queen move to f4 is a blunder because it abandons the protection of the pawn on g2. Black can answer with Qxg2#, delivering immediate checkmate and turning a position that was winning by a decisive three‑pawn margin into a forced loss. The engine’s best continuation was Rd1, which would have kept White’s material edge and avoided the mate.
student: By playing Qf4 White leaves the pawn on g2 completely undefended and walks straight into Black’s forcing line. After the natural reply Qxg2#, the queen captures the hanging pawn and delivers immediate mate, turning a winning position into an instant loss. The engine indicates that the correct defence would have been Rd1, which would have avoided the fatal fork. In short, the blunder costs White a decisive advantage and forces a forced mate in one.

teacher: Black ends the game with Qxg2#, a forced checkmate that leaves White’s king on g1 without any defence. By capturing on g2 the queen eliminates the last shield in front of the king, and the resulting isolated pawn on h2 and the weakened pawn cover cannot stop the mate. Even though White was up a pawn, the decisive queen infiltration together with the open b‑file for Black’s rook makes any continuation impossible, converting the engine’s “mate in 1” into an immediate win.
student: By playing Qxg2# Black finishes the game immediately, converting the earlier forced mate into a clean win. The capture not only eliminates White’s last pawn but also leaves White with an isolated h‑pawn and a weakened pawn shield around the king, while Black’s rook on b8 already dominates the open b‑file. Although White remains a pawn up, the position is lost because the forced mate was already available.

teacher: White opens with 1 e4, the engine’s top‑rated move, and it preserves the modest edge that existed from the start. The evaluation shifts only marginally, from +0.34 to +0.38 pawns, so White’s position remains only slightly better. In the principal variation Black would answer …c5, after which White can continue with Nf3, Black …e6 and White d4, keeping the same small advantage.
student: White opens with e4, keeping the modest edge that existed before the game and even nudging it up to roughly +0.38 of a pawn. The engine rates this as the best continuation, noting that Black’s most natural reply would be …c5, after which White can develop with Nf3 and later strike in the centre with d4. In short, the move preserves White’s slight advantage while preparing to contest the centre.

teacher: Black meets White’s central thrust with the classical 1…e5, a perfectly sound reply that leaves material equal and the evaluation essentially unchanged – White still enjoys a tiny edge of about 0.4 pawn. The engine rates the move as excellent, though it is not the top‑ranking option; 1…c5 would have given Black a marginally better standing. In the continuation the engine expects White to develop with Nf3, after which Black could answer Nf6, allowing White the tactical shot Nxe5 followed by …d6.
student: Black answered 1.e4 with …e5, a solid central thrust that leaves material equal and keeps the engine’s assessment virtually unchanged – White remains only a fraction of a pawn ahead. The engine preferred 1…c5, but …e5 still preserves Black’s position without worsening it. In the principal variation White would continue Nf3, after which Black can meet Nf6 and later play …d6, keeping the balance intact.

teacher: White’s 2 d4 tries to open the centre by striking at Black’s e5 pawn, but after the natural …exd4 the pawn structure changes: the d‑file becomes semi‑open for White while Black gains a semi‑open e‑file and doubled pawns on d‑file. This concession costs White about a third of a pawn, dropping the evaluation from a slight edge to near equality. The engine judged Nf3 as the stronger continuation, preserving the modest advantage instead of allowing the exchange. In the main line Black would capture on d4, after which White can develop with Nf3 and Black’s best try is …Bb4+, after which White can meet it with Nbd2.
student: White launches the central pawn break 2.d4, directly challenging Black’s e‑pawn and hoping to open the d‑file after the natural …exd4. After the capture the d‑file becomes semi‑open for White while Black ends up with doubled pawns on that file, but the resulting structure leaves the balance essentially even – the engine’s evaluation slips from +0.40 to about +0.10, meaning White’s slight edge evaporates by roughly a third of a pawn. The engine judged Nf3 to be superior, as it would have kept more pressure without conceding the extra pawn‑value. In practice, however, the move does not lose material and still creates concrete threats.

teacher: White steps the queen back to e3, eliminating the immediate threat to the queen. While the material balance remains unchanged, the engine’s numbers show the position slipping by roughly a tenth of a pawn against White. The move is judged “good” and is indeed the engine’s top choice; Black can now continue development with …Nf6, after which White may answer with Nc3.
student: White’s retreat Qe3 simply eliminates the immediate danger to the queen, allowing it to remain safe while preserving material equality. The engine rates the move as good and confirms that it was indeed the best continuation, though it nudges Black’s edge from about a fifth of a pawn to a little more – a modest deterioration for White. In the principal line Black would continue with …Nf6, after which White can develop further with Nc3, Bb4 and a3.

teacher: White’s 5.Bd2 simply develops the c1‑bishop to d2, but it is not the most accurate continuation. The engine rates the move as “good” yet notes that it costs White roughly a quarter of a pawn, leaving Black slightly better (about –0.36) compared with the roughly equal position before. A more precise choice would have been 5.Nc3, which the engine flags as the best move and would have kept the evaluation near equality.
student: White develops the bishop to d2, but the engine judges that this costs him about a fifth of a pawn compared with the more accurate  Nc3. After 5.Bd2 Black can reply …Be7, after which White would have been able to continue with Nc3 and keep the balance. The evaluation therefore slides from roughly equal to a small edge for Black. In short, the move is solid but not optimal, leaving Black with a slight advantage.

teacher: By playing …Bb4 Black pins the white bishop on d2 to the king on e1, so the bishop cannot move without exposing the king. The engine, however, shows that this concession costs Black about three‑tenths of a pawn, turning a slight advantage into an almost equal position; the stronger continuation would have been …Be7. White can meet the pin with a3, after which Black would capture on d2 with check and White recaptures, leading to a balanced position after …O‑O. Thus the move is decent but not optimal.
student: By playing …Bb4 Black creates a pin on White’s bishop on d2 against the king on e1, so that the bishop cannot legally move. The engine still rates the position as roughly equal after the move, but it notes that the evaluation slipped by about a third of a pawn compared with the optimal continuation. The engine preferred 5…Be7, which would have kept Black’s slight edge instead of conceding the modest advantage. In practice the pin does not change the material balance and leaves the game balanced.

teacher: White develops the queen’s knight to c3, blocking the bishop on b4 and shielding the king from the diagonal. However, the knight lands on a square attacked by that bishop, so Black can keep the pressure and White’s evaluation slips by roughly half a pawn. The engine rates a3 as the better try, which would have chased the bishop away and kept the balance. From the resulting position Black can simply castle (O‑O) and retain the slight edge.
student: White develops the knight to c3, but the engine judges that this costs him about half a pawn compared with the more accurate  a3. After 6.Nc3 Black can simply castle, after which White would have to castle again and then play Re8, allowing Black to keep the initiative. The evaluation therefore slides from an almost equal balance to a slight edge for Black. In short, the move is good but not optimal, worsening White’s standing by roughly half a pawn.

teacher: By playing Re8 Black brings the rook onto the semi‑open e‑file, while White’s rook on the d‑file uses the semi‑open d‑file, preserving the modest edge that existed before the move. The engine rates the move as the best, with the evaluation staying at roughly –0.5 pawn in Black’s favour. In the suggested continuation White would try Qf4, after which Black can meet it with Ne5, followed by f3 and c6.
student: By placing the rook on e8 Black immediately occupies the semi‑open e‑file, giving the piece active play against White’s rook that already sits on the d‑file. The engine rates this as the best continuation, and the evaluation stays at roughly –½ pawn in Black’s favour, confirming that the move preserves the slight edge without creating any new weaknesses. In the principal variation White would continue with Qf4, after which Black can answer Ne5, keeping the balance intact.

teacher: White develops the bishop to c4, where it pins the f‑pawn to the black king on g8. This pin curtails Black’s pawn moves and nudges the evaluation in White’s favour by roughly a tenth of a pawn, shrinking Black’s edge from –0.57 to –0.43. The engine, however, prefers the more incisive  Qf4, which would keep even tighter pressure on the f7 pawn. Nonetheless, Bc4 is a solid, improving move in a position where Black’s rook enjoys the semi‑open e‑file and White’s rook the semi‑open d‑file.
student: By playing Bc4 White places the bishop on a square that immediately pins the f‑pawn to the black king on g8, so the pawn cannot legally move and thus limits Black’s coordination. The engine rates the move as a modest improvement for White – it nudges the evaluation from a slight Black edge of about half a pawn to roughly four‑tenths of a pawn in Black’s favour. Although the suggested continuation would be …Na5 followed by Be2, Qf4 was judged the optimal reply, but Bc4 still secures a small gain despite Black’s active pieces.

teacher: Black’s …d6 simply advances the queenside pawn majority, giving him four pawns against White’s three on that wing. The move does not alter the material balance, but it reduces Black’s advantage – the evaluation shifts from a 0.43‑pawn advantage for Black to only 0.25‑pawn, so Black’s position is slightly worsened. The engine preferred …Na5, which would have preserved a larger advantage. Nevertheless, the pawn push is a sound “good” move that keeps the position solid.
student: By playing …d6 Black pushes his queenside pawn majority forward, gaining space and preparing to expand on that flank. The advance does not change the fact that White’s bishop on c4 still pins the f‑pawn to the black king, so Black’s pieces remain cramped while White’s rook enjoys the semi‑open d‑file. The engine rates the move as good but notes it costs Black about a fifth of a pawn compared with the optimal Na5, which would have kept more pressure. In short, the move solidifies Black’s pawn structure but allows White to retain some activity along the d‑file.

teacher: By playing …Be6 Black eliminates White’s bishop pressure that was pinning the f7‑pawn to the king, thus removing the immediate threat to that pawn. If White captures, the natural reply Bxe6 is met by Rxe6, keeping material equal while the rooks continue to contest the semi‑open e‑ and d‑files. Although Black gives up the bishop pair, the engine rates the move as excellent because the evaluation changes by only a few hundredths of a pawn, preserving Black’s slight edge.
student: By playing …Be6 Black eliminates the immediate danger to the f‑pawn, allowing White’s bishop to capture and pin that pawn to the king while Black surrenders the bishop pair. The exchange leaves material equal and the engine still rates the position as a slight Black edge – roughly half a pawn – so the move preserves Black’s modest advantage without worsening the score. With both sides’ rooks already active on their respective semi‑open files, the continuation would likely see White recapturing with Bxe6, after which Black can answer Rxe6 and keep the pressure. This precise defensive resource therefore earns the “excellent” label.

teacher: Black’s capture on e6 eliminates White’s bishop, removes the immediate threat to the f7 pawn and places the rook on the semi‑open e‑file, keeping Black’s slight edge (the engine still rates Black a few tenths of a pawn better). The exchange also forces White to give up the bishop pair, leaving material equal and the position essentially unchanged in value. White can answer with Ng5, forking the rook on e6 and the pawn on f7, after which Black would typically meet the fork with Re8 according to the principal variation. This line shows why Rxe6 was the only move that preserves Black’s modest advantage.
student: By playing Rxe6 Black eliminates White’s active bishop on e6, thereby removing the immediate threat to the pawn on f7 and keeping material equal. The capture also puts the black rook on the semi‑open e‑file, where it can exert pressure while Black’s own bishops remain cramped – the bishop on b4 has only two safe squares and White’s bishop on d2 just one. Although White could try Ng5, forking the rook on e6 and the pawn on f7, Black’s position stays slightly better (about three‑tenths of a pawn) and the engine rates the move as excellent.

teacher: White’s  h4  simply advances the kingside pawn majority, gaining a little more space on that flank. student: White pushes h4 to advance his four‑pawn majority on the kingside, a natural way to increase pressure in an otherwise balanced position. The engine still judges the position as slightly better for Black – about six‑tenths of a pawn worse for White – and notes that the move keeps the evaluation essentially unchanged, costing roughly a tenth of a pawn compared with the optimal continuation. Nevertheless, it is a solid “good” move because it does not worsen White’s standing further.

teacher: Black’s subtle pawn push h6 is a move that preserves the slight edge, keeping the evaluation at roughly a pawn in Black’s favour. By leaving the bishop on b4 with only two safe squares and the rook on the semi‑open e‑file fully active, the move does not alter material and therefore is judged the best continuation. student: By playing …h6 Black reinforces the centre and keeps the pressure along the semi‑open e‑file that his rook already dominates. The move also respects the cramped situation of both bishops – White’s bishop on d2 has only one safe square while Black’s own bishop on b4 is limited to just two safe squares. With material still equal and the engine’s assessment barely shifting from a slight edge to a clear advantage of roughly a pawn, …h6 is rightly judged as the best continuation.

student: White’s queen slides to g3, a quiet but precise maneuver that leaves material even and keeps the engine’s assessment virtually unchanged – Black remains only a fraction of a pawn ahead. By occupying the g‑file, White preserves the balance of the position while Black’s bishop on a5 still has its single safe retreat and both sides continue to use their respective semi‑open files (the d‑file for White and the e‑file for Black). The engine rates Qg3 as the best continuation, with the most likely follow‑up being …Nd4 followed by White’s natural Qd3 in the principal variation.

teacher: White chose 15 f3, pushing the kingside pawn majority forward and taking the e4‑ and g4‑squares away from Black’s knight on f6, but the move allows Black the freeing …b5, after which the b‑pawn is left en prise and Black emerges with roughly a pawn’s worth of advantage. The engine judged Nd5 to be the superior continuation, preserving White’s pressure, whereas 15 f3 cost White about 0.6 of a pawn. Although the pawn push does not lose material outright, Black’s rook on e8 already enjoys the semi‑open e‑file and the bishop on a5 remains cramped, giving Black a clear edge. student: White’s 15 f3 tries to advance his kingside pawn majority and deprive Black’s knight on f6 of the e4‑ and g4‑squares it had been eyeing. In practice the move lets Black reply …b5, after which the pawn on b5 becomes vulnerable – a line that the engine notes would give Black a clear edge of about a pawn. The evaluation therefore slides from roughly equal to a clear advantage for Black, a moderate worsening of White’s position by roughly two‑thirds of a pawn. The engine preferred 15 Nd5, which would have kept the balance instead of allowing this inaccuracy.

teacher: By playing Nh3 White both removes the immediate danger to the knight and lifts the queen on g3 and the bishop on d2 into a discovered attack on Black’s g7 and h6 pawns. With Black’s bishop on a5 confined to a single safe square and each side’s rook already occupying a semi‑open file, the new pressure forces Black to devote resources to defending his kingside pawns and narrows his edge. The evaluation improves from a slight Black advantage of about half a pawn to only a third of a pawn, a gain of roughly a quarter pawn for White. This modest but concrete increase explains why the engine rates Nh3 as the best move.
student: By retreating the knight to h3 White not only eliminates the immediate danger to that piece but also uncovers two new lines of pressure: the queen on g3 now eyes the pawn on g7 and the bishop on d2 attacks the pawn on h6. This creates concrete threats while leaving Black’s bishop on a5 with essentially only one safe retreat square, so the engine rates the move as the best choice, improving White’s standing by about a quarter‑pawn. The continuation suggested by the engine would be …Nc4, after which White can meet it with Nb1 and later exchange on d2, keeping the initiative alive despite Black’s slight edge.

teacher: Black’s capture on d5 wins a knight, but it is a tactical blunder: White can simply play Bxa5, which both removes Black’s bishop and uncovers a discovered attack by the rook on d1 against the knight that just moved to d5. The engine’s preferred move, Bxd2+, would have given check and kept the initiative, whereas the line after Nxd5 leaves Black down about a pawn’s worth despite being up material. As a result the evaluation swings from roughly equal to a clear White advantage, a loss of roughly a pawn for Black.
student: By playing …Nxd5 Black simply wins a piece but immediately hands White the initiative with Bxa5, which both recaptures the bishop and uncovers a discovered attack by the white rook on the newly‑placed knight. The engine shows that this exchange costs Black roughly a pawn’s worth of evaluation, turning an essentially equal position into one where White is clearly better. The stronger continuation would have been Bxd2+, a checking capture that also removes the bishop on d2 while keeping the balance. Consequently, the move is a clear mistake.

teacher: By playing Bxa5 White removes Black’s bishop and, more importantly, uncovers a discovered attack from the rook on d1 against the knight on d5. The capture therefore nudges the already clear advantage (+1.27, about a pawn) a little higher. Black’s most forcing reply would be Ne3, forking the rook on d1 and the pawn on c2, yet White still remains clearly better.
student: By taking on a5 White not only wins a piece but also uncovers a discovered attack by the rook on d1 against Black’s knight on d5, exploiting the semi‑open d‑file that White already controls. The capture therefore improves White’s standing, nudging the evaluation up by roughly a sixth of a pawn. Black can try …Ne3, forking the rook on d1 and the pawn on c2, yet even after that reply White remains clearly better. This precise exchange makes Bxa5 the clear best continuation.

teacher: Black’s 21…b5 pushes the queenside pawn majority forward, a natural way to gain space on the side where he has four pawns against White’s three. By doing so he also leaves the semi‑open e‑file for the rook on e8, preserving its activity while the evaluation stays essentially unchanged – White remains a little better, roughly a pawn’s worth. The engine’s top‑choice was 21…a5, which would have kept a bit more tension on the a‑file, but the b‑pawn advance is still a very strong continuation, costing Black only a tiny swing of about six hundredths of a pawn.
student: By pushing …b5 Black expands his queenside pawn majority to four versus White’s three, gaining space and preparing to activate the rook that already enjoys the semi‑open e‑file. The advance leaves material equal and the engine still judges White to be about a pawn ahead, with the evaluation shifting by only six hundredths of a pawn in Black’s favour. Although the move is solid, the engine prefers the more aggressive …a5, which would have offered Black a slightly larger edge. In practice, however, …b5 keeps the balance intact without creating any new weaknesses.

teacher: White’s 22 f4 is the engine‑recommended move, simply pushing the pawn to expand the kingside majority to four versus Black’s three. The advance leaves the evaluation essentially unchanged at about a pawn’s worth in White’s favour, while Black’s rook on e8 continues to sit on the semi‑open e‑file. Black can meet the thrust most accurately with …Nc6, removing the pressure on the knight on c6 and leading to a line such as Qg6 – Qe6 – Ng4.
student: By playing f4 White expands his four‑pawn majority on the kingside, gaining space and preparing to push further with the remaining pawns. The advance leaves the position essentially unchanged – White remains about a pawn ahead – while Black’s rook continues to enjoy the semi‑open e‑file that it already controls. Black can meet the thrust most simply with …Nc6, removing the immediate pressure on the knight, after which White would continue with Qg6 and keep the initiative. This precise pawn push therefore preserves White’s clear advantage without creating any new weaknesses.

teacher: White’s retreat of the queen to d3 is a clear mistake; it allows Black’s rook on e8 to exploit the semi‑open e‑file, and the evaluation drops from a comfortable +2 pawns to only about +1 pawn – a loss of roughly a pawn’s worth of advantage. The engine’s preferred move was Rh3, which would have kept White’s edge much larger. After Qd3 Black can continue with Qa6, and the resulting line shows how the pressure on the e‑file now favors Black.
student: White’s queen retreat to d3 does nothing to meet Black’s active rook on the semi‑open e‑file and simply hands the initiative back to Black. The engine shows that the far stronger continuation would have been Rh3, keeping the rook on the main diagonal and preserving White’s sizable advantage. By playing Qd3 White’s evaluation drops by roughly a pawn, turning a clear +2‑pawn edge into only about a pawn’s worth. In short, the move costs White about a pawn in evaluation.

teacher: Black’s a5 tries to press the queenside pawn majority and deprive White’s bishop on c3 of the b4 square, but it allows White the pawn break a4, which attacks the b5 pawn. The engine shows the move costs Black roughly half a pawn, with White’s evaluation climbing from about +0.9 to +1.4, and the stronger continuation would have been Qa6. Even though Black’s rook on e8 enjoys the semi‑open e‑file, the loss of the b5 pawn’s stability outweighs that advantage.
student: By playing …a5 Black tries to push his queenside pawn majority and deprive White’s bishop on c3 of the b4 square, but the advance does not improve his position and actually lets White increase the pressure. The engine shows that this inaccuracy costs Black roughly half a pawn, leaving White with a clear advantage of about one pawn. A more accurate continuation would have been …Qa6, keeping the queen active and preserving the balance. After …a5 White can now strike with the pawn break a4, attacking the b5 pawn.

teacher: By playing 24 g4 White advances the kingside pawn majority, gaining space and nudging the evaluation from a clear +1.4‑pawn edge to a much better +1.8‑pawn advantage—a moderate gain of roughly a third of a pawn. The move leaves Black’s rook on e8, which already enjoys the semi‑open e‑file, untouched. Although the engine rates the move as strong, it still prefers the pawn break 24 a4, which would strike directly at Black’s b5 pawn; after 24 g4 the most likely continuation is …Qa6, 25 g5, …b4, 26 gxf6.

The advance also leaves Black’s rook on e8 with a semi‑open e‑file to operate while White’s pieces remain active, so the evaluation climbs from roughly a pawn to almost two pawns in White’s favour. Although the engine prefers the more ambitious a4, which would strike directly at Black’s b5 pawn, the g4 push still improves White’s standing by about a third of a pawn.

teacher: By playing b3 White unwittingly leaves the a‑pawn hanging; Black can simply capture with Nxa3, winning the pawn on a3. This inaccuracy costs White roughly a pawn’s worth of evaluation, dropping the score from a clear +2 to only about +1. Moreover, Black’s rook on the semi‑open e‑file already exerts pressure, so weakening the queenside only compounds White’s problems.
student: White’s 25 b3 looks natural but it leaves the pawn on a3 hanging, allowing Black to reply …Nxa3 and capture that pawn outright. This concession costs White roughly a pawn’s worth of advantage, as reflected by the evaluation slipping from +2.0 to +1.0. The engine points out that the far stronger continuation would have been 25 g5, a pawn break that strikes at both the f6‑ and h6‑pawns and keeps White’s edge intact. By opting for b3 instead, White missed this more active chance and turned an already comfortable lead into a modest one.

teacher: Black’s …b4 creates a direct fork on White’s a3‑pawn and the bishop on c3, striking at the pawn on a3 and fixing White’s b‑pawn on a light square while pushing the queenside pawn majority forward. Nonetheless, …b4 is still a good move, keeping pressure on the queenside despite the slight drawback.
student: By pushing …b4 Black creates a fork on White’s a‑pawn and the bishop on c3 while also fixing White’s b‑pawn on a light square and advancing his queenside pawn majority. The engine rates the move as good but notes that it costs Black roughly a tenth of a pawn, leaving White still clearly better by about a pawn’s worth. A more accurate continuation would have been Nxa3, which both eliminates the threat to the knight on a3 and wins the pawn on a3 outright. After White’s forced bxc4 the b‑file becomes semi‑open for White and Black’s queenside pawn majority (four pawns against three) is reinforced, while White is left with isolated pawns on a3, c2 and c4. The exchange restores material balance, yet the resulting pawn structure gives White a modest initiative, which the engine reflects by still rating White about a pawn ahead. Black’s rook on e8 now enjoys the semi‑open e‑file, supporting the position.
student: By taking on c4 Black eliminates White’s queen and at the same time removes the immediate threats to the pawn on c7 and the knight on f7. After the forced recapture bxc4 the b‑file becomes semi‑open for White while Black retains a four‑pawn versus three‑pawn queenside majority, leaving White with isolated pawns on c2, a3 and c4. The engine rates the capture as good – it is the best continuation despite the modest swing in evaluation that leaves White still a little better.

teacher: White’s 32.Rg3 brings the rook onto the semi‑open g‑file, giving it activity that matches Black’s own rook on the e‑file. This concession costs White roughly a tenth of a pawn, turning a slight +0.09 edge into a roughly equal –0.05 evaluation. student: White’s 32.Rg3 puts his rook on the semi‑open g‑file, but it also leaves the pawn on c4 undefended. Black can simply capture on h5 with …Rxh5, after which White would have to retreat the rook to h3 before Black’s Nd8 and White could answer Nf2, so the engine judges the move as costing about a tenth of a pawn compared with the optimal continuation. teacher: By capturing the pawn on h4 Black not only recovers a pawn but also opens the h‑file, allowing the rook on h4 to dominate that newly opened line while the other rook already exerts pressure on the semi‑open e‑file. In this rook‑and‑minor‑piece ending the open h‑file gives Black a small but concrete edge, keeping the evaluation around a third of a pawn in Black’s favour. The engine confirms that Rxh4 is the best move, preserving Black’s slight advantage.
student: By capturing on h4 Black eliminates White’s last pawn and opens the h‑file, giving his rook full control of that line while the other rook continues to operate along the semi‑open e‑file. The exchange leaves material equal in this rook‑and‑minor‑piece ending, but it preserves Black’s slight edge – the engine still rates the position as about four‑tenths of a pawn better for Black. student: White’s 36.Rb1 is a clear mistake because it does nothing to stop Black’s active rooks – the engine shows that after the natural …Rh2+ the pawn on g7 becomes en prise and the evaluation swings from a slight Black edge to a clear one‑pawn advantage. student: By moving the king to b2 White uncovers the rook on b1’s line against Black’s rook on h1, creating an immediate tactical threat that can be met with …Rb8+. After the forced Ka2, Black would capture on b1 with his rook, but White can recapture with the knight, preserving material equality in this rook‑and‑minor‑piece ending. The move therefore does not win material, which is why the engine’s evaluation slips slightly from about a pawn’s worth to a little less, yet it is still the best continuation in this rook‑and‑minor‑piece ending. Keeping the open h‑file for his remaining rook while neutralising White’s semi‑open g‑file rook leaves Black with a clear, though modest, advantage.
student: By playing Rbxb1 Black eliminates White’s active rook on b1, removing the immediate danger to his own rook on h1 in this rook‑and‑minor‑piece ending. The capture initiates an exchange that will be answered by Nxb1, restoring material balance but leaving Black with a clear advantage – roughly a pawn ahead. Although the engine notes a slight dip of about a sixth of a pawn, the move remains the best choice because it neutralises White’s pressure without conceding any material.

teacher: By taking on b1 White eliminates Black’s rook on b1 and restores material balance in this rook‑and‑minor‑piece ending. Black can reply with …Rf1, forking the newly placed knight on b1 and the pawn on f4, yet White’s rook on g3 still enjoys the semi‑open g‑file, giving enough counterplay to hold the position. student: By taking on b1 White eliminates Black’s active rook, leaving material equal in this rook‑and‑minor‑piece ending. The capture also leaves White’s rook on g3 free to exploit the semi‑open g‑file while Black’s rook continues to dominate the open h‑file. Although the engine still judges Black to be about a pawn ahead, the move is excellent because it neutralises Black’s most dangerous piece without worsening White’s position. Black could reply with …Rf1, forking the knight on b1 and the pawn on f4, but even that does not improve Black’s standing.

teacher: White eliminates Black’s pawn on g5, removing the immediate danger to that pawn and forcing the exchange that will open the f‑ and g‑files. student: By playing fxg5 White eliminates Black’s immediate pressure on the g‑file and forces the natural reply Nxg5, after which the f‑file becomes semi‑open for White while the g‑file opens. student: White’s king steps to b3, keeping it active in this rook‑and‑minor‑piece ending where both sides already enjoy their own semi‑open files. student: White launches the pawn break c5, aiming to strike at Black’s d‑pawn and later create a passed e‑pawn while opening the d‑file. student: By playing …dxc5 Black opens the d‑file and pushes his queenside pawn majority forward, even though it creates isolated and doubled pawns on the c‑file.
