student: By playing Ne5 Black eliminates the immediate danger to the pawn on c6, while also leaving the g‑pawn hanging. The engine rates the move as excellent and notes that it keeps Black’s slight edge – the evaluation shifts by only about five hundredths of a pawn. In this rook‑and‑minor‑piece ending both sides already have active pieces on their respective semi‑open files, so the knight retreat does not create new weaknesses but simply preserves Black’s modest advantage.

teacher: White’s 47.Kb6 simply sidesteps with the king while the rooks continue to battle on their respective semi‑open files, allowing Black to play …g4. That pawn‑push removes the threat to Black’s pawn on g4 and lets Black consolidate, pushing the evaluation to about a pawn in Black’s favour. The engine judged 47.Rg2 as the correct continuation, keeping the rook active on the g‑file and preserving equality; by playing Kb6 White worsened the position by roughly 0.6 of a pawn.
student: White’s king step to b6 does little in this rook‑and‑minor‑piece ending and simply hands Black the chance to increase his advantage. By moving away from the centre, White allows …g4, which eliminates the pressure on the g‑pawn and leaves Black with a clear edge – the evaluation slides from a slight Black lead to roughly a pawn’s worth. The engine indicates that the more accurate continuation would have been Rg2, keeping the rook active on the semi‑open g‑file and preserving White’s chances. Consequently, Kb6 is an inaccuracy that costs White about two‑thirds of a pawn.

teacher: By pushing …g4 Black creates an advanced passed pawn on the g‑file, removing the immediate threat to that pawn. In this rook‑and‑minor‑piece ending the new pawn is isolated, and White’s rook on g3 already controls the semi‑open g‑file, so the passer does not yield a large increase in Black’s advantage. The continuation would likely see White replying Rg2, after which Black can keep up the pressure with Re3 and later capture on a3.
student: By pushing …g4 Black creates a passed pawn deep in White’s camp, eliminating the immediate danger that had been hanging over it. The advance does leave the pawn isolated, but in this rook‑and‑minor‑piece ending it gives Black a clear long‑term asset while White’s rook remains confined to the semi‑open g‑file. The engine rates the move as good and the best available, though the evaluation slips by roughly a tenth of a pawn because Black’s advantage shrinks marginally. In the principal line White would try Rg2, after which Black can continue with Re3 and later capture on a3 if needed.

teacher: By moving the king to g5 Black immediately reinforces the advanced passed pawn on g4 and curtails White’s rook, which is the only piece that can exploit the semi‑open g‑file. This king activation nudges the evaluation from a modest –1.38 to a clearer –1.64, a gain of about a quarter pawn for Black, and therefore the engine flags Kg5 as the best move (!!). In the principal variation White would try Rg2, Black replies Kf4, White checks with Rf2+ and Black meets it with Ke3, illustrating how the king’s presence will dominate the ensuing play.
student: By moving to g5 Black brings his king into the centre of this rook‑and‑minor‑piece ending, directly attacking White’s rook that sits on the semi‑open g‑file. The engine rates the move as the best, improving Black’s evaluation by roughly a quarter of a pawn even though White remains a pawn ahead. In the principal variation White would try Rg2, after which Black can continue with Kf4, keeping the pressure on the white rook.

teacher: Black’s king steps to f4, bringing the monarch closer to the action in this rook‑and‑minor‑piece ending and staying near the advanced g‑pawn, which is a key asset for Black. Although the engine notes a small drop of roughly a third of a pawn, the position is still “much better” for Black and no alternative improves the score. White’s most forcing continuation would be the checking rook lift Rf2+, which Black can meet without endangering the passed pawn.
student: By moving to f4 Black brings his king into the centre of this rook‑and‑minor‑piece ending while preserving the advanced passed pawn on g4. The engine still judges the position as clearly better for Black – about a pawn ahead even though White remains a pawn up – and notes that the move costs him roughly a third of a pawn compared with the previous evaluation. White’s most forcing reply would be Rf2+, after which Black can answer Ke3 and continue with …Rf5 and …Nf3, keeping the pressure on the semi‑open g‑file.

teacher: White checks with Rf2+, using the open f‑file to drive the black king away. After the forced Ke3, White can keep the rook active on the f‑file with Rf5, preserving the one‑pawn material edge in this rook‑and‑minor‑piece ending where Black’s passed g‑pawn looms. The move does not improve the engine’s assessment – Black is still much better, well over a pawn – but it is the best continuation, keeping White’s only advantage intact.
student: White’s rook slides to f2 delivering a checking blow, keeping the rook active on the open f‑file in this rook‑and‑minor‑piece ending where Black already enjoys an advanced passed pawn on g4. The engine rates the move as the best possible continuation, leaving the evaluation virtually unchanged at roughly –1½ pawn for White while preserving his one‑pawn material edge. In the principal line Black would reply Ke3, after which White can continue with Rf5, followed by Nf3 and Rf8, maintaining the pressure despite Black’s clear advantage.

teacher: White places the rook on g2 to press the semi‑open g‑file and attack Black’s advanced pawn on g4, but Black can simply meet the move with …Ne5, which shields the pawn and eliminates the only active threat White created. This reply leaves Black clearly better – the evaluation jumps from a modest Black advantage to a “well over a pawn” edge, costing White roughly 0.8 pawn of evaluation. The engine’s preferred move, Re2, would have kept the pressure without allowing the defensive knight hop. Hence 51.Rg2 is an inaccuracy that significantly worsens White’s position.
student: White’s 51.Rg2 tries to press the semi‑open g‑file in this rook‑and‑minor‑piece ending, but it does nothing to stop Black’s dangerous passed pawn on g4. After the natural reply …Ne5, the pawn becomes safe and Black can continue with …Rxe2, winning material and pushing the evaluation from a modest disadvantage to a clear one‑pawn deficit. The engine shows that the correct continuation was 51.Re2, which would have kept the balance instead of allowing the loss of roughly eight‑tenths of a pawn. Consequently, Rg2 is an inaccuracy that costs White about a pawn of standing.
violations: calls the position decisive/winning at -1.75

teacher: By pushing 53 a4 White does obtain a queenside passed pawn, yet the pawn becomes isolated and the move does nothing to stop Black’s active rook on the semi‑open e‑file or the dangerous g‑pawn. The engine’s evaluation drops from a slight Black edge to a clear one‑pawn advantage, because Black can reply …c5+ with check, after which the newly created c5 pawn will be left en prise. The computer’s preferred continuation was the checking move Rf2+, which would have kept the initiative. In short, the pawn advance worsened White’s position by roughly a pawn’s worth.
student: By pushing a4 White creates a passed pawn but leaves it isolated on a4, allowing Black to continue with …c5+ – a checking move that also attacks the newly created pawn. The engine shows this costs roughly a pawn’s worth of evaluation, turning a slight Black edge into a clear one despite White still being up a pawn in material. In contrast, the best continuation would have been Rf2+, delivering a direct check and keeping the balance much tighter. Consequently, a4 is a mistake that hands Black a comfortable advantage.

teacher: Black responds with the checking pawn thrust 53…c5+, forcing the king to retreat. After the forced Kb3 the white pawn on e4 is left en prise, giving Black a concrete target that more than offsets the newly created isolated, en‑prise pawn on c5. The tactical gain pushes the evaluation from a modest pawn advantage for Black to a clearer edge for Black – roughly a quarter‑pawn swing in Black’s favour – justifying the move’s “best” rating.
student: Black’s …c5+ is a forcing check that forces White to move his king away in this rook‑and‑minor‑piece ending. The pawn lands on c5 where it is left en prise, but the engine shows the move nudges the evaluation from roughly –1½ to –1¾ pawns, improving Black’s standing by about a quarter of a pawn. After the natural reply Kb3, White would be forced to defend the e4 pawn, leaving Black’s dangerous passed g‑pawn untouched. This precise checking idea therefore secures the most favorable continuation despite being down a pawn overall.

teacher: White’s king steps to b3, the only move that averts an immediate collapse, but it still leaves the e‑pawn vulnerable and the knight on c3 pinned by Black’s rook on e3. After this move Black can reply Kf3, forking White’s rook on g2 and the pawn on e4, which pushes the evaluation down to about a two‑pawn disadvantage. Nevertheless the engine rates Kb3 as the best continuation, meaning every other try would have been still worse for White.
student: White’s king steps to b3, but it immediately leaves the pawn on e4 undefended – Black can reply …Kf3, forking the rook on g2 and the pawn that just moved there. The engine rates this as the best continuation despite the modest worsening of White’s standing (about a third of a pawn worse than before), because any other try would allow Black to increase his advantage further. In this rook‑and‑minor‑piece ending Black still enjoys an advanced passed pawn on g4 while his rook on e3 pins the white knight on c3, so the king move does not change the overall balance.

teacher: By pushing …g3 Black creates a passed pawn on the g‑file, but the pawn is isolated and does not improve the already cramped rook‑and‑minor‑piece ending. The move therefore costs Black about a pawn of evaluation, dropping the advantage from a clear lead to only roughly a pawn’s worth and allowing White to remain a pawn up. Engine analysis shows that the far stronger try would have been Kf3, which forks White’s rook on g2 and the e4 pawn, preserving the larger edge.
student: By pushing …g3 Black creates a passed pawn but does so at the cost of an isolated pawn on g3, which immediately weakens his structure in this rook‑and‑minor‑piece ending. The engine shows that the far stronger continuation would have been Kf3, forking White’s rook on g2 and the pawn on e4 while keeping the king active. After …g3 the evaluation drops by roughly a pawn, leaving White a full pawn ahead despite Black still being clearly better. Consequently the move is judged an inaccuracy.

teacher: White pushes a5, creating an advanced passed pawn but leaving it isolated on the a‑file. This allows Black’s king to step to f3, where it can fork the rook on g2 and the pawn on e4, and after the fork the g3 pawn becomes vulnerable. The engine rates the move an inaccuracy, costing White roughly two‑thirds of a pawn and increasing Black’s edge from about a pawn to well over a pawn. A better continuation would have been Rg1, keeping the rook active and avoiding the fork.
student: By pushing a5 White creates a passed pawn but does so at the cost of leaving it isolated on a5, while Black’s own passed pawn sits on g3. The advance also leaves White’s king exposed to a fork after …Kf3, which attacks both the rook on g2 and the e‑pawn, and the engine shows that this inaccuracy pushes the evaluation down by roughly two‑thirds of a pawn. In contrast, the stronger continuation would have been Rg1, keeping the rook active and avoiding the tactical liability. Consequently, White’s position slips further into Black’s favour.

teacher: By stepping to f3 Black activates his king, forking White’s rook on g2 and the pawn on e4 and instantly raising the pressure on White’s pieces. Although the pawn on g3 is left en prise, the fork more than compensates, and the engine rates the move as the best, improving Black’s standing by roughly a third of a pawn (from a clear advantage to an even larger one). White’s most accurate reply would be Rg1, removing the threat to the rook on g2, after which Black can continue with Kf2 and a timely …c4+ as shown in the principal variation. The move therefore consolidates Black’s superior position in this rook‑and‑minor‑piece endgame, where both sides have dangerous passed pawns.
student: By moving the king to f3 Black creates a fork, attacking White’s rook on g2 and the pawn on e4 at once. The engine rates this as the best continuation, improving Black’s already sizable advantage by roughly a third of a pawn even though the move leaves the g‑pawn vulnerable. White can meet the threat with Rg1, which would remove the immediate danger to the rook, but Black still retains a clear edge in this rook‑and‑minor‑piece ending.

teacher: In this rook‑and‑minor‑piece ending White’s rook on g1 was under attack, and the simple retreat Rg1 eliminates that threat. The engine rates the move as excellent and notes that it leaves the evaluation essentially unchanged – Black remains much better, with an advantage of more than two pawns even though White is up a pawn in material. Black can reply with Kf2, removing the danger to the pawn on g3, and the suggested continuation would be Rd1, after which White could try c4+ and Black would answer Kb4.
student: By playing Rg1 White eliminates the immediate danger to his rook, allowing him to keep the extra pawn in this rook‑and‑minor‑piece ending. The engine rates the move as excellent and the best continuation, with Black’s most natural reply being Kf2, which would simply remove the pressure on the g3 pawn while preserving Black’s sizable advantage. After that, White can continue with Rd1, keeping the rook active against Black’s king and the distant passed pawn on g3.

teacher: By pushing …g2 Black does obtain a passed pawn, but the pawn is isolated and the move lets White retain a material edge, cutting Black’s lead to roughly a pawn. The engine judged this an inaccuracy, noting that the alternative …Re1 – even though it would leave the rook on e1 en prise – would have preserved a larger advantage. In the continuation the engine expects White to press on the queenside with a6, after which Black’s best try would be …Nc6 followed by …Re1.
student: By pushing …g2 Black creates a passed pawn but does so on an isolated square, allowing White to keep the initiative in this rook‑and‑minor‑piece ending where both sides already have dangerous passed pawns. The engine rates the move as an inaccuracy, costing roughly eight‑tenths of a pawn compared with the optimal continuation Re1, which would have kept the rook active while preserving Black’s larger advantage. After …g2 White can continue with a6, after which Black could try Nc6 and then bring the rook back to e1, keeping the pressure alive. In short, the pawn push gives White counterplay without improving Black’s standing.

teacher: White pushes the last queenside pawn to a6, turning it into an advanced passed pawn and extending the 2‑vs‑1 pawn majority on that flank, although the pawn becomes isolated. In this rook‑and‑minor‑piece ending Black still has the far‑more dangerous passed pawn on g2, so the engine continues to rate Black about two pawns better and the move even nudges the score a little lower for White (≈ ‑0.3 of a pawn). Nevertheless a6 is the only move that improves White’s chances and is therefore the correct choice.
student: By pushing a6 White creates a passed pawn on the a‑file, turning his two‑pawn queenside majority into a concrete asset in this rook‑and‑minor‑piece ending. The advance does leave the new pawn isolated, but it also gives White a clear long‑term target while Black’s own passed pawn sits on g2. Although the engine still judges Black to be clearly better—about two pawns ahead—the move is the best available for White, costing him roughly a third of a pawn compared with the previous evaluation.

teacher: White’s king walk to c4 is a serious blunder: although it removes the immediate threat to the pawn on e4, it hands Black the decisive initiative. After Kc4 Black can answer with Re1, and despite the rook on e1 being left en prise, the resulting line (Re1 – Ra4 – g1=Q – a7) gives Black a winning advantage and a clear path for the passed g‑pawn. The engine shows that the move costs White about two pawns of evaluation, turning a modest –2 pawn disadvantage into a decisive –4 pawn loss. The correct move would have been Rd1, which keeps the rook active and avoids the crushing infiltration.
student: White’s king walk to c4 was intended to eliminate the immediate danger to the e‑pawn, but it walks into Black’s tactical shot …Re1, after which the rook on e1 becomes vulnerable. The engine shows that this blunder costs roughly two pawns of evaluation, turning a clearly worse position for White into a winning one for Black. The correct continuation would have been Rd1, keeping the rook active and preserving White’s chances. Consequently, Kc4 is a clear blunder that dramatically worsens White’s already inferior standing.

teacher: Black’s best reply, Re1, preserves the decisive advantage that the engine evaluates as a winning edge, even though it nudges the evaluation down by only a tenth of a pawn. The rook on e1 is left en prise, but White’s most natural continuation, Ra2, would simply remove the threat to the rook without changing the overall balance. In this rook‑and‑minor‑piece ending, Black’s passed pawn on g2 and the winning advantage remain overwhelming despite the temporary tactical vulnerability.
student: By playing Re1 Black finally brings his last heavy piece onto the board, even though the rook will be left en prise. The engine still judges the position as a decisive Black win, but White can answer with Ra2, which would remove the immediate danger to the white rook on a1. After that line Black can continue with …g1=Q, after which White’s best reply is a7 and Black captures on a7, preserving the winning edge. Thus the move is good because it activates the last heavy piece in this rook‑and‑minor‑piece ending, although it costs a tiny fraction of a pawn compared with the previous evaluation.

teacher: Moving the king to g3 is a mistake because it lets White answer with the checking rook lift Ra3+. That check not only forces the Black king away but also leaves the knight on d1 en prise, and after the forced …Kh4 White can continue Ne3 and promote the g‑pawn. The evaluation therefore drops from a decisive –4.5‑pawn edge to about –3.5, roughly a pawn of material loss for Black, whereas the engine‑recommended Ke2 would have preserved the winning advantage. This loss of tempo and the exposed knight markedly weaken Black’s chances in the rook‑and‑minor‑piece ending.
student: By moving the king to g3 Black walks into White’s forcing line Ra3+, which both checks the king and leaves the knight on d1 hanging. The engine shows that this blunder costs roughly a pawn, dropping the evaluation from a decisive –4½‑pawn edge to about –3½. The far stronger continuation would have been Ke2, keeping the king out of the attack and preserving the larger advantage. Consequently, Kg3 is a clear mistake in this rook‑and‑minor‑piece ending.
violations: describes a check that did not happen

teacher: With Ra3+ White forces a check while simultaneously attacking the undefended knight on d1, leaving it en prise.  The move does not erase Black’s decisive edge, but it nudges the evaluation up by roughly a third of a pawn and even puts White a pawn ahead.  Black’s most resilient reply would be Kh4, after which White can continue Ne3, and if Black then queens with g1=Q White has the forcing Nf5+ in response.  The dual purpose of the check and the hanging knight makes Ra3+ the clear best move in this rook‑and‑minor‑piece ending.
student: White’s checking rook lift to a3 forces Black’s king to step back – the engine’s line continues with …Kh4 – while simultaneously leaving the white knight on d1 hanging. By creating this tactical liability White improves his standing by roughly a third of a pawn in a position where Black already enjoys a decisive edge. The move also preserves White’s advanced passed pawn on a6 against Black’s distant g‑pawn, keeping the balance as tight as possible.

teacher: White’s 62.Ne3 was meant to protect the pawn on e4 and the knight, but it simply gives Black the time to push the far‑advanced g‑pawn to promotion. Black can reply g1=Q, which promotes the pawn to a queen on g1 and turns the already decisive Black edge of about four pawns into an even larger advantage of roughly five pawns. The engine’s preferred move was a7, keeping White’s passed a‑pawn active and avoiding the loss of tempo. Thus Ne3 is a clear mistake, costing White about a pawn’s worth of evaluation.
student: White’s Ne3 does eliminate the immediate danger to the e‑pawn and the knight itself, but it allows Black to continue with …g1=Q, which would capture the white king on c4 and turn the already decisive edge into a much larger one. The engine shows that this concession costs roughly a pawn in evaluation, worsening Black’s winning chances by about a pawn. In contrast, the best continuation was a7, which would have kept the king safe and avoided the forced queen sacrifice. Consequently, Ne3 is a clear mistake that deepens Black’s winning advantage.

teacher: By queening on g1 Black both opens the g‑file and eliminates the lingering threat to the newly created queen. The promotion leaves the engine’s assessment essentially unchanged at a decisive –5½‑pawn advantage, even nudging it slightly in Black’s favour. White’s most natural try would be 63 Kb5, forking the pawn on c5 and the knight on c6, but Black can meet that with 63…Qg6, preserving the winning material edge.
student: By promoting on g1 Black not only creates a new queen but also opens the g‑file, removing the immediate danger to the newly created queen. The engine rates the move as the best continuation, keeping Black’s decisive edge virtually intact – the evaluation shifts by only about a tenth of a pawn in White’s favour. If White tries the natural king infiltration Kb5, Black can answer with Qg6, after which White would capture on c5 and Black continues with Na7, preserving the material lead.

teacher: By playing Qxe3+ Black not only wins the rook on e3 but also gives a check that simultaneously attacks White’s king on c5 and the pawn on e4, a classic queen fork. The capture preserves Black’s overwhelming material lead – up the equivalent of nine pawns – and the engine still judges the position a decisive Black advantage, only a shade less favorable than before. White’s most natural reply would be Kxc6, capturing the knight on c6, yet even after that continuation Black remains winning.
student: By playing Qxe3+ Black wins the white rook with check while forking White’s king on c5 and the pawn on e4, preserving his material edge in this endgame. The capture also leaves Black’s knight on c6 vulnerable to Kxc6, so White must recapture with the king. Although the engine notes a slight dip of about a tenth of a pawn, Black remains decisively ahead – roughly four‑and‑a‑half pawns down. This continuation therefore justifies the “good” label as the best move.

teacher: White finally eliminates Black’s last minor piece by taking on c6, turning the position into a queen ending. The capture also leaves White with an advanced passed pawn on a6 that could become a focal point in the ensuing queen versus king endgame. Yet the engine still judges Black as winning by roughly four and a half pawns, and the move even nudges the evaluation a little deeper in Black’s favour (about a quarter of a pawn).
student: By taking on c6 White eliminates Black’s last minor piece and forces the game into a pure queen ending. The capture also leaves White with an advanced passed pawn on a6, but it does not improve the evaluation – the engine still judges Black to be decisively better, now about four‑and‑a‑half pawns ahead. Nevertheless, Kxc6 is the best continuation available, as any other try would allow Black to keep the initiative.

teacher: White advances the queenside pawn to c4, turning the two‑pawn majority into a passed pawn but leaving it isolated on c4. The move improves White’s score by only a few hundredths of a pawn, yet Black remains decisively ahead with a winning advantage. The engine, however, rates 67 c3 as superior – it would keep the pawn on the same file, though the pawn would still be isolated, offering White a marginally better defensive chance.
student: By pushing c4 White creates a passed pawn and extends his two‑pawn queenside majority, even though the new pawn will be isolated. In this pure queen ending the engine still judges Black to be decisively better – roughly five pawns ahead – so the move does not improve White’s chances. The engine preferred c3, which would have been marginally stronger, but c4 leaves the evaluation virtually unchanged, costing White only about half a pawn in the assessment.

teacher: White pushes the queenside pawn to c5, converting the two‑pawn majority into a passed pawn but leaving that pawn isolated and en prise. Black can simply answer Kxe4, snatching the e‑pawn and keeping the decisive material edge; the engine rates the move as slightly worse for White (about two‑tenths of a pawn). The engine’s top choice was Kc6, which would have preserved a more solid stance. Nonetheless, the move is still classified as good, even though it does not improve White’s already losing position.
student: By pushing c5 White creates a passed pawn on the queenside but immediately leaves it en prise, so Black can simply capture the pawn on e4 with Kxe4. The engine rates the move as “good” yet notes that it costs White about a fifth of a pawn compared with the optimal king move Kc6, which would have kept the evaluation roughly the same. In this queen‑ending the move does not improve White’s chances – Black remains decisively ahead, still up six points of material.

teacher: Black’s king steps to e5, keeping a central presence in the queen‑endgame, but by forgoing the capture on e4 it allows White to retain the pawn on e4 and the engine’s evaluation slips by about a fifth of a pawn. The engine judged the move “good” yet not optimal; Kxe4 would have taken the pawn on e4 and preserved a larger winning margin. White’s remaining threats – the advanced passed pawns on c5 and a6 – remain, and the continuation suggested by the engine (c6, Qb8+, Kc4, Qb6) shows White can still try to activate the c‑pawn while Black’s queen checks from the side.
student: Black’s king steps to e5, keeping it active in this queen‑ending where White’s passed pawns sit on a6 and c5. The engine rates the move as good but notes that it costs about two‑tenths of a pawn compared with the optimal capture Kxe4, which would have taken the pawn on e4. After Ke5 White can answer with c6, removing the pressure on the c‑pawn, after which Black could continue with …Qb8+ followed by …Qb6. Even so, Black remains decisively ahead with a material lead of six pawns.

teacher: By moving the king to c6 White walks into a forced queen capture on a6, allowing Black to check with Qxa6+ and win the advanced passed pawn. This blunder costs roughly another pawn, deepening Black’s decisive advantage from about –5½ to –6½ pawns. The engine’s preferred move was the pawn push c6, which would have removed the queen’s threat to the pawn on c6 and kept the material balance more favorable for White.
student: White’s king walk to c6 does nothing to meet Black’s looming queen capture on a6; after …Qxa6+ the black queen checks while taking the pawn that was defended by the c‑pawn, leaving White with no compensation for the loss of material. The engine shows this costs roughly a pawn in evaluation, pushing the already decisive Black edge from about –5½ to –6½. In contrast, the simple pawn push c6 would have removed the immediate danger to the c‑pawns and kept the balance much tighter. Consequently, Kc6 is a clear mistake, worsening White’s position by about one pawn.

teacher: By playing Qxa6+ Black eliminates White’s a‑pawn, opens the a‑file and gives a checking blow that leaves the white king with no refuge. The queen on a6 together with the black king on e5 forces a forced mate in 11, turning the already decisive material advantage into a concrete win. Consequently the engine rates the move as the best (‑6.48 → mate in 11).
student: By playing Qxa6+ Black not only wins the pawn on a6 but also opens the a‑file and forces White’s king to step back with Kc7. After that, Black can continue Ke6, then e5, and finally Qa7+, delivering a forced mate in eleven moves. The capture therefore converts a large material edge into a decisive win, as reflected by the evaluation swing from a decisive –6½‑pawn advantage to a forced mate.

teacher: White’s 70 Kd7 is a serious blunder that collapses a forced mate in 11 into a forced mate in just three moves. By moving onto d7 the king allows Black’s queen to give check on b7, which simultaneously forks the king and the e‑pawn, and the engine’s line Qb7+ Ke8 Ke6 c6 shows how quickly Black can deliver mate. The engine notes that the correct retreat was 70 Kc7, which would have kept the mate farther off. With the passed pawn on c5 and the pawn on e4 remaining, White cannot escape the inevitable checkmate.
student: White’s retreat to Kd7 walks straight into Black’s forcing line: after the natural …Qb7+, the queen checks the king while also attacking the advanced e‑pawn, leading to a forced mate in three instead of the previous eleven moves. The engine shows that the correct defence was Kc7, which would have kept the mating net far longer. By playing Kd7 White not only loses the extra time but also allows the immediate fork and mate threat.

However, this move abandons the forced mate that existed – the engine shows that the superior check Qb7+ would have forked the king and the e4 pawn and kept a mate‑in‑three. By playing Qb5+ Black still wins a huge material advantage (about seven pawns), but the inaccuracy costs the immediate forced win and reduces the result to a decisive but non‑mating advantage.
student: Black’s checking queen on b5 looks tempting, for it does fork White’s king on d7 and the advanced pawn on c5, but it walks into a simple tactical shot. After the natural reply c6, the pawn on c6 becomes en prise, allowing White to capture it with his king and erase Black’s mating net. The engine shows that the correct continuation was Qb7+, which would have kept the forced mate instead of conceding the extra material. teacher: White pushes the last remaining pawn to c6, creating an isolated passed pawn that is left en prise but, because Black’s queen on b5 pins it to the white king on d7, it cannot be captured immediately. The advance of the queenside majority gives White a tiny improvement – the engine now rates the position about a sixth of a pawn better for White despite Black’s decisive material lead. Black could answer with Qa4, forking the e4‑pawn and the newly created c6‑pawn, but even that continuation cannot erase Black’s overwhelming advantage.
student: By pushing c6 White creates an advanced passed pawn that can be exploited in this queen‑ending, even though it becomes isolated and is technically en prise. The pawn is pinned by Black’s queen on b5 to the white king on d7, so White cannot capture it immediately, but the new passed pawn gives White a concrete target despite the disadvantage. The engine rates the move as the best available, improving White’s standing by roughly a sixth of a pawn while Black still enjoys a decisive material edge. Black could try Qa4, forking the e4 pawn and the newly created c6 pawn, yet White remains the most resilient side in the position.

teacher: Black’s queen rushes to d5 with a double‑purpose check: it attacks the White king and simultaneously forks the king and the advanced pawn on c6. With the king forced away, White cannot stop the inevitable mating net, and the engine shows the forced mate shrinks from nine to eight moves. In this pure queen‑ending the move leaves White with only a lone pawn and a king on d6, while Black’s queen and king coordinate to deliver the final blow. This precise check is therefore the only winning continuation, justifying the “!!” annotation.
student: Black’s queen jumps to d5 with a checking fork, hitting both White’s king on d6 and the advanced pawn on c6 at once. The engine shows that this forces a win by forcing the white king onto c7, then Ke5, Kb6 and Kd6, cutting the mate from nine moves to eight. In this pure queen‑ending the extra tempo makes the move absolutely decisive.

teacher: White’s king steps onto c7, the only move that keeps the advanced passed pawn on c6 from being lost immediately. In this queen‑ending Black still has a forced mate in eight moves, and the engine confirms that no alternative king move would improve White’s chances. The suggested continuation (Ke5 – Kb6 – Kd6 – c7) shows White trying to escort the pawn, but the inevitable mate cannot be avoided.
student: White’s king steps to c7, the only square that keeps the game alive and therefore earns the “best” label. In this queen‑endgame with Black’s king already on e4 and a passed pawn on c6, any other move would have surrendered the position immediately. The engine still evaluates the position as a forced mate for Black in eight moves, but Kc7 at least delays the inevitable.

teacher: In this queen endgame White’s only chance is to keep the king as close as possible to the advanced passed pawn on c6, and Kb6 does exactly that. The engine’s principal variation shows that after Black’s best reply Kd6 White can push c7, after which Black checks with Qb3+ and White replies Ka6, but the line still ends in a forced mate in seven for Black. Although the move does not alter the evaluation—Black is still up 8 points and mates in seven—it is the best defensive try in a hopeless position.
student: White’s king steps to b6, the only move that keeps the game alive and therefore earns the “best” label. In this queen‑endgame with Black’s king on e5 and the white king on b6, the engine still sees a forced mate in seven for Black, but Kb6 at least prevents immediate capture or loss of the passed pawn on c6. The continuation would likely be …Kd6, then White pushing c7, followed by Qb3+ and Ka6, yet the position remains hopeless for White.
violations: describes a capture that did not happen

teacher: Black’s king steps to d6, the only move that preserves the forced mate and even speeds it up to a six‑move win. By centralising the king in this queen‑endgame, Black readies the queen’s decisive infiltration while White’s advanced pawn on c6 remains free to advance. White can only try 1.c7, but after 1…Qb3+ 2.Ka6 Kxc7 Black’s queen and king combine to deliver mate in a few moves, confirming the move’s brilliance.
student: By moving the king to d6 Black brings his monarch into the centre of this queen‑ending and forces White’s only realistic try — the pawn push c7 that would remove the immediate danger to the white pawn on c6. After that reply Black can continue with …Qb3+, driving the white king away from the pawn and then capture it on a6, completing the forced mate in six moves. The engine rates Kd6 as the best continuation, improving the previous mate‑in‑seven evaluation by one step.

teacher: White pushes the last pawn to c7, turning it into an isolated passed pawn and removing the immediate threat to it while advancing the queenside majority. In this queen‑endgame Black still has a forced mate in six; the best continuation would be …Qb3+ checking, after which White must go to a6, Black captures on c7 and the mating net continues. Thus 75.c7 is the only move that preserves a passed pawn, but it does not change the inevitable forced mate for Black.
student: By pushing c7 White creates an advanced passed pawn and activates his lone queenside pawn, turning a hopeless position into one where Black still mates in six moves but at least has no immediate way to win material. The advance also eliminates the previous threats to the pawn, though it leaves the pawn isolated on c7. Black’s most forcing continuation would be Qb3+, checking the king and leading to the sequence Ka6‑Kxc7‑Ka5 that finishes the game. In this queen‑ending the move is rightly judged as the best possible defense.

teacher: By capturing the pawn on c7 Black not only wins material but also opens the c‑file, giving the queen unobstructed access to the white king. This simple capture shortens the forced mate from six to five moves, confirming it as a winning continuation in this queen endgame. After 76…Qxc7 White’s best try would be 77.Kb5, but Black can reply 77…Qc2 and, after 78.Kb6, finish with 78…Qb2+ delivering mate.
student: By taking on c7 Black eliminates White’s last pawn and opens the c‑file for his queen, turning this into a pure queen ending where Black already enjoys a forced win. The capture not only wins material but also shortens the forced mate from six to five moves, as reflected by the evaluation swing. With the c‑file now clear, Black can continue with …Qc2, then …Qb2+, delivering immediate checkmate. This precise queen sacrifice therefore secures an even more decisive advantage.

teacher: Black’s check with Qc5+ is a clear mis‑step: although it does give check, it allows White’s king to slip away and lengthens the forced win. Before the move Black already had a forced mate in five, but after the check the quickest line stretches to six moves, costing a tempo. The engine’s preferred continuation, Qc2, would have kept the mate in five, making the queen check a needless delay in this queen endgame.
student: Black’s checking move Qc5+ looks natural but actually costs a tempo, turning a forced mate in five into a forced mate in six. The engine shows that White can simply answer Ka6 and then continue with …Qc7, after which Black must play Kb5 and finally finish with Qc2, whereas the correct continuation was Qc2. In short, the check delays the inevitable win by one move, making it a clear mistake.

teacher: White’s king move to a4 is a clear mistake: the position was already a forced mate in six, and by stepping onto a4 White walks straight into Black’s winning line, allowing Black to continue with …Qb6 and shorten the mate to five moves. The engine indicates that the only better try was Ka6, which would have kept the forced mate at six instead of five. In this queen‑endgame, with Black up nine points of material, the move merely accelerates the inevitable defeat.
student: White’s king walk to a4 does nothing to stop Black’s looming queen infiltration and actually deepens the mating net – the evaluation slips from a forced mate in six to five moves. The engine shows that the correct defence would have been Ka6, which would have kept the mate at seven moves instead of eight. After Ka4 Black can continue with …Qb6, forcing the white king back to a3, then …Kc5 and finally …Ka2, delivering mate as planned. In this queen‑ending the king move therefore costs White about half a move and turns an already hopeless position into an even more dire one.

teacher: White’s king walk to a4 is a fatal blunder: it walks straight into Black’s forced mate, allowing …Qb4# on the very next move. The engine shows that before the move White was only facing mate in three, but after Ka4 the mate shrinks to one, a dramatic loss of two moves. The only move that would have kept the game alive was Ka2, which would have delayed the inevitable mate.
student: By moving the king to a4 White walks straight into Black’s winning line. After Ka4 Black can play …Qb4#, delivering immediate mate and turning an already lost position into a forced loss for White. The engine shows that the correct defence was Ka2, which would have kept the game alive by avoiding the fatal queen check. Consequently the move costs White about three pawns of material and forces a forced mate in one.

teacher: Black could have finished the game instantly with Qb4#, a direct checkmate, but instead chose Kc4. The king step simply creates the threat Qa7#, so after White’s only sensible reply Ka3 Black still mates in one with Qb3#. In this queen‑endgame Black remains overwhelmingly ahead—up the equivalent of nine pawns—and the evaluation stays a forced mate in one.
student: By moving to c4 Black immediately creates the mating threat Qa7#, forcing White’s king onto a4 and then delivering mate with …Qb3#. The engine notes that this line already guarantees a forced win for Black, but the more accurate continuation would have been Qb4#, which also delivers mate outright. In short, Kc4 keeps the same winning edge while preserving the immediate mate‑in‑one plan.

teacher: Black answers 2…c5 with a modest pawn advance that leaves the evaluation virtually unchanged – the engine’s assessment moves only a hundredth of a pawn in Black’s favour. Although the move is solid, the engine notes that the more ambitious 2…d5 would have been a pawn break striking at White’s e4 pawn, offering greater central pressure. By choosing c5 Black forgoes that immediate challenge, yet the position stays roughly equal.
student: Black answered with …c5, a quiet central thrust that leaves material even and keeps the engine’s assessment essentially unchanged – still about a tenth of a pawn in White’s favour. The move does not contest White’s centre; the engine preferred the more ambitious …d5, which would have struck directly at the e4 pawn. In practice, however, …c5 preserves equality without creating any new weaknesses.

teacher: White chose to push the f‑pawn to f4, a move that leaves the position essentially unchanged but gives Black a small edge (about a tenth of a pawn). Although it is not a blunder, the engine prefers 3.Nf3, which would have kept White’s standing more solid. Black can answer with the pawn break …d5, striking at White’s e4 pawn. As a result, White’s position is now slightly worse, though material remains equal.
student: White’s third move f4 does not change the balance – the engine still judges the position as roughly equal and even gives Black a slight edge after the move. The engine preferred Nf3, which would have kept the evaluation around zero. After f4 Black can answer with the thematic …d5 pawn break, striking at White’s e‑pawn and gaining space. In short, the move is solid but misses the more accurate development idea.

teacher: Black answered 4…g6, a modest pawn move that keeps material level but nudges the evaluation a little in White’s favour. The engine rates the move as “good” yet notes it worsens Black’s standing by roughly a quarter of a pawn compared with the more accurate 4…Be7. In the principal variation White can continue with 5 c3, Black replies 5…d5 and later Black may develop the bishop to g7, but the immediate choice of g6 already gives White a small edge.
student: Black’s …g6 is a modest pawn push that leaves material unchanged but nudges the evaluation in White’s favour by about a quarter‑pawn, turning an essentially equal position into one where White holds a slight edge. The engine rates the move as “good” yet not optimal – …Be7 would have kept the balance more closely and avoided the small swing. In the suggested continuation White can play c3, after which Black might reply d5, followed by Be2 and Bg7. Thus the move is acceptable but costs Black a modest amount of equality.

teacher: Black answers White’s castling with the natural developing move Nge7, bringing the second knight into the game while keeping the pawn structure intact. The engine rates it as the best continuation, leaving the evaluation essentially unchanged at roughly equal. In the main line the game can proceed 7.c3 O‑O 8.Be3 d6, with both sides maintaining a balanced position.
student: Black’s …Nge7 simply brings the knight to its natural square, completing development and leaving material perfectly balanced. The engine rates it as an excellent move, keeping the evaluation at roughly equal – a swing of only about a tenth of a pawn in White’s favour. In the principal variation White would continue with c3, after which Black can safely castle and later play …d6, preserving equality.

teacher: Black chose the thematic pawn break …f5, directly challenging White’s e‑pawn and trying to open lines in the centre. However, the advance also creates holes in front of the Black king, and the engine evaluates the move as having cost roughly a third of a pawn compared with the position before the move. A more precise continuation would have been …b5, which keeps Black’s slight edge intact. If White replies with the natural a4, Black can continue b6, after which White’s Na3 would allow Black to capture on e4, but the missed …b5 already left Black a little worse.
student: Black’s …f5 tries to open lines against White’s e‑pawn by striking at it, but the advance also loosens the pawn shield that covers his own king. The engine rates the move as a moderate worsening for Black – roughly a third of a pawn compared with the optimal continuation …b5, which would have kept the evaluation around –0.5. After …f5 White can answer with a4, after which Black may reply …b6 and later capture on e4, leaving Black still a little better but not as clearly so.

teacher: White’s 10.Nbd2 develops the queen‑side knight, but the engine shows it lets Black’s edge grow from a modest –0.21 to –0.49, a deterioration of roughly a quarter of a pawn. The computer‑recommended 10.a4 would have kept the balance more favourably for White, with the continuation …b6 11.c3 Qd7 12.Bb3 in the principal variation. In short, the move is playable and labelled “good”, yet it costs White a small amount of pressure compared with the sharper pawn thrust.
student: White develops the queen’s knight to d2, but the engine judges that this costs him about a quarter‑pawn compared with the more accurate continuation a4. After Nbd2 Black can answer with …b6, after which White would have to meet it with c3 and later bring the bishop to b3, leaving Black still a little better. The evaluation therefore slides from –0.21 to –0.49 in Black’s favour. In short, the move is solid but not optimal, costing White roughly a quarter‑pawn of advantage.

teacher: Black’s 12…d5 looks like a natural pawn break against White’s e4 pawn and tries to deprive the knight on d2 of the c4 square, but the thrust is premature. With the knight on e7 already without safe squares and both White bishops cramped, the pawn push merely opens lines for White, who can answer with e5 (the engine’s continuation) and seize the initiative, flipping the evaluation from a Black edge to a White edge of about a pawn. The engine shows that the simple queen move Qd7 would have preserved Black’s modest lead, whereas 12…d5 costs roughly one and a half pawns in positional terms, justifying its “mistake” label.
student: By playing …d5 Black tried to open lines against White’s e‑pawn and to deprive the knight on d2 of the c4 square, but the thrust does nothing to relieve the cramped situation of his own pieces – especially the knight on e7, which already has no safe retreats. The engine shows that this concession flips the evaluation from a clear Black edge to a similar advantage for White, costing roughly a pawn in practical terms. A far stronger continuation would have been …Qd7, keeping the pressure without giving White the chance to equalise. Consequently the pawn break was a mistake, worsening Black’s standing by about one and a half pawns.

teacher: White’s advance e5 locks Black’s pawn on e6 onto a light square and leaves the bishop on g7 short of squares, sharply curtailing its activity. By fixing the pawn structure—White’s pawns now sit on dark squares while Black’s are stuck on light ones—the move secures a modest but lasting positional edge, which the engine still rates as a slight advantage for White. Although the evaluation slips a fraction of a pawn, e5 is the correct and best continuation.
student: By playing e5 White locks Black’s pawn on e6 onto a light square and further restricts the already cramped bishop on g7, which now has virtually no useful retreat. The advance also leaves Black’s pieces with very limited options – the bishop on g7 is short of squares while White’s own pawns stay fixed on dark squares. Although the engine notes a slight dip in White’s edge (about a sixth of a pawn), the move remains the best continuation and preserves White’s modest advantage.

teacher: White’s 14.c3 is a solid, improving move that removes the b4 and d4 squares from the Black knight on c6, thereby strengthening White’s dark‑square pawn chain. The position remains one where White’s pawns sit on dark squares, Black’s on light, and the Black bishop on g7 is still confined to its only safe diagonal. Although the move keeps White clearly better, the engine rates 14.d4 as the stronger alternative—a pawn break that would strike at Black’s c5 pawn and generate more pressure. As a result, 14.c3 costs White about a tenth of a pawn in the evaluation, and Black could reply with …d4, immediately targeting the newly placed pawn on c3.
student: White’s 14.c3 simply blocks the b4‑ and d4‑squares that Black’s knight on c6 could otherwise use, thereby limiting its activity while leaving material equal. The engine still judges White to be clearly better – roughly a pawn’s worth – but notes that the more ambitious 14.d4 would have struck at Black’s c5 pawn, offering White a sharper continuation. By opting for c3 instead, White missed this immediate pawn break and the evaluation slipped by about a tenth of a pawn. Nonetheless, the move keeps the position solid and preserves White’s modest edge.

teacher: White’s knight hops to c4, a natural square that meshes with White’s dark‑square pawn chain while leaving Black’s bishop on g7 with only a single safe retreat. The move preserves White’s modest edge – the engine still rates the position as slightly better for White, only a fraction of a pawn down from the previous evaluation. Black could try Rb8, after which White would have the strong reply Nd6, continuing the pressure.
student: White’s knight jumps to c4, a natural developing move that fits the static structure – White’s pawns sit on dark squares while Black’s are locked on light squares and Black’s bishop on g7 already has very few safe retreats. The engine rates it as the best continuation, though the evaluation slips from roughly +0.7 to +0.5 because Black can answer with …Rb8, after which White would continue Nd6 and keep the slight edge. In short, Nc4 preserves White’s modest advantage without creating new weaknesses.

teacher: By playing …dxc3 Black eliminates White’s pawn on c3 and, as noted, uncovers a discovered queen attack on the pawn d3. White can recapture with bxc3, restoring material balance, opening the b‑file for White and the d‑file for Black, and leaving White with an isolated pawn on a4, yet the engine now scores the position about a third of a pawn worse for Black (White +0.8 versus +0.49 before). The engine’s preferred move was Rb8, which would have avoided the exchange and kept Black’s evaluation more favorable. Consequently, the capture is a good tactical idea but it costs Black roughly a third of a pawn in the overall assessment.
student: By playing …dxc3 Black opens the d‑file and creates a queen‑to‑d3 line, but after White’s natural reply bxc3 the b‑file becomes semi‑open for White while Black gains a temporary half‑open d‑file. The capture also leaves White with an isolated a‑pawn, yet it does not win material – the engine shows that the evaluation shifts to roughly a pawn in White’s favour despite Black being up a pawn before the exchange. Consequently the move costs Black about a third of a pawn compared with the optimal continuation Rb8, which would have kept the balance without giving White the extra activity.

teacher: By retreating the bishop to b3 White creates a powerful pin on the e‑6 pawn, which now cannot move without exposing the black king on g8. The move fits neatly with White’s dark‑square pawn chain and the fact that Black’s light‑square pawns and the g7‑bishop are already cramped, further limiting Black’s counterplay. Black’s most natural reply, …Nd5, would simply try to lift the pin on e6, but even after the forced exchange sequence the engine still judges White to be well over a pawn ahead, with the move itself adding roughly a quarter‑pawn to the advantage.
student: By playing Bb3 White places his bishop on the long diagonal and immediately pins the e‑pawn to Black’s king on g8, so the pawn cannot move without exposing the king. This subtle pin deepens White’s already sizable advantage – the engine now evaluates the position at roughly +1.85 pawns, about a quarter‑pawn more than before. Black’s most natural reply would be Nd5, which simply removes the pressure on the e‑pawn, after which White can capture with Bxd5 and continue with d4, keeping the initiative. The move therefore solidifies White’s lead while limiting Black’s defensive options.

teacher: White’s queen retreat to g3 is an inaccuracy because it leaves the pawn on c3 en prise, allowing Black to win a pawn and reducing White’s advantage from about a pawn‑and‑a‑half to roughly a single pawn, as the evaluation drops from +1.73 to +1.14. The engine’s top choice, Bxd5, would have captured the knight on d5 and, by pinning the e‑pawn to the king, kept the initiative. By playing Qg3 White also missed the chance to exploit the fact that Black’s bishop on g7 has only one safe square. The position remains clearly better for White, but the advantage has been noticeably diminished.
student: White’s queen retreat to g3 looks natural but it carelessly leaves the pawn on c3 hanging, allowing Black to reply Rxd6 and win the knight on d6. That capture not only removes the knight but also leaves the rook on d6 vulnerable, so White’s advantage drops by roughly half a pawn compared with the engine‑recommended continuation. The engine judged Bxd5 to be far stronger – it would have captured the knight on d5 while pinning the e6‑pawn to the black king, preserving White’s clear edge. Consequently, Qg3 is an inaccuracy that modestly reduces White’s lead.

teacher: White’s 23.Qf3 does create a pin of the d5‑knight against Black’s queen on b7, but the move does not improve the position and actually reduces White’s advantage by about half a pawn. The engine rates 23.Nf3 as the superior continuation, which would have preserved White’s larger advantage while developing the knight. By opting for the queen move White leaves the material balance unchanged and lets Black’s position become slightly more comfortable. The pawn structure remains locked on opposite colours and Black’s bishop on g7 is still confined to its only safe square.
student: White’s queen retreat to f3 creates a pin of the d5‑knight against Black’s queen on b7, but it does not improve the already solid structure – the pawn chain remains locked on dark squares and Black’s bishop on g7 still has very few safe squares. The engine rates the move as an inaccuracy, dropping the evaluation by roughly half a pawn compared with the optimal continuation Nf3. In the principal variation Black would reply …Qc6, after which White could try Qh3, followed by …b5 and then Nf3, preserving the advantage.

teacher: White strikes with the pawn break 24 g4, directly attacking Black’s pawn on f5 and exploiting the fact that Black’s bishop on g7 is confined to a single safe square. The advance also opens the g‑file, giving White active play at the cost of slightly weakening the pawn shield in front of his king. The engine judges this pressure worth about a sixth of a pawn, improving the evaluation from +1.23 to +1.39. The suggested continuation Rg8‑Rg2‑b5‑c4 shows how White can follow up the break with active piece play.
student: White’s pawn thrust g4 is a sharp break that attacks Black’s f5‑pawn and tries to open lines for his pieces while leaving the king’s pawn shield a little thinner. The engine rates it as the best continuation, nudging the evaluation up by roughly a sixth of a pawn even though it does weaken the king’s cover. With White’s pawns locked on dark squares and Black’s bishop on g7 confined to its single safe square, the advance creates concrete threats without compromising material.

teacher: White’s gxf5 captures the pawn on f5, starting an exchange that temporarily gives White a pawn advantage (material up one pawn) but after the expected recapture Nxf5 material will be equal, while nudging the evaluation up by about a quarter pawn. After the forced Nxf5 the f‑file becomes semi‑open for Black while the g‑file is now semi‑open for White, Black is left with an isolated pawn on e6 and White retains the bishop pair; additionally Black’s bishop on g7 has only one safe square. The reply Nxf5 also leaves Black’s pawn on g6 en prise, giving White further targets. This combination of structural and piece‑activity gains makes the move the clear best choice, justifying the !! annotation.
student: By playing gxf5 White eliminates Black’s central pawn and forces the natural reply Nxf5, after which the f‑file becomes semi‑open for Black while the g‑file opens for White. The capture also leaves both sides with isolated pawns – Black’s e6 and White’s h2 – but it does not restore material equality because Black must recapture with the knight. This exchange nudges the evaluation from roughly +1.7 to about +1.95, confirming that White remains clearly better despite the slight structural concession.

teacher: Black’s queen captures the pawn on d3, opening the d‑file and leaving White with an isolated pawn on c3. However, this is a mistake because it ignores the far stronger continuation Nxf5, which would have taken the pawn on f5 and left Black’s g‑pawn en prise; after that White could reply f6, forking the knight on e7 and the bishop on g7. Consequently White’s evaluation jumps from a modest +2 to a winning +3½, a swing of roughly a pawn in White’s favour.
student: By playing Qxd3 Black wins the pawn on d3 but immediately hands White the chance to increase the pressure. The capture opens the d‑file and leaves White’s pawn on c3 isolated, while the engine shows that White can reply f6, forking the knight on e7 and the bishop on g7, which pushes the evaluation from a modest +1.95 to a decisive +3.58 in White’s favour – roughly a loss of about a pawn for Black. The engine’s preferred continuation was Nxf5, which would have taken the pawn on f5 despite leaving the g6 pawn vulnerable. Consequently, the move costs Black a clear edge.

teacher: White finally took the enemy queen on d3, but the capture merely initiates an exchange that Black can answer with Rxd3, restoring the material balance and leaving White with only a modest edge. By removing the immediate threat to the bishop on d2 the move does solve a tactical problem, yet it forfeits the far stronger continuation f6, which would have forked the knight on e7 and the bishop on g7 and kept the decisive advantage. Consequently the evaluation slides from a winning +3.5‑pawn lead to a comfortable +1.9‑pawn lead, a loss of roughly one and a half pawns.
student: By playing Qxd3 White wins the black queen but immediately allows …Rxd3, restoring material balance and wiping out about a pawn‑and‑a‑half of White’s earlier edge. The capture also eliminates the immediate danger to the bishop on d2, yet it does not generate any compensation – the engine shows that the far stronger continuation would have been f6, which forks the knight on e7 and the bishop on g7. Consequently the evaluation drops from a decisive +3.58 to a modest +1.93, making the move a clear mistake.

teacher: By playing 26…Rxd3 Black finally eliminates White’s queen, restoring material equality; the engine’s evaluation barely changes, with White still about a pawn better. The capture also leaves Black’s bishop on g7 with only one safe square while the rook on f8 continues to use the semi‑open f‑file. White’s most dangerous reply would be 27 Nxg6, forking the knight on e7 and the rook on f8 and leaving the pawn on f5 en prise.
student: By playing Rxd3 Black finally eliminates White’s queen, restoring material balance but leaving White still clearly ahead by about two pawns. The capture also leaves Black’s bishop on g7 with its sole safe square while the rook on f8 continues to use the semi‑open f‑file. White can reply Nxg6, forking the knight on e7 and the rook on f8, yet after the forced recapture Nxg6 the pawn on f5 becomes vulnerable, giving Black counterplay despite the engine’s assessment that the position remains roughly equal in practical terms. This precise exchange therefore earns the “best” label.
violations: calls the position equal at 1.89

teacher: Black’s 28…Ncd5 is the only move that can at least blunt White’s bishop on b3, because the knight now sits on d5 and deprives the bishop of the e6 square. Although it is the engine’s top choice, the move still leaves Black a pawn down and the evaluation slides from a +1.21 to about +1.47 in White’s favour – a small deterioration of roughly a quarter pawn. White’s dangerous passed g‑pawn and his bishop pair give him a clear edge, while Black’s bishop on g7 has no safe squares. If White replies with the natural pawn break 29 f5, Black can capture with exf5, and after 30 Rg3 Black can exchange on g3, keeping the pressure.
student: By playing …Ncd5 Black removes the e‑6 square from White’s bishop on b3, curbing its activity and limiting the scope of that piece in the endgame. The engine still judges White to be clearly better – roughly a pawn ahead – but the move costs Black a little more than the previous evaluation, worsening the score by about a quarter of a pawn. In the principal variation White can try the pawn break f5, which would strike at the e6 pawn and leave the e5 pawn vulnerable, yet Black remains the best continuation despite the slight disadvantage.

teacher: White’s 29.Ng2 keeps the bishop pair and the advanced passed pawn on g6, but it also leaves that pawn en prise, a drawback the engine points out. Consequently White’s advantage shrinks from about a pawn‑and‑a‑half to roughly a pawn, a moderate worsening of the position. The engine’s top choice was 29.f5, a pawn break that would hit the e6 pawn and, after …b5, would pressure White’s a4 pawn, preserving a larger edge. By contrast, after Ng2 Black can now consider the pawn thrust …b5, targeting the a‑pawn, as shown in the principal variation.
student: White’s 29.Ng2 looks active but it leaves the advanced g‑pawn hanging, so Black can answer with …b5 and strike at White’s a‑pawn instead of the more dangerous …b5‑…Bc2 plan that the engine preferred. The evaluation therefore slips from roughly +1.5 to about +1.0 – a loss of four‑tenths of a pawn for White. The engine judged f5 to be superior because it would have opened a pawn break against Black’s e‑pawn while also attacking the e5 pawn, keeping the pressure on Black’s centre. In short, Ng2 is a good try but it costs White a modest amount of advantage.

teacher: White captures the pawn on b5, opening the a‑file and removing Black’s pawn that was a potential target; the exchange does not change the material balance, so White’s two‑pawn lead is preserved. With the a‑file now clear, White’s rook can become active while Black’s bishop on g7 remains without safe squares and White’s advanced passed pawn on g6 together with the bishop pair continue to dominate the position. The engine still rates the move as excellent, but it does not improve the evaluation (the score stays around +1.1 pawn) and a more precise continuation would have been 30.Bc2, which keeps the same material while maintaining a slightly higher pressure. In short, the move keeps White’s clear advantage essentially unchanged.
student: By playing axb5 White eliminates Black’s pawn on b5 and opens the a‑file, but the capture merely initiates an exchange that will be restored after Black’s natural recapture. The engine still judges the position as clearly better for White – roughly a pawn’s worth – and even notes that the move leaves the evaluation essentially unchanged at about +1.15. Although the suggested continuation would have been Bc2, which the engine rates as the optimal move, the chosen move is nevertheless excellent because it keeps White’s advantage intact while creating useful play on the newly opened file.

teacher: White retreats the bishop to c2, preserving the bishop pair and keeping the advanced passed pawn on g6 supported while the black bishop on g7 remains without safe squares. The move is judged good, although it trims White’s edge by roughly four‑tenths of a pawn, leaving a clear but smaller advantage. Black’s most accurate reply would be Rh3, which would eliminate the threat to the rook on h3. The continuation suggested by the engine proceeds Rh3 Rge1 Nxc3 Bxc3.
student: By retreating the bishop to c2 White preserves the powerful bishop‑pair and keeps the advanced passed pawn on g6 alive while Black’s bishop on g7 remains without safe squares. The engine rates Bc2 as the best continuation, even though it costs White roughly four‑tenths of a pawn in evaluation. Black can answer with Rh3, which would remove the immediate threat to the rook on h3, after which White could continue with Rge1 and later capture on c3.

teacher: White captures the knight on f5, creating a fork on Black’s rook h3 and pawn e6, but Black can simply answer Rxf5, eliminating the fork and giving up the bishop pair. By removing the active knight and keeping the powerful passed pawn on g6, White’s position is nudged a little higher, the evaluation climbing from about a third of a pawn to roughly half a pawn in White’s favour. The engine’s top‑ranking alternative was Be1, yet Bxf5 still improves the score by about a seventh of a pawn despite the inevitable exchange.
student: By playing Bxf5 White eliminates Black’s active knight on f5 and simultaneously creates a fork on the rook on h3 and the pawn on e6, forcing Black to answer with Rxf5. After the forced exchange White loses the bishop pair but retains the advanced passed pawn on g6 and the fact that Black’s bishop on g7 has no safe squares, which together keep the slight edge. The engine rates the capture as a modest improvement – about a sixth of a pawn – yet it is not the top choice; Be1 would have preserved the bishop pair without giving up the material gain.

teacher: By playing …Rxf5 Black eliminates White’s bishop on f5 and at the same time removes the immediate threat to the e‑6 pawn and the rook on h3. The capture also leaves Black with an active rook on the semi‑open f‑file, while White is reduced to a single bishop on d2. White still enjoys a slight material edge and an advanced passed pawn on g6, but the exchange costs Black virtually nothing – the evaluation remains at about +0.5 for White, a change of only +0.04 pawns. For these reasons the engine rates …Rxf5 as the best move.
student: By playing Rxf5 Black eliminates White’s active bishop on f5, thereby removing the immediate threats to the e‑pawn and the rook on h3. The capture also leaves Black with a semi‑open f‑file that his rook can use while White remains down a piece, so the engine still judges the position as only marginally better for White (+0.47). Although White now holds a small material edge, the move keeps the balance essentially unchanged, justifying its “best” label.

teacher: White’s 35.Nh4 is a subtle invitation to Black’s rook: by landing on h4 the knight tempts …R3xh4, which would fork the h‑ and f‑pawns but simultaneously leaves the attacking rook itself en prise. After the capture White can answer Bxh4 and then Rxh4, after which the rook can swing to f1, preserving the extra pawn and keeping the powerful passed g‑pawn alive while Black’s bishop on g7 remains cramped. The move therefore maintains the roughly equal evaluation, but it secures White’s material edge and exploits the limited squares available to Black’s pieces.
student: White’s knight jump to h4 is the engine‑recommended continuation, even though it leaves the f‑pawn hanging. Black could reply …R3xh4, which would fork the h2‑pawn and the newly placed f4‑pawn while also threatening immediate mating threats such as Rxh2#. After the forced exchange White recaptures Bxh4 and then plays Rgf1, keeping the balance despite being a pawn ahead. The move therefore preserves equality in this endgame, where White already enjoys an advanced passed pawn on g6 and a rook dominating the open d‑file.

teacher: By playing Rgf1 White eliminates the immediate threat to the pawn on f4, allowing the advanced passed pawn on g6 to stay alive without having to be defended by the rook on d1. In this rook‑and‑minor‑piece ending Black’s bishop on g7 is confined to its only safe square, while White’s pieces remain harmoniously placed. The engine rates the move as the best, keeping the evaluation at equality. Black could reply Kg8, after which White can continue f5, then Bxe5 and fxe6, preserving the balance.
student: By playing Rgf1 White eliminates Black’s immediate pressure on the f‑pawn, thereby preserving the balance in this rook‑and‑minor‑piece ending where White already enjoys an advanced passed pawn on g6 while Black’s bishop on g7 is cramped to its sole safe square. The engine rates the move as the best choice, leaving the evaluation at equality despite material being level. In the principal variation Black would reply Kg8, after which White can continue with f5, keeping the tension alive without conceding any advantage.

teacher: Black’s retreat Bf8 is a clear mistake: the bishop already has only two safe squares and the move does nothing to stop White’s dangerous passed pawn on g6. By stepping back, Black allows White to play the pawn break f5, striking at the e‑6 pawn and activating the majority, which the engine evaluates as giving White almost two pawns of advantage. The engine’s preferred move was Kg8, which would have kept the king on a safer square and avoided the costly pawn break.
student: By retreating the bishop to f8 Black leaves it with only two safe squares in this rook‑and‑minor‑piece ending where White already boasts an advanced passed pawn on g6. The engine shows that the far stronger continuation would have been Kg8, keeping the king active and preserving equality. After …Bf8 White can immediately strike with f5, attacking the e6 pawn and exploiting the cramped bishop, which pushes the evaluation to about +1.8 for White – roughly a pawn’s worth of advantage. In short, the retreat costs Black about one pawn and hands White a clear edge.

teacher: White pushes f5, a pawn break that strikes at Black’s e6 pawn and pushes forward the kingside majority of four pawns against Black’s two. The advance also leaves Black’s bishop on f8 with only two safe squares while White’s passed pawn on g6 already looms deep in Black’s camp. Black’s most forcing reply would be Ne3, forking the rooks on d1 and f1, yet even after that tactic White’s evaluation remains around +1.8 pawns, confirming f5 as the best continuation.
student: White’s pawn thrust f5 is a sharp break that strikes directly at Black’s e‑pawn and pushes the four‑pawn kingside majority forward. In this rook‑and‑minor‑piece ending it also leaves Black’s bishop on f8 with very few safe squares while White’s own passed pawn on g6 remains far advanced. The engine rates the move as the best continuation, keeping White’s advantage essentially unchanged at about +1.9 pawns. Black could try Ne3, forking the rooks on d1 and f1, but even after that White can meet the threat with Rd8 and later capture on f8, preserving the edge.

teacher: Black’s …Ne3 jumps into the enemy camp and forks White’s rooks on d1 and f1, exploiting the cramped bishop on f8 that has only two safe squares. White can meet the threat precisely with 38.Rd8, attacking the bishop on f8 and removing the danger to the d‑file; after the natural continuation …Nxf5 39.Rxf8+ Kg7 the material balance is unchanged and White still enjoys a clear pawn‑plus advantage. The move therefore fulfills its tactical idea but does not alter the overall evaluation, which remains a little under two pawns in White’s favour.
student: By jumping to e3 Black creates a fork, attacking both White’s rooks on d1 and f1 at once. The engine rates it as the best continuation, even though the evaluation stays around +1.9 for White because White can answer with Rd8, pinning the bishop on f8 to the king and removing the immediate danger to the rook on d8. After that reply Black would be able to capture on f5, after which White could continue with Rxf8+, but the material balance remains equal and the position stays clearly in White’s favour.
violations: mentions two rooks, but the mover has 1

teacher: White’s pawn push f6 creates a passed pawn on the f‑file and, with the rook on d8 pinning Black’s bishop on f8, threatens an immediate mate by Rxf8#. By advancing the kingside pawn majority (four pawns against Black’s two) and eliminating the previous danger to the f‑pawn, White not only consolidates the attack but also improves the engine’s assessment by roughly a pawn, raising the advantage to a decisive level. It is therefore rightly marked as the best move in the position.
student: By pushing f6 White creates a direct mating threat – Black’s king must answer Kg8, after which White can capture on f8 with check, delivering mate. The advance also bolsters the already‑advanced passed pawn on f6 while advancing the four‑pawn kingside majority against Black’s two. With the rook on d8 pinning the black bishop to the king, Black has no legal way to stop the attack, and the engine rates the move as improving White’s evaluation by about a pawn. In this rook‑and‑minor‑piece ending the move therefore secures a decisive advantage for White.

teacher: By playing Rxh2+ Black does win a pawn, but the check opens the h‑file for White and shatters the pawn shield in front of the white king. White can meet the check with Kg1, after which Black’s rook is forced to the second rank and White immediately threatens the winning mate Rxf8#. The engine’s preferred move was Kg8, which would have avoided this weakening and kept the evaluation roughly unchanged; instead the capture worsens Black’s position by about two pawns. Thus the material gain is far outweighed by the loss of defensive resources, making the move a clear mistake.
student: By playing Rxh2+ Black wins a pawn but immediately hands White a clear mating threat. After the capture White can answer Kg1, which would threaten Rxf8# and turn the already decisive White edge into a crushing one – roughly a two‑pawn swing against Black’s six‑point material lead. The engine rates the move as a mistake, costing about a pawn compared with the safer Kg8, which would have kept the evaluation much more favorable for Black. In this rook‑and‑minor‑piece ending the new passed pawn on h6 does not compensate for the loss of tempo.

teacher: By retreating the king to g8 Black not only missed the immediate checking fork Rg2+, but also allowed White’s rook on d8 to pin the bishop on f8, further restricting Black’s pieces. The engine rates the move as a mistake, worsening Black’s position by about one‑and‑a‑half pawns and increasing White’s decisive advantage to roughly eleven pawns. In contrast, Rg2+ would have given check and created a fork of the king and the g‑pawn, offering Black the best practical chances. This passive king move therefore deepens White’s winning edge despite Black’s material lead.
student: By moving the king to g8 Black walks into White’s pin on the f‑file – the white rook now attacks the black king while the bishop on f8 remains immobilised by the pin. This allows White to continue with g7, after which Black would have to capture the rook with check, but the resulting line leaves Black still down about one and a half pawns in a position where White already enjoys a decisive edge. The engine indicates that the far stronger try was Rg2+, a checking fork that would hit both the white king on g1 and the pawn on g6 even though the rook would become en prise. Consequently, Kg8 costs Black roughly two pawns of evaluation and is rightly judged a mistake.

teacher: By advancing the pawn to g7 White creates a passed pawn that, together with the f‑pawn, locks down the kingside and forces a forced mate in 13. The rook on d8 already pins the black bishop on f8, so Black cannot stop the pawn’s promotion; even the only realistic try …Rg2+ (which leaves the checking rook en prise) is met by Kxg2 Kf7 gxf8=Q+, after which the new queen delivers the decisive blow. The move therefore turns a material deficit into a decisive forced checkmate, justifying the !! annotation.
student: By pushing g7 White creates a second passed pawn and strengthens his three‑pawn kingside majority, while the rook on d8 continues to pin Black’s bishop on f8 to the king on g8. This advance forces a forced mating net: after Black’s best reply Rg2+ the rook lands on g2 where it is immediately taken by the white king, then White can continue with Kf7 and finally capture the queen on f8 with checkmate in thirteen moves. The engine rates the move as the best possible, converting a decisive material edge into a win that would otherwise have been impossible.
violations: names a queen on f8, but there is none

teacher: Black’s 43…Ne3+ is a serious blunder: instead of trying to keep the forced mate at twelve moves, the checking knight actually shortens White’s winning sequence to six moves. Although the move does give check and removes the immediate threat to the knight on e3, it does nothing to stop White’s overwhelming attack in this rook‑and‑minor‑piece ending, where the white rook on d8 pins the black bishop and White’s passed f‑ and g‑pawns are already marching forward. The engine’s top choice, 43…Kf7, would have kept the mate at twelve, but the knight check hands White a much quicker win despite Black being up a pawn.
student: Black’s Ne3+ does give a check while removing the immediate danger to the knight, but it fatally shortens White’s winning line from a forced mate in twelve to just six moves. After the check White can simply play Kf3, forcing Black’s king back with …Kf7, then capture on f8 with check and continue Kg6, leaving White with a decisive attack. The engine indicates that the correct defence was Kf7, which would have kept the mating net far longer. Consequently, Ne3+ is a clear blunder, costing Black about half a move of life.

teacher: Black meets White’s flank opening with the central thrust …e5, which the engine rates as the strongest reply and leaves the evaluation essentially unchanged at roughly equal. By contesting the centre immediately, Black maintains material balance and keeps the position balanced. The engine’s principal variation suggests White will likely continue 2.g3, after which Black can develop …Nf6 and …Nc6, preserving the equality.
student: Black answers with …e5, the engine’s top choice and the most accurate continuation in this opening. The pawn push leaves material perfectly balanced and keeps the evaluation at roughly +0.1 pawn for White, so the balance of the position is preserved. According to the principal variation, White would likely continue with g3, after which Black can develop with Nf6 and later bring the knight back to c6, maintaining equality.

teacher: Black’s …Nf6 modestly improves his standing, cutting White’s edge from roughly two‑thirds of a pawn to just over half a pawn.
