The move is solid, but the engine indicates that …g6 would have been even more accurate. Consequently, while …Nf6 is a respectable choice, it leaves Black a little worse than the optimal continuation.
student: Black’s …Nf6 simply develops the knight to its natural square and nudges the evaluation in Black’s favour by roughly a tenth of a pawn, shrinking White’s lead from about +0.66 to +0.54. The engine still prefers the more active …g6, which would have kept the pressure a little higher, but …Nf6 is a perfectly sound developing move that improves Black’s standing without creating any new weaknesses. In the principal variation White could continue with e3, after which Black would reply …Nc6 and later play g6, preserving the modest edge.

teacher: White places his knight on e2, keeping material even and nudging the evaluation up from a clear +0.76 to about +0.93, a modest but tangible gain. The engine confirms it as the best continuation, and after Black’s most natural reply …Be6 White can press in the centre with d4; if Black captures, White recaptures with exd4, preserving the advantage. This line shows why the move is rated a brilliant !!.
student: White’s knight jumps to e2, nudging the evaluation up by roughly a sixth of a pawn and confirming it as the clear best continuation. The engine rates the move as “best” and notes that Black’s most natural reply would be …Be6, after which White can continue with d4, keeping the initiative. In short, Nge2 preserves White’s modest edge while preparing the central thrust that follows in the principal variation.

teacher: Black’s bishop on c8 is cramped, with only two safe squares, so the quiet retreat Bd8 simply puts the bishop on a secure post and leaves the material balance untouched – White still enjoys a modest advantage of roughly a pawn. The engine rates the move as the best, and the line it suggests continues with White’s Nec3, Black’s Be6, White’s Qe2 and Black’s Rc8.
student: By retreating the bishop to d8 Black places it on one of its only two safe squares while preserving material equality and leaving the engine’s assessment virtually untouched – White remains about a pawn ahead. The move therefore keeps the balance as closely as possible for Black in this middlegame position. According to the engine, White can continue with Nec3, after which Black would answer …Be6, followed by Qe2 and Rc8.

teacher: White launches the pawn break b4, striking at Black’s c5 pawn and, after the natural capture cxb4, makes the b‑file semi‑open for his rooks while handing Black doubled pawns on that file and leaving White with an isolated a‑pawn. Although the break creates a semi‑open line for White, it does not improve the evaluation – the engine’s assessment falls from about a pawn’s worth to just under one, a loss of roughly 0.2 pawns. The engine judged Nec3 to be a stronger continuation, which would have preserved more of White’s advantage. Black can simply capture on b4 with cxb4, after which the structural changes described above materialise.
student: White launches the thematic pawn break b4, aiming to strike at Black’s pawn on c5 and open the b‑file while leaving Black with a semi‑open c‑file. After the natural reply cxb4, White can recapture with axb4, but the exchange leaves White with an isolated pawn on a3 and gives Black doubled b‑pawns, which explains why the engine’s evaluation drops by roughly a fifth of a pawn. The move is still good – it creates concrete threats and improves White’s activity – yet it is not the most accurate continuation; Nec3 would have kept more pressure without conceding the structural weaknesses that follow the capture.

teacher: Black’s 13…b5 tries to open lines with a pawn break against White’s c4 pawn, but after the natural reply 14.cxb5 White simply captures and leaves Black with an isolated a‑pawn while the b‑file becomes semi‑open for Black and the c‑file for White. This exchange also gives White doubled pawns on the b‑file, yet the resulting structural imbalance is enough to push the evaluation from a slight White edge to a clear one‑pawn advantage, a moderate deterioration for Black. The engine points out that the more accurate 13…cxb4, which would have taken the pawn on b4, would have avoided this loss of ground. Consequently, although the move is not a blunder, it is inferior to the best alternative.
student: Black’s …b5 tries to open lines by striking at White’s c‑pawn, but after the natural reply cxb5 the b‑file becomes semi‑open for Black while White gains a semi‑open c‑file and ends up with doubled b‑pawns, leaving Black with an isolated a‑pawn. This structural concession costs Black roughly four‑tenths of a pawn, turning a slight White edge into a clear advantage. The engine judged that the more accurate continuation would have been …cxb4, which simply removes the b‑pawn without creating these new weaknesses. Consequently, despite being “good”, the move moderately worsened Black’s position.

teacher: By playing …Rxb5 Black merely captured the pawn on b5 and removed the immediate threat to the knight on c6, but he completely ignored White’s dominant knight on d5. The engine’s preferred move, 14…Nxd5, would have eliminated that knight and kept the balance, whereas …Rxb5 lets White’s advantage swell from roughly +¾ of a pawn to almost +2 pawns – a loss of about a pawn for Black. Although the rook now occupies the semi‑open b‑file, this activity does not offset the missed tactical shot, making the move a clear mistake (?).
student: By playing Rxb5 Black eliminates White’s immediate pressure on the knight on c6 and wins the pawn on b5, but the capture does nothing to stop White’s active pieces. The engine shows that this costs Black roughly a pawn‑and‑a‑half, turning an already modest White edge into a clear advantage. A far stronger continuation would have been Nxd5, which captures the white knight on d5 and keeps material balanced. Consequently, the rook grab is a mistake that hands White a comfortable lead.

teacher: The knight retreat to c3 looks natural but it simply lets Black neutralise the pressure on the semi‑open b‑file. After 15.Nec3 Black can answer with …Rb8, removing the threat to the rook on b8 while White’s bishop on b2 still has only one safe square, and the evaluation drops from a clear +1.9 pawn to about +0.9 – roughly a pawn’s worth of advantage lost. The engine’s preferred move was 15.Qa4, which would have preserved White’s edge. Consequently the move is rightly marked as a mistake.
student: White’s retreat Nec3 does nothing to relieve the pressure on his cramped bishop on b2 or to stop Black’s active rook on the semi‑open b‑file, and it allows Black to meet the move with …Rb8, removing the immediate danger to that rook. After …Rb8 White can capture on f6, but Black recaptures with Bxf6, leaving White still down roughly a pawn in evaluation despite being “clearly better” before the move. The engine rates Qa4 as the correct continuation, preserving White’s advantage without conceding material. Consequently Nec3 is a clear mistake, costing White about a pawn’s worth of standing.

teacher: White captures the knight on f6, using its fork on h7 and the queen on e8 to force a response. Black can answer with Bxf6, which eliminates the immediate threats but places the bishop on a cramped square with limited prospects. The move gives White a temporary material advantage of a piece, which is neutralised after Black’s recapture, and the engine’s evaluation only slips by about a tenth of a pawn, so White remains clearly better. In short, the move trades a piece while worsening Black’s piece placement and preserves White’s advantage.
student: By taking on f6 White not only wins a piece but also creates a fork, attacking both the pawn on h7 and Black’s queen on e8 while the knight lands on a square that limits Black’s pieces – the black knight on c6 already has only one safe retreat and the bishop on f6 will soon have few useful squares after the forced …Bxf6. After the natural reply Bxf6, the fork disappears and the material balance is restored, leaving White still a little better (about three‑quarters of a pawn). The engine rates the capture as the best continuation, with the evaluation remaining essentially unchanged at roughly +0.6.

teacher: By retreating the bishop to d8, Black secures the only safe square for the knight on c6 while keeping the rook on the semi‑open b‑file fully active. The move also restricts White’s bishop on b2, which now has only two safe squares, and leaves the balance of material untouched, so the evaluation stays at roughly a pawn’s worth in White’s favour. The engine notes that White could answer with fxe5, but Black’s position remains solid and the move is judged excellent.
student: By retreating the bishop to d8 Black preserves the balance in this position, keeping material equal and leaving White’s modest edge virtually unchanged at roughly +0.68 pawn. The retreat also respects the fact that Black’s knight on c6 has only one safe square while the rook on b8 already enjoys the semi‑open b‑file. If White were to capture on e5 with fxe5, Black can recapture Nxe5 and continue with …Qc2, maintaining the pressure without worsening his standing. This precise defensive resource earns the engine’s “excellent” rating.

teacher: By pushing …e4 Black freezes White’s pawn chain on dark squares and cramps the bishop on g2, which now has very few useful diagonals. The advance also leaves the g7‑pawn technically en prise, but White’s bishop on c3 pins it to the king on h8, so the pawn cannot legally move. This subtle restriction improves Black’s standing by about a tenth of a pawn, as reflected in the evaluation swing. White could try the pawn break d3 to challenge the e4‑pawn, but Black’s position remains slightly better.
student: By pushing …e4 Black not only attacks White’s central pawn but also fixes it on a dark square and leaves the g‑pawn hanging, while White’s bishop on g2 becomes cramped with few useful retreats. The engine rates the move as the best, improving Black’s standing by roughly a tenth of a pawn even though the pawn on g7 remains temporarily vulnerable. White can try the thematic pawn break d3, striking at the new e‑pawn, after which Black would continue with …Ba6 and later capture on e4, keeping the pressure alive.

teacher: White captures on c5, but Black can simply recapture with …dxc5, opening the b‑file for White while the d‑file becomes semi‑open for Black. The exchange restores material balance, leaves White with an isolated pawn on a3 and gives Black an isolated pawn on c5, which together push the evaluation a little further in Black’s favour. The engine rates the move only as good and points out that the stronger continuation would have been the pawn break d3, directly challenging Black’s e4 pawn. As a result White’s choice costs roughly a sixth of a pawn compared with the optimal line.
student: By playing bxc5 White opens the b‑file and gives Black a semi‑open d‑file after the forced …dxc5, but the capture also leaves White with an isolated pawn on a3 while Black’s pawn on c5 becomes isolated. The engine rates the move as “good” yet notes that it costs about a sixth of a pawn compared with the optimal continuation, which would have been the pawn break d3 striking at Black’s e4 pawn. After the natural reply …dxc5 the evaluation slips further in Black’s favour, confirming that the exchange does not improve White’s standing despite gaining a pawn.

teacher: White’s capture on c6 creates a tempting fork on a7 and the rook on b8, but the knight can be taken immediately, and after Black’s natural …Qxc6 the material balance is restored, leaving the position essentially equal (+0.02). The engine therefore rates the move as only “good” and notes a moderate drop of about a third of a pawn for White. A more accurate continuation would have been Na6, which would have forked the pawn on c5 and the rook on b8 while also eliminating the threat to the knight on a6. Thus, although the capture initiates an exchange, it forfeits White’s slight pre‑move edge.
student: White’s capture on c6 looks attractive at first glance – it forks Black’s a‑pawn and the rook on b8 – but after …Qxc6 the fork disappears and the material balance is restored, leaving the position essentially equal. The engine rates Na6 as the superior alternative because it would have created a similar fork on c5 while also removing the immediate danger to the knight on a6. By opting for Nxc6 instead, White gave up about a third of a pawn in evaluation, turning a slight edge into a roughly balanced game.

teacher: Black’s queen captures on c6, wiping out White’s knight and instantly eliminating the threat to the a7 pawn and the rook on b8. By removing that attacker, Black neutralises White’s pressure while keeping material level, and the engine still judges the position roughly equal, with only a tiny edge for Black. The exchange respects the locked pawn structure—White’s pawns are fixed on dark squares and Black’s on light squares—so no new weaknesses arise. Hence Qxc6 is rightly celebrated as the best move.
student: By playing …Qxc6 Black eliminates White’s active knight on c6, simultaneously removing the immediate danger to the a‑pawn and the rook that had been under attack. The capture restores material balance while leaving the position still roughly equal, as reflected by the tiny swing in the engine’s assessment. With White’s pawns locked on dark squares and the g7‑pawn pinned by the bishop on c3, Black’s pieces remain well‑placed, confirming the move as the clear best choice.

teacher: White slides the queen back to c2, a quiet move that leaves the pawn structure untouched – White’s dark‑square pawns stay fixed and the bishop on c3 continues to pin the g7‑pawn to the black king. The engine, however, points out that the move Rb1 would have been stronger, keeping the balance, whereas Qc2 lets Black gain a small edge (about a third of a pawn). Consequently White’s position is now slightly worse, though material remains equal.
student: White’s retreat Qc2 does little more than preserve the existing pin of the g‑pawn against Black’s king and leaves the material balance untouched. The engine rates it as a slight deterioration for White – about a third of a pawn – because the stronger continuation would have been Rb1, which keeps the pressure on Black’s queenside while improving piece coordination. After Qc2 Black can continue with …Bb3, after which White could try Qb2, but the evaluation remains in Black’s favour. Thus the move is good, yet not optimal compared with the suggested Rb1.

teacher: By playing …c4 Black creates an isolated pawn on c4, a structural weakness that costs him roughly a third of a pawn and turns his earlier slight edge into a roughly equal position. The move also leaves Black’s light‑square pawn chain fixed while White’s dark‑square pawns and the bishop on c3 keep the g7 pawn pinned to the king on h8, limiting Black’s counterplay. Although the move is still sound, the engine judged 22…Bb3 to be better, as it would have preserved Black’s modest advantage.
student: By pushing …c4 Black creates an isolated pawn on the fourth rank and gives White a clear target in the centre. The engine rates the move as “good” but notes that it costs Black about a third of a pawn compared with the optimal continuation …Bb3, which would have kept the slight edge. After …c4 White can reply Rfb1, after which Black’s best try would be …Rc8, yet the evaluation slides back to near equality despite material being unchanged. In short, the pawn push neutralises Black’s modest advantage while leaving the position roughly balanced.

teacher: White slides the rook from f1 to c1, simply joining the queen and bishop on the c‑file. The pawn structure stays the same and the bishop on c3 continues to pin the g7‑pawn, so the move creates no new threats and lets Black retain the comfortable balance, as reflected by the engine’s drop of roughly a tenth of a pawn (the evaluation moves from –0.03 to –0.15). The engine’s preferred continuation was 23.Rfb1, which would have moved the rook to the b‑file and preserved more flexibility. After 23.Rfc1 Black can answer with …Bg8, after which White’s best try is Be5, leading to an essentially equal position.
student: White’s rook slides to c1, keeping it active while the bishop on c3 continues to pin Black’s g‑pawn to the king. The engine still rates the position as roughly equal but notes that the move costs White about a tenth of a pawn compared with the optimal continuation Rfb1. In other words, Rfc1 is a solid choice, yet it is not the most accurate – the engine prefers the alternative rook lift to b1.

teacher: Black’s Bxc3 captures the white bishop on c3 and therefore starts the only sensible exchange in the position. After White’s expected Qxc3 the material balance is restored, but the trade eliminates both sides’ bishop pair – Black temporarily loses its pair while White gives up the bishop that had been on c3 – so the evaluation remains essentially unchanged, with Black still a fraction of a pawn better. In addition, the queen on c3 will pin the g7‑pawn to the black king, confirming the soundness of the exchange.
student: By taking on c3 Black eliminates White’s active bishop and forces an immediate queen exchange. After the inevitable Qxc3 the material balance is restored, but White surrenders the bishop pair while Black retains it, leaving both sides with their own bishops. The capture also leaves the g‑pawn pinned by the white queen, yet Black remains a shade better – roughly three‑tenths of a pawn – because his pieces stay well‑coordinated. This precise simplification makes Bxc3 an excellent continuation.

teacher: By capturing on c3 White eliminates Black’s active bishop and, with the queen now on c3, pins the g7‑pawn to the king on h8, removing the immediate threat to the rook on a1. The exchange also costs Black its bishop pair, leaving the remaining light‑squared bishop hemmed in by its own pawns while White’s dark‑square pawn structure stays solid. Black could answer with …Qd7, which would defend the pawn on g7, but even after that the engine still rates the position as only a slight edge for Black, meaning the move kept White’s evaluation essentially unchanged. Hence Qxc3 is an excellent, fully justified exchange.
student: By playing Qxc3 White eliminates Black’s active bishop and simultaneously pins the g‑pawn to the black king, thereby removing the immediate danger to the rook on a1. The capture also leaves material equal while preserving White’s dark‑square pawn structure, which fits with Black’s light‑squared bishop being cramped behind its own pawns. Black can reply with Qd7, which would relieve the pressure on the g7 pawn, but even after that continuation White remains a shade worse – the engine still evaluates the position as “slightly better for Black” (about three‑tenths of a pawn). This precise queen sacrifice therefore earns an excellent rating.

teacher: By shifting the rook to b5 Black simply places it on a useful square without disturbing the locked pawn structure, where White’s pawns sit on dark squares and Black’s on light squares and the light‑squared bishop remains hemmed in by its own pawns. The move leaves material unchanged and the engine’s assessment essentially the same (roughly equal +0.04), which is why it is judged the best. If White replies with the natural Rb2, Black can meet it with Rxb2, after which Qxb2 and a follow‑up …Rb8 keep the balance. In short, the rook move preserves equality in a position where neither side can generate new chances.
student: By playing …Rb5 Black finally brings his last heavy piece onto the board, directly challenging White’s queenside and exploiting the fact that White’s pawn chain is locked on dark squares while Black’s own pawns sit on light squares. The engine rates this as the best continuation, keeping the evaluation essentially unchanged at roughly equal. In the principal variation White would reply Rb2, after which Black can capture on b2 with the rook, then retreat to Rb8, preserving the balance. This precise placement of the rook neutralises any latent threats and maintains the equilibrium.

teacher: With the pawn structure locked—White’s pawns fixed on dark squares, Black’s on light squares and the light‑squared bishop hemmed in by its own pawns—Black’s 35…Rb3 simply re‑positions the rook to b3, preserving the material balance and leaving the evaluation unchanged. The engine rates this move as the best continuation, keeping the position roughly equal. In the principal line White can try 36 a5, Black answers 36…h5, White brings the other rook to c2 and Black steps the king to h7, and the balance remains.
student: By sliding the rook to b3 Black immediately attacks White’s king, exploiting the fact that White’s pawn chain is locked on dark squares while Black’s own pawns sit on light squares and the light‑squared bishop remains cramped behind its own pawns. The engine rates this as the best continuation, leaving the evaluation essentially unchanged at equality. In the principal line White could try a5, after which Black would answer with …h5, followed by …Rcc2 and a quiet king move to h7.

teacher: White’s 38.Rc3 looks natural, reinforcing the third rank, but it unintentionally leaves the d‑pawn undefended, so Black can now target that pawn and improve his already slight edge. The engine shows the position slipping from a −0.33 to a −0.46 pawn disadvantage – a modest worsening of about a tenth of a pawn – and rates the move only “good” rather than best. Given the fixed dark‑squared pawn chain for White, the light‑squared pawn chain for Black, and Black’s cramped light‑squared bishop, the move is not a blunder, but Kf2 would have been a stronger move and would have kept the evaluation a little more favorable for White.
student: White’s 38.Rc3 looks active but it leaves the pawn on d2 hanging, so Black can capture it and increase the pressure. The engine rates the move as a slight worsening for White – about a tenth of a pawn – because the evaluation slides from –0.33 to –0.46. A more accurate try would have been 38.Kf2, which keeps the king safer and avoids giving Black the immediate target on d2. After 38.Rc3 Black could continue with …h6, after which White might play R3c2, keeping the tension alive.

teacher: Black tried the pawn break 41…c3, hoping to strike at White’s d‑pawn and to uncover the bishop on f7 against the rook on a2. After the forced 42.dxc3 the d‑file opens and White gains a passed pawn on c3, while Black’s already cramped light‑squared bishop stays hemmed in. This exchange swings the evaluation from a slight Black edge to a clear White advantage of roughly a pawn. The engine’s best move was the quiet 41…h5, which would have kept Black’s modest lead.
student: By playing …c3 Black tried to strike at White’s d‑pawn and uncover the bishop on f7 against the a2 rook, but the pawn push simply allows White to capture with dxc3, opening the c‑file for Black while giving White a passed pawn on c3. This exchange flips the evaluation from a slight Black edge to a clear White advantage – roughly a pawn’s worth – because the newly opened file gives White active play without compensating for the loss of material. The engine indicates that the more accurate continuation would have been …h5, which would have kept the balance instead of handing White the extra pawn. Consequently, …c3 is a mistake that costs Black about one and a half pawns of standing.

teacher: By capturing on c3 White eliminates Black’s advanced pawn, opens the d‑file and creates a passed pawn on c3, taking full advantage of Black’s light‑squared bishop being hemmed in by its own pawns. Although the capture leaves White with an isolated pawn on c3, the dynamic possibilities more than offset this static drawback, and the engine still judges the position about a pawn better for White, with the evaluation essentially unchanged. Black’s most natural reply would be …Rb3, removing the threat to the rook on b3, after which White can continue with Rd1, forcing an exchange on d1. This continuation preserves White’s clear edge and justifies the move’s “best !!” rating.
student: By playing dxc3 White opens the d‑file and creates a passed pawn on c3 while advancing his queenside majority, even though that pawn will be isolated. The capture also leaves Black’s light‑squared bishop cramped behind its own pawns, so the position remains favorable for White despite the slight structural concession. Black can answer with Rb3, which would remove the immediate pressure on the rook on b3, but White still enjoys a clear advantage of roughly a pawn. This precise pawn push therefore justifies the “best” label.

teacher: White’s 44 Rd1 is a solid, defensive resource that keeps the material edge and leaves the balance essentially unchanged, the evaluation slipping by only about a tenth of a pawn. By placing the rook behind White’s dark‑square pawn chain while Black’s light‑squared bishop remains hemmed in, the move does not create any immediate tactical threats but simply preserves the status quo. Engines, however, judge Rb1 to be the sharper continuation; after 44.Rd1 Black can capture with …Rxd1, after which White would recapture 45.Qxd1 and the line continues 45…Rxc3 46.Rxc3, leaving the material balance the same. Thus Rd1 is an excellent defensive move, even though it is not the absolute engine‑best.
student: White’s Rd1 simply preserves the balance – the engine still evaluates the position as roughly equal and even notes that the move leaves White a pawn ahead. By keeping the rook on the second rank, White maintains the pressure while Black’s light‑squared bishop remains cramped behind its own pawns. The engine preferred Rb1, but Rd1 is an excellent defensive resource that does not worsen White’s standing. If Black were to capture with …Rxd1, White could recapture with Qxd1 and continue with Rxc3 Rxc3, preserving the material edge.

teacher: White’s rook lifts to d4, removing the immediate threat to the pawn on e3. Although this solves the problem, the engine indicates that the queen move Qc1 would have done the same job more accurately, and the rook shift costs White about a quarter of a pawn of the earlier advantage. The position stays in White’s favour, with his dark‑squared pawn chain solid and Black’s light‑squared bishop still cramped behind its own pawns. Thus the move is good, but not the optimal choice.
student: White’s 45.Rd4 simply eliminates Black’s immediate pressure on the e‑pawn, removing the threat that had been looming over it. The engine still rates the position as slightly better for White – roughly three‑quarters of a pawn – but the evaluation drops by about a quarter pawn compared with the optimal continuation. The engine preferred 45.Qc1, which would have removed the same threat while keeping the advantage intact. In short, the move is solid and keeps White’s edge, yet it costs a modest amount of positional value.

teacher: Black captures the pawn on c3, placing his rook on c3 where it forks White’s rook on c2 and the pawn on e3 and opens the c‑file. Nevertheless, the move does nothing to relieve the cramped, “bad” light‑squared bishop or to change the fixed pawn structure, and the engine now judges White to be about a pawn better – a clear deterioration from the previous slight edge. The engine’s top choice, 45…Be6, would have kept the tension without conceding the fork and would have allowed Black to meet the natural 46.Rd8+ more resiliently. Thus 45…Rxc3 is an inaccuracy that costs Black roughly half a pawn of evaluation.
student: By playing Rxc3 Black wins the pawn on c3 but immediately creates a tactical liability: White can answer with Rd8+, checking the king while also leaving the rook on d8 and the pawn on e3 hanging. This reply turns an already slight White edge into a clear advantage of roughly a pawn’s worth, as reflected by the evaluation swing. The engine judged Be6 to be the correct continuation, which would have avoided the fork and kept material equal. Consequently, the capture is an inaccuracy that costs Black about half a pawn.

teacher: White captures the rook on c3, but the move merely starts an exchange; Black can answer with Qxc3, which both restores material balance and forks White’s queen on a1 and the pawn on e3. By allowing this queen fork, White’s modest lead of about a pawn disappears, and the position is evaluated as roughly equal. The engine’s preferred move, Rd8+, would have given check and left the white rook on d8 and the white pawn on e3 en prise, preserving White’s advantage. Hence 46.Rxc3 is an inaccuracy that costs White about three‑quarters of a pawn in evaluation.
student: By playing Rxc3 White simply trades a rook for Black’s rook, but the capture merely initiates an exchange that Black can answer with Qxc3, removing the threat to his queen while forking White’s queen on a1 and the pawn on e3. This concession erodes White’s earlier +0.9‑pawn edge, leaving the evaluation essentially level – a loss of about three‑quarters of a pawn. The engine’s preferred continuation was Rd8+, which would have kept the initiative with a checking rook and avoided the fork. Consequently, the move is marked as an inaccuracy.

teacher: White delivers check by sacrificing the queen on c3, a move that simultaneously forks the a5 pawn, Black’s king on g7 and the rook on c8. After the forced Rxc3 the queens disappear and the game slips into a rook‑and‑minor‑piece ending where the position remains roughly equal. The engine prefers Qd1, which would keep the queen on the board and avoid the exchange, but the alternative leaves the e3 pawn vulnerable and the evaluation difference is only about 0.05 pawns. In practice Black will capture with the rook, removing the fork and restoring material balance.
student: White’s capture Qxc3+ forces Black’s only sensible reply Rxc3, which both eliminates the fork and trades queens while leaving the material balance unchanged. After the forced exchange the game simplifies into a rook‑and‑minor‑piece ending where White retains his extra pawn advantage despite being down a queen. The engine rates the move as excellent because it keeps the evaluation essentially equal, but it notes that Qd1 would have been marginally stronger – it would have removed the threat to the rook on d8 and the queen on d1 without giving Black the immediate queen exchange. In short, the sacrifice costs White about half a pawn in evaluation, yet the resulting position remains roughly balanced.

teacher: White’s rook lifts to d7, pinning Black’s bishop on f7 to the king on g7 and thus freezing that piece completely. In this rook‑and‑minor‑piece ending, where White’s pawns sit on dark squares and Black’s on light, the pin leaves Black with very little active play. Black’s most accurate reply would be Rc2, which would pin White’s bishop on e2 to the king on f2, but White can answer with Ke1 and the position remains balanced, as the principal variation shows. Consequently, the move perfectly preserves the equality and is rightly judged the best move.
student: By playing Rd7 White places his rook directly behind Black’s bishop on f7, pinning it to the black king on g7 and rendering that piece immobile in this rook‑and‑minor‑piece ending where both sides’ pawn structures are locked on opposite colours. The engine rates the move as the best continuation, leaving the evaluation essentially unchanged at equality. Black could try Rc2, which would pin White’s bishop on e2 to the white king on f2, but even after that reply White remains balanced.

teacher: Black’s king steps to e7, preserving the delicate balance of this rook‑and‑minor‑piece ending in which White’s pawns sit on dark squares and Black’s on light squares. The move leaves material equal and the engine’s evaluation unchanged, confirming it as the strongest continuation. White could try Ra6, which would remove the pressure on the rook on a6, after which Black can meet the ensuing play with …Bb3 and keep the position level.
student: Black’s king steps back to e7, a safe square that leaves the material balance untouched in this rook‑and‑minor‑piece ending where White’s pawn chain sits on dark squares while Black’s is locked on light squares. The engine rates Ke7 as the best continuation, keeping the evaluation at equality. White can try Ra6, which would remove the immediate danger to the rook on a6, but after …Bb3 Black remains balanced with the same light‑square pawn structure.

teacher: By sliding the rook to a6 White eliminates the immediate danger to the piece, preserving the balance in this rook‑and‑minor‑piece ending. With both sides’ pawns locked on opposite colours—White’s on dark squares, Black’s on light—the move simply maintains the status quo, leaving the evaluation unchanged at equality. The engine confirms Ra6 as the optimal choice; Black’s most natural reply would be …Bb3, after which White can continue with Bb5, keeping the position level.
student: By sliding the rook back to a6 White eliminates Black’s immediate pressure on that piece, thereby preserving the balance in this rook‑and‑minor‑piece ending where both sides’ pawn structures are locked on opposite colours. The engine rates Ra6 as the best continuation, leaving the evaluation at roughly equal despite material being level. In the principal variation Black would continue with …Bb3, after which White can answer Bb5 and later bring the rook to a7+, keeping the position stable.

teacher: By moving the rook to c2 Black pins White’s bishop on e2 to the king on f2, so the bishop cannot legally move without exposing the king. This simple resource holds the balance in the rook‑and‑minor‑piece ending, as the engine’s evaluation stays at zero and material remains equal. Although the engine’s top choice would be 51…Bb3, the rook move is still strong enough that White’s most forcing reply, 52.Ra7+ (checking and forking the a‑pawn and king), only leads to a checked sequence that returns to an equal position after …Kf6 and …Bb3. Thus 51…Rc2 is a solid, best‑in‑spirit move that keeps the game level.
student: By playing Rc2 Black places his rook on the second rank where it pins White’s bishop on e2 against the king on f2, so the bishop cannot move without exposing the king. In this rook‑and‑minor‑piece ending – with White’s pawns locked on dark squares and Black’s on light – the pin neutralises any immediate threats while keeping material balanced. The engine rates the move as “best” but notes that Bb3 would have been marginally stronger, because after Rc2 White can try the forcing line Ra7+, checking the king and forking the a‑pawn and the king, yet Black still retains equality.

teacher: By playing Ke1 White walks into a decisive tactical shot: Black can answer with Rxe2+, checking the king and simultaneously forking the king on e1, the h‑pawn and the e‑pawn, leaving the rook on e2 en prise but winning material. The engine’s evaluation swings from equality to a roughly five‑pawn advantage for Black, turning the balanced rook‑and‑minor‑piece ending into a winning one. White’s alternative, Ra7+, would have given a checking fork on the a‑pawn and Black’s king, preserving equality. In this endgame with White’s pawns fixed on dark squares and Black’s on light squares, the king move was a clear blunder.
student: White’s retreat to e1 is a serious blunder that turns an equal rook‑and‑minor‑piece ending into a clearly winning one for Black. By moving the king instead of checking with Ra7+, White missed the tactical shot that would have forked the black king on e7 and the a‑pawn, allowing Black to reply Rxe2+ with a double attack on the white king, the h‑pawn and the e‑pawn. After the forced line Rxe2+ Kd1 Bb3+ Kxe2, Black emerges with a decisive edge – roughly five pawns in evaluation. The engine’s best continuation was Ra7+, which would have kept the balance.

teacher: By capturing on e2 Black not only wins a bishop but also checks the white king while simultaneously forking the king, the h‑pawn and the e‑pawn. The rook on e2 is left en prise, yet the move preserves Black’s decisive material edge—only a tiny drop of roughly a tenth of a pawn in the engine’s score. In the ensuing line White’s king must step to d1, after which Black can continue with a bishop check such as Bb3+, keeping the initiative in this rook‑and‑minor‑piece ending.
student: By playing Rxe2+ Black wins the white bishop with check, creating a fork that attacks the king on e1, the pawn on h2 and the pawn on e3 while also leaving the rook on e2 temporarily en prise. The capture preserves Black’s decisive material edge in this rook‑and‑minor‑piece ending, where White’s pawns sit on dark squares and Black’s on light squares. Although the engine notes a slight dip of about a tenth of a pawn, the move remains the best continuation and keeps Black clearly ahead.

teacher: White captures the rook on e2, removing the immediate threat to the e‑3 and h2 pawns, but by stepping onto e2 the king walks into a checking fork after …Bc4+, which attacks both the king and the rook on a6. This allows Black to win back material and pushes the evaluation from a decisive Black advantage of about five pawns to an even larger gap of roughly six pawns – a deterioration of about a pawn and a half for White. The engine’s preferred move, Kd1, would have avoided the fork and kept White’s material edge. In the main line Black can continue with Bc4+ and then Bxa6, regaining the exchange and leaving White in a losing endgame.
student: By playing Kxe2 White wins the rook but immediately walks into Black’s tactical shot …Bc4+, forking the king on e2 and the rook on a6. The engine shows that this fork pushes the evaluation down by roughly a pawn, turning an already losing position into one where Black enjoys a decisive edge. The correct continuation would have been Kd1, which keeps the king out of danger and preserves White’s chances. Consequently, the capture costs White about a pawn in practical terms.

teacher: White opens with 1 e4, a classic central thrust that preserves the slight edge the position already afforded (+0.29 → +0.35, essentially unchanged). The engine rates it as the best move, improving White’s standing by about 0.06 pawn. If Black replies naturally with 1…c5, the usual continuation would be 2 Nf3 Nc6 3 c3, leading to an open‑game structure.
student: White opens with e4, keeping the modest edge that existed before the game and even nudging it up to roughly three‑tenths of a pawn. The engine rates this as the best continuation, noting that Black’s most natural reply would be …c5, after which White can develop with Nf3 and later bring the c‑pawn into play. In short, the move preserves White’s slight advantage without creating any new weaknesses.

teacher: Black meets 1.e4 with 1…c5, the engine’s top reply, keeping material equal. The evaluation slides from a slight White edge of +0.35 to +0.47, meaning the move costs Black about a tenth of a pawn. From here the game can continue in a typical Sicilian fashion with 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bb5 Nf6.
student: Black’s reply …c5 is the engine‑recommended continuation and keeps material equal while preserving the balance of the opening. The evaluation shifts only marginally – White remains a little better, about four‑tenths of a pawn – so the move does not worsen Black’s standing but also does not improve it. In the principal variation White would develop with Nf3, after which Black can continue …Nc6, followed by Bb5 and Nf6.

teacher: White seizes the initiative with the thematic pawn break d4, striking directly at Black’s pawn on c5. Black can answer cxd4, which opens the c‑file for Black but gives White a half‑open d‑file and leaves Black with doubled pawns on that file – a clear structural concession. The engine rates the move as excellent, and the evaluation stays essentially unchanged, confirming that White has preserved his slight edge without losing anything.
student: White strikes in the centre with d4, directly challenging Black’s pawn on c5 and opening lines that will be useful later. If Black replies cxd4, the exchange leaves Black with doubled pawns on the d‑file while the c‑file becomes semi‑open for Black, giving White active play along the d‑file. The engine rates the move as excellent and the best continuation, keeping White’s slight edge essentially unchanged.

teacher: Black removes White’s central pawn with …cxd4, opening the c‑file for Black while, after White’s forced Nxd4, giving White a semi‑open d‑file. The capture technically puts Black a pawn up, but White’s recapture restores material balance, so the engine’s evaluation stays essentially unchanged and White remains only a fraction of a pawn better. The natural continuation Nxd4 Nf6 … follows the principal variation, keeping the position balanced.
student: By playing …cxd4 Black eliminates White’s central pawn and forces the natural reply Nxd4, which opens the c‑file for Black while giving White a semi‑open d‑file. The capture therefore initiates an exchange that leaves the overall assessment unchanged – White remains only a fraction of a pawn ahead – but it secures a temporary material edge for Black before the forced recapture. In the engine line White would take back with Nxd4, after which Black can continue with …Nf6, keeping the position balanced despite the slight disadvantage.

teacher: Black answered with the modest pawn move a6, the only reasonable continuation that keeps material balanced. The engine’s evaluation shifts from a small White edge to a clearer one (about a pawn’s worth), meaning the move cost Black roughly two‑tenths of a pawn. Nevertheless, it is still the best move available; the engine expects White to continue with Be3, after which Black can reply e5, followed by Nb3 and Be7 in the principal line.
student: Black’s …a6 is the engine‑recommended reply, keeping material equal and preserving the balance in this opening. The evaluation shifts from White being “slightly better” to “clearly better”, roughly a pawn’s worth, so the move costs Black about two‑tenths of a pawn compared with the previous position. Nevertheless it is still judged good because it does not create any new weaknesses or concessions. In the principal variation White would continue with Be3, after which Black can answer …e5 and later bring the bishop back to e7.

teacher: Black’s 7…g6 is an inaccuracy that lets White’s edge grow from a modest +0.29 to a clear +0.87, a swing of about half a pawn. The move does nothing to meet the looming threat to the f7‑pawn; the engine’s top choice was 7…e6, which would have removed that danger. As a result White can continue with Bg5 (the principal‑variation continuation), preserving the pressure and solidifying the larger advantage.
student: Black’s …g6 does nothing to meet White’s pressure and simply allows White to increase the edge, as the evaluation jumps from a slight White advantage to roughly a pawn’s worth. The engine points out that the more accurate reply would have been …e6, which would have removed the threat to the f‑pawn and kept the balance. By playing …g6 instead, Black’s position slipped by about half a pawn in the assessment.

teacher: White completes development by placing the dark‑squared bishop on e3, the engine’s top choice in the position. The move leaves the evaluation virtually unchanged, keeping White about a pawn ahead. Black would most naturally reply …Bd7, after which White can continue with Qd2 and later castle long, preserving the modest but clear advantage.
student: White’s bishop retreats to e3, keeping the modest edge that existed after Black’s …Bh7 and preserving the roughly pawn‑size advantage. The engine rates it as an excellent continuation, with the evaluation slipping by only three hundredths of a pawn – essentially unchanged from +0.81 to +0.78. In the principal line Black would reply …Bd7, after which White can meet it with Qd2 and continue development without losing ground.

teacher: Black’s knight moves to d7, a safe developing square that does not further restrict the already cramped bishops on b7 and g7. The move nudges the evaluation in Black’s favour by roughly a tenth of a pawn, cutting White’s lead from about +0.63 to +0.51. While solid, the engine still prefers Nc6 as the optimal continuation, but Nbd7 remains a sound choice that modestly improves Black’s position.
student: By developing the knight to d7 Black brings another piece into play while keeping the cramped bishops on their limited squares – each now has only two safe retreats. The engine rates the move as a modest improvement for Black, shaving roughly a tenth of a pawn off White’s advantage and leaving material equal. Nevertheless, the engine preferred Nc6, which would have been marginally stronger. In practice the move solidifies Black’s position without creating new weaknesses.

teacher: White’s queen retreat to e2 turns a modest plus into a clear minus, worsening the evaluation by about a pawn and a half. By abandoning the d‑file, White leaves the knight on d4 – which has only one safe square – vulnerable, and Black can immediately strike with …e5, forcing the knight to capture on b5 and after …axb5 Black can comfortably castle long. The engine’s preferred move was 11.Qd2, which would have kept the position more balanced. As a result, the move costs White roughly one and a half pawns in the assessment.
student: White’s retreat Qe2 does nothing to improve his cramped pieces – Black’s bishops remain confined to just two safe squares each and White’s knight on d4 still has only one safe haven – so the evaluation swings from a slight edge for White to a clear advantage for Black. The engine shows that the far stronger continuation would have been Qd2, which keeps the pressure on Black’s queenside while preserving White’s modest lead. By playing Qe2 instead, White allows Black to consolidate with …e5, after which White could try Ndxb5 but loses material in the ensuing exchange, leaving Black comfortably better.

teacher: By taking on c3 White wins the rook and opens the b‑file, giving a clear material edge of two pawns. The capture, however, leaves White with isolated pawns on a3, c2 and c3 and doubled pawns on the c‑file, weakening the pawn shield in front of the castled king. Black can immediately exploit the new weaknesses with …Qa5, forking the a‑ and c‑pawns and generating dangerous pressure. Nevertheless, the rook win outweighs the structural drawbacks, making bxc3 the best continuation.
student: By playing bxc3 White wins the rook on c3, but the capture leaves him with isolated and doubled pawns on the c‑file and weakens the pawn shield in front of his king. The engine rates the move as good even though it costs roughly four‑tenths of a pawn, because Black’s most natural reply would be …Qa5, which would fork the a3‑pawn and the newly created c3‑pawn. After that continuation White can continue with Kb2, then castle and later play h4, keeping the pressure despite the structural weaknesses.

teacher: Black’s queen jumps to a5, forking White’s a‑pawn and c‑pawn and forcing White to deal with the double attack. The move costs Black a small amount of the edge—its evaluation drops from about a pawn’s worth to a little less than a pawn—but it remains the strongest continuation in a position where Black’s king is still in the centre and the g7‑bishop has limited safe squares. The most natural follow‑up would see White’s king step to b2, after which Black can continue with …Nb6, …Qf2 and eventually bring the king to safety by castling.
student: By playing …Qa5 Black creates a powerful fork, attacking both the a‑pawn and the c‑pawn at once. The engine rates it as the best continuation even though the evaluation slips by roughly a fifth of a pawn because Black’s king remains in the centre while White already enjoys a clear edge. In the principal line White would reply Kb2, after which Black can continue with …Nb6, keeping the initiative alive.

teacher: White’s 15 Ba2 creates a pin on the f7‑pawn, but the move misplaces the bishop and gives Black the tempo to improve. After the natural reply …Rc8 the f7‑pawn becomes en prise, and the engine now judges the position as about a pawn and a half better for Black despite White’s material edge. The engine’s top alternative was the pawn thrust 15 h4, which would have kept the tension without allowing …Rc8. Thus Ba2 is a clear mistake, costing White roughly a full pawn in the evaluation.
student: By playing Ba2 White creates a pin of the f‑pawn against Black’s king, but the move does nothing to stop Black’s active pieces and actually lets Black improve his position. After the natural reply …Rc8 the pawn on f7 becomes en prise, allowing Black to consolidate his advantage – the evaluation swings from a slight edge for Black to a clear one‑and‑a‑half‑pawn lead. The engine indicates that the correct continuation was h4, which would have kept the balance, whereas Ba2 costs roughly a pawn in practical terms.

teacher: White’s knight hops to b3, eliminating the direct threat to the pawn on c3. By securing that pawn, White preserves the semi‑open d‑file for the rook, while Black’s bishop on g7 remains limited to only two safe squares and White’s own bishop on a2 still lacks a safe haven. The engine still judges the position clearly better for Black and the move costs White roughly a sixth of a pawn, but it is the best move available, earning a “good” assessment.
student: By retreating the knight to b3 White eliminates Black’s immediate pressure on the c‑pawn, thereby preserving the extra pawn and keeping the rook active on the semi‑open d‑file. The engine still judges Black to be clearly better—about a pawn ahead—but the move costs White roughly a sixth of a pawn compared with the previous evaluation. With Black’s bishop on g7 confined to just two safe squares and White’s own bishop on a2 without any safe retreats, the knight’s redeployment is the most accurate way to maintain the material edge.

teacher: Black’s 16…Rc8 looks natural on the semi‑open c‑file, but it abandons the far more active 16…Ne5 that the engine preferred. By shuffling the rook instead of improving piece activity, Black lets White consolidate and the evaluation flips from a clear Black edge to a modest White advantage – roughly a pawn’s worth, and White even emerges a pawn up in material. The move also leaves Black’s bishop on b7 cramped (it still has only two safe squares) while White’s bishop on a2 remains without a safe retreat, offering no compensation for the loss of momentum. In short, the rook move significantly worsened Black’s position, costing about two pawns in practical terms.
student: By playing Rc8 Black simply abandoned the pressure that existed along the semi‑open c‑file and allowed White to equalise, turning a clear Black edge into a modest White advantage. The engine’s preferred continuation was Ne5, which would have kept the initiative and preserved Black’s lead. After Rc8 White can reply with Bc1, after which Black could try Qa4, but the evaluation swings back in White’s favour by roughly two pawns. In short, the move cost Black about one and a half pawns of value.

teacher: White’s retreat Bc1 is the only move that preserves his modest edge while neutralising Black’s latent pressure on the semi‑open c‑file. By placing the bishop on c1 White both shelters the piece that had no safe squares and blocks the c‑file, curbing the rook on c8 that was the only active Black piece on that line. The engine rates the move as the best, nudging the evaluation from a clear plus‑½ pawn to about three‑quarters of a pawn in White’s favour. Black’s most natural continuation would be Qa4, simply removing the queen’s exposure without changing the overall balance.
student: By retreating the bishop to c1 White eliminates any immediate danger and preserves the modest edge that existed before the move. The retreat also leaves Black’s bishop on b7 with only two safe squares while the rook on c8 continues to dominate the semi‑open c‑file, so White remains comfortably ahead. Black’s most natural reply would be Qa4, removing the pressure on the queen, after which White can continue with Rd4 and keep the advantage. The engine rates Bc1 as the best move, improving the evaluation by roughly a tenth of a pawn.

teacher: Rxc4 looks active, but it simply hands the rook to Black: after the forced bxc4 the pawn both removes the queen‑threat on a4 and captures the rook, leaving White without any compensation. Because White’s bishop on a2 has no safe squares, the exchange cannot generate counterplay, and the resulting position swings the modest +0.7 edge into a clear –2.0 advantage for Black—a loss of roughly three pawns. The engine’s best continuation was the quiet Bb2, which would have kept material intact and avoided this costly blunder.
student: By playing Rxc4 White simply trades a rook for another and opens the b‑file while leaving Black’s pawn on c4 permanently fixed on a light square. After the forced …bxc4 the material balance is restored, but Black’s pawn becomes isolated on a6 and the c‑file loses its semi‑open character, giving Black active play that outweighs any compensation. The engine shows this costs roughly three pawns, turning a clear +0.7 advantage into a –1.9 disadvantage. The blunder could have been avoided by the quiet developing move Bb2, which would have kept White’s modest edge without creating these structural weaknesses.

teacher: White’s Nd2 eliminates the immediate threat to the knight, even though it leaves the pawn on c2 hanging. With the bishops on a2 and c1 cramped – the former has only one safe square and the latter only two – there is little else to improve the position, so the move simply neutralises Black’s pressure. Black can answer with the pawn break d5, striking at the e4 pawn, but the evaluation remains essentially unchanged, confirming that Nd2 was the most accurate continuation despite White’s material edge.
student: White’s retreat Nd2 eliminates the immediate danger to his knight and leaves the position essentially unchanged – Black remains about two pawns ahead, with the engine still judging it as “much better” for Black. The move does leave the pawn on c2 hanging, but the loss of that piece would have been even more costly, so the sacrifice is acceptable in this cramped middlegame. Black can now try the thematic …d5 break, striking at White’s e‑pawn, after which the continuation Bxc4 – dxc4 – Qxc4 follows the principal variation.

teacher: Black finally breaks with …d5, striking at White’s e‑pawn and advancing the queenside pawn majority of three against two. The thrust also leaves White’s only active minor piece cramped – the knight on d2 now has only one safe square and both bishops (a2 and c1) are limited in mobility. Although the engine notes the move makes Black’s position a little worse (about two‑tenths of a pawn), it is still the best continuation; after the natural 21.Bxc4 Black can recapture with …dxc4, and after 22.Qxc4 continue with …Nb6, keeping the pressure.
student: By playing …d5 Black finally opens the queenside with a pawn break that attacks White’s e‑pawn and pushes his three‑pawn majority forward while leaving White’s knight on d2 with virtually no useful squares. The advance also leaves White’s bishop on a2 without any safe retreats and further restricts the already cramped piece. Although the engine notes a slight dip in Black’s evaluation (about 0.2 pawn), the move remains the best continuation because it creates concrete threats and keeps Black clearly ahead. If White answers with the natural Bxc4, Black can recapture with dxc4 and then continue with …Nb6, preserving the pressure.

teacher: White captures on d5, uncovering the queen’s line from e2 to the pawn on e7 and leaving the e‑file semi‑open for White. After Black’s most natural reply Nxd5, the d‑file becomes open and the material balance is restored, but Black is left with an isolated pawn on c4 and a newly opened d‑file that White can later exploit. Although the engine notes a slight –0.12‑pawn swing, the move remains the best choice, preserving White’s clear advantage of about a pawn.
student: By playing exd5 White opens the d‑file and creates a discovered attack on Black’s e7 pawn with the queen on e2, while also opening the e‑file for his pieces. After the natural reply Nxd5, Black would capture the pawn but leave an isolated pawn on c4, giving White active play along the newly opened files. The engine rates the move as good and the best choice, though it costs a small fraction of a pawn in evaluation because the material advantage remains clear.

teacher: Black’s capture Nxd5 not only captures a pawn but also opens the d‑file and eliminates the threat to the e‑pawn, improving Black's position by roughly a quarter‑pawn. By removing the d‑pawn, White is left with isolated pawns on c2 and c3 while the bishop on b2 remains pinned by Black’s queen on b5, severely restricting White’s piece activity. White’s most accurate reply would be Qxc4, which captures the pawn on c4 and eases the pressure on c3, but Black can continue with Nxc3+ followed by Nxa2, keeping the initiative.
student: By taking on d5 Black eliminates White’s immediate pressure on the e‑pawn and opens the d‑file for his pieces while also removing the threat to that pawn. The capture leaves White with isolated pawns on c2 and c3, further limiting their activity, and the queen on b5 continues to pin the bishop on b2 to the king, so White can no longer generate counterplay. Although White remains a pawn ahead, the engine rates Nxd5 as the best continuation, improving Black’s standing by roughly a quarter of a pawn. White could try Qxc4, which would remove the threat to the c3 pawn and recapture the pawn on c4, but even after that Black still holds the slight edge.

teacher: By playing Qxc4 White eliminates Black’s pawn on c4, turning the c‑file into a semi‑open line for Black but, more importantly, removes the immediate threat to the pawn on c3 and creates a passed pawn duo on c2 and c3. The capture also leaves Black’s queen on b5 still pinning the bishop on b2 to the king on b1, while White’s bishop on a2 has only one safe square. Black could try Nxc3+ with check, winning the c3 pawn and leaving the f7 pawn en prise, but the engine judges White’s queen capture as the optimal continuation, preserving the roughly one‑pawn advantage. The evaluation stays essentially unchanged, confirming the move’s excellent quality.
student: By taking on c4 White eliminates the immediate danger to the pawn on c3 and wins a pawn, leaving him two points ahead in material. The capture also creates a passed pawn duo on c2‑c3 while the c‑file becomes semi‑open for Black, but Black’s queen on b5 still pins the bishop on b2 to the king, so the new queenside pressure does not translate into concrete threats. Black’s most forcing reply would be Nxc3+, delivering check and capturing the pawn on c3, yet even that line leaves White with a clear advantage of roughly a pawn. Consequently the engine rates Qxc4 as an excellent, best‑move choice.

teacher: Black’s 23…Nxc3+ is an excellent checking capture that wins the pawn on c3 while the white queen on c4 pins the f‑pawn to the black king, leaving that pawn en prise but unable to move. The check forces White’s king to b1, after which Black can continue with …Nxa2, winning a bishop and heading for the queen exchange shown in the principal variation. The engine rates the move as the best and notes that it leaves the overall evaluation essentially unchanged, with White still about a pawn ahead.
student: By playing Nxc3+ Black not only wins the pawn on c3 but also delivers a checking blow that forces White’s king to move. The capture leaves the pawn on f7 hanging because White’s queen on c4 pins it to the black king, and after the forced Ka1 the continuation Nxa2 followed by Qxb5 and axb5 leaves White still a little better – roughly a pawn’s worth. This precise sequence makes the move an excellent choice, keeping the evaluation essentially unchanged despite White being up a pawn.

teacher: Black’s 24…e6 is the right move, bolstering the kingside pawn majority (four pawns against three) and removing the immediate threat to the f7‑pawn. By tightening the pawn structure it also curtails White’s bishop on a2, which already has only two safe squares. If White tries the natural 25.Qxb5, Black can answer 25…axb5 and, after 26.Nb1, win the bishop on a2 with 26…Nxa2, showing how the pawn push neutralises White’s active ideas. The engine still rates the position clearly in White’s favour, but the move improves Black’s standing by about a quarter of a pawn and is the best available.
student: By playing …e6 Black both strengthens his four‑pawn majority on the kingside and eliminates White’s immediate pressure on the f7 pawn, thereby improving his standing by roughly a quarter of a pawn. The advance also leaves White’s bishop on a2 with only two safe squares, limiting its activity further. If White tries the natural Qxb5 fork, Black can answer axb5 and later capture on a2, keeping the initiative alive despite being down a pawn overall. This subtle improvement makes …e6 the clear best choice in the position.

teacher: By playing …axb5 Black eliminates White’s queen, opening the a‑file and removing the immediate threats to the bishop on b7 and the knight on d7. The capture does leave Black with an isolated pawn on b5 and gives White a semi‑open b‑file, while White’s bishop on a2 is now cramped to only two safe squares. Although the engine still rates the move as good, the evaluation shifts a little in White’s favour (from about a pawn ahead to roughly a pawn‑and‑a‑bit).
student: By playing axb5 Black eliminates White’s queen and simultaneously opens the a‑file while removing the immediate threats to the bishop on b7 and the knight on d7. The capture does leave Black with an isolated pawn on b5 and gives White a semi‑open b‑file, but it also curtails the bishop on a2, which already has very few safe squares. Although the engine still judges White to be about a pawn ahead, this exchange is objectively the best continuation available in the position.

teacher: By delivering a check with Bd5+, Black drives the white king onto the a‑file (the continuation Ka1 Bf8 Rd1 f5 shows how the bishop pair can keep the initiative in this rook‑and‑minor‑piece ending. The move not only checks but also nudges the evaluation in Black’s favour by roughly a tenth of a pawn, even though White still holds a clear material edge. In a position where Black enjoys the bishop pair, this active check is the most precise way to retain counterplay.).
student: Black’s best reply is to give a checking blow with Bd5+, forcing White’s king to step back to a1. After the forced Ka1, Black can continue with …Bf8, keeping the pressure while preserving the bishop pair in this rook‑and‑minor‑piece ending. The engine rates the move as improving Black’s standing by roughly a tenth of a pawn, though White still retains a small edge.

teacher: White improves the coordination of his pieces in this rook‑and‑minor‑piece ending by placing the knight on c3, a square that increases White's control of key squares while keeping the material edge of a pawn. The engine’s evaluation drops only slightly, from about a pawn’s worth to roughly 0.7 of a pawn, so White remains clearly better. Black’s most natural continuation would be …Bc6, which would remove the threat to the b5 pawn, but even after that reply White’s advantage persists.
student: White’s knight hops back to c3, keeping it active in this rook‑and‑minor‑piece ending where Black enjoys the bishop pair but White’s bishop on b2 is already cramped with only two safe squares. The engine rates the move as good and the best choice, even though the evaluation slips by roughly a tenth of a pawn because Black can answer with …Bc6, which would eliminate the pressure on the b5 pawn. Nevertheless, White remains clearly better – about three‑quarters of a pawn ahead – and the continuation shown by the principal variation (…Bc6 Rd1 Be7 Ne4) indicates that White can continue to press without losing ground.

teacher: By playing …f5 Black pushes his kingside pawn majority forward, gaining space but simultaneously loosening the pawn shield in front of his king. In this rook‑and‑minor‑piece ending, where White’s bishop on b2 already has only two safe squares and Black enjoys the bishop pair, that weakening lets White’s advantage creep from roughly a pawn to almost a full pawn. The move is still sound – it is labelled “good” – but the engine prefers …Be7, which would have kept the king’s safety intact and avoided the slight deterioration. In effect the pawn advance costs Black about 0.18 of a pawn.
student: By playing …f5 Black tries to push his four‑pawn majority forward, but the advance also thins the pawn shield in front of his king. In this rook‑and‑minor‑piece ending White’s bishop on b2 already has very few safe squares, so the weakening of the king’s cover costs Black roughly a fifth of a pawn, as reflected by the evaluation swing. The engine judged …Be7 to be superior, keeping the king more protected while preserving the same material balance without worsening Black’s position. Consequently, despite being the best move available, …f5 is a good but suboptimal choice that lets White keep the edge.

teacher: White’s 33.Nd3 leaves the material balance unchanged and nudges the evaluation from a slight +0.40 to +0.50, essentially preserving White’s modest edge. In this rook‑and‑minor‑piece ending White already controls the open d‑file with the rook, while Black enjoys the bishop pair, so the knight move does not alter the basic imbalances. Nevertheless, the engine prefers the quieter 33.Kb1, which would keep the same advantage while improving the king’s safety. According to the suggested continuation, Black could answer 33…Bd6, after which White might play 34.Bc3, followed by 34…Ke6 and 35.Bb4.
student: White’s knight hops to d3, keeping the rook on d1 active on the open d‑file in this rook‑and‑minor‑piece ending where Black enjoys the bishop pair. The engine rates the move as a slight improvement for White – the evaluation rises from +0.40 to about +0.50 – but it is not the most accurate continuation; Kb1 would have been preferable. After Nd3 Black can continue with …Bd6, after which White could play Bc3, followed by …Ke6 and Bb4, preserving the modest edge.

teacher: Black’s Ke6 is rated an excellent move even though the engine preferred Bd6. It leaves the material balance untouched and the evaluation shifts by only a hundredth of a pawn, so White’s slight edge remains essentially the same. In this rook‑and‑minor‑piece ending Black already enjoys the bishop pair while White’s rook dominates the open d‑file, and the king move does not deteriorate that standing. The engine’s line would have continued Bc3 Bd6 Re1 e4, but Ke6 still preserves the balance.
student: Black’s king steps to e6, keeping it active in this rook‑and‑minor‑piece ending where White’s rook dominates the open d‑file. The engine rates the move as excellent because it leaves the balance virtually untouched – White remains only a fraction of a pawn ahead. Although the engine preferred Bd6, which would have improved Black’s piece activity, Ke6 still preserves the bishop pair and avoids any immediate tactical problems.

teacher: Black captures on e4, creating an advanced passed pawn while opening the f‑file and leaving the e‑file semi‑open for White. In this rook‑and‑minor‑piece ending the pawn on e4 is isolated, but Black retains the bishop pair and a 3‑to‑2 kingside pawn majority, giving him active chances despite being a pawn down. The move slightly worsens Black’s evaluation (by about a sixth of a pawn) yet remains the best continuation.
student: By capturing on e4 Black creates a passed pawn that will be difficult to stop in this rook‑and‑minor‑piece ending, even though it leaves the pawn isolated. The exchange also opens the f‑file while the e‑file becomes semi‑open for White, giving White active play but not enough compensation – the engine still judges White to be a little better after the capture. With the bishop pair and the new passed pawn, Black retains a clear kingside majority despite the slight increase in White’s edge.

teacher: Black’s 37…Kf5 simply shuffles the king without affecting the key features of the position – a rook‑and‑minor‑piece ending where Black already has the bishop pair and an advanced passed pawn on e4. The engine judges the move to have slightly worsened Black’s standing, the evaluation sliding from a small White edge to about a half‑pawn advantage. A more precise try would have been 37…Bxh2, which would capture the pawn on h2 and eliminate White’s material edge.
student: By moving the king to f5 Black steps out of the line of White’s rook but does nothing to improve his cramped position in this rook‑and‑minor‑piece ending. The engine shows that the far stronger continuation would have been Bxh2, directly capturing the pawn on h2 and keeping the balance more favorable for Black. Consequently the evaluation slipped from a slight White edge to roughly half a pawn in White’s favour – a loss of about two‑tenths of a pawn for Black.

teacher: By playing 38…h5 Black pushes the last pawn of his kingside majority, trying to generate a passed pawn on that flank. The pawn advance, however, leaves Black a pawn down and the evaluation now favours White by a small margin (about a quarter of a pawn). The engine judged 38…b4 to be the stronger try, as it would have preserved material equality and offered Black better prospects.
student: By pushing …h5 Black tries to advance his three‑pawn majority on the kingside, but in this rook‑and‑minor‑piece ending White already enjoys a small edge – the engine now evaluates the position as about a quarter of a pawn better for White. The move also leaves Black’s advanced passed pawn on e4 untouched while giving White active play with the king moving to c1. The engine preferred  …b4, which would have kept the balance more closely. Consequently, …h5 costs Black roughly a quarter of a pawn compared with the optimal continuation.

teacher: By playing 42…g5 Black expands his kingside pawn majority, turning the three‑pawn wedge against White’s two pawns and removing the f4‑ and h6‑squares from the white bishop on e3. In this rook‑and‑minor‑piece ending the advance also supports Black’s advanced passed pawn on e4 while the bishop pair remains active. The engine keeps the evaluation at a slight edge for Black (about a quarter of a pawn) and rates the move as the best continuation, leaving the balance essentially unchanged.
student: By pushing …g5 Black expands his three‑pawn majority on the kingside while simultaneously depriving White’s bishop on e3 of the useful squares f4 and h6. In this rook‑and‑minor‑piece ending the advance preserves Black’s advanced passed pawn on e4 and keeps the bishop pair intact, leaving the engine’s assessment virtually unchanged at a slight edge for Black. The engine rates the move as the best continuation, with the most likely line being Kc1 followed by …h4, Rd1 and Nxh2.

teacher: By playing …b4 Black creates an isolated pawn on b4 and removes the c3 square from White’s knight on d1, but the pawn sacrifice erodes Black’s slight edge, turning a –0.36 pawn advantage into a roughly equal position with White now up a pawn. The idea of restricting the opponent’s minor piece is understandable in this rook‑and‑minor‑piece ending, yet it costs Black about a third of a pawn. Engine analysis indicates that the more accurate …h4, a pawn break against White’s g3 pawn, would have kept Black’s advantage. Hence the move is judged good but not optimal.
student: By pushing …b4 Black creates an isolated pawn on the b‑file and deprives White’s knight on d1 of the c3 square, but in doing so it hands White a pawn advantage – the evaluation swings to equality after the move. The engine judged that the more accurate continuation would have been the pawn break h4, which strikes directly at White’s g3 pawn and keeps Black’s slight edge. Consequently the move costs Black about a third of a pawn, turning a modest plus into a perfectly balanced position.

teacher: White’s checking move Ne3+ looks natural but it actually hands Black a much easier game; after Black’s reply …Kh3 the black king steps out of danger and Black can soon neutralise White’s limited bishop on c1. The engine shows that the position swings from a slight Black edge to a clear advantage of almost two pawns, a loss of about a pawn‑and‑a‑half for White despite being up material. The correct checking move would have been Nf2+, which keeps the black king more confined and preserves White’s chances. In the line after Ne3+ Black’s king can go to h3, White would try Bb2, Black replies Bd6 and White is forced back to Bc1, illustrating how the mis‑timed check costs White dearly.
student: White’s Ne3+ looks like a forcing check, but it does nothing to stop Black’s dangerous passed pawn on e4 or to improve the cramped bishop on c1. The engine shows that the simple Nf2+ would have kept the pressure while preserving more chances for the bishop, whereas Ne3+ simply lets Black slip ahead by roughly one and a half pawns – a swing of about –1.45 pawns in evaluation. After the check Black can answer Kh3, after which White’s best try Bb2 leaves Black with active pieces and a clear advantage. In short, the move costs White a large amount of ground despite being up a pawn.

teacher: White’s 47.Bf6 is a serious blunder, worsening the evaluation by roughly two‑and‑a‑half pawns and turning a already inferior position into a clearly winning one for Black. In this rook‑and‑minor‑piece ending Black’s bishop pair and the advanced passed pawn on e4 dominate, and the move does nothing to stop that pressure. The engine’s top choice, 47.Bc1, would have kept White’s material edge without conceding the decisive advantage that follows after Black’s natural reply …Bc5. Consequently the move costs White a decisive edge and hands the initiative to Black.
student: White’s retreat Bf6 is a serious blunder that turns a already inferior position into a clearly losing one – the evaluation drops by roughly two‑and‑a‑half pawns. By moving the bishop to f6 White does nothing to stop Black’s looming …Bc5, after which the engine predicts White must answer with Nf5, allowing Black to continue with e3 and then capture on g5, cementing a decisive edge for Black. The engine’s preferred move was Bc1, which would have kept the bishop active and avoided this costly continuation. Consequently Black now enjoys a winning advantage despite being down a pawn in material.
violations: describes a capture that did not happen

teacher: By pushing …e3 Black creates a passed pawn deep in White’s camp, bolstering his three‑pawn kingside majority and keeping the evaluation essentially unchanged at a decisive –4½‑pawn advantage. The pawn is isolated, but its advance forces White to react; the engine’s principal variation shows White’s most active reply would be 48 g4, striking at the h‑pawn, after which Black can answer …h4 and later improve his bishops. This continuation preserves Black’s winning edge without creating new weaknesses, which is why the move is judged excellent.
student: By pushing …e3 Black creates a passed pawn deep in White’s camp, turning his three‑pawn kingside majority into a concrete asset even though it will be isolated. In this rook‑and‑minor‑piece ending the advance preserves Black’s bishop pair and keeps the decisive edge – the engine still evaluates the position as a winning one for Black despite being down a pawn. White can try the thematic g4 pawn break to strike at the h5 pawn, but Black remains comfortably ahead.

teacher: White captures the pawn on e3, but the knight lands en prise and Black can simply recapture with Bxe3, regaining the material and opening the e‑file. This exchange neutralises White’s two‑pawn lead and pushes the evaluation further in Black’s favour by about half a pawn. The engine notes that a far stronger try would have been the pawn break g4, striking at the h5 pawn and preserving White’s chances. As a result, the capture costs White roughly 0.45 of a pawn in the assessment.
student: White’s capture Nxe3 wins a pawn but immediately leaves the knight on e3 hanging, allowing Black to reply Bxe3. After that recapture the e‑file opens and the material balance is restored, leaving White with no compensation for the loss of the piece. The engine rates the move as “good” yet notes it costs roughly half a pawn compared with the superior pawn break g4, which would have struck at Black’s h5 pawn and kept more pressure in this rook‑and‑minor‑piece ending. Consequently Black remains decisively ahead.
violations: claims material is won, but the capture is an exchange

teacher: Black’s check with Nd2+ looks tempting because it uncovers the bishop on c6’s attack on White’s rook on h1, but the move also leaves the g‑pawn hanging and forfeits the immediate chance to win material. By playing Nd2+ Black’s evaluation slipped from a decisive –5.0 pawn advantage to about –4.1, roughly a pawn’s worth, since the engine’s preferred continuation was Bxe3, which would have captured the white knight on e3. In other words, the check sacrificed a clear winning capture for a modest, temporary threat, turning a winning position into a merely winning one.
student: Black’s 49…Nd2+ checks the king while uncovering the bishop on c6’s line against White’s rook on h1, but it also leaves the g‑pawn hanging. The engine rates the move an inaccuracy because it costs roughly a pawn compared with the winning continuation Bxe3, which would have captured the white knight and preserved Black’s decisive edge. After the check White can simply retreat to Kc1, after which Black could continue with Bxe3, keeping the pressure alive. In short, the check does not improve Black’s already winning position and even weakens his own pawn structure.

teacher: White’s Re1 is the only move that eliminates the immediate danger to the rook on e1, allowing the rook to continue dominating the open e‑file in this rook‑and‑minor‑piece ending. The move does leave the pawn on h2 hanging, but the priority of saving the rook outweighs that drawback, and the engine rates the move as excellent even though the evaluation stays at a decisive Black advantage (about four pawns). Black’s most forcing continuation would be the discovered check Nc4+, which also removes the threat to the bishop on e3, but even this line cannot improve White’s already lost position.
student: By playing Re1 White eliminates the immediate danger to his rook, placing it safely on the open e‑file in this rook‑and‑minor‑piece ending where Black enjoys the bishop pair. The move does leave the pawn on h2 en prise, but the engine rates it as the best continuation, keeping the evaluation virtually unchanged at roughly –4½ pawns for White. Black’s most forcing reply would be Nc4+, giving a discovered check from the bishop on e3, after which White can capture on e3 but Black recaptures with the knight, preserving the decisive edge.

teacher: Black’s check with Nc4+ is the only move that preserves his winning edge. By moving the knight to c4 the bishop on e3 now gives a discovered check while the knight simultaneously removes the immediate threat to that bishop. White is essentially forced to answer Rxe3, after which the rook on e3 is left en prise and Black can recapture with the knight, keeping his material advantage. The engine rates the move as good, noting only a tiny dip of about a tenth of a pawn in an already decisive position.
