The engine rates the move as excellent and the evaluation stays essentially unchanged, leaving White a pawn up. Black’s most natural reply would be Kxb4, after which White can continue with Rxc6, preserving the material edge.
student: By playing Rxc5+ White not only wins the black knight but also creates a fork that attacks both the king on c4 and the pawn on c6, turning the game into a pure rook ending. The capture checks the king while the rook sits on the semi‑open c‑file, giving White active play in an otherwise balanced position. Black’s most natural reply would be Kxb4, after which White can continue with Rxc6, keeping the slight edge. The engine rates the move as excellent and the evaluation remains at roughly +0.21 pawn.

teacher: By capturing on c6 White both wins the pawn and opens the c‑file, allowing the rook to dominate that line while eliminating the threat that Black’s pawn posed to the rook on c6. The exchange leaves Black with an isolated pawn on b5, giving White a clear material edge in an otherwise balanced rook ending. With the c‑file now open White’s rook exerts pressure, while Black’s rook remains confined to the e‑file. The engine rates the move as excellent, keeping the evaluation essentially equal but converting it into a pawn advantage.
student: By taking on c6 White eliminates Black’s pawn and opens the c‑file for his own rook, while also removing the immediate danger to that piece. The capture leaves Black with an isolated pawn on b5 and gives White a clear material edge in this rook ending. With both sides’ rooks contesting opposite open files – White’s rook on c6 versus Black’s rook on e8 – the engine rates the move as excellent and the evaluation remains essentially equal, confirming it as the best continuation.

teacher: White improves his king’s safety by stepping to g2, a move that leaves the position essentially unchanged – the evaluation stays at roughly equal with a tiny material edge for White. In this rook ending Black’s rook on h8 already enjoys the semi‑open h‑file, while White’s rook on c6 controls the open c‑file, so the kings simply avoid any immediate danger. Although the engine’s top choice is Kg3, Kg2 is still a top‑class move; Black’s most forcing reply would be Rg8+ giving check, after which White can meet it with Kh2 and the game would continue with Rd8 and Ra6.
student: White’s king steps to g2, keeping it out of the way while preserving the one‑pawn edge in this rook ending. The engine still rates the position as roughly equal, with the evaluation shifting by only three hundredths of a pawn. Although Kg3 would have been marginally stronger, Kg2 leaves the balance essentially unchanged and allows Black the checking idea …Rg8+, after which White can meet the pressure with Kh2 and continue with Rd8 and Ra6. Thus the move is solid but not the most precise continuation.

teacher: White’s rook slides to c2, eliminating the immediate danger to the a‑pawn and keeping the rook active on the open c‑file. In this rook‑ending the position remains roughly equal, with White only about a pawn ahead, and the move leaves the evaluation essentially unchanged (a tiny 0.02‑pawn swing). Although the move is excellent in neutralising the threat, the engine judged Rc5 to be a better continuation, preserving more pressure on Black’s position.
student: By playing Rc2 White eliminates the immediate danger to the a‑pawn, keeping the material edge intact in this rook ending where Black’s rook already occupies the semi‑open h‑file. The engine still rates the position as roughly equal, with the evaluation shifting by only about two hundredths of a pawn, so the move does not worsen White’s standing despite being slightly inferior to the optimal continuation. Although Rc5 would have been marginally stronger, Rc2 remains an excellent defensive resource that preserves White’s one‑pawn advantage while maintaining control of the open c‑file.

teacher: By pushing …b4 Black willingly creates an isolated pawn, yet it is the only move that preserves the balance in this rook ending. The pawn advance leaves Black’s rook fully active on the semi‑open h‑file while White’s rook continues to dominate the open c‑file, so the evaluation stays essentially equal even though White is a pawn up. The engine’s continuation (Kg3 Rg8+ Kf4 Rf8+) shows Black can keep up checking chances with the rook, underscoring why …b4 is judged a brilliant best move.
student: By pushing …b4 Black creates an isolated pawn on the b‑file in this rook ending, but the move preserves the balance and leaves the evaluation essentially unchanged at roughly equal. The engine rates it as the best continuation, noting that White’s most natural reply would be Kg3, after which Black can continue with Rg8+ forcing Kf4 and then Rf8+, keeping the rooks active on their respective files. Although White remains a pawn ahead, the positional resources of both sides keep the game level.

teacher: After 56…Rh8 Black simply re‑positions the rook onto the semi‑open h‑file, a sensible square in this rook ending but one that does not alter the balance. The engine still prefers 56…Rc8, keeping the rook more active on the c‑file, and the evaluation remains roughly equal even though White is a pawn up. Thus the move leaves the material deficit unaddressed while White’s rook on f2 continues to dominate the open f‑file.
student: By sliding the rook to h8 Black puts it on the semi‑open h‑file, where it can contest White’s rook that dominates the open f‑file in this pure rook ending. The engine rates the move as keeping the balance exactly the same – the evaluation remains at zero despite White being a pawn ahead – and notes that the alternative Rc8 would have been marginally stronger. In practice the position stays roughly equal, with both sides still holding their pieces without any clear advantage.

teacher: Black’s checking move 57…Rg8+ forces the white king to step aside, preserving the balance in this rook ending where Black’s rook dominates the open g‑file while White’s rook holds the f‑file. After the only sensible reply Kh2, Black can continue with …Re8 and later …Re3, keeping the position roughly equal despite being a pawn down. The move therefore perfectly maintains the status quo, which is why the engine rates it as the best move.
student: Black’s Rg8+ delivers a checking blow to White’s king in this rook ending, forcing it to step aside and allowing Black to keep the initiative. The engine rates the move as the best continuation, leaving the evaluation essentially unchanged at equality despite White being a pawn ahead. After the forced Kh2, Black can continue with Re8, keeping the pressure while White’s rook remains confined to the f‑file.

teacher: Black’s 58…Rh8+ simply checks the white king, exploiting the semi‑open h‑file in this rook ending. White can answer with Kg3, after which the pawn on h3 becomes en prise, but the engine still rates the move as a small step backwards for Black, turning a slight edge into an even position. The engine’s preferred continuation was 58…Rg1, which would have preserved Black’s modest material advantage.
student: Black’s Rh8+ checks the white king and makes use of the semi‑open h‑file in this rook ending. White can answer with Kg3, after which the pawn on h3 becomes en prise, but the engine still evaluates the position as roughly equal because Black has lost about a fifth of a pawn compared with the optimal continuation. The engine preferred Rg1, which would have kept the slight edge without conceding the extra pawn. Thus the move is good, yet it costs Black a small advantage.

teacher: White’s king walk to g4 unfortunately leaves the h‑pawn hanging and grants Black the immediate checking idea …Rg8+, after which White is forced to Kh4 and Black can continue with …Rg1, seizing the initiative in this rook ending. The engine judges the move only “good” and notes a slight swing of about a quarter pawn in Black’s favour. A stronger try would have been Kg3, which also leaves the h‑pawn en prise. In the resulting position Black’s rook on the semi‑open h‑file is more active than White’s rook on the open f‑file.
student: White’s king step to g4 does leave the h‑pawn hanging, and Black can immediately answer with …Rg8+, forcing the white king to retreat and allowing the rook to infiltrate on the h‑file. This concession costs White about a quarter of a pawn in evaluation, turning an equal position into a slight Black edge despite being up one pawn overall. The engine judged Kg3 to be superior because it also leaves the h‑pawn vulnerable while keeping the king more flexible. Consequently, although not a blunder, Kg4 is a sub‑optimal choice that hands Black a modest advantage.

teacher: Black’s Rh8+ gives a check with the rook that sits on the semi‑open h‑file in this rook ending. White can reply Kg3, after which the pawn on h3 is left en prise and Black could continue with Rg8+ as the engine suggests. However, the engine rates Rg1 as the superior continuation – it would have preserved Black’s extra pawn more safely – so the check only kept the evaluation essentially unchanged, leaving White still a pawn up.
student: Black’s Rh8+ delivers a checking blow to White’s king, forcing it to step aside and allowing Black to keep the balance in this rook ending. The engine rates the move as excellent because it neutralises any immediate threats while preserving equality – the evaluation remains essentially unchanged at roughly equal. However, the engine preferred Rg1, which would have been marginally more accurate, and after the check White can reply Kg3, leaving the pawn on h3 en prise. In short, the move secures the status quo but misses the optimal continuation.

teacher: White’s king steps to g3, keeping his rook on f2 active on the open f‑file. The move does leave the h‑pawn hanging, but White still remains a pawn up and the position stays roughly equal. Black’s most forcing reply would be Rg8+, after which White can retreat to h2 and the balance is maintained. Thus Kg3 is rightly judged the best move, preserving the material edge without worsening the evaluation.
student: White’s king steps to g3, keeping the balance in this rook ending despite leaving the h‑pawn vulnerable. The engine rates it as the best continuation, and after any sensible reply Black can try Rg8+ checking, but White can meet that with Kh2 and continue with Re8 followed by h4, preserving the one‑pawn material edge. In short, Kg3 maintains equality while preparing the most accurate defensive resource.

teacher: In this rook ending Black’s check with Rg8+ forces the white king to move, exploiting the open g‑file that the black rook now dominates. By keeping the white king off the g‑file and preserving active rook play, Black neutralises White’s extra pawn and the engine’s evaluation remains essentially equal. The continuation shown by the engine (Kh2 Re8 …) illustrates how the check leads to a balanced rook‑versus‑rook fight despite the material deficit.
student: Black’s Rg8+ delivers a checking blow to White’s king in this rook ending, forcing it to step aside and allowing Black to keep the initiative. The engine rates the move as the best continuation, leaving the evaluation essentially unchanged at equality despite White being a pawn ahead. After the forced Kh2, Black can continue with Re8, keeping the pressure while White’s rook remains confined to the f‑file.

teacher: White steps his king to h2, getting it out of the dangerous open g‑file that Black’s rook on g8 dominates. In this rook‑ending both sides already control their respective open files—Black on g and White on f—so the key is simply to keep the king safe while preserving the material edge. After Kh2 the engine still sees an equal balance, and Black’s most natural continuation would be …Re8, after which White can press on with h4.
student: By moving to h2 White steps out of Black’s line of fire along the open g‑file, where Black’s rook already dominates that file. The engine rates this as the best continuation, leaving the evaluation essentially unchanged at equality while preserving White’s one‑pawn material edge in this pure rook ending. In the principal variation Black would continue with …Re8, after which White can push h4 and later bring the rook to d2, keeping the balance intact.

teacher: By moving the rook to g8 Black lines his heavy piece up the open g‑file, directly bearing down on White’s king. In this rook‑endgame the rook on g8 does control the file, but the shift allows White a small edge – the evaluation drifts from roughly equal to White being about a quarter of a pawn better. The engine prefers 63…Rd8, which would have kept the balance more accurately than the chosen “good” move.
student: By playing Rg8 Black places his rook on the open g‑file, where it bears down on White’s king and gives him active control of that line in this rook ending. The engine still rates the position as slightly better for White – about a quarter of a pawn – so the move costs Black roughly a sixth of a pawn compared with the optimal continuation. A more precise alternative would have been Rd8, which keeps the rooks on the d‑file and preserves the balance. After Rg8 White can continue with h4, after which Black could try Rc8, but the advantage remains with White.

teacher: By shifting the rook to c2 White places it on the open c‑file, directly counter‑balancing Black’s rook that dominates the semi‑open h‑file. This simple file‑play maintains White's one‑pawn material advantage and the engine still evaluates the position as roughly equal, the move costing only about a seventh of a pawn compared with the optimal Kg3. Although Kg3 was judged the best continuation, Rc2 is an excellent practical choice that preserves equality in this rook ending.
student: By sliding the rook to c2 White places it directly on the open c‑file, complementing the pawn on a2 and keeping the rook active in this pure rook ending. The engine still rates the position as roughly equal, but the evaluation slips by about a seventh of a pawn because the more precise Kg3 would have been preferable. After Rc2 Black’s best reply would be …Rh8, after which White can continue with Re2, preserving the balance while maintaining control of the file.

teacher: In this pure rook ending Black’s move to h8 places the rook on the semi‑open h‑file, giving it active play that mirrors White’s rook on c2, which dominates the open c‑file. By doing so Black does not eliminate White’s extra pawn, and the engine’s evaluation remains roughly equal after the move. The move therefore fulfills the best‑move criteria, preserving equality in a position where the rooks each control their respective open files.
student: By sliding the rook to h8 Black puts it on the semi‑open h‑file, where it can contest White’s rook that dominates the open c‑file in this pure rook ending. The engine rates the move as the best continuation, leaving the evaluation essentially unchanged at equality despite White being a pawn ahead. In the principal variation White would try Re2, after which Black can answer Rd8 and keep the balance.

teacher: White’s 70 Ra4 simply re‑positions the rook onto the a‑file, keeping it active in a rook ending where Black’s rook is confined to the semi‑open h‑file. The engine’s evaluation is virtually unchanged at a slight plus for White, confirming that the move preserves the modest edge. In the principal variation White can improve his king with Kc3, after which Black’s best reply Kg3 would lead to Rg6+ and a forced king walk, but the overall balance remains the same.
student: In this rook ending White’s king steps to h2 and brings the rook to a4, keeping the rooks opposite each other while Black’s rook continues to occupy the semi‑open h‑file. The engine rates the move as the best, noting that it leaves White still a little better – roughly a third of a pawn – and even nudges the evaluation a touch higher after the natural reply Kc3. After that, White can continue with Kg3 and later force a check with Rg6+, preserving the slight edge.

teacher: Black’s king steps to the edge on b2, a safe but more passive square. This allows White’s rook to swing to the fourth rank (Ra4) and the evaluation slides from a slight White edge to roughly a pawn’s worth, a loss of about half a pawn for Black. The engine notes that the more accurate Kd4 would have kept the king nearer the centre and limited White’s advantage. Nonetheless, the move is still judged “good,” even though it costs Black a noticeable amount of ground.
student: Black’s king step to b2 does little in this rook ending and simply allows White to improve his king with Ra4, after which Black can only retreat to c3 and then meet White’s Kg3 with …Rg6+. The engine rates the move as a moderate worsening – roughly half a pawn worse for Black – because it lets White consolidate while Black’s rook remains passive on the semi‑open h‑file. A more accurate try would have been Kd4, keeping the king nearer the centre and preserving the balance. Consequently White now enjoys a clear advantage of about a pawn.

teacher: Black’s king steps to a3, a safe square that stays out of the way of White’s rook on the semi‑open b‑file while keeping the black rook active on the semi‑open h‑file. The move leaves the engine’s assessment essentially unchanged, with the position still judged roughly equal even though White is a pawn up. In the principal variation White would press on the b‑file with Rb8, after which Black can maintain the balance with Ra6 and later …Ra4.
student: By moving his king to a3 Black brings it into the centre of this rook ending while keeping the balance intact – the engine’s evaluation remains essentially equal despite White being a pawn ahead. The move also respects the fact that both sides have rooks operating on their respective semi‑open files (White’s rook on b7 and Black’s on h6). In the principal variation White would continue with Rb8, after which Black can answer Ra6, preserving the equality.

teacher: White continues the rook ending with a forcing check, Ra7+, driving the black king away. After the check Black’s most natural reply is Kb2, and after this move White is up a pawn, although the engine evaluation remains roughly equal. The move leaves the position roughly equal, preserving White’s slight material edge while the black rook remains tied to the semi‑open h‑file.
student: White’s Ra7+ simply checks the black king while keeping his one‑pawn edge intact in this rook ending. The engine rates the move as “best” but notes that it leaves the balance exactly the same – the evaluation remains at zero and White stays a pawn ahead. In contrast, the engine’s top alternative would have been Rb8, which also delivers a check but costs a little more material. After the check Black can answer with Kb2, after which the game continues with the same equality.
